How a Kamala Harris administration would regulate the technology is less clear, but her recent statements have given crypto fans hope. In September, she promised to help grow “innovative technologies” including “digital assets.” Then she announced that she would support regulations that enable “Black men who hold digital assets to benefit from financial innovation” while keeping those investors “protected”—a strange and careful framing that implicitly acknowledged how many Black men have lost money on crypto. These comments could just be campaign rhetoric meant to fend off attacks by the crypto lobby. But they show that Harris is listening to the industry’s arguments, particularly those couched in the language of opportunity and equity. Harris is, if nothing else, sensitive to the direction of political winds. If a newly crypto-friendly Congress were to pass the industry’s desired legislation in a bipartisan way, a President Harris might feel great pressure to sign it. And even if Trump and Harris do nothing to help crypto, the technology has by now proved its indestructibility. As if to drive home the point, 99Bitcoin’s obituary tracker seems to have dropped off this year. The last entry is from April. I messaged the site’s owner to ask if he was still updating it. He didn’t respond. Support for these stories was provided in part by the William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. The Atlantic maintains full editorial control over its content.

item.title: Revenge of the Office
item.description:
Source: Business : The Atlantic Score: 2.77
More than a year since the World Health Organization declared the end of the pandemic public-health emergency, you might expect the remote-work wars to have reached a peace settlement. Plenty of academic research suggests that hybrid policies, which white-collar professionals favor overwhelmingly, pan out well for companies and their employees. But last month, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy announced that the company’s more than 350,000 corporate employees must return to the office five days a week come January. In a memo, Jassy explained that he wants teams to be “joined at the hip” as they try to out-innovate other companies. His employees don’t seem happy about it. The Amazon announcement was met with white-collar America’s version of a protest—a petition, angry LinkedIn posts, tense debates on Slack—and experts predict that some top talent will leave for companies with more flexible policies. Since May 2023, Amazon has allowed corporate employees to work from home two days a week by default. But to Jassy, 15 months of hybrid work only demonstrated the superiority of full-time in-office collaboration. Many corporate executives agree with him. Hybrid arrangements currently dominate white-collar workplaces, but a recent survey of 400 CEOs in the United States by the accounting firm KPMG found that 79 percent want their corporate employees to be in the office full-time in the next three years, up from 63 percent the year before. Many of America’s executives have had enough of the remote-work experiment, and as the Amazon announcement suggests, some are ready to fight to end it. They seem to be fighting not only because they believe that the evidence is on their side, but also because they long to return to the pre-pandemic office experience. (Management professors even have a name for this: “executive nostalgia.”) Quite simply, they are convinced that having employees in the office is good for business—and that having them in the office more is even better. Managers have some empirical basis for preferring in-person work. A 2023 study of one Fortune 500 company found that software engineers who worked in proximity to one another received 22 percent more feedback than engineers who didn’t, and ended up producing better code. “When I was on Wall Street, I learned by showing up to the office,” Imran Khan, a hedge-fund founder and the former chief strategy officer of Snap, told me. “How do you learn if you don’t come to work?” Remote work can also take a toll on creativity and culture. A study of Microsoft employees found that communication stalled when they went remote during the pandemic. Another found that people came up with less creative product pitches when they met over Zoom rather than in person. Eric Pritchett, an entrepreneur and a Harvard Business Review adviser, had the ill fortune to launch Terzo, his AI start-up, in March 2020. He left California for Georgia, where social-distancing rules were laxer and he could call people into the office. “You think of these iconic companies,” he said, counting off Amazon, Tesla, and Nike. “These iconic companies didn’t invent themselves on Zoom.” (Even Zoom, in August 2023, told employees to come into the office two days a week.) Jassy, the Amazon CEO, wrote in his back-to-office memo that he wanted Amazon to operate “like the world’s largest startup.” But some Amazon employees don’t buy Jassy’s argument. CJ Felli has worked at Amazon Web Services since 2019. When the pandemic sent workers home, he was apprehensive about spending every day at his Seattle apartment. Now he’s a work-from-home evangelist. “I was able to deliver projects,” he told me. “I could work longer than I could in the office, I could eat healthier, and I was able to get more done.” He earned a promotion during the pandemic and was praised for his efficiency, which he sees as further evidence of his productivity gains. His colleagues who have kids or who get distracted in Amazon’s open-floor-plan office tell him that their work has improved too. If remote work is such a drag, its defenders ask, then why has business been booming since the pandemic? Profits are up, even as employees code in sweatpants or practice their golf swing. As one Amazon employee wrote on LinkedIn, “I’d rather spend a couple of days being really productive at my house, taking lunch walks with my dog (or maybe a bike ride). This is how my brain works.” One mid-level manager at Salesforce, who spoke on condition of anonymity in order to publicly criticize his employer’s policies, pointed to the company’s success throughout the pandemic. “We’re not machines either,” he told me. “People aren’t meant to just be wrung like a towel to get every drip of productivity out of them.” The big-picture data are a bit fuzzy. Some studies have found a modest negative effect on productivity—defined as work accomplished per hour on the clock—when companies switch to fully remote work. But this can be at least partly offset by the commuting time that workers regain, some of which they spend working longer hours. “There is no sound reason to expect the productivity effects of remote work to be uniform across jobs, workers, managers, and organizations,” as one academic overview puts it. The debate between bosses and workers “feels a lot like my view of how productive my teenager is being when she says she’s working while talking to her friends on her cellphone,” Nicholas Bloom, a Stanford professor who co-authored the study, told me. “She’s probably doing more work than I think—which is zero—and probably less work than she thinks, which is a lot.” In theory, hybrid work should be the compromise that satisfies both sides. A May Gallup poll found that only 7 percent of employees wanted to work in person five days a week, 33 percent wanted to be fully remote, and 60 percent wanted some kind of hybrid arrangement. A study by Bloom found that employees of the travel site Trip.com who spent three days in the office were just as likely to be promoted as their fully in-person counterparts. They wrote code of the same caliber, and were more likely to stay at the company. Crucially, after a six-month trial, managers who had initially opposed hybrid work had revised their opinion. All of that helps explain why the percentage of companies with a hybrid policy for most corporate employees doubled from 20 percent at the start of 2023 to about 40 percent today, according to the Flex Index, which tracks work arrangements. But as Amazon’s announcement shows, the decisions around work arrangements were never going to be just about the data. When Jassy spoke last year about the company’s decision to move from a remote policy to a hybrid one, he said that it was based on a “judgment” by the leadership team but wasn’t informed by specific findings. Executives might just have an intuition that in-office work is better for the companies they helped build. It may make their jobs easier to have everyone close by. They also seem to find it hard to believe that their employees are doing as much work when they’re at home as when they’re in the office, where everyone can see them. Eric Schmidt, the former CEO of Google, said the company fell behind in the AI arms race because employees weren’t in the office. “Google decided that work-life balance and going home early and working from home was more important than winning,” he said in a speech at Stanford. “The reason start-ups work is because the people work like hell.” (He later claimed that he “misspoke about Google and their work hours.”) “I largely do believe we are moving toward some truce between executives and employees,” Rob Sadow, the CEO of Flex Index, told me. “But I also think this is much less settled than the average person thinks it is.” He predicts that the battle will drag on for years. Companies might have trouble actually enforcing a full-time in-office policy for workers who have gotten used to flexibility. Talented coders are still in high demand. Theoretically, if enough people from Amazon decamp to Microsoft, say, then Jassy could be all but forced to backtrack. Bloom has followed one company that officially requires people to be in the office three days a week; most employees spend fewer than two days in person. He was skeptical that Amazon would discipline a high-performing employee who preferred to code from the couch. The middle manager at Salesforce told me that he is preparing a list of excuses he can offer to executives who ask why his team isn’t in the office. But executives have tools at their disposal too. Amazon and Google have already begun tracking badge data and confronting hybrid workers who don’t show up as often as they’re told to. (An Amazon spokesperson told me that the company hopes to eventually stop surveilling employees’ work locations.) Even if bosses struggle to penalize their employees, perhaps they can lure them in with promises of career advancement. Eighty-six percent of the CEOs in the KPMG survey said they would reward employees who worked in person with promotions and raises. “You’re a young person coming out of college, and you want to be CEO someday—you will not get there via remote work,” Ron Kruszewski, the CEO of the investment bank Stifel, says of his company. “It just won’t happen.” Support for these stories was provided in part by the William and Flora Hewlett Foundation. The Atlantic maintains full editorial control over its content.

item.title: Marine anti-tank missilemen are getting attack drones for a new precision-strike role
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.94
US Marine Corps anti-tank missilemen trained to destroy enemy armored vehicles are getting a new weapon: one-way attack drones that can hunt and strike targets far beyond the reach of their traditional missiles, a top general told reporters recently. The first Marine units are set to receive the loitering munitions in January, part of the service's broader redesign of its ground force for large-scale combat in the Pacific and for battlefields increasingly filled with drones and disrupted communications. The changes underway within the Corps represent a marked shift from the post-9/11 wars that saw Marines involved in counterterrorism and counterinsurgency operations in Iraq and Afghanistan. The Corps has already shed its tanks and some other heavy equipment, created new units focused on coastal warfare, and prepared to disperse Marines across remote islands and coastal areas inside an adversary's weapons range. The new loitering munitions provide small Marine units with their own ability to conduct precision strikes at distances that previously would have required calling in strikes from nearby aircraft or artillery. The Marines set to receive these weapons first are troops whose core mission has long been engaging and destroying tanks and armored vehicles with Javelin and TOW missiles. Lt. Gen. Jay Bargeron, the Corps' director of strategy, plans, and policy, told reporters last week that the service is set to field its Organic Precision Fires-Light system in January. These loitering munitions — explosive attack drones — can fly out, locate a target, and strike it. "What I'm trying to do is bring precision strike capabilities down to the lowest level," Bargeron said. "That's a great example of using advanced technology to enhance the lethality of Marines that are already doing that job." Though the missleman job title isn't changing, the Corps is describing troops with the added role as "precision strike Marines" in a move that reflects how drones are dramatically reshaping ground combat. But the same technology giving Marines new offensive capabilities also creates a growing defensive problem. The US military is still searching for reliable ways to defeat drones at scale, even as the Corps begins fielding systems meant to help small units detect and destroy individual threats. "This is really about buying back or ensuring we have the right firepower and staying power in those ground combat units to do things like seize and defend a piece of ground when it's necessary," Bargeron said. The service has already fielded the first 80 sets of an organic system for countering small drones, with 300 more planned this year. The equipment includes a drone detection capability, new electronic-warfare systems to help defeat drones, and a new type of ammunition Marines can fire from standard-issue rifles at drone targets. That new equipment requires more training, making "task saturation" — giving troops more responsibilities and adding to their cognitive loads — a complicating factor, Bargeron said. A new three-day counter-drone course is in development for rifle squads, groups of roughly a dozen infantry Marines, at the Corps's major combat training center, Twentynine Palms, California, the general said. That work builds on the service's offensive and defensive attack drone teams, which are driving the development of drone tactics within the Marines. The essential ability for the lowest level, the lowest echelon units — teams of anywhere from a dozen to two hundred Marines — to defend against one-way attack systems, "is really maybe one of the biggest holes in our swing," Bargeron said. "So we're working hard on that."

item.title: OpenAI is about to make its biggest push yet into the legal industry
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.75
OpenAI wants to sell large enterprises on its technology. Now, it's taking its case to law firms. The ChatGPT maker is planning to launch new integrations with third-party legal software companies, according to people familiar with the matter. An OpenAI spokesperson declined to comment. The company has been in talks with multiple legal software providers about allowing OpenAI's chatbot to plug into their tools and data sources, the people said. This way, lawyers could update a file, negotiate contracts, or search a legal database, without leaving ChatGPT. Law firms are under pressure from clients to move faster and show they're not billing associates for work that software can do. In-house legal teams are looking for ways to automate more work themselves, so they can send less to outside counsel and shrink their legal bills. That demand has produced a flood of startups addressing legal work. For years, those companies have built on top of large language models supplied by frontier research labs such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Now the labs appear to want a closer relationship with the users themselves. Anthropic and Google have both begun packaging their models as products for legal departments and law firms, selling directly to enterprises rather than only supplying the models themselves. That effort has been rippling through the public markets. Anthropic's February contract-review plugin helped ignite the "SaaSpocalypse," a stock sell-off driven by fears that AI companies could absorb work once handled by stand-alone software. OpenAI enters the legal market with an unusual advantage. ChatGPT is already the best-known chatbot among the lawyers it hopes to win over. A Law360 survey found ChatGPT was the profession's most-used tool, with 54% of respondents reporting they use it, ahead of Microsoft Copilot, Gemini, Harvey, and Claude. But the consumer brand is also a hurdle in a profession where confidentiality and precision are paramount. Lawyers may trust ChatGPT to plan their holidays in St. Barths. Persuading them that it belongs inside a firm's most sensitive workflows is another matter. Chatbots have already landed lawyers in hot water with judges for making up cases and mangling their meanings. The company is making its legal push three months after hiring Jason Boehmig, an executive who spent more than a decade figuring out the slow, messy business of selling software to lawyers. He had left a Big Law job to start Ironclad, a company that helps corporate legal departments manage contracts. Lawyers will be watching OpenAI's launch closely. The tech industry, meanwhile, is about to find out how much room the company intends to leave them.

item.title: Amazon's fight with the FTC contains an uncomfortable lesson for advertisers
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.21
CMOs are digesting an explosive lawsuit filed by the Federal Trade Commission against Amazon this week. The advice from marketing insiders on the next steps: Check your exposure and double down on independent measurement. The FTC's lawsuit accuses the retail giant of manipulating ad auctions to artificially inflate ad prices. Nick Manning, founder of the media consultancy Encyclomedia, said the suit's allegations present another sign to CMOs that "walled gardens and black boxes hold all the cards." The suit centers on "second-price auctions," which are common across the digital ad landscape. At their most simple: an advertiser sets the maximum price it's willing to pay — say, $1 — but if the next-highest bid is only $0.50, the advertiser would end up paying around $0.51. These auctions grew in popularity because advertisers could bid high to boost their chances of winning an auction without necessarily forking out the entire sum. The FTC, which was joined in its suit by 22 states, alleges that Amazon sometimes secretly used a "soft reserve" — effectively inserting its own synthetic bid into the mix — to raise the final auction price without advertisers knowing. The complaint alleges that this scheme likely extracted more than $20 billion from advertisers since it began in late 2018. On Monday, Amazon posted a lengthy response to the suit, which it described as "misguided." It said the FTC's argument leans "on a handful of simplified communications to allege a companywide effort to deceive," which it said was "patently false." The company said its ranking formula gives more weight to ad relevancy over bid amount, and that it properly explains its pricing and auctions to advertisers, such as on its Amazon Ads help pages. So what action, if any, should CMOs take? Ruben Schreurs, CEO of marketing consultancy Ebiquity, said he's guiding clients to "remain calm and pragmatic" over what are, at present, just allegations. Ebiquity recommends that CMOs, through their media teams or agencies, investigate how much they spent on the ad products detailed in the suit over the period it references. Schreurs advised CMOs to obtain a statement directly from Amazon that unequivocally confirms that none of their spending was exposed to the alleged issues. That can be useful if they want to pursue a claim later down the line. Alan Chapell, a privacy attorney and regulatory analyst, said advertisers should already be investing in alternative ways to check the efficacy of their ad spending on big platforms like Amazon. "This demonstrates that, if anything, they need to double down on that component," Chapell told me. We've been here before Big Tech giants have faced several high-profile lawsuits over alleged manipulations of their ad systems in recent years. However, repeated transparency scandals haven't dented ad spending, as CMOs grow ever more reliant on the largest platforms that provide vast audiences, targeting, and measurement tools. That's no excuse for CMOs to take their eyes off the ball, though. "Price setting" is key, Encyclomedia's Manning said. "You have to decide whether the price you're paying on something like Amazon, Google, or Meta meets your requirements, even if there's an uncontrollable and untransparent margin for the platform in there," Manning told me. "You just have to use your own metrics and your own systems." Amazon, in its statement, said the FTC's claim "fundamentally misunderstands how advertisers operate," arguing that marketers adjust their bids based on performance rather than auction mechanics. The company estimated that advertisers saved more than $8 billion between 2021 and 2025 because it prioritizes "ad relevancy" over selecting ads on bid price alone. It said that with this approach, approximately "92% of selected Sponsored Products ads" in 2024 were not the highest bid, "often by a wide margin." The point about performance is why Luke Stillman, of the consulting firm Madison and Wall, doesn't think Amazon's ad business will take a major hit as a result of this suit. Advertisers decide where to spend "based on whether the advertising works and the return they're getting from their campaigns," Stillman wrote. "That is more true in commerce media than in any other channel." Stillman added that if Amazon were forced to change its auction dynamics, it could cause ad prices to fall in the short term, benefiting advertisers. That could also help Amazon in the long term: If marketers find it more efficient, they'll allocate more budget to the platform. The lawsuit's allegations will likely reignite existing tensions in the advertiser-Amazon relationship. In April, Million Dollar Sellers, a community of more than 700 Amazon sellers, arranged a 24-hour boycott of Amazon's ad platform to protest several policy changes that the group's cofounder called "cash extraction." "These allegations, if established as true and systematic, would add to the grievances," Jamie MacEwan, an analyst at Enders Analysis, told me.

item.title: See where aspiring entrepreneurs are showing the most interest in starting a business, ranked
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 5.08
Los Angeles County and Sheridan County, Wyoming, don't share many similarities, except for one main area: a high volume of business applications. That's one of several findings from the US Census Bureau's most recent business application data release in June. The data track applications for Employer Identification Numbers (EINs) submitted to the Internal Revenue Service. Business Insider sorted the data by which US counties saw the most EIN applications and calculated the percent change compared to 2024 data, while also cross-referencing with the agency's 2025 county population dataset to determine the rate of applications per 1,000 residents. These applications did not necessarily result in a business being formed. Overall, the US saw a roughly 8% increase in business applications in 2025, rising to 5.6 million from 5.2 million in 2024. That could be loosely tied to an economic shift during President Donald Trump's first year of his non-consecutive second term, including a weaker labor market that may have pushed some laid-off or out-of-work Americans toward entrepreneurship. The boom in artificial intelligence, too, has torn down some obstacles that previously barred entrepreneurs from starting and running a business, ushering in an AI startup golden age. While most of the top counties include large metropolitan areas like Philadelphia and Miami, a small county called Sheridan in the US' least-populated state, Wyoming, ranked 16th, with 47,787 business applications in 2025; its population is just 33,241 residents. That's more than half of the state's 79,024 applications overall. George Mocsary, a professor and corporate and small-business law expert at the University of Wyoming, told Business Insider that Wyoming is attractive to entrepreneurs because it has an industry built around simple, low-cost business formation services, particularly for small LLCs, including registered agents that provide designated addresses for receiving official notices. When applying for an EIN, he said businesses can use an address associated with their registered agent, in this case, Sheridan, making it appear as though tens of thousands of businesses are opening in the small Wyoming county when they may actually operate elsewhere. "You've got an entire industry in the state, and in Sheridan in particular, that's set up to let you [start a company]," Moscary said. item.title: Burning Man 2026: Satellite images show how the Nevada desert transforms into Black Rock City
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.85
Burning Man is transforming Nevada's Black Rock Desert into a temporary metropolis once again. Thousands of participants began entering the gates at midnight on August 30, hauling the food, water, shelter, and supplies needed to survive a week in the remote playa about 80 miles north of Reno. Roughly 70,000 people are expected to attend the art festival, described as an annual experiment in radical self-expression, communal effort, and civic responsibility. Burning Man has also long attracted prominent Silicon Valley figures, with Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Jeff Bezos, and Sam Altman among its past attendees. Early arrivals spent the Sunday raising shade structures, building camps, and installing artwork as hammers, power tools, and dance music echoed across the dust. This year's creations include a metal octopus and a shattered Eiffel Tower, along with the Man, a human-shaped effigy, and the Temple of the Moon, a 170-foot-wide sanctuary for reflection and remembrance. Both structures are made to be burned in separate ceremonies near the end of the event. Temperatures are forecast to hover around 80 degrees during the first half of the week, though gusty winds could whip up the playa's notoriously punishing dust. Here are this year's satellite images showing the progress of Black Rock City. Laying the groundwork Before Burning Man opens, survey crews mark Black Rock City's clock-face plan on the empty playa. Radial avenues extend from the Man, while curved streets form the surrounding semicircular camping area. Work on Black Rock City begins roughly a month before the event, when crews mark the city's center and begin surveying the street grid. Over the following weeks, they build roads, gates, service compounds, Center Camp, and ceremonial structures before artists and the general public arrive. The entry queue Burners arriving by car formed long lines across the Black Rock Desert over the weekend, funneling through temporary lanes toward the event's entrance gates. The sprawling queue is a familiar part of arrival at Black Rock City, where organizers inspect tickets and vehicle passes before admitting participants. From above, the rows of cars resemble a temporary highway etched into the playa, leading toward the semicircular desert city beyond. The Black Rock City Municipal Airport The Black Rock City Municipal Airport, which springs up for just 13 days a year, appears to be in full swing based on satellite images. Instead of asphalt, the airport is built from scratch each year on the dusty playa. Staffed almost entirely by volunteers, the temporary airport serves general aviation and private planes, as well as Burner Express Air, which is a designated event charter flight that carries some attendees between the temporary airport and Reno, the San Francisco Bay Area, or Southern California during the event. Center Camp Center Camp sits near the 6 o'clock edge of Black Rock City. Its acre-wide canopy provides shade and hosts performances, art, drinks, and gatherings. Mostly staffed by volunteers who handle scheduling, daily operations, and bartending in the ring of interactive camps that surrounds the plaza, the area is one of Black Rock City's main civic spaces and natural meeting points. The Cryptomeria pavillion At Black Rock City's geographic center, the Man is taking shape above the Cryptomeria, a tree-inspired pavilion with rootlike approaches and spiral stairways that climb nearly 60 feet. This year's pavilion was named and designed by designer and inventor Alexander Rose, a longtime burner. Around it, temporary installations are expected to gradually spread across the open playa, creating an outdoor gallery. The Temple of the Moon Art installations are taking shape across the playa. The Temple of the Moon installation made especially for the 2026 Burning Man, as pictured, is a 170-foot-wide sanctuary inspired by the Queen of the Night cactus and lunar cycles. Its petal-like forms surround a chamber reaching 52 feet. The installation was created by artist James Gwertzman alongside the Moonlight Collective and Temple Build Crew as a quiet space for grief and remembrance.

item.title: Inside the world's largest college dorm, a 1.4 million-square-foot Naval Academy building with over 4,600 beds and its own ZIP code
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.81
Bancroft Hall at the US Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, is named for former Navy Secretary George Bancroft, but to the midshipmen who call the dormitory home, it is affectionately known as "Mother B." The largest single college dormitory in the world, Bancroft Hall, houses all roughly 4,400 midshipmen throughout their four years of study at the elite military academy. Bancroft Hall's center section and first two wings, designed by Ernest Flagg, a Beaux-Arts architect known for his grand, classical designs, were completed in 1908. The dormitory was expanded in 1921, 1941, and 1961 and now features eight wings. The enormous 1.4-million-square-foot complex houses 1,639 dorm rooms and 4,663 beds, and contains 33 acres of floor space and 4.8 miles of hallways, which midshipmen refer to by their maritime term, "passageways." The dorm is so big that its internal post office uses the unique ZIP code, 21412. Incoming freshmen, known as "plebes," march into Bancroft Hall through the center doors after their Oath of Office Ceremony on Induction Day, the first official day of Plebe Summer before the academic year begins. From then on, midshipmen are not permitted to walk through the center doors until after graduation. (Civilians, officers, and non-midshipmen are allowed to use the center doors.) The front doors of Bancroft Hall open into a decorative rotunda accessible to visitors. Memorial Hall, a space honoring fallen alumni of the US Naval Academy, is publicly accessible through the staircase in the rotunda. Bancroft Hall also features student services, including gyms, a uniform store, a bookstore, a tailor, a cobbler, laundry rooms, and dental and medical facilities. The greater Bancroft Hall complex also includes Mitscher Hall, located in the courtyard, which houses an auditorium and a small chapel. The Levy Center inside Mitscher Hall includes a synagogue, conference rooms, and the Honor Court, a midshipman-led body that investigates alleged violations of the USNA Honor Concept. Midshipmen keep their dorm rooms shipshape Attending the US Naval Academy requires adherence to strict rules, including in the dorms. Uniforms and shoes must be stored in order from light to dark, and beds must be neatly made with hospital corners each day. Rooms are also inspected regularly. The rooms, housing at least two people, are single-sex. Each room includes a twin bed above a desk, a closet, storage, and its own shower and sink. Communal toilets are located in the halls. The dormitory is co-ed. As of 2024, the student body was around 70% male and 30% female. Rooming assignments are organized by the roughly 150-person companies that midshipmen are placed in upon arrival. The companies also eat and study together, and compete for points each semester that earn special distinctions. Meals are served in King Hall, which was completed in 1953 and is located within Bancroft Hall. At breakfast, lunch, and dinner, the Naval Academy serves 4,500 meals at once in less than 10 minutes — enough for virtually every midshipman to eat at the same time. In total, it serves 13,500 meals a day. Aside from housing the entire student body, Bancroft Hall's most important role, US Naval Academy public affairs officer Lieutenant Commander Kara Handley told Business Insider, is shaping future leaders. "For over 120 years, the US Naval Academy has built warfighters behind the doors of Bancroft Hall," Handley said. "Serving as the structural heart of the Yard, Bancroft Hall not only houses the Brigade of Midshipmen as the largest, single dormitory complex in the world but also provides a training ground to reinforce military discipline, unit cohesion, high standards, and accountability."

item.title: CreatorFi raised $45 million to bet on creators with 'cult-like' audiences
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.76
The creator economy has led to a swell of new media companies, but few have access to capital to expand. One of the companies trying to change that is CreatorFi, and it just raised $45 million in new financing to fund creator-led media businesses, Business Insider exclusively learned. CreatorFi advances capital to creators against the revenue they earn from platforms like Roblox, Spotify, TikTok, and YouTube. It also offers traditional business loans. CreatorFi's cofounders said they saw an opportunity as technology makes it easier for people to build IP-based businesses without institutional backing. "It used to take hundreds of millions of dollars to publish a game that will make a couple million dollars a month, and now, in Roblox, in Fortnite, kids are doing it in their basement," said Billy Huang, CreatorFi's CEO and cofounder. CreatorFi raised a $12 million credit facility in 2025. The new financing is a combination of equity and debt. The equity financing was led by Escape Velocity (EV3) with Uncorrelated Ventures, Protagonist, and other investors participating, including executives from State Street, JPMorgan Chase, and Periscope. The debt financing was led by VerisFi Capital. Creators have reached a point of maturity where their platform earnings can be systematically backed, and CreatorFi was attractive because of its data-driven approach to evaluating creators, said Salvador Gala, managing partner at Escape Velocity. "It just shows a maturity in capital markets to acknowledge creators as businesses," CreatorFi cofounder Jack Cameron said. How CreatorFi works CreatorFi backs creators of varying sizes, with a focus on gaming, music, digital content, and live events. It writes checks that typically start at $500,000 and can go up to $5 million, in exchange for a percentage (usually 50%) of the creator's platform revenue and the requirement that the creator make new IP, such as a number of new songs by a certain date. If CreatorFi thinks the company it's backing has a high key-person risk, it might require the person to take out life insurance. Those it's backed include music label Coasthill IV; Mythical Games, a venture-backed company that developed the "FIFA Rivals" game with FIFA; and YouTubers Lah Mike and The Danza Project. CreatorFi starts with how much a creator earns from a given platform, then looks at indicators of their fan engagement. "We try to figure out what is the strength of the IP," Huang said. "We really love creators that have a cult-like following. They don't necessarily need to be big." The creator funding battle A growing number of investors are battling to back creator-led companies. There's Spotter, which primarily works with YouTubers like MrBeast and Dude Perfect. In addition to traditional record companies, firms like beatBread and Sound Royalties advance money to artists. There's still a gap in funding for the early- to mid-stage companies that CreatorFi is backing, so more capital entering the space is good, said Andy Cloyd, a former venture capitalist and now CEO of Superfiliate, a creator marketing platform. CreatorFi says it differs from Spotter by investing across multiple platforms. When it comes to music, CreatorFi sees itself as focused on an artist's long-term commercial growth, advancing them money against their future earnings to create new IP. It doesn't acquire catalog rights in exchange for payments. Besides advancing money, it also promotes itself as having a big ecosystem that can benefit creators. When a musician it backed went on tour, for example, CreatorFi tapped other creators it had backed for promotion. "We want to be able to vertically integrate and say, 'Hey, not only can you do this with your copyright and your royalties, we can also extend you into the physical world and help promote you within our ecosystem,'" Huang said.

item.title: OpenAI does a victory lap for its new AI model: 'Welcome to the AGI era'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.67
OpenAI says that its new model has reached the AI industry's most sought-after milestone. "Welcome to the AGI era," Greg Brockman, the company's president, said at the end of a press call announcing the arrival of OpenAI's Astra model on Thursday. AGI stands for artificial general intelligence, a fuzzy concept that nonetheless has become a core goal for AI development. OpenAI defines it as "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work." The company pitched Astra as a major research breakthrough and a shift in what's possible to delegate to AI. It's rolling out to customers this week. Brockman has described reaching AGI as a gradual process. On the Thursday call, he said that in the future, he thinks people will look back and think AGI was created "about this time, and I think it might be about this model." "For me personally, I do think we're there," he said. GPT-6 Astra comes about a year after OpenAI launched its GPT-5 model family and about two months after its most recent upgrades, dubbed GPT-5.6. The company called Astra "the world's most intelligent and aligned model," and a "step change in professional work." The model will also improve ChatGPT's "computer use" abilities, the company said. OpenAI employees told Business Insider last month that those tools — which run tasks autonomously on a user's desktop computer or internet browser — have reached an inflection point. The blog post said Astra can fill out forms, format documents, schedule appointments, and operate software. Although successful "computer use" AI agents have been a long-standing goal of OpenAI and other tech giants, the technology is tricky because there's such a wide variety in people's desktop work, and so far, the tools have been fairly slow. "Anything you can do on a computer, Astra can do for you. Fast," OpenAI wrote on X. OpenAI previously said it delayed Astra's release until September after identifying improvements in its cybersecurity capabilities. The company wrote earlier this week that it needed to ensure Astra's safeguards block its use by bad actors for hacking and that the model itself is aligned to do what's asked of it. Like Brockman, other tech leaders have held up AGI as a goal. Google DeepMind cofounder Demis Hassabis said at the company's May conference that he expected AGI to arrive as soon as 2030, adding that humanity is standing "on the foothills of the singularity." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, for his part, told the Sources podcast in a recent appearance that AGI is, at best, "a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it's like an irrelevant marketing term." item.title: Warren Buffett piled into Alphabet to bet big on AI, successor Greg Abel says
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.66
Warren Buffett bet on Alphabet to tap into the AI boom, and he's still helping to call the shots at Berkshire Hathaway, Greg Abel says. The legendary investor was succeeded by Abel at the start of this year after nearly six decades as Berkshire's CEO. During a rare on-air interview with CNBC on Wednesday, Abel shed light on Buffett's surprising tech bet and his ongoing role as chairman. The Berkshire CEO explained why Buffett built a nearly $38 billion stake in Alphabet from scratch in under a year. Google's parent company was the third-largest position in Berkshire's stock portfolio at the end of June. Abel pointed to AI's material impact on businesses and beyond, Berkshire having a "lot of visibility" into AI and its benefits through its myriad subsidiaries, and Alphabet being a "significant player" in the space. "Now there's a lot more to Google than what I just said in why we like it, but those were the fundamental reasons as to why we took a serious look at Google, and now have a significant investment in it," Abel said. Berkshire bolstered its Alphabet stake earlier this year by participating in a private placement. Abel said Berkshire was invited in late May to take part, and he promptly called Buffett to discuss the opportunity. Consulting with his predecessor was "very much consistent with how we manage Berkshire," Abel said. The pair agreed on a $10 billion investment at a 6.5% discount to Alphabet's market price, Abel said, and the transaction went ahead. Buffett has eschewed tech companies for most of his career, preferring to invest in more predictable, attractively valued businesses he understands deeply. But Alphabet and Berkshire have some shared DNA. Alphabet's bosses modeled it on Berkshire and its web of decentralized, autonomous subsidiaries after visiting Buffett in Omaha in the mid-2000s. In addition to Google, Alphabet is the parent company of YouTube, Android, Waymo, and others. Google's cofounders, Larry Page and Sergey Brin, also said that Buffett's essays and "owner's manual" for Berkshire shareholders were the main inspirations for the shareholder letter they included in Google's 2004 IPO prospectus. Buffett previously broke from tradition when he bought into Apple in 2016. The iPhone maker has proven to be one of his most successful investments, and remains Berkshire's biggest stock position. Buffett and Abel The Alphabet position is one of many topics of discussion for Berkshire's chairman and its CEO, Abel said. He and Buffett have a "great working relationship," he told CNBC, and speak regularly as "we love talking business, we love talking about what we're seeing across our portfolio." Berkshire owns scores of businesses, including See's Candies and Geico, and holds multibillion-dollar stakes in public companies such as American Express and Coca-Cola. Abel, speaking from Japan during a visit to Berkshire's business interests there, told CNBC that he stopped by Buffett's 96th birthday celebration in Omaha on Sunday, and sensed some FOMO from the business icon. "Warren absolutely loves the Japanese investments," Abel said, "so I could tell it wasn't easy for Warren that off I went to Tokyo."

item.title: The US Navy's top admiral says lasers are key to keeping cheap drones from eating into warship missile magazines
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.59
The US Navy's top admiral sees laser weapons as a strategic answer to the cost challenge of combating cheap drones. The Navy has been looking to laser and directed-energy weapons as a potentially cheaper means of neutralizing uncrewed systems, preserving limited and much more expensive interceptor missiles for higher-end threats. Laser weaponry, however, has been tricky to develop, as its effectiveness in combat depends heavily on power, cooling, and other shipboard systems. In a Wednesday op-ed for The Washington Post, Adm. Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations, identified the cost imbalance of using multimillion-dollar interceptors to take out low-cost drones as a "defining challenge for the US Navy." "Recent conflicts have demonstrated how quickly low-cost drones, one-way attack aircraft and other relatively inexpensive weapons can pressure even advanced air and missile defenses," the admiral explained, cautioning that "a defender who fires multimillion-dollar interceptors against inexpensive drones may win the immediate engagement while losing the larger campaign of endurance." "This is why directed energy weapons — especially high-powered lasers — matter strategically," Caudle said. As the sea service battled the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen from October 2023 to May 2025, Navy warships routinely relied on missiles to eliminate drone threats. The Navy also regularly used top interceptors to combat ballistic missiles, straining stocks. Last year, Adm. James Kilby, the acting chief of naval operations at that time, told Business Insider that the way the service had been heavily leaning on its interceptors in the Middle East would not be sustainable in a high-tempo fight. During his July 2025 confirmation hearing for the CNO position, Caudle told the Senate Committee on Armed Services that the Navy faced a "learning curve" choosing the right weapons. He said that lessons from the Red Sea led the Navy to look to cheaper air-to-air weapons and electronic warfare when possible, but further consideration is necessary. The war with Iran this year, which has seen the US military face both drone and missile threats, has also demonstrated how quickly American forces can expend key stockpiles of high-value defensive munitions. The fighting added to concerns already sharpened by the Red Sea campaign over how long US interceptor stockpiles might last in a lengthy conflict. While the defense industry is expediting and expanding the production of critical munitions, recent conflicts have turned up the pressure on the military to find more cost-effective, more sustainable solutions for defending against large numbers of drones. Laser weapons are a promising capability to meet that threat and preserve those stockpiles, Caudle wrote, arguing that "lasers offer the possibility of shifting part of naval defense away from finite stored munitions toward shipboard electrical power." That said, "lasers are not magic weapons," he wrote. Lasers are line-of-sight weapons bound by combat realities like the atmosphere, ocean environment, beam strength and accuracy, and power and cooling requirements. To properly support laser weaponry, warships need enough power and the correct coolants to keep it from overheating. That means ship design has to be considered alongside weapon design. Caudle stressed that laser weapons are not a replacement for high-end interceptor missiles. Instead, he added, directed-energy capabilities should be deployed as part of a larger, layered defense, employed against certain lower-cost threats. The admiral said that the Navy needs to start incrementally readying the sea service for laser weaponry with more manageable, self-contained systems on ships rather than waiting for "perfect megawatt-class systems." He said that such systems would not represent a "final answer," but rather "a practical bridge between promising technology and an operational capability the fleet can learn from, improve, and scale." The Navy has been working on laser weapons for years, evaluating them for maritime missions at its Directed Energy Systems Integration Laboratory in California. The sea service installed an early operational laser demonstrator, the Laser Weapon System, on the Austin-class amphibious transport dock USS Ponce in the 2010s, and then it installed a 150kW Solid State Laser Technology Maturation demonstrator, or SSL-TM, on the San Antonio-class amphibious transport dock USS Portland in 2019, using it to successfully destroy a drone target in May 2020 before it was uninstalled in 2023. Additionally, the Arleigh Burke-class destroyer USS Preble is equipped with Lockheed Martin's High Energy Laser with Integrated Optical-dazzler and Surveillance, or HELIOS. Lockheed Martin said earlier this year that HELIOS eliminated four drones during a Navy-operated demonstration last year. Some other destroyers are equipped with the lower-powered Optical Dazzling Interdictor, Navy, or ODIN, which is used mainly to disrupt the optical sensors on drones and other threats. Other services have explored the use of lasers as well. Last week, the US Army saw a laser weapons win, using the Army Multipurpose High Energy Laser to eliminate three drug cartel-linked drones at the southern US border.

item.title: What the big bond sell-off means for your wallet
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.41
With America's debt mounting and oil prices on the rise again, the bond market has been gripped by a sell-off this week. Market jitters were first triggered last week, following Scott Bessent's plan to have the Treasury as much as double its long-dated bond purchases. The move briefly quelled yields, but they rose again as investors feared the government wasn't tackling the big fiscal issues that have been driving yields higher all year. In the days that followed, a flare-up of US-Iran tension has driven oil back within striking distance of $100 per barrel, throwing fuel on inflation fears and recalibrating rate outlooks. The 10-year Treasury yield on Wednesday was about 4.8%, the highest since 2023. From consumer prices to personal finance, here's how the big bond market sell-off could impact your wallet. What it means for your investment account Higher bond yields can present a problem for stocks for a couple of reasons. For one, they offer a compelling alternative to equities. The thinking is, why risk the stock market when you can get a nearly risk-free rate of 5% socking your money into Treasurys. The other reason has to do with higher borrowing costs and credit risk for companies. A higher cost of debt eats into earnings. For companies with shakier balance sheets, rising borrowing costs could threaten the overall health of the company. All of this means one thing: potentially weaker stock returns. The stock market has already shed some of its summer gains as government bonds have convulsed this week, but more volatility could be coming. 5% has been the threshold to watch for the 10-year to know if more pain might be coming for stocks. For stock investors looking to hedge rising yields, BlackRock's top US strategist this week told Business Insider to focus on dividend-paying stocks and quality stocks, defined as shares of companies with stable earnings growth, high free cash flow, strong balance sheets, and strong competitive advantage. Consumers could see higher mortgage rates and a tougher job market It's not just investors who need to know what's going on in the bond market. Higher yields have implications for Main Street, too. The bond market is signaling that it sees higher rates on the horizon for a variety of reasons. For consumers, that's important because it suggests that the Federal Reserve likely won't cut interest rates soon. Chair Kevin Warsh has held rates steady this summer, though they remain historically elevated. Some economists — and Fed governors — expect at least one hike this year. Some banks see as many as three hikes through early 2027. Warsh said in his Jackson Hole keynote address last week that his top priority is taming inflation. According to Marcus Sturdivant Sr., managing member at advisory firm, The ABC Squared, bond market volatility will impact anyone with adjustable rate payments, most likely those dealing with mortgage or auto loans. "The cost of borrowing for Main Street and the requirements to obtain capital will tighten or restrict," he told Business Insider. Treasury yields influence a variety of consumer loan products, and their rise could lead to more expensive mortgage rates, auto loans, credit card rates, and personal loans. However, a silver lining may be higher rates paid on savings accounts. The already-sluggish real estate market in many areas could be poised for a sharper slowdown. Higher mortgage rates mean higher monthly payments. The 30-year mortgage rate edged toward 6.8% this week, pumping up borrowing costs while home prices remain elevated. Higher mortgage rates could also exacerbate the "lock-in effect," with current owners opting to stay put rather than move and buy a new home at higher rates than their current mortgage. Business leaders, meanwhile, might find themselves pinching pennies. The ripple effects of a bond sell-off and high interest rates will mean that it costs more to borrow money, leaving companies with less money to hire workers and offer raises. Job seekers could see a slowdown in an already brutal market.

item.title: VC founder says he doesn't invest based on FOMO. Here are the 4 traits he looks for instead in founders.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.29
Skip the FOMO approach if you're pitching Nicolas Sauvage. The founder and president of venture capital firm TDK Ventures said founders can't sway him with claims that other investors are already buying in or that a funding round is quickly filling up. Sauvage told Business Insider that TDK Ventures takes a deliberate approach to investing, conducting what he calls a "deep exploration" of a chosen discipline before making a decision. The firm, founded in 2019, manages $500 million across four funds and invests in tech entrepreneurs. The team rigorously challenges its own assumptions before committing capital, he said. "We are protecting ourselves, thanks to our process," said Sauvage, who leads the firm's global investment activities in deep tech sectors. When TDK Ventures evaluates an investment, Sauvage said the firm looks for four core qualities. No. 1 is "first-principles thinking," which he describes as the ability of founders to recognize what they know and don't know, follow evidence rather than consensus, and keep learning until they understand the problem enough to act. That may be even more important in today's rapidly shifting workplace. Sauvage recently published a blog expanding on this topic, including the framework he recommends for using AI to expand capabilities while preserving human judgment and accountability. As leaders race to use AI more, they can easily measure workflows, prompts, and hours saved. However, the less quantifiable measures may matter more, he said. "Are people making better decisions, discovering what they missed, verifying consequential claims, and understanding the work they deliver under their own names?" he wrote in the blog. The second trait he looks for in founders is being "magnetic," Sauvage said. "They can attract people to join the journey when it is so uncertain, so risky," Sauvage said. "And yet they manage to get people to coalesce around them." That magnetism is what allows them to win over investors and customers before a product is even ready. Sauvage said it matters because no entrepreneur can succeed alone. It is part of a founder's "superpower" — his third investment criterion. "They have to have a superpower that is something no one else has," Sauvage said. A founder's "superpower" could be deep knowledge of a particular area, a specialized skill, industry insight, or access to an opportunity that others might not know about. Sauvage compared it to a superhero movie — audiences want to see heroes join forces, but each needs a distinct strength to bring to the group. He added that founders need strong writing skills alongside verbal communication. If they cannot clearly communicate in writing, he said, they will struggle to scale their business and build relationships with customers and partners. "Being limited to always have to talk and to be explaining everything verbally through calls or through meetings is a scaling challenge that may not be obvious when the company is three people or 10 people," Sauvage said. However, Sauvage said that once the startup grows to 50 people, the challenge becomes more obvious. At 100, it becomes a bottleneck. "They need to have that magnetism not just in person, but also when they are not present," Sauvage said. That requires being "very, very good" at writing, he said.

item.title: So, how bad is Bill Simmons' proxy betting mishap? We asked legal experts what could happen.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.09
Bill Simmons has said he authorized another person to place sports bets on his behalf, but don't expect the podcasting star to get more than a slap on the wrist. Simmons, who runs Spotify's podcast strategy, said on his show on Sunday that he'd enlisted his daughter's boyfriend to log into his account and place NFL futures bets for him. The issue is that Simmons lives in California, where online sports betting is illegal, and his daughter's boyfriend lives in Massachusetts, where it's legal. So-called "proxy betting" is illegal under Massachusetts state law. Simmons' bets have caused a stir, especially since he said they were placed on the online sportsbook FanDuel, which has major sponsorship deals with Spotify and The Ringer, the sports-and-culture site Simmons started. However, legal experts say that the Spotify executive likely won't be in too much trouble. Simmons is "an unlikely candidate" for aggressive civil penalties, though he appears to have violated online gaming laws in Massachusetts, said Mark Gottlieb, a law professor at Northeastern University in Boston. Simmons may get a 'good-faith determination' Under Massachusetts law, sportsbooks can only accept bets from people who are 21 or older and are physically present in the state. Sportsbooks can't allow customers to have more than one account or to place bets on behalf of someone else. If sportsbooks find that users have multiple accounts, including through a proxy, the law says they "shall implement procedures to terminate all accounts" associated with them. Sportsbooks can make exceptions if they investigate the account and make a "good-faith determination" that the violator's behavior "was not intended to obtain a competitive advantage," according to the Massachusetts Gaming Commission's rules. Richard McGowan, an associate professor at Boston College who studies gambling, said he'd "really be surprised" if Simmons received a penalty, other something like than a one-month suspension from FanDuel. A FanDuel spokesperson said the company "became aware of the issue" and handled it according to its terms, which meant reporting it to the Massachusetts Gaming Commission and voiding the bets. Sportsbooks like FanDuel can also suspend or close an account at their discretion for severe or repeated violations of their terms. A spokesperson for the Massachusetts Gaming Commission said they're "aware of the comments made on the Bill Simmons Podcast" and that "staff are currently reviewing the matter" but declined to share specifics. Simmons put himself in 'a very awkward place' Gottlieb said proxy betting is so common that Simmons may not have realized he could be breaking the law. Simmons said on his Tuesday show that he "did not know about the proxy rules" but that he "did learn." Not knowing isn't a bulletproof defense, though. "The law presumes that people know the law — even if they do not," said Jeffrey Eilender, a civil litigation partner at New York-based Schlam Stone & Dolan LLP. While FanDuel might decline to drop the hammer on Simmons, who regularly promotes the sportsbook to his audience, this incident could be a wake-up call in the fast-shifting world of sports betting. "It puts FanDuel and Bill Simmons in a very awkward place," Gottlieb said. "He shouldn't have been doing this in the first place, and he shouldn't have announced it."

item.title: Ukrainian soldiers are finding deceptive uses for their unjammable fiber-optic drones as ambush tactics spread
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.88
Ukraine is using fiber-optic drones in increasingly deceptive ways, relying on their resistance to electronic warfare and close-range video feeds to scout Russian positions, study bunkers and dugouts, and create unusual openings for attacks, a soldier said. These jamming-resistant drones have been on the battlefield for over two years, and they have become an important tool for both sides, allowing troops to surveil and attack without their drones being brought down by electronic warfare. Dmytro "Liber" Zhluktenko, a former drone operator who is now an analyst in Ukraine's 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment "RAID," told Business Insider that Ukrainian operators are increasingly using fiber-optic drones in atypical ways — such as deception and ambush — to "create tons of chaos." He said that some operators have their drones play dead or purposefully lie in wait on the battlefield, exploding at just the right time to kill an approaching soldier or expose a protected enemy position rather than simply flying directly into a target and detonating on impact. He said fiber-optic drones are also helpful for studying Russian bunkers and dugouts because they can capture high-quality video of "all of the entrances, because you get the perfect footage, you could literally figure out what type of cover that they have on their entry to their dugout, and what you should do to open it." Close-range reconnaissance is one of the drone's best uses, Zhluktenko said. Before hitting Russian dugouts and bunkers, drone operators can gather "very good intel" and "very precise intelligence at very, very close range." While they can be used to chase and attack, he said, there are limitations that make them less than ideal for those missions. These drones, which are connected to the operator by a thin data cable, are slower than the untethered FPV drones, and the fiber-optic cables can "break quite easily when you just give it a full throttle." For fiber-optic drones, pilot commands and video feeds are transmitted through a physical cable instead of over radio frequency connections, which can be jammed by electronic warfare. The cable is delicate and can snap if caught on trees or obstacles. Some soldiers carry scissors to cut through any cables they come across. A US veteran who has fought for Ukraine told Business Insider on the condition of anonymity that there are "very simple ways to bring them down," including by cutting their wires. "In the wintertime," he said, "the cold will break them half the time." Still, these systems are considered necessary given the prolific electronic warfare threat. Zhluktenko said the cable was becoming more expensive, which has limited how often the drones are used. He said Ukraine was finding other ways to try to get the same stable connection, including by using masses of signal repeaters to keep radio connections online, but fiber-optic drones remain in play. The deception and ambush tactics Zhluktenko described are part of a growing trend on both sides of this war. A British medic working in Ukraine who spoke to Business Insider on the condition of anonymity said that Russia places drones in positions for ambushes. Russian drones, she said, will "actually sit within the grass or the verges, and a group of soldiers will either go past or drive past, and these things will literally activate and just almost jump out of nowhere and hit. " "We have this image of drones flying, making a great noise and making a great presence, but that is not the case," she said. "They can be quiet, insidious, and the one minute you'll be, shall I say, walking along a tree line, the next thing, you hear the noise, and then we see an explosion, and it's just so incredibly rapid. And because they're so fast, it's often way beyond your reflexes to actually react." Another US veteran who fought in Ukraine told Business Insider that Russian soldiers will use "land mine tactics," where they put the drone next to a road and leave it there, waiting for a vehicle or another target to approach. Ukrainians have called attention to these tactics as well. Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, then serving as a drone warfare advisor to Ukraine's defense ministry, said last year that Russia was using fiber-optic drones for "ambush" tactics, including lying in wait for targets along roadways. "This is one of the tactics involving fiber-optic drones," he said. "It's effective and causes us a lot of problems." Russia is also using solar-powered drones that can lie dormant for this tactic. "The drones hide on roads and at intersections," Beskrestnov said. "They're often placed on forest trails, waiting for a target. When they spot a vehicle, they take off and strike quickly, leaving little time to react."

item.title: Volkswagen plans 50,000 more job cuts amid biggest overhaul in its history
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.80
Volkswagen plans to cut roughly 50,000 more jobs worldwide. On Thursday, the company's supervisory board approved its "Future Plan 2030," a 12-part restructuring effort that Volkswagen calls the "most extensive transformation program" in its history. Volkswagen said a "fundamental adjustment" of its global workforce — including management roles — will be necessary beyond its existing cost-cutting programs. It did not say where the positions would be eliminated, when the reductions would happen, or whether they would come through layoffs, buyouts, or attrition. The job cuts are one piece of a much broader reset. Volkswagen plans to halve its model portfolio by 2035 and reduce the complexity of its vehicle offerings by about 75%. It also aims to sell about 9 million vehicles annually and reach a 9% operating margin by 2030. That will mean fewer models and variants, higher volumes for the cars it keeps, and lower costs across its sprawling group of brands, which includes Volkswagen, Audi, Porsche, Škoda, Seat, Cupra, Bentley, and Lamborghini. The company has been facing steep competition from lower-cost Chinese automakers, especially on its home turf in Europe. The expensive transition to electric vehicle development, US automotive tariffs, and high energy prices are not helping either. It's part of a larger trend in the auto industry: Car companies have gone through a decluttering era as they try to reduce costs as they face the compounding headwinds. Volkswagen is one of the most dramatic examples. On Thursday, the automaker said its European factories have capacity for more than 500,000 vehicles beyond current demand. That leaves the future production plans for four German factories — Emden, Zwickau, Hanover, and Neckarsulm — uncertain from 2031 through 2034. Volkswagen said it is considering alternative uses for the plants. The new workforce reduction comes on top of existing programs. In 2024, Volkswagen AG agreed with labor representatives to cut more than 35,000 jobs at its German sites by 2030. Volkswagen didn't immediately respond to Business Insider's questions about how its new global target overlaps with those earlier planned reductions.

item.title: Uber is laying off 10% of its staff as it seeks to cut management layers. Read the CEO's memo.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.49
Uber is laying off 10% of its corporate staff, joining other tech firms in cutting management layers. The ride-hailing company's move will eliminate roughly 3,300 positions, the company said on Wednesday. The job cuts focused on management and coordination roles, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi wrote in a memo to staff. While Uber's recent financial results have largely surpassed analysts' expectations, the company has become more complex over the last five years, Khosrowshahi wrote. "We have reduced roles primarily focused on coordination, and have clarified the remit of the coordination roles that remain," he wrote. Uber "also cut down the number of management layers by broadening manager scopes," Khosrowshahi wrote. The layoffs were earlier reported by Bloomberg News. The layoffs are the latest example of a tech company taking aim at managers' jobs to save money. From Meta to Coinbase, other companies have either cut back on such roles or asked managers to start producing themselves — often with help from AI. Uber's Wednesday announcement did not mention AI. Khosrowshahi did, however, point to examples of cutting management layers, from combining teams responsible for its delivery business to eliminating about half of teams with one or two direct reports — a setup that Uber calls a "micro-team." Uber is also asking almost all its employees to return to working in an office at least three days a week, Khosrowshahi wrote. Less than 1% of Uber's corporate workforce will remain remote, he added. The layoffs are the latest round of job cuts for Uber, which eliminated roles in customer service and HR earlier this year. In July, the company laid off 10% of its customer service team, citing increased use of AI. Read the memo that Khosrowshahi sent to Uber employees: Team, Today, we're making a number of significant organizational changes across Uber. We are removing layers, simplifying team structures, refining our global location strategy, and focusing our people and investments against the biggest opportunities ahead of us. As a result, we will be reducing the size of our team by about 10%. Everyone whose role has been affected has already been notified, except in countries where we will follow the required local process. This wasn't a decision we made lightly, because it will have a real impact on our teammates and friends who have worked hard for Uber. It's important to say that these changes are about how we're organized and what we're prioritizing, not about anyone's contributions to Uber, which we will always value. I'm sure you're asking, 'Why, and why now?'—particularly since our business is performing so well. Over the last 5+ years, Uber has grown by orders of magnitude, with our top line nearly tripling. We've built new products, expanded into new businesses, reached more consumers and supported more earners, and become a much larger and stronger company. But that growth has also brought complexity: more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale. Our opportunity from here is enormous: we have the chance to bring Uber to hundreds of millions more people; to invest even more in drivers, couriers and merchants; and to innovate across our core businesses and build the autonomous future. To do those things, we need to make deliberate choices about where we put our people, our time, and our capital. The changes we're making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future. A leaner organization will mean clearer ownership, faster decisions, and more time spent building rather than coordinating. It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years. It's our job as leaders to make these difficult calls, and to give you transparency into our thinking and our decision-making process. Here's what we are doing and why: - Organizational health: In Pulse surveys and conversations with many of you, we've heard that too much work requires coordination across teams, debates take too long, and decision-making rights are unclear. I'm sure many of you have felt that you spend too much time "aligning" rather than building, shipping, or serving customers. To improve this, we have reduced roles primarily focused on coordination, and have clarified the remit of the coordination roles that remain. We also cut down the number of management layers by broadening manager scopes, particularly where we had "micro-teams" of only 1-2 reports. In all, we've reduced the number of employees who sit 7+ layers from the CEO by 20% and the number of micro-teams by nearly 50%. The outcome is a simpler org chart geared toward building versus managing. - Team simplification: We brought together teams where fragmentation was creating duplication and slowing decisions. The most significant example of this is Mac's decision to combine our three current Delivery Ops teams (across Restaurants, Retail, and Direct) into single-threaded teams at the global, regional, and country levels. Running these three businesses separately made sense in their early days, but that structure is no longer serving us at scale. Bringing the P&Ls together under single owners will reduce overlap, clarify accountability, and allow GMs to allocate capital more efficiently and effectively based on their strategic imperatives. Another example of this: in Tech, we're combining our Core Services Engineering and Science teams, mirroring the structure we already have on Mobility and Delivery. - Location strategy: The benefits of sitting together, collaborating in person, and solving problems as a team are clearer than ever in our post-Covid world. With that in mind, we're establishing clearer principles for where roles and teams should be based, with the goal of concentrating teams in a smaller number of key hubs. Global teams will be concentrated in our largest global hubs, NY and SF; regional teams in designated regional hubs; local teams in country hubs; and tech teams in tech hubs. We'll prioritize co-location between managers and their teams wherever possible, particularly for earlier-career employees. We are also asking the vast majority of remote employees to move to an office, and going forward, only ~1% of employees will be remote. We'll also continue to reinforce compliance with our hybrid work policy, which requires three days a week in the office. You can read more about our location strategy here. I realize this is a lot of change, but we decided it was better to make one big shift rather than multiple small ones. We also know organizational changes can be hugely distracting, and our job is to create an environment that allows you to focus and do your best work. With these decisions now made, our focus is on the future. We have tremendous momentum, significant financial capacity, and opportunities in front of us that are larger than at any point since I joined the company. The decisions we're making today are difficult, but they will help us build an even stronger Uber for the years ahead. You can read more about the changes across the company here, and please be sure to read specific follow-up information you'll receive from your leaders about what this means for your team, so we can all keep building together. Uber on, Dara Do you have a story idea about Uber? Contact this reporter at abitter@businessinsider.com or via encrypted messaging app Signal at 808-854-4501. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

item.title: I've been to all of the Canadian provinces. Forget Ontario — these are the 3 you really ought to visit.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.73
Canada is pretty massive. The country spans almost 4,700 miles from east to west, touches three oceans, and hosts six different time zones. Fortunately, I've been able to visit all 10 of its provinces. And with so many options, I know it can seem overwhelming to choose where to explore next. Although I enjoyed learning and experiencing what makes each province unique, a few places stand out — and they aren't in Ontario, Canada's most-touristed province. Here are the three Canadian provinces I loved visiting, plus highlights I experienced that'll make you want to plan your own trip to each. Explore the Earth's mantle and freshwater fjords in Gros Morne National Park in Newfoundland and Labrador. Humans tread on the Earth's crust, but it's not every day that you experience the second component below it, the mantle. However, in the Tablelands in Gros Morne National Park, parts of the Earth's mantle are exposed, and visitors get a rare chance to admire this distinct structure without any digging. When I explored the south end of this UNESCO World Heritage site, the rust-colored terrain made me feel as if I were on Mars. I loved learning about the local carnivorous pitcher plants and feeling the texture of the rusty rocks. There, I opted for a guided group walk along the beautiful Tablelands Trail, which is around 5 miles out and back. After walking on the mantle, I headed north of the park to visit Western Brook Pond. This freshwater fjord was carved thousands of years ago by retreating glaciers, and it's nothing less than breathtaking. I took a guided boat tour through the fjord and learned all about it. If you want a panoramic view of it, take the day to hike to the top of the Western Brook Pond Trail. Take in the scenery while cycling along Prince Edward Island's numerous trails. Prince Edward Island is famous for its potatoes, red-sand beaches, and picturesque countryside. The red sand is due to the soil's rich iron content, which oxidizes (turns reddish) when exposed to air. During the summer, there are usually more than 20 supervised beaches on the island. Instead of admiring the area by car or on foot, my family and I have enjoyed exploring it by bicycle. Biking allowed us to slow down, be present with where we were, and get a taste of the laid-back island lifestyle. We chose to pedal along the Confederation Trail, which stretches from one tip of the island to another and covers about 278 miles. It helped us connect to special towns like Cardigan, where we visited Canada's smallest library. The Confederation Trail has labeled stretches that range from easy to hard, so you can choose your own cycling adventure. If you're looking for a strenuous trail, I recommend gearing up on the Gairloch or O'Leary Mountain Bike Trail. But if you're not confident in your cycling skills, consider taking a guided ride or renting an e-bike to help you go the distance. British Columbia is a popular province in Canada for a reason. British Columbia is an adventurer's playground with impressive natural beauty. It's hard to get bored with the beautiful Pacific coastline and legendary old-growth forests. Johnstone Strait, a glacier-carved channel between mainland British Columbia and Vancouver Island, is especially beautiful — and you might even see a humpback whale in the water if you visit at the right time. One of my favorite experiences on the province's Vancouver Island is kayaking around the shores in the morning. I watched Steller sea lions glide through the water, and a river otter play on a nearby dock. Once you're done with the water, venture to nearby picturesque communities like Telegraph Cove and Hanson Islands. Or perhaps find your footing and try the Haddington Beach Trail (just under 2 miles out and back) or the Salmon River Estuary Trail (under a mile out and back). While there, I suggest learning about the area's diverse ecosystem — and there's perhaps no one else better to teach you than members of the Tlowitsis Nation, a group acknowledged as being among the first to originally live on this stretch of land.
