item.title: Where Was 'The Shards' Filmed? Where ‘80s LA Nostalgia Still Exists Today
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.82
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favorite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Shards filmed? The Shards, FX’s new adaptation of American Psycho author Bret Easton Ellis’s 2023 autofiction thriller, opens with protagonist and narrator Bret (Igby Rigney) driving to the Bruin Theater in the Westwood neighborhood of Los Angeles. He buys a ticket at the booth out front and sits down to watch The Shining in 70-mm. His present-day voice-over floats in, remarking on how strange it was to see a movie in 1980, without distractions like smartphones and social media. While waiting, he glances at the ornate Art Deco ceiling, taking note of every gorgeous detail. In reality, the Bruin is now shuttered; there was never a ticket booth out front, and the ceiling featured in the show is from the Fox Theater across the street. But thanks to production designer and native Angeleno Cat Smith, Bret’s day at the cinema feels as true as memory. Memory is central to The Shards, as a fictionalized Ellis recounts how he and his elite prep school pals were targeted by a serial killer nicknamed “The Trawler” during their senior year. While Smith was thankfully never the subject of a manhunt, she did go to an LA prep school in the ‘80s, and it’s her ultra-specific memories of the time that flesh out such an authentic and believable backdrop for the show. I spoke with Smith about The Shards, the city so integral to its story, and how she went about recreating such a distinct version of it—here are some excerpts from our conversation. The Shards is so intrinsically LA that it feels like a character. When you began this process with Ryan Murphy and Bret Easton Ellis, what was the main thing they asked of you in curating the vibe of the city? I’m a local, so I know the city really well. And I also went to a private school in Los Angeles, kind of in the period just about when Bret wrote his book. So I had a really intrinsic memory of that, and we just try to get as close to the actual as we can. Ryan’s influence from the beginning was American Gigolo, and what’s great about that movie is that it was filmed in 1981. He takes walks through areas of Los Angeles that are completely authentic to the time because it wasn’t a period piece, and it’s amazing what he sees. The entire Westwood Village was there. Ryan thought of a very muted palette, grays and whites, and this is ‘81, so it’s not the height of ‘80s design, just the edge. You’re turning into the ‘80s from the late ‘70s, where you would have those browns and reds, while the ‘80s were those pastels and stronger colors that came later. So it was kind of a combination of those two distinct eras. Are there any places in the city that have stayed in that same design style as in American Gigolo? We did shoot in the Westwood Village, and the Bruin and Westwoods theaters are the same because they were built in the ‘30s. Although the theater [Bret] went into was closed temporarily, and it didn’t have a concessions booth outside, so we had to build that. But when you come outside, we were able to copy the street from Westwood at the time. When you pass by the theater and you look behind, all of those are façades we put up, but that street was mainly still the architecture of that time. There’s this beautiful shot of the ceiling of the Bruin Theater in the pilot. Why are design details like that so important in your storytelling? Right! Because that’s what you’ll find in LA, those theaters kept those details. That’s something that either we, as a city, thought was worthwhile, or they renovated it. In this particular case, it’s actually the Fox Theater interior. We cheated it. They really loved the way the Bruin looked on the outside, but the inside of the Fox was in better shape. There’s certain things that people find important, that they keep. And one of those things that they don’t keep is shopping malls. Were you guys shooting in the [Sherman Oaks] Galleria? No. The Galleria, even though it still exists under that name, is not what you would see then. They shot Fast Times at Ridgemont High there, and that’s what it would’ve looked like at that very time. I had to find something that looked like the Galleria in 1980, and there’s not a lot in Los Angeles that would give you that. I mean, the most memorable thing was this amazing skylight that covers the whole ceiling and glass elevators and escalators that go up three stories. So we went to the South Coast Plaza, and they do have all of that, but the problem is, of course, they’ve renovated it probably more than once. Now it would be a shopping experience that’s recognizable to you today: it’s all glass, the signage is either very subtle or completely crazy. And the stuff they have is so specific to today, like they have this weird virtual reality room. None of it is appropriate for the ‘80s, so we had to go there and figure out exactly what our shots were, and then redo the facades of like ten spaces. We did the movie theater, Orange Julius, Licorice Pizza, Swensen’s Ice Cream—although you never saw that one—and we did Vince’s Pets. All those existed in the Galleria. We did a Casual Corner, Judy’s, this horrible place called One Potato, Two Potato. It was so much fun. We weren’t given a huge budget, but I wanted it to recall that very strong memory I had of shopping in the Galleria and going to movies in that theater. How do you think your experiences as an LA native helped create such an authentic depiction of that time period without feeling forced? Well, I was a little bit disdainful going into this, thinking “I’m gonna show them what it was really like.” And then I realized everybody who worked on this, who had lived through it, has a different memory of what it actually was, which I think leads to more interesting design, because then you end up with layers. This person remembers this, and that person remembers that, and when you put them together, that’s what it really was. But also AI has completely corrupted people’s view of what the ‘80s was, so I had to be really careful that I wasn’t getting mesmerized by these fake images of what the ‘80s was versus an actual advertisement for a bedroom set or a picture from Architectural Digest from that year. You always see something unexpected there that you don’t see in the AI images, like weird artwork or way too many plants. You’ve got to throw it into a blender because it gets so caught up in what people’s personal tastes were, which weren’t always great. They may see something in an Architectural Digest and their version of it in their own house is not quite as tasteful as you’d want it to be. I love that. We did a lot of location scouting of houses where they kept the ‘80s design, which is crazy if you think about it. There was this street in the Valley that looked almost untouched from the ‘80s, even the signage wasn’t that bad. What do you think The Shards says about LA as a city now? It’s very insular. I always worry that when people come to LA, they’ll be very lonely. It’s hard to meet people, you have to get around by car. There’s people who already have a community who don’t allow new people to be a part of that community. But the interesting thing about LA is that there’s so many layers here, I’m never bored looking around. I’ll look around and see the craziest detail. It’s such an ambiguous place that the detail stands out, because you’re not looking in a sea of that. You’re looking at a sea of blankness when this beautiful thing appears that tells you something about life situations. And we’re living in a time that’s very similar to the 80s. I always told my son: “You shouldn’t love the 80s, it was a dark, depressing time.” There were a lot of drugs, a lot of gun violence, everybody was out for themselves. The rich were kings. Sound familiar? And then I left him this world that was identical.

item.title: Seeking Texas's Sartorial Soul in Forth Worth, an Apex of Cowboy Culture and Craft
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.72
Inside Fort Worth's Cowboy Coliseum, a historic 1908 indoor rodeo venue in the heart of the city's famous Stockyards, the gunpowdery smell of pyrotechnics lingers in the air. It's the first round of the Professional Bull Riders (PBR) World Finals, and the very tan and blond singer Charly Reynolds delivers the national anthem in front of a giant screen showing billowing American flags. The bull riders—including the current champion, 20-year-old John Crimber—stand with their cowboy hat over their heart, boots shuffling nervously in the dirt. More fireworks throw sparks into the air and the crowd cheers. Minutes later the finalists will fight to stay on the back of 2,000-pound animals with names like Man Hater and Buck Nasty for eight excruciating seconds, and then dodge the bull's hooves and horns when they're tossed to the ground. Well-heeled locals—the men in sport coats and starched jeans, the women in dresses with yoked tops and embroidery—fill the narrow metal seats to watch. All of them are in boots; most of them wear hats. Chad Blankenship, a friend of a friend and the general manager of the Ariat Texas Rattlers, the local PBR bull-riding team, reserved a ticket for me, thinking—correctly—that it would be a good opportunity to see Fort Worthians in action and explore the Stockyards scene. Every year about 12 million visitors who want some of the Stockyards' rustic-luxe swagger to rub off on them flock to this district on Fort Worth's North Side, which sat at the end of the Chisholm Trail and where cattle drovers traded livestock by the millions beginning in the late 1800s. By the 1970s the area was derelict and prime for reinvention. Thanks to some savvy local developers who fought to preserve its charm, it now sees nearly double the number of visitors as the Eiffel Tower per year. As I look around the coliseum, there is ample evidence confirming my belief that Texans don't do subtle and they don't want to blend in. Texans have always seemed to relish their otherness, maybe even more so now that, in our age of globalization, so much sameness has infiltrated most American and international cities. I flew to Fort Worth from my hometown of Los Angeles with the hope of seeing some of this bold individualism firsthand and to check out how this North Central Texas city has grown into the epicenter of the haute-rodeo lifestyle and the premier destination for custom high-end Westernwear. “I grew up here, and it's interesting to watch Fort Worth and the Stockyards mature without losing their essence and wild frontier spirit,” says Taylor Sheridan, actor, writer, producer, and the creator of the Yellowstone television drama universe. He has dreamed up a show rooted in Fort Worth's history (1883) and another in its present day (Landman), and is at least partially responsible for the city's renaissance. He lives in nearby Weatherford, where Bella Hadid is a neighbor, and owns the 600-acre Bosque Ranch near town, which he uses for filming and production. Many tourists are drawn to the city because they're hooked on the lifestyle Sheridan embraces in his storytelling. “It was the place where people would come and supply up for the season, and it was the last place to stock up before heading West,” he tells me. “It's always been the center of the ranching world. It's still clinging very firmly to its roots.” No place is ushering that classic Texan spirit into modern life quite like Bowie House, Auberge Collection, owned by Jo Ellard, a cutting horse legend and breeder who was a champion of the Western equestrian event that showcases a horse's ability to work gracefully with cattle. The hotel is my home base for the next few days. It's mastered the rich-ranch aesthetic: A seven-foot-tall leather revolver sculpture stands in the lobby lounge, leather and calfskin hides cover much of the seating, and there's an on-site boutique from designer Lela Rose that looks like an updated version of Dale Evans's closet, replete with vintage turquoise belt buckles and long embroidered skirts. I drop my bags and head out to explore. “If you remember seeing one of these as a kid, then we can guess how old you are,” boot fitter Jeff Stevens says with a wink, walking toward me with a vintage metal Brannock device to measure my feet. I'm at Rod Patrick Bootmakers, a 51-year-old local brand in Arlington Heights, not far from my hotel in the Cultural District. It's known for carrying sizes 4 through 17 with a whopping 13 different widths. The walls are lined with photos of rodeo-star customers, and a classic from the Charlie Daniels Band that I haven't heard since the '80s plays through the speakers. Stevens determines, based on my relatively high arch, that I'm a 9.5. He brings out a $2,000 pair of soft black ostrich-skin boots, warning me that it will be hard to go back to stiffer goat or cow leather once I slip the boots on (with the help of two hooks looped into the pull tabs). He isn't wrong. “A well-fitting boot should feel like a handshake around your ankle,” he explains. Long before a cowboy boot became a fashion statement, its form was rooted in function. A narrow pointy-toe boot slipped easily into stirrups. Round or blunt toes were better suited to long days working the ranch. The tall boot shaft was built for protection, and the stitching helped the leather retain its shape as it softened. I don't walk out with a new pair, but I do have a new appreciation for a well-made boot and the incredibly skilled craftspeople in South Texas and León, Mexico. Next up is a drive down Camp Bowie Boulevard, with its historic red brick pavers and mature trees, to the affluent River Oaks neighborhood to meet Jo Latham at her fine jewelry store inside the larger You Are Here boutique. Latham, a chic 50-something Snow White doppelgänger, knows how to buy for those who understand quality and appreciate a little whimsy, including wealthy locals, visiting Texas Christian University parents, and women from across Texas and Oklahoma who make regular shopping trips to town. She shows me a $50,000 diamond-encrusted horseshoe necklace before sending me down the block to Chieffalo Americana, a Westernwear shop that sells reworked vintage and American-made clothing, Montana Silversmiths belt buckles, and refurbished short-brimmed Shady Oak hats. “People here love to live large and look good while doing it,” says Jackie Chieffalo, a stylist who owns Chieffalo Americana with her husband, Rodger. “They do not want to look like everybody else.” She tells me that The Fort Worth Stock Show & Rodeo, an annual three-week-long event at the Will Rogers Coliseum and the adjacent Dickies Arena beginning in January, is the social and fashion event of the year. “There are people who go every night and want to wear something different every time,” she says. “If you have something custom-made, isn't that the ultimate luxury? It's a mindful purchase, an investment that can be handed down.” As I wander around the Stockyards the following afternoon, there's a polished boomtown energy in the air. Seniors from TCU in purple graduation gowns and cowboy boots pose for photos in front of a longhorn steer tied up on the sidewalk. Outdoor bars and tents are being set up for the crowds expected for the bull-riding event that evening, and couples of all ages hold hands and wander the brick streets. “During the day the Stockyards is like the Paris of the West,” says Sheridan. “At night the North Side bars open up and it's a different story. They're the kind of places where you get into fights at the pool table. There was a time in my youth when that would have been a good night out, but now I want a nice place to take my wife for dinner and a drink.” Sheridan closed that gap by revitalizing the Cattlemen's Steak House, a 1947 classic in the heart of the Stockyards, and adding a lower-level members-only club. When I arrive for an early dinner, the dining room's leather booths are already packed with groups of friends in plaid shirts with mother-of-pearl buttons and dressy denim, and stylish couples in sport coats and silky twilly scarves. My server calls me “darlin',” and I order the best steak salad of my life, washed down with perfectly salted “ranch water,” tequila and sparkling water with lime. The next morning I start my day with a visit to Maverick Fine Western Wear, opened in 1987 by the adorable Gayle Hill. Today, Hill is wearing a royal blue cowboy hat with matching eyeglass frames, and her store is stocked to the rafters with colorful dresses, vests, fringed jackets, hats, and homewares. She sells one-off silver and turquoise jewelry from designers like Texas native Richard Schmidt, and Louis Vuitton handbags revamped with whipstitching by Austin-based Leather and Vodka. Hill's sales team, including James, a skateboarding graphic artist turned hat shaper working behind an antique carved wood bar, knows how to sell the lifestyle. Hill leaves me with James for a custom hat shaping and says, “Holler if you get thirsty.” James, sensing this is my first metaphoric rodeo, offers some selections that “suit my coloring.” I land on a tobacco brown felt hat. After measurements come a few compliments from Gayle about my large but symmetrical head (“You'd be surprised how many people have heads like a cashew”), and some deliberation over whether the curled brim should be flat or have a dip in the front (I chose a slight dip). I feel perfectly normal when I walk out in my new lid, a dramatic feather tucked into the hatband. I head across the street to the Murrin family office to meet Hill's son Philip Murrin and his wife, the painter Sarah Murrin. Philip and his brother Stephen manage the family's commercial real estate business that their father, Steve “Cowboy” Murrin Jr., started in the '70s. The elder Murrin is credited with saving the Stockyards from demolition and transforming it into a historic zone; he also invested in the famous local honky-tonk Billy Bob's. He's still easy to spot with his bushy white moustache and tall hat. When I ask Sarah about Fort Worth's unique creativity and appreciation for craft, she suggests that the city's arts scene plays a part. The Fort Worth Circle, a group of midcentury painters, put the community on the contemporary-art map. The Amon Carter Museum of American Art, designed by Philip Johnson, celebrates masterworks and photography with roots in the West. And, she tells me, the Louis Kahn–designed Kimbell Art Museum houses a world-class collection, including Michelangelo's first painting. When we switch to the topic of fashion, Sarah says that “people dress like they do here because it's a way of life. It's authentic, not for show.” I feel a little sheepish about my new hat. “We've seen the trends come and go,” Philip chimes in, in the tone of a longtime resident dealing with the headaches that growth brings. Old-timers like his dad remember the 1980 frenzy over John Travolta in the movie Urban Cowboy. Sarah adds, “Now we have Landman.” Because, I'm told, no trip to the Stockyards is complete without a visit to retailer M.L. Leddy's, I take a look. It started as a custom saddle and boot shop in the 1920s and opened its handsome Stockyards location in 1941; now it's a favorite among professional horse trainers and well-dressed cowboys. It has its own hat-shaping bar and a line of handmade boots that start at about $1,500 a pair. Upstairs is the saddlery. Also on offer are hand-tooled leather belts that can be stamped with your initials, and silver money clips and buckles by legendary Texas silversmith Clint Orms. There is a team of consultants and master tailors at the ready to design and sew a full custom wardrobe. Feeling buoyed by my boot education, and left out because I still don't have a pair, I walk to Hotel Drover, where I'm staying for my last night, and into the Lucchese Custom Collection off the lobby. Lucchese has been an iconic Texas brand since 1883 and sets the standard for fashion-forward handsewn boots. Its primary location, on Exchange Street, is its top-performing retail outlet in the US, but the smaller Drover location is where the team measures for custom boots in exotic skins and dozens of color combinations. I sit in a leather chair and place my foot on a page of a large paper ledger, while a stylish young fitter with a perfect manicure traces my feet, taking five key measurements. While I'm not ordering boots today, I can start the design process and have the specifications sent to its South Texas factory at any time. People choose emblems, like a star or a flower, for a little flair. If you've seen boots with a tulip design on the shaft, that's brand founder Salvatore “Sam” Lucchese's signature. “The starting price point for custom is about $1,500,” says store manager Nate Hill. “After that we'll make as many modifications as you like. The sky is the limit.” He's not kidding. A $10,000 pair is not out of the ordinary. “We take orders for up to 10 custom pairs per day, and anywhere from 180 to 200 hands touch each boot we make.” Suddenly the $700 off-the-shelf Luccheses feel like a bargain. I land on a dressy black pair with graceful brown stitching and walk out two inches taller. My last stop before the evening's bull riding is The Best Hat store. Owner Susan Maddox, wearing a denim shirt and an Hermès scarf tied around her shoulders, welcomes me. She opened the shop with her late husband, Keith, in 1996, then they bought the American Hat Company factory in Conroe, Texas, in 2003. She has run the business with help from her younger daughter, Mercedes, since Keith's death in 2019. Maddox and her daughters, including Treasure, who works in marketing for Auberge, embody the modern Fort Worth aesthetic: refined, colorful, and unabashed. They post their outfits of the day on social media and wear a high-low mix (Chanel with Zara) and Miron Crosby boots—sometimes with an American Hat adorned with their signature “Positive Times” emblem. But when they are asked to describe what makes the local style unique, it's hard for the matriarch to sum things up: “We love a nice elevated Western look, and I don't think we overdo it. We don't put on airs. People who settled here have a very bold spirit and a kind of grit that was required to make it. You can see that spirit in the people here today.” Sometimes it takes an outsider's perspective to decipher what makes the local panache so compelling. I ask Blankenship, my rodeo-ticket connection, who moved here in 2022 to work with the Rattlers, for his take on the town. “I grew up in Oklahoma,” he says. “We always thought of Texans as being very proud and maybe a little annoying about it. Now that I live here, I get it. It's an authentic place, where a handshake still counts as a contract. Yes, there's a lot of local pride, but it's not bragging. It's like people are saying, ‘Let me show you all of our awesome.’” Where to stay The 106-room Bowie House, Auberge Collection has a luxury-ranch aesthetic with large, spotless rooms, a clubby, cozy lobby bar, and an indoor-outdoor restaurant to create a truly unique stay. For the property, owner Jo Ellard selected 400 paintings, collages, photos, and sculptures sourced from antiques sales, Art Basel shows around the world, and her own private collection. Most of it is available for purchase. If you can't score an invitation to a private ranch, a stay at Hotel Drover, Autograph Collection in the heart of the Stockyards, may be the next best thing. The 200-room property is a short walk from some of the city's historic treasures, but it's surrounded by peaceful gardens, a resort pool, and outdoor terraces for drinking and dining. With its warm minimal interiors and crisp, colorful furnishings, The Crescent Hotel, Fort Worth reflects the city's more restrained side. Bonuses: an on-site Canyon Ranch Wellness Club and the elegant (and beautifully lit) Emilia's restaurant. Where to eat and drink The 1947 classic Cattlemen's Steak House, which was given a new life—along with a members-only club in its basement—by mega-producer Taylor Sheridan, features modern steakhouse go-tos. Order ranch water and a steak salad at the bar, and enjoy the world-class people-watching. No trip to Fort Worth is complete without a visit to bustling family-owned Tex-Mex institution Joe T. Garcia's and its sprawling patio. Join the always festive crowd for strong, salty margaritas and classics like enchiladas and chiles rellenos, and mariachi on Friday and Saturday nights and all day Sunday. A piled-high plate of ribs and brisket and an ice-cold beer is a Texas standard, and no one in Fort Worth does it better than Railhead Smokehouse BBQ, a 40-year-old barbecue joint owned by state representative Charlie Geren. Where to find westernwear Realtor Rodger Chieffalo inherited a short-brimmed beaver felt hat beloved by legendary local businessman Amon G. Carter, then began sourcing and refurbishing similar hats to give as gifts to clients. The passion became Chieffalo Americana which now includes upscale American-made and reworked Western vintage wear. Owned and operated by the Franklin family for three generations, M.L. Leddy's sells its own line of custom boots and hats—and anything else a well-heeled Texan might want. The store's rich, wood-trimmed interior smells like saddle leather and oil money. Packed to the rafters with fashionable Western clothing and accessories, Maverick Fine Western Wear is a must-stop shop in the heart of the Stockyards. Owner Gayle Hill hosts several designer trunk shows a year for her loyal customers, who rely on the Maverick buyer's eye for heirloom-quality pieces. Dallas-born designer Lela Rose has elevated and adapted cowgirl chic to appeal to the Net-a-Porter crowd. Her shop inside Bowie House sells clothing, home accessories, and boots from her Lucchese collaboration. At Crissy Jean Faulconer's appointment-only Proper Supply Co. in Weatherford (a ranch community near Fort Worth), Faulconer sells jeans stitched from rare Texas denim and custom sterling silver belt buckles made using vintage molds from Bohlin Company, a favorite of Western stars like Roy Rogers. Diplo is a customer. Where to peruse jewelry The fine jeweler Jo Latham sources unique pieces for discerning shoppers who appreciate craftsmanship with a wink—like horseshoe pendants from French Lebanese designer Selim Mouzannar or a diamond-encrusted pistol charm. “Chief” Garren Still, who is half Cherokee, crafts and sells a curated selection of sterling and American-mined turquoise jewelry, like ornate cuffs and statement necklaces at Weatherford establishment Chief's Trading Post. Where to try on hats The marquee in front of the Best Hat Store reads “Positive Times,” and the optimistic “+ x” symbol is embroidered onto the store's signature hat patches. Inside, rows of in-house brand American Hat Company (manufactured in Bowie) line the walls, and customers queue up for sessions with its team of experienced shapers. The Mule Alley Flea Style, the most successful of the 10 locations owned by Dallas-based former magazine editor Brittany Cobb, caters to a trendy customer who loves the cowboy lifestyle but spends little time on a ranch. Shoppers choose their hat shape and then browse bins of artfully curated bits and bobs sourced from flea markets to adorn it. Where to strut in boots To the trained eye, a Lucchese boot is as identifiable (and aspirational) as a Louboutin. The Texas-based boot brand founded in 1883 has a reputation as one of the world's finest boot makers for men and women, using lemonwood-peg construction (instead of metal tacks) and soft, sturdy leather that's comfortable straight out of the box. Built to last, well-worn pairs can get a factory refurbishment for a few hundred dollars. Rod Patrick, known for its wide spectrum of available sizes among the 15,000 pairs of in-stock boots, sells premium and bespoke boots to a discerning client who appreciates attentive service. Its relatively rapid custom timeline—delivering boots in 6 to 12 months—is also a plus. This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: 16 Idyllic Hotels in the Catskills, Where Design Meets the Upstate Wild
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.26
I’ve been going to the Catskills for as long as I can remember, and I still adore the feeling when the drive north begins to feel less like a commute and more like a true escape from the city. As a native New Yorker, I’ve spent years getting to know this upstate mountain region in every season: summer afternoons bouncing between swimming holes and farm stands, brilliant fall drives beneath canopies of red and gold, spring weekends when the woods suddenly turn electric green, and winter stays where a fire and a good dinner can easily constitute the entire itinerary. These feelings of comfort, simplicity, and adventure are part of what makes the region such an enduring weekend escape—and what makes its hotel scene so appealing. The best hotels in the Catskills range from characterful country inns and beautifully restored motels to secluded woodland retreats and sprawling estates, many with fireplaces, pools, standout restaurants, and rooms that invite you to linger just a little longer. Some are destinations in themselves; others put you in just the right spot for hiking, antiquing, swimming, or wandering through the region’s small towns. After a lifetime of returning to the Catskills, these are the hotels I’d book for an upstate New York getaway, no matter the season. Our top picks: - Best for families: Urban Cowboy Lodge - Best for design lovers: Hotel Lilien - Best for spruced-up glamping: Postcard Cabins Eastern Catskills - Best for barnhouse wellness: Inness - Best for an upscale, farm-to-table retreat: Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection FAQ: Where should I stay in the Catskills? From trailhead lodges to art-filled inns, the decision of where to stay depends on the tone you want to set for your getaway. In towns like Phoenicia, Big Indian, and Tannersville, you’ll find restored mountain lodges and design-forward motels surrounded by waterfalls, hiking trails, and swimming holes. Big Indian, in particular, offers a quieter, more secluded slice of the Catskills—dense forest, winding roads, and stays that put you within minutes of Slide Mountain and the Esopus Creek. Around Woodstock and Kingston, expect artsy spots that nod to the region’s bohemian legacy, with galleries, vintage shops, and standout farm-to-table dining. For winter ski escapes on the slopes of Hunter and Windham, look for hotels with mountain views and cozy fireplaces. Come summer, lakefront stays near Catskill and Saugerties trade snow for sun and live music nights. When is the best time to visit the Catskills? The Catskills are basically four destinations in one, each season reshaping the landscape and the mood. Spring, from April to June, brings thawed rivers, waterfalls in full rush, and wildflowers along hiking trails. Summer, from July to late August, hums with lake swims, tubing on the Esopus Creek, and outdoor concerts in Woodstock and Saugerties. Fall, from late September to early November, is peak magic for fiery maples, cider festivals, and mountain drives through Hunter and Windham. Winter, from December to around March, draws skiers and comfy-vibe-seekers to slopeside lodges and fireside dining. Which hotels in the Catskills offer the best views and amenities? The top stays in the Catskills balance mountain views with top-notch modern amenities. Eastwind Oliverea Valley captures Nordic simplicity amid forested peaks—its saunas, hammocks, and riverside setting are ideal after a day on the trails. Nearby, The Bradstan Boutique Hotel at the Eldred Preserve brings waterfront, tree-covered luxury, blending eco-minded design (hello, floor-to-ceiling windows with panoramic forest views) with cozy interiors. For architecture lovers, Piaule Catskill redefines the modern cabin with glass-walled rooms that seem to float amongst the trees, complete with a spa and soaking pools. How we choose the best hotels in the Catskills Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: Booking.com Promo Codes & Coupons | September 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.03
From flights to car rentals to cruises, Booking.com does it all—but perhaps what it’s most known for is scoring travelers spectacular rates on hotels around the world. You can book every aspect of your trip on one platform, including taxis to and from the airport and attractions in your favorite cities, like Tokyo and Montreal. Plus, you’ll be able to scroll through thousands of options for hotels and packages featuring reviews from real-life travelers like you, and nothing beats the ability to compare prices, locations, and ratings across all of your top picks. Whether you’re planning a three-week vacation in Thailand or a quick weekend getaway upstate, on Booking.com you’ll find everything you need to turn your perfect trip into a reality—with tons of coupons, promo codes, and expert tips for saving $500+ this month. Get at least 15% off with Booking.com getaway deals Book a dream getaway for less with Booking.com getaway deals. You can save at least 15% on top hotels around the world. Look for the Getaway Deal tag when you use Booking’s online search tool to save on both domestic and international stays. No promo code is needed at checkout. Thousands of their highest-rated properties are offering discounts, including destinations such as Kyoto from $24 per night, Paris from $82, and Los Angeles starting at $89 per night. Be sure to book (and stay) by September 30, 2026, to enjoy your savings. 10% off Booking.com coupon for new customers If you’ve never booked with Booking.com before, now’s the time. New customers get to enjoy even more rewards—those who sign up for the free Genius Loyalty Program will immediately receive a 10% Booking.com coupon on select stays and rental cars. Once you unlock Level 2 of the loyalty program—which can be done by completing five bookings within two years—you’ll start receiving up to 15% off on select stays, followed by discounts of up to 20% off when you reach Level 3 (unlocked by completing 15 bookings in two years). Loyalty members at Level 2 will also receive free room upgrades and free breakfast. Plus, once you unlock a level, those rewards are yours for life—you’ll never be demoted or downgraded. More ways to save on Booking.com hotels, rental cars, and flights To secure the lowest prices, you’ll want to book your flight and accommodations together to unlock vacation package deals. Right now, expect savings of over $1,000 on select hotel and flight packages to Cancún and hundreds of dollars of savings on car and hotel packages in Las Vegas. Choose from any combination of a Booking.com hotel, rental car reservation, or round-trip flights to get money off in bundle discounts. Browse everything from luxury properties in Paris to cozy boutique hotels in Mexico City. Simply pop in your travel dates, then let their online tool go to work. Not only will you unlock better rates, but you can also customize each part of your travel itinerary to fit your budget. Think you can find a better deal somewhere else? If the same reservation is listed at a lower price on another website, you can contact Booking.com to request a price match up to 24 hours before your check-in time. Save 15% with a Booking.com student discount Study hard and save more with Booking.com’s student discount. Those who can verify their student status can get up to 15% off stays, flights, and car rentals across the website. To reap your rewards, create an account through the platform StudentBeans and verify your status. There are no additional fees you’ll have to worry about when navigating through StudentBeans, and the codes can be used (and reused) throughout the duration of your schooling. Student codes are unique for each person, so they can’t be used across groups, and can sometimes be stacked on other sales to make the most of your money. What to know about Booking.com promo codes and travel coupons Did you know that you can earn Booking.com discount codes from their partner travel brands, too? Simply shop as you usually would, making sure to use the same email linked to your Booking.com account. Then keep an eye on your email inbox where you may receive a unique coupon code that can be redeemed through the travel coupons center on Booking.com's site. Once you enter your code and email, the credits will be added to your Wallet when you log in to your account. Easily track any rewards you've earned from both credits and vouchers here and use them like a coupon on future bookings. To see which properties accept rewards, check to see if there's a “Pay with Wallet” badge on the booking, then select it as your form of payment during checkout. What to do if your Booking.com promo code is not working Ready to reserve your next trip but your Booking.com promo code isn’t working? There are a few things you can do at home to troubleshoot. First, confirm that you’re typing in the promo code correctly: double-check that there are no accidental capitalizations, spaces, or incorrect look-alike characters (like zero and the letter O). Once that’s done, take a look at the code restrictions. Has the expiration date passed? Perhaps there’s a minimum spend limit or the code only applies to specific categories. If all seems to be correct, make sure you’re not trying to stack a coupon code that isn’t applicable on an already discounted purchase. Finally, consider restarting your browser, switching to a new device, or clearing your cookies and cache. You can also reach out to Booking.com’s customer service team for additional help.

item.title: The UK’s oldest recorded town has more than 2,000 years of history – and where it is may surprise you
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.97
When I found out where the UK’s oldest town was, I wasn't expecting it to be a place I've passed through quite so frequently, or one still thriving today. I’ve been lucky enough to travel the breadth of Britain over my 31 years, from tiny hamlets in the Scottish Highlands to artsy towns in Cornwall. I’ve spent half my life calling London home and the other half in East Anglia; holidayed in Wales, visiting beaches accessible only by wooden swing; slept in cabins in the Cotswolds; road-tripped through Northern Ireland; and spent years studying in Newcastle. All of which is to say, if you’d asked me to guess where it was, I’d have imagined a barely-there archaeological site somewhere in rural Northumberland, rather than a thriving modern city in Essex, close to the Suffolk border and just 60 miles northeast of London. I’m talking, of course, about Colchester. Today, the city is popular for its fast commuter trains into the capital, relatively affordable housing, open green spaces and, of course, its rich history. But in around AD 43, it was known as Camulodunum: the first major Roman city and the initial capital of Roman Britain, before it was destroyed during Boudica’s rebellion in AD 61. The story of the Roman settlement didn’t end there, however, and Colchester was rebuilt in the years that followed. During the Anglo-Saxon era, the city was largely neglected before later falling under Viking control. In AD 917, Edward the Elder drove the Vikings out, and Colchester began to regain its former stature. Following the Norman Conquest, Colchester Castle was built in 1066 over the ruins of an earlier Roman temple. Dating to the 1070s, it became the first and largest of the Normans’ great keeps, cementing Colchester’s importance as one of England’s key centres. But the city’s history stretches back even further than the Roman conquest. Colchester began as an Iron Age settlement, ruled by Cunobelin, known as the ‘King of the Britons’. Evidence of this early history can still be found in the city today, including a collection of Iron Age and Roman artefacts at Colchester & Ipswich Museums. There’s something slightly confusing about calling Colchester the oldest town in the UK, given that it is also one of the country’s newest cities. It gained city status in November 2022 as part of the late Queen’s Platinum Jubilee Civic Honours, one of eight towns to receive the upgrade. It joined Doncaster, Milton Keynes, Dunfermline, Bangor, Wrexham, Douglas and Stanley. Of course, when compared with some of the world’s oldest cities, Colchester is relatively young in the grand scheme of human history. Jericho, on the West Bank near the Jordan River, is thought to have been inhabited as early as 9000 BCE, and is often described as the world’s oldest known walled city. Across Britain, several places lay claim to the title of oldest town, from Thetford in Norfolk and Ipswich in Suffolk to Amesbury, near Stonehenge, where evidence of settlement dates back as far as 8820 BC. Colchester’s claim rests on a specific point of difference: it is officially recognised as the UK's oldest town on record, based on a reference to the settlement by the Roman writer Pliny the Elder.

item.title: Is your vagus nerve the real reason travel wrecks you?
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.89
Scroll far enough on social media and you'll hit a quick fix promising to calm your nervous system in seconds. The vagus nerve in particular has become wellness shorthand for ‘calm on demand’ but there's actual science behind how you do it properly – and it goes far beyond a 15-second clip. So, what is the vagus nerve? Essentially, the longest cranial nerve in the body, travelling from the brainstem down through the neck and chest into the abdomen, brushing past the heart, lungs and gut. It's the main line of the parasympathetic nervous system – rest, digest, repair – as opposed to the sympathetic system that gears you up to handle a threat. “If you think of your body as a car, the autonomic nervous system is the drivetrain and brakes,” says Lou Atkinson, clinical wellbeing lead of Yōjō, a health and wellness platform specialising in vagus nerve stimulation or VNS. “The sympathetic nervous system is the accelerator, while the vagus nerve is your essential braking system, slowing your heart rate, initiating digestion and lowering inflammation.” Activating the vagus nerve can help us feel calmer, but the issue with quick fixes is that we are treating the symptoms of nervous system dysregulation – like anxiety, insomnia, a need to control everything – rather than the dysregulation itself. “If we treat the symptom without ever getting to the root cause, it becomes a tireless battle managing something that cannot dissipate unless we leave the state we're in,” explains Sarah Baldwin, a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner. What happens to our nervous system when we travel? Travel obliterates almost all our comforting routines and habits. “It’s essentially a stress-test for your autonomic nervous system, and vagal tone takes the hit," says Human Potential Coach and Breathwork Practitioner, Rob Rea. “Crossing time zones desynchronises the body's rest-and-digest rhythm from local day and night – a large part of why jet lag brings poor sleep, a racing heart and low mood, not just tiredness.” Short nights, dry cabin air, dehydration, alcohol and caffeine all tip the body further towards fight-or-flight, leaving less room for recovery. For some, it goes way deeper than jet lag. Leaving a familiar environment removes our daily safety anchors, and unresolved stress can resurface as anxiety or hypervigilance amid the unpredictability of new places. “Long after we’ve arrived, and the danger has passed, the body can keep replaying that same protective response – that’s why so many of us feel anxious or shut down for reasons we can't quite explain, especially when travelling,” trauma psychotherapist Emmy Brunner says. “Release isn't about forcing it – it happens through small, repeated doses of safety, not pushing through.” In practice, this looks like having a vagus nerve toolkit you can turn to when you need it most. "Splash cold water on the face – cold exposure activates the vagus nerve and can pull you out of a spiral almost instantly,” Brunner advises. Another tip she says is to: “Slowly look around the room and name a few things you can see – it reminds the nervous system it's present and safe." Another surprising method that works is quiet humming. “It stimulates the vagus nerve directly through the vocal cords,” says Atkinson. If you feel too conscious doing this in a public place, longer exhales also help engage it: "Breathe gently through your nose, inhale for four seconds and exhale for six," says Rea. "Let the breath become quieter rather than bigger, and continue for two to five minutes." Making travel easier on our nervous systems Perhaps the best advice is to think of nervous system work as part of your pre-travel prep, along with your packing and booking. “People often wait until they're deeply dysregulated to start regulating, but the earlier you start, the better,” Baldwin advises. She recommends getting outdoor light at both ends of the day to recalibrate your circadian rhythm, before, during and after your trip. As is having a piece of home with you. “Bringing something familiar, a candle, a journal, a photo and orienting to a new room by consciously noticing its colours and sounds both help signal safety, too,” she adds. For frequent flyers wanting something more hands-off, wearable vagus nerve stimulators like yōjō deliver gentle electrical pulses to the ear's auricular branch, nudging the body into rest-digest mode without requiring meditation mid-flight – wearable while working, watching a film or trying to sleep. But ultimately it’s about incorporating vagal nerve work into your daily life. “The goal is not a quick fix; it’s to discharge small amounts of activation to lessen our dysregulation by even 5 per cent,” Baldwin says. Our nervous systems need something called disconfirming experiences. “These are moments where we show, not tell, our nervous systems that the thing it thinks is dangerous is actually safe,” she says. After doing that, our nervous system has enough data points to see that the perceived danger is actually safe, and we no longer experience the anxiety we once did. None of this promises to make flying enjoyable – particularly if you struggle with it. But understood and practised properly, vagal tone could be the deciding factor in whether a trip leaves you restored or wrung out. That’s worth knowing, next time you're stuck in seat 34C convincing yourself it's turbulence, when it’s actually your nervous system on overdrive. - Emmy Brunner’s residential retreats combine hypnosis and somatic practice. The Compass, a four-week online course, fuses evidence-based clinical tools with belief and identity repatterning. - Sarah Baldwin’s online programs Navigating Your Nervous System and Nervous System Essentials can be found here. Listen to her podcast, You Make Sense Podcast, on Apple or Spotify. - Rob Rea’s Autumn Equinox Day Retreat will be at 1 Hotel Mayfair, London. Follow him online.

item.title: The Indonesian island that time forgot is one of travel’s most exciting new destinations
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.07
There are not many places left in the world like the tip of Rote. It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell and bathymetry. There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach – good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there. Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote & Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels – a few hundred miles apart – front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property. One night I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance, storytelling and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the firepit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument the sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student. Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders – and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” This is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile – on the harbour, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land and are now building a cottage. I borrow a bike to explore the main coastal road, sealed but potholed and set back from the seafront, with sandy lanes trailing down to the beaches. Village merges into village, and the only demarcations are bollards painted “Selamat Datang” – welcome – or a trio of life-sized crucifixes, prettily decorated despite being a symbol of execution: one is painted lavender, another strewn with flowers. The churches here are enormous and numerous, towering vaulted monuments, one resembling a gigantic Noah’s Ark. Catholic, a man tells me, then to be contradicted by his wife: no, Presbyterian. Another says Methodist. The pastor tells me Calvinist. Tropical Christianity, let’s agree on, and fervent. At Easter, I’m told, crowds enact the Stations of the Cross, parading through the streets in the garb of Roman soldiers. The rest of the year there’s not much more than a scrap of traffic. One day I drive 40 minutes and count two motorbikes and one water bowser. I reach the end of a road that peters out into scrub, nothing beyond and nowhere for me to go. Although there are few vehicles, there are scads of roadside vendors selling petrol in fancy glass bottles that look more like love potions. Lines of laundry flap. Animals are everywhere: languorous cows, silky-haired goats atop bathroom-tiled gravestones and broods of chickens crossing the road, I could only assume, to get to the other side. This easy-going scene belies the region’s bloody colonial history. Timor was fought over by the Dutch and Portuguese – a battle rooted in the sandalwood and spice trade – resulting in its split into East and West. The British muscled in, but only for a few years, and the Japanese occupied the area during the Second World War. Remnants of history and cultural heritage are not obvious at first glance; some can be seen in the weaving of tessellated tenun ikat textiles, and the Ti’i Langga, resembling a ten-gallon cowboy hat made of lontar palm, worn by men, with a phallic spike on the brim. The best way to explore Rote, with its offshore islands, reefs and consistent breaks, is by boat. At one rocky outcrop I find a vast cave of screeching fruit bats; I drop into the water with a mask and snorkel, and fast-float in the choppy current to spy triggerfish and parrotfish. I was told oceanic manta ray and whale sharks congregate here, so I focus my eyes towards the deep, which falls away fast; the next strike of land is Australia. I check out surf sites, ending up on the far side of Ndana Island, Indonesia’s most southerly point. Nobody is around. I spend most of my time crashing and splashing, but nothing can beat the occasional moment standing aloft, feeling the push of a wave, the water so clear I can see fish dashing about the coral. A couple of haggard, sun-smashed Aussie surfers arrive close to the end of the day, so I bow out of the wave, instead bobbing about straddling my board to watch the colours of the sky shift. Back on land I meet locals and newcomers with surf shacks, market stalls and motorbike hire shops. Hotelier Mick Fogarty is just opening on Rote, after more than 30 years in Bali running the fabled Mick’s Place on Bingin Beach. When I ask him if he feels an ache about leaving Bali, he says “no” before I’ve finished the question. He and his Danish wife, Sascha Hansen, have three pretty self-catering bungalows, and, sensibly, used the best land to build a house for themselves. “We were going to build a restaurant but then thought, why don’t we build a home,” says Fogarty. That sums up the spirit of those who come to Rote. “Everyone moves here for the lifestyle,” he continues, “not to turn a profit, just to sustain a life.” After sunset, when everyone lopes back from the beach, there are a few couples hitching their gear onto motor scooters and a few families carrying babies, bags and boards, toddlers in tow. Everyone’s sandy with wet, tangled hair. It’s a strong, fit, healthy scene: “no drugs, no nightclubs”, as I keep hearing on repeat. One hotel owner points out, “Many of the people here already had their 20 crazy years, so now we can all chill.” Another labels Rote a “retirement village for surfers, who come for peace and quiet”. Carla Lázaro Ferro from the Canary Islands calls it differently. She lived here, then moved to Berlin, where she found herself “crying for Rote”. “Here you feel you can give back; life is more meaningful, more chaotic, more free,” she tells me. On my last night, I sleep out on the deck of my villa at Ferro’s dreamy resort, Bo’a Vida, overlooking the Bo’a wave and the Timor Sea. Here on the southern edge of Indonesia, the stars glow like light bulbs, even on the horizon. Only the dazzle of the rising moon dims them. I feel as far away as I could be. Shacks, bungalows, resorts and more NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy Following the success of its sister resort in Sumba (to the west of Rote), this 21-villa property on Bo’a Beach opens the renowned surf sites to top-end travellers. Villas are a mix of one-bedroom, duplex and family-style set-ups, and larger residences are planned. The westerly rooms have the best views of the Bo’a break. An on-site training academy allows guests to give back to the community. Bo’a Vida Owner Carla Lázaro Ferro opened a thatched shack 15 years ago atop a rocky outcrop at the end of Bo’a Beach, overlooking the legendary wave of the same name and the sunset beyond. Now she has six climate-conscious villas, five of which were designed by her husband, award-winning architect Álvaro Carrillo Eguilaz, with stone paths meandering down to slips of sand and the yoga sala. Ferro also runs Indika café in town, which serves fruit bowls until 5.30pm, when everyone heads out to catch a wave. Rote Island Huts Nat and Matt Thistlewaite came here from Australia in 2011 after finding the island of Rote on Google Earth. They arrived with the aim of creating a nonprofit holiday retreat that channelled income into local education and the community. There are five simple huts: three are family-style with bunks, all have beachfront access. It’s a heartening enterprise and they are now preparing to hand over management to local Rotenese, as they always intended. Sardine Beach Rote Pika and Pascal Chevillot, a Slovenian and a Frenchman, used to own Sardine, one of Bali’s top restaurants. Here on Rote they’ve created a spectacular three-villa property in five acres of gardens on one of the island’s best beaches. The rooms use lontar palm and coconut leaf to create traditional roofing, panelled walls and sconces. Pascal’s breakfast is a real event, with Parmesan omelettes and smoked Spanish mackerel. I notice a copy of Tao Te Ching on a side table, which just about sums up the place. Mick’s Place Rote Aussie Mick Fogarty and Sascha Hansen from Denmark are the creators of these three delightful beachfront bungalows with private courtyards in a glade of coconut trees. The couple are strong on sustainability, harnessing solar power, reusing grey water for the gardens and lending bicycles for guests to get around on. The lap pool is set to be the gathering place. Minimum one-week stay. 81 Palms Close to the T-Land break at Nemberala Beach, Spaniards Julia Davila Solana and Jose Miguel Murgui have built six A-frame cabins on the soft sand, plus they’ve recently opened four smaller bungalows at their new Next Door property. The Spanish restaurant is the best place for dinner in Rote, with former Michelin-starred Murgui in the kitchen cooking up gazpacho, tapas and seafood paella. Natural World Safaris (01273 691642) can arrange an 11-day trip combining a B&B stay at COMO Uma Ubud on Bali and a seven-night full-board stay at NIHI Rote & Hospitality Academy on Rote, from £5,800 per person. The price is based on two people sharing and includes all transfers and domestic flights. International airfare is excluded.

item.title: 12 authors on the books that inspired them to travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.88
Reading a good book can be a way to unwind after a stressful week at work, a way to escape reality for a little while, and a way to learn more about the world around us. However, books can also serve as some indirect inspiration for travel too – especially when a writer has transported you to a particular place or environment. I had this very experience recently whilst reading Carley Fortune’s latest romance novel, Our Perfect Storm. She’s an author who uses location as a character in itself and writes about it so beautifully, and this book has made me want to visit Tofino in Canada. And I’m not the only one who has been inspired by reading to plan or visit a new destination. To aid with your holiday planning, we asked a group of authors to tell us about the books that inspired them to travel to somewhere new and why. Dalia Al-Dujaili recommends Little Women by Louisa May Alcott When I was in New York alone for the first time in 2023, I decided to spend a few days exploring Boston and New England. I had romanticised ideas of the East Coast from my American Literature degree – The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, Little Women, and the poetry of Robert Frost and Mary Oliver. So I boarded a 6am Greyhound to Boston – very main character! – with no money and barely anything to eat except nuts and American trail mix. Five hours later, I checked into a random hostel, completely unprepared but enjoying the spontaneity. The next day, I had planned to take a ferry to Provincetown, where Mary Oliver lived, but a storm cancelled the ferries. Instead, I took the train to Salem. It was late October, so the town was full of pumpkins and candlelit New England houses. I spent the next few days exploring forests, visiting Louisa May Alcott’s house, browsing vintage bookshops, and eating lobster rolls. It was one of the best trips I’ve ever taken alone! Dalia Al-Dujaili is the author of Babylon, Albion Julia Armfield recommends Solo Faces by James Salter Solo Faces is perhaps one of the most compelling novels I've ever read about the combined ugliness and beauty of climbing. His passages about the cruelty and yet astonishing grace to be found in the Alps are just incredible and made it more or less imperative for me to visit the Swiss Alps myself. Travelling entirely by train from London enables you to witness an outrageous cross-section of landscapes and really adds to the sense that you are growing incrementally further and further away from reality, the higher up you get. Julia Armfield is the author of Our Wives Under The Sea and Up To The Light Sian Meades-Williams recommends The Stone Boudoir by Teri Maggio I bought this book on a slight whim from a bookshop in Greenwich, where the author visited because her grandmother said there was ‘nothing there’, and I not only completely fell in love with Sicily but wanted to see it for myself. It was incredible; I’ve been back a few times since my first trip and my partner and I even got engaged in that tiny town with ‘nothing to see’. Sian Meades-Williams is the author of The Pyjama Myth Beth Ashley recommends Fault Lines by Emily Itami The writing is so beautiful in the way it describes the environment of Tokyo you honestly feel like you can see it. Itami is so descriptive and romantic in her prose, and having the main character have a job where she shows people around is such a brilliant narrative device, also showcasing Tokyo to the reader. And when I finally took a trip to Tokyo, I ended up re-reading Fault Lines. Beth Ashley is the author of Sluts Tahmina Begum recommends Without Reservations by Alice Steinbach Without Reservations is a memoir by a Pulitzer-winning journalist and single working mother. At the time of writing, Steinbach’s children had grown up, her nest empty and there is a level of contentment with her career, while a level of discontentment with her life. The date marked in the library stamp at the front says I took this out on 3 April 2018. I would have been 23. Although Steinbach was writing on the other side of life, I vividly remember the impact this book had on me. My own version of Eat, Pray, Love. In fact, my first solo trip to Malta came shortly after this. I may not have lived as long as Steinbach when reading Without Reservations, but I had at that point been interning and working a few writing jobs in newsrooms, all at the same time, for already five years by then. I was similarly becoming more content in my career decisions while feeling, as though I was not living enough. So I did what many South Asian Muslim women are not asked to do that Steinbach was also seeking: joyful memories that were just for herself. Tahmina Begum is the author of Womanhood Rioghnach Robinson recommends Outline by Rachel Cusk It's been five years since I visited Greece, and longer since I first read Rachel Cusk's Outline, so I can't remember whether the book's diamond-cut Mediterranean descriptions really did drive me to Athens. But I do remember landing in 115-degree heat as that summer's wildfires bore down on the city, and the tinkling music in the sprawling, deserted restaurants near the scorching beach, and a long, one-sided conversation with a stranger about the organisation of Greek transit. So: Rachel Cusk clearly made Athens feel like Outline to me, and now, when I reread, Outline feels like that summer's Athens. Rioghnach Robinson is the author of Bad Words Stephanie Wrobel recommends Misery by Stephen King Misery inspired me to write my own cat-and-mouse thriller set in the publishing industry, but instead of an author held captive by his number-one fan, Revenge Plot pits a literary agent against an unhinged aspiring writer. I knew I needed somewhere suitably remote to trap them together, which led me to an Airbnb treehouse in the Catskill Mountains in New York and eventually to spending a few nights there alone for research. The reality was more unsettling than I’d anticipated. The treehouse had no cell service, and its walls were made of glass. It was beautiful during the day; after dark, all I could think about was how easily someone could be standing among the trees, watching me. Needless to say, plenty of that unease found its way into the book. Stephanie Wrobel is the author of Revenge Plot Fiona Valpy recommends The Weight Of Water by Anita Shreve I love Anita Shreve’s books set along the New England coastline. The Weight of Water is a dual-timeline novel about a historical murder and a contemporary relationship in freefall on the mysterious Isles of Shoals in the Gulf of Maine. I’m planning a trip there next year to explore more of the coast, and to visit Celia Thaxter’s beautiful garden. She was a poet who made her summer home on one of the rocky and inhospitable islands, planting a garden that inspired some of the paintings by the American Impressionist painter Childe Hassam. Fiona Valpy is the author of Sisters of the Midnight Sun Meg Charlton recommends Weetzie Bat by Francesca Lia Block If I said I moved to Los Angeles because of Weetzie Bat, I would not be alone. This is, apparently, a common reaction to reading Francesca Lia Block’s psychedelically overstuffed ode to the city. Block's LA is a smoggy, fizzy heaven for freaks and rebels, the young and young at heart, anyone willing to see the beauty glinting out between the strip malls and dying palms. A YA novel that flutters into magical realism might feel a tad overheated for some adult readers. But then again, LA can feel like that itself: Too big, too much. Sprawling and tacky and totally, utterly sublime. Meg Charlton is the author of Voyagers Charles Cumming recommends the James Bond series by Ian Fleming In the 1980s, as a pupil at the sort of cloistered boarding school with which Ian Fleming would have been familiar, I read every James Bond book going. 007 travelled far and wide – to the Bahamas and Japan, to Paris and Berlin – but it was the Istanbul of From Russia With Love that I longed to visit. Years later, researching a spy novel of my own, I finally came face-to-face with the crumbling Ottoman buildings, subterranean passages and magnificent mosques so vividly depicted in Fleming’s classic. Istanbul was crowded and sensual, a hub of skulduggery and corruption, still the perfect setting for a story of espionage. Charles Cumming is the author of ICARUS 17 Anna Deacon recommends The Living Mountain by Nan Shepherd I've always been inspired by great travel writing, and my bookshelves are full of dog-eared Lonely Planet books that have travelled with me in a backpack to many far-flung places, but one book I return to time and time again is The Living Mountain by Nan Shepherd. Even though I've spent a great deal of my life in the Cairngorms in Scotland and know the area really well, this book offers a whole different view of this rugged, wild landscape. Nan's writing is so visceral and descriptive, and her adventures inspire the reader to explore, not only these wild places, but themselves too. I've taken this book on so many adventures and it never stops inspiring me to plunge in icy river pools, quietly observe nature, and walk until I find myself. Anna Deacon is the author of The Wild Fix Scotland C.J. Tudor recommends The Shining by Stephen King The Shining is one of my favourite books and I’ve always wanted to visit the creepy Overlook Hotel featured in the film. In 2023, I travelled to Alaska to research my novel, The Gathering, and booked an isolated lodge in the mountains: Talkeetna Lodge. Everything about it, from the snowy mountain views to the huge lounge with its high vaulted ceiling, reminded me of the Overlook. It had only just opened for the season, so it was almost deserted, adding to the eerie feel, although disappointingly, the bartender was not called Lloyd! C.J. Tudor is the author of Serenity Falls

item.title: 14 best loungewear brands: upgrade your airport uniform with these luxury pieces actually worth the hype
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.79
Comfy, layered, security-friendly and stylish: the best loungewear brands are having a moment. Gone are the days when cosy equated to frumpy. Slouchy joggers, sharp sweatshirts, leggings and hoodies are now de rigueur in the business class lounge and economy cabin alike. Traveller writers and editors have learned that a smart yet comfortable loungewear set is the go-to for surviving red-eye flights, prioritising cashmere co-ords and silky soft, thermoregulating bamboo to create a chic, elevated set you won't feel sheepish to wear out of the house. Below, we’ve curated the definitive guide to the best loungewear brands to know in 2026, so your next flight will be the most comfortable yet – and you won't have to compromise on style. Varley It’s the fabrics that Varley uses that makes its separates so supremely comfortable, and despite initially investing in a few of its sportswear separates for a wellness escape in Ibiza, it’s become one of my most revisited brands at home, too. Now, I wear its oversized sweatshirts on travel days, when working from home and on route to the gym. The simplistic silhouettes are easy to style (read: you don’t need to do much to make them look good) and if you’re partial to a print, the leggings are a fun way to amplify your off-duty wardrobe. Sarah Bannerman Uniqlo Uniqlo remains the ultimate destination for affordable lounge essentials, with its signature mix of minimal Japanese design paired with pleasingly high quality fabrics. The result is stylish everyday wear that’s comfortable as anything. Tactile textures elevate downtime dressing in the brand's loungewear offerings – think soft washable knit ribbed trousers and ultra-cosy fleece pieces that are still smart enough to wear out of the house. These low-maintenance separates work equally well for a quiet morning at home, afternoons running weekend errands and to keep you comfy on your yearly far-flung long haul flight. Tala Founded by former fitness influencer Grace Beverley, British brand Tala balances style, functionality and a dose of cool, alongside a strong commitment to sustainability. Pieces are made with organic cotton and recycled blends. The brand excels at crafting relaxed cuts twinned with modern touches – your classic tracksuits gets an instant upgrade thanks to rich shades like deep Americano. Whether you are working from home, heading to a Pilates class, or travelling, these heavy-weight, peachy-soft sets make off-duty dressing feel intentional rather than slapped together. Asceno Everyone at Traveller rejoiced when pyjama-inspired fashion entered the scene. We’ve always wanted to wear our cosiest nightwear on a flight (especially those we’d like to try and sleep on), and now it’s not only socially acceptable, but actively stylish. Asceno is unbeatable on this front – Its signature Aurelia trousers and London shirt are made from 95 per cent lambswool and five per cent UK-sourced cashmere, for a look that’s as easygoing as it is effortlessly chic. Pangaia We previously tested a jacket from Pangaia that used flowers as down – the brand is an industry leader in innovative sustainable practices. Its loungewear is no exception, banishing manmade materials in favour of a 50/50 split of organic and recycled heavyweight cotton, which is both casual enough for the sofa and cool enough to wear into town. You can even get a set for the whole family, as Pangaia makes their colour-popping separates for women, men and children. Cos Known for its minimalist aesthetic and understated cuts, Cos stands out as one of the cooler high street fashion brands offering clothes at a pleasing price point. It has a strong year-round loungewear offering, including a lovely selection of cashmere pieces that wouldn’t look out of place in the office, let alone in an aeroplane cabin. H&M H&M are masters of the high street, consistently offering soft, effortless pieces that punch above their price point. This season’s collection runs the gamut from lightweight, breezy fabrics for warm afternoons to plush brushed cotton ready for when the nights start to draw in. There are plenty of styles that work well for mixing and matching, too. Lilysilk Not content with creating ultra-luxurious sheets for your bedroom, Lilysilk turned its attention to creating a silk clothing range too. The brand’s loungewear collection is crafted from a premium silk-blend knit, turning your comfy clothes into elegant, breathable mainstays that, with good care, should keep you cosy for years to come. Pieces are designed to move naturally and fluidly with the body – if you’re after casual separates that feel as luxurious as eveningwear, the below make good options. Alo Yoga If you love the slouchy style of the Adanola tracksuits but you want something less sporty, more elegant, Alo Yoga is the best loungewear brand for you. There’s a reason the style set is regularly spotted kitted out in this US activewear brand. They’re known for creating quality, fashion-forward pieces that take the likes of Gigi Hadid, Taylor Swift, Kendall Jenner and Hailey Bieber seamlessly from pilates class to brunch. Although some of these sets are loose-fitting, with comfort and freedom of movement at the forefront of the designs, others are more body-sculpting, if you prefer a form-hugging look. Adanola Sportswear brands are the easy win when it comes to loungewear and Adanola treads the line between style and functionality especially well. Instead of choosing the boldly labelled sweatshirts and socks that have become the brand’s signature, choose more subtle pieces like the leg-lengthening wrap-over yoga pants in black, or the light-grey knitted two-piece. The latter combines to make for a polished yet easy look that’s as soft as sleepwear but worthy of a Business class plane seat. Sarah Bannerman Adidas Originals Adidas Originals has made a fashion comeback of late. Despite launching almost 30 years ago, it was the 2024 collaboration with Wales Bonner that secured its spot as fashion brand first, sportswear choice second. Simply stroll the streets of London and you’d be hard-pushed not to spot a pair of suede Sambas or a track jacket worn ironically (consciously or not) in a nod to the 90s. We’ll call that one the Oasis effect. I’ll admit it took me a minute to jump onboard with the return of the three-stripe trackpant, but styled with a chunky knit and a leather jacket, the burgundy pair has quickly become my airport-to-city go-to. Sarah Bannerman Lululemon Lululemon’s leggings remain the gold standard for flights – multiple Traveller editors rave about their buttery-soft finish, elevated design, gentle compression and squat proof waistbands that looks as at home in the yoga studio as in a business class airport lounge. Its loungewear brings all the same technical precision, flattering fits and quality materials in a cosier, snugglier form. Sporty & Rich Canadian founder Emily Oberg used to work in magazines, so she’s always had an eye for style. She founded Athleisure-luxe label Sporty & Rich in 2015, more as a creative outlet than a genuine business idea, but the brand’s vintage-leaning all-American sensibilities soon garnered a following, and now it’s a beloved staple for discerning types, made with a triple-threat of nostalgic cuts, vibrant colours and quality, sustainable materials. Vuori Californian fashion is synonymous with laid-back chic and Vuori brings that relaxed West Coast feel to its extensive range of active pieces and loungewear with its thoughtful, minimalist designs crafted with sustainability in mind. The brand requires all suppliers to sign and uphold a code of conduct covering labour, working conditions and environmental practices, while prioritising ethically grown cotton. I have multiple Vuori pieces – from leggings to joggers to t-shirts, and not one has bobbled, lost its shape or faded after two-plus years of washes – and I’ve worn them on flights everywhere from Saint-Tropez to India to Finland.

item.title: 15 best treehouses to rent in the UK, for a magical woodland escape
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.71
There's something magical about the thought of a few nights holed up in one of the UK's best treehouses, especially when the summer leaves start to fall and autumn staycations become the order of the day. From luxury two-bed treetop dwellings with families in mind to cosy cabins perfectly designed for two, this is our pick of the most charming places to stay in England's woodlands. So whether you're dreaming of the Cotswolds and want to feel close enough to a spa that you're dabbling in nature but close to hotel luxuries, or prefer to go all-out and book a spot with an outdoor stove in lieu of a kitchen, there's a home in our list to suit. item.title: 15 best hotels in Amsterdam 2026 for the ultimate canal-side break
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.57
As a city of web-like canals and quirky corners, when it comes to the best hotels in Amsterdam, expect rooms of all shapes and sizes, interiors from the hip to the headily luxurious, and all manner of decor, from starkly minimalist to antique-store clutter and the summits of contemporary design. The city's hotel restaurants are often among the most adventurous in town, and the bars are way out front on the best bars in Amsterdam scene. All combined, and Amsterdam is a city where the hotel stay is part of the experience. From canal-views to Gothic style architecture, and even hotels with their own canal boats, here we list the very best places to stay in Amsterdam. Editor's picks of the best hotels in Amsterdam - For luxury: Rosewood Amsterdam - For a central location: Mandarin Oriental Conservatorium - For an affordable stay: The July, Boat & Co. - For families: Pulitzer Amsterdam Which part of Amsterdam is best to stay? For the quintessential Amsterdam experience, a hotel in the historic central Canal District, happening De Pijp, museum-filled Zuid or über-charming Jordaan is a must, but there are also great places to be found in quarters west and east of the centre and across the water behind Amsterdam Centraal Station. What are the best cheap hotels in Amsterdam?
