No timeline for testing to resume An Iranian institution that administered TOEFL exams told DW that new registrations had stopped following the latest sanctions changes. The institution added that the suspension could be temporary, but no date had been given for exams to resume. That uncertainty is particularly serious for students approaching university and scholarship deadlines who have spent months preparing and paying application-related costs. The suspension follows earlier problems with IELTS (British equivalent of TOEFL) testing in Iran. An IELTS center in Tehran told DW that sanctions-related difficulties transferring money had become one of the main obstacles to continuing exams. Some Iranian applicants had already been traveling to countries such as Turkey and Armenia to take IELTS. TOEFL and GRE candidates may now have to do the same. Rising costs for applicants Alireza, who is preparing to apply to a university in Italy, said the suspension of TOEFL had disrupted a backup plan he had arranged after IELTS testing became unavailable. "European universities usually accept IELTS. But because IELTS has been suspended in Iran, after extensive correspondence with the university, they agreed to let [Iranian students] meet the required score through an equivalent TOEFL result," he told DW. "But now TOEFL has also been suspended in Iran. Traveling to a neighboring country just to take the exam is very expensive, especially given Iran's current economic situation," added Alireza. Another candidate told DW that taking the exam in Turkey or Armenia would mean paying for travel and at least one night's accommodation on top of the test fee. For students hoping to secure scholarships or full funding, those additional expenses can be significant. Students launch petition Iranian TOEFL and GRE candidates have launched an online petition urging ETS to restore access to the exams. The petition says thousands of students are losing access to tests required for university admissions, scholarships, graduate programs and other academic opportunities. Many, it says, have spent months preparing, paid exam-related costs and built their application schedules around specific test dates. "Students should not lose years of preparation or their chance to pursue higher education because access to required examinations has suddenly been removed," the petition states. Narges, an Iranian applicant affected by the suspension, said she had seen the petition circulating in Telegram groups used by language learners and students applying to foreign universities. "I doubt it will have any impact," she said. "Still, I'm going to sign the petition." The organizers are calling on the US Treasury Department's OFAC to provide a specific exemption for standardized academic testing, and on ETS to restore TOEFL and GRE services in Iran as soon as legally possible. They argue that sanctions aimed at the Iranian government should not restrict educational opportunities for ordinary citizens who have no role in state policy. When sanctions impact education Until recently, the General License G had provided a legal channel for certain academic exchanges and educational services despite broader US sanctions on Iran. For many students, the suspension is the latest in a series of barriers to studying abroad. Bahar, who is applying for Ph.D. programs, said many Iranian students had already shifted their focus from the United States because obtaining visas had become increasingly difficult. "American universities were our first choice because they generally offer funding for Ph.D. programs more readily than European universities," she told DW. Now, she said, applicants are increasingly turning to Europe and Australia, but the testing suspension has created a new hurdle. "There is effectively no difference between IELTS and TOEFL for us now, because in either case, we have to leave Iran to take an English language test," Bahar said. For students approaching admissions deadlines, postponement may not simply mean waiting a few months. It can mean missing an entire admissions cycle, losing scholarship opportunities or delaying academic plans by a year or more. While ETS says it is examining possible ways to restore testing in Iran, there is currently no indication of when that might happen. For many applicants, the immediate choice is limited: wait without knowing when testing will return, or spend considerably more to take the same exam abroad. Edited by: Ole Tangen Jr

item.title: Inside the sea cucumber smuggling boom
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.98
When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade. Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering. Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory — local biologist Sangamesh Uday said they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks." The 1,500 or so species of sea cucumber around the world are great marine recyclers. They eat organic material including bacteria and microalgae, break it down and excrete clean oxygenated sand. This keeps vital nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorous in circulation and suppresses coral diseases. It also boosts ocean alkalinity levels which helps to slow down acidification, which is becoming a huge issue as rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere cause oceans to warm. In short, it's hard to overstate the environmental importance of these innocuous looking lumps. Why are they being smuggled? To their detriment, sea cucumbers are also considered a delicacy, especially in China and Southeast Asia. Historical records show they were traded between Indonesian fishers and Chinese merchants even 800 years ago. They are used in soups, served as pickled sides or turned into traditional medicine. And though there is some scientific evidence that the omega-3 they contain is a useful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, they're mostly popular because they're quite phallic — and therefore considered an aphrodisiac. Since the 1980s, commercial sea cucumber harvesting has expanded globally, with better access as well as higher incomes and demand in East Asia acting as the main drivers. Though many countries have outlawed the practice, some like Sri Lanka and Madagascar do allow fishing and aquaculture. Of the existing sea cucumber fisheries, 70% have become overexploited globally. The combination of the increasing demand and legal complexities has drawn the attention of minor and major mafias. Some of the largest Mexican cartels and even the Japanese Yakuza have been reported as diversifying their portfolios by using sea cucumbers and other sea creatures to keep the money flowing. These illicit groups enter every aspect of the supply chain — from extorting fishermen to the final smuggling of illegally-caught cucumbers across borders. They exploit weak environmental regulations and a lack of official knowledge around rules and species. Sea cucumbers are sometimes marked as legal fish consignments or smuggled into countries that do allow trade in the species. Teale Phelps Bondaroff, a leading expert on sea cucumber crime, said awareness is critical in dealing with the issue. "While many law enforcement officers may be on the lookout for drugs, weapons or well-known wildlife contraband like ivory, rhino horns or shark fins, sea cucumbers may slip past," he told DW. Poachers from overseas drawn to Andaman Islands The Indian government began regulating sea cucumbers in the 1980s and introduced a blanket ban on fishing them in 2001, when it saw the impact of the illicit trade on local populations. Since then, India has become the country with the strongest protections for the species. Anyone who catches one faces a seven-year jail term — the same sentence handed down for poaching a tiger or elephant. As a result, sea cucumbers close to the Andaman Islands have generally thrived. In the ocean around Myanmar, around 50 kilometers (30 miles) further north, it's a different picture. Civil war in the country has severely impacted local livelihoods and local black-market agents are using the instability to offer comparatively higher sums for a boatload of illegally caught sea cucumbers. And as their numbers in local waters dwindle, poachers head south. It is no easy game, however. They have to dodge the Indian coast guard, navy and police, evade local fishermen and even dense populations of crocodiles. They survive on fish, freediving using hookah pipes to breathe, and spend months rationing their diesel to ensure they have enough to make it back home — evading the Myanmar authorities and pirates looking to try and steal their catch. Many poachers are caught by the regional Andaman and Nicobar police, who are being specifically trained to comb the mangrove islands to find them. At least 50 people have been arrested in the past year, some as young as 16 and some in their 60s. Several have come back for the second or third time — risking being incarcerated again after completing full sentences. Is there a way to stop the illegal trade? Despite the efforts of the Indian authorities, the number of poachers coming in, year after year, has stayed stable. Bondaroff sees a need to sound the alarm at a global level. Other similar trades, like that of shark fins, have been slowed thanks to increased awareness about its cruelty and impact on the ecosystem — making it less socially acceptable. "The solution must include educating consumers about the harms of unsustainable and illegal sea cucumber extraction and tackling seafood fraud." Other suggestions include India opening up small areas of its waters where sea cucumbers can be legally fished, or introducing community-based aquaculture that is easier to regulate and would also benefit local fishers. But Bondaroff thinks that tackling the problem also requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue. "This means liaising and information sharing between governments and law enforcement agencies," he said. "And working together to address the complex financial crimes that enable sea cucumber crime." This report was supported by the Pulitzer Center. Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Cargo ship with 10 crew sinks off Turkey coast — authorities
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.83
Turkish authorities are searching for 10 people aboard a cargo ship that sank after a collision with another vessel in the Marmara Sea near Istanbul early Wednesday. "We believe, and have more or less confirmed, that the Tugberk Imamoglu has sunk," Transport Minister Abdulkadir Uraloglu told reporters in Istanbul. Uraloglu said all 10 crew members aboard the vessel were Turkish nationals and that attempts to reach them by mobile phone had been unsuccessful. "We can say that the sinking occurred rapidly in 11 minutes. No one has been found alive," he added. The bulk carrier Tugberk Imamoglu and the chemical tanker Alsu collided at around 3 a.m. local time (0000 GMT) off the city's western Silivri district, the Istanbul governor's office said in a statement. Two helicopters and 12 search and rescue vessels are scouring the area. The Transport Ministry's maritime directorate said that life-saving equipment, including a lifeboat belonging to the Tugberk Imamoglu, had been found floating on the surface. "Unfortunately, the crew members were not inside," it added. What else do we know about the missing ship? The 90-meter (295-foot) Turkish-flagged bulk carrier was en route to the Black Sea port of Eregli from Iskenderun when the collision happened. According to the maritime directorate, it was carrying 4,200 tons of rolled steel. Authorities believe it sank in waters around 900 meters deep. The 91-meter Turkish-flagged Alsu, was sailing from Kocaeli, east of Istanbul, to the Aegean port of Aliaga. It was empty at the time of the collision and did not appear to have suffered any damage, the governor's office said. The Sea of Marmara forms part of one of the world's busiest shipping corridors, linking the Mediterranean to the Black Sea via the Bosporus and Dardanelles straits. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Ukraine: Zelenskyy warns airlines to avoid Russian airspace
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.61
What you need to know This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading. Read below for developments regarding Russia's war in Ukraine on Wednesday, September 2. - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warns drone surge is making Russian airspace unsafe for civil aviation - Zelenskyy also says Germany and Ukraine are finalizing a drone deal - Two civilians reported killed in Russian attacks on central Ukrainian city of Dnipro Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Putin to not stop at Ukraine, German minister warns A Russia win in the war in Ukraine would encourage autocrats all around the world, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said. "If Russia, if Vladimir Putin wins this war, then that is a blueprint for all the autocrats in this world to say: what do I care about the law, the sovereign rights of other nations?" Pistorius said in the northern German city of Braunschweig. "Vladimir Putin will not stop if he were to take Ukraine," the Social Democrat warned. Germany says EU countries handing out too many visas to Russians Berlin is pushing for other EU members to cut down on tourist visas to Russian citizens, essentially calling for stricter rules across the entire EU. More than 600,000 short-stay visas were issued by EU countries in Russia last year. Italy, France and Spain issued the most, while Germany approved a mere 20,000. Berlin says it wants to make sure that people who could pose a security risk are not allowed to enter the EU. The call comes as tensions between Germany and Russia peak over Berlin’s accusation that Moscow was the mastermind behind an attempted drone attack a German airport in August. Russian ship seized in Norway Norway has seized a Russian ship due to a request by Ukrainian state company Naftogaz, the company said. According to Naftogaz — which has been looking for compensation from Russia since 2016 due to its expropriation of Naftogaz property — the seizure was meant to ensure that Russia meets its outstanding obligations. It was ordered by the Nord-Troms and Senja District Court. The vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was Russia-owned. "Russia cannot evade responsibility by refusing to comply with an international arbitral award, " Naftogaz's acting CEO Sergii Fedorenko said. Belgium's position on frozen Russian assets unchanged Belgium's opposition to using frozen Russian assets has remained in place, the country's foreign minister said. This comes after several European Union countries called the bloc to move forward with the move last week. According to Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot, the idea "generated little enthusiasm" among the bloc's foreign ministers, adding the Brussels government's objection to the move stems from reasons that "have not magically disappeared." About 210 billion euros (243.4 billion dollars) of Russian assets were immobilized following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Belgium last year rejected the European Commission's proposal to use the assets for a loan to Ukraine due to fears it would not be singled out by potential lawsuits by Russia. READ MORE: Should Germany intensify its response after the failed Leipzig attack? The German government is holding Russia responsible for an unsuccessful attack in Leipzig. Yet many feel that its response has been too mild. Read the full story: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war?' Pressure on Russia to grow, EU foreign policy chief says The European Union's foreign policy head Kaja Kallas said the bloc is interested in tightening the enforcement of sanctions against Russia. The move should also come with increasing pressure on Moscow, as well as increasing support for Ukraine. "Attempts to intimidate Europe will fail," Kallas said.
Childrens' hospice founder arrested after war criticism The founder of a Russian children's hospice has been detained and charged with deliberately spreading false information about the war in Ukraine. Lida Moniava, who is known for her engagement for sick children, took to Telegram to call the war a crime and said it must end. According to Russian investigators, Moniava posted false information "presented as credible reports" about the Russian army's actions against civilian population in Ukraine. The childrens' hospice Moniava founded in Moscow said it will continue to operate as usual, without adding further information. EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig attack The European Union's foreign policy head Kaja Kallas summoned the Russian envoy in Brussels following Germany's announcement that Russia was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport last month. WATCH: Why are books becoming a casualty of war in Ukraine? Ukraine says Russian airspace 'not safe' amid drone surge Kyiv says it has formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) that Russian airspace is "not safe" as a result of increasing Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian territory. Ukraine has also asked the UN agency to prohibit member countries from using Russian airspace, according to a government letter to the ICAO cited by Reuters. It came after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned airlines to stay away. "We in Ukraine do not want innocent lives to be lost. That is why we are warning our partners: the safe days in Russia's skies are over," Zelenskyy said. "Drone-infested skies are no place for civilian aviation," he added. "The sky over Russia is currently for drones ... as long as the war continues." Last week, Zelenskyy threatened to deploy up to 1,000 long-range drones per day. The ICAO has not commented on the request from Ukraine. Russia's aviation watchdog regularly closes airports in response to the Ukrainian drones. Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the war started in 2022. While European and US carriers do not fly over Russia due to the conflict, the airspace is used by other airlines from China, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates and other Gulf countries. Russia has stepped up its strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks. Ukraine has responded with long-range drone strikes on Russian energy and military infrastructure. Kyiv under attack for 7th straight day, 2 civilians killed in Dnipro Russian drones hit central Kyiv for a seventh day in a row on Wednesday, injuring seven people and damaging residential and university buildings, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The attack on a downtown university forced some 160 people to take shelter, he added. Also on Wednesday, Russia struck electricity facilities in the southern Odesa region, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes, authorities said. Two people were also killed and eight wounded in Russian strikes on the southeastern city of Dnipro, officials said. According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia fired 174 attack drones, as well as two ballistic missiles and two plane-launched missiles at Ukraine overnight. Meanwhile, Russia said its air defenses destroyed 130 Ukrainian drones overnight. Ukrainian drone attacks on Wednesday killed two people in Russia's Belgorod border region and wounded 16 more, officials said. Ukraine and Germany close to inking drone deal, Zelenskyy says Ukraine is close to finalizing a drone deal with Germany, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday after a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. "This will, among other things, certainly enhance the defense capabilities of both Germany and Ukraine," the Ukrainian president wrote on Telegram. The agreement, initially proposed by Ukraine several months ago, is expected to involve the joint development of several types of drones, missiles and related software. Zelenskyy thanked Germany and said he would meet with the chancellor to sign the deal in person. Welcome to our coverage Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned airlines to avoid Russian airspace amid a surge in Ukrainian drone activity. Kyiv formally notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that Russian airspace was "not safe." Moscow, in response, said it was improving flight safety and would not allow Ukraine to seriously disrupt aviation. More than four years after Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the two countries continue to trade daily strikes. Russian attacks on Wednesday killed two civilians and wounded six in the central Ukrainian city of Dnipro, local officials said, while the capital Kyiv was targeted for a seventh day in a row. Meanwhile, Zelenskyy said he held a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and that their two countries were close to finalizing a drone deal. We'll be following these developments, along with other key events in Russia's war against Ukraine, throughout the day in this blog.

item.title: Russia's hybrid attacks on Germany: When is it 'war?'
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.55
Fortunately, nothing bad happened this time around. Had the attack succeeded, however, who knows what the consequences might have been: On the evening of August 4, a drone outfitted with explosives and a detonation device was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes in the security area of Leipzig/Halle Airport. The airport serves as a hub for military aid to Ukraine. The German government hesitated for a long time before publicly holding Russia responsible. But now it has announced its findings. On Tuesday, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that the methods used in the attempted attack were consistent with those seen in other Russian hybrid operations, citing the drone's construction, various components, explosives and detonation technology. He noted that the attack had been planned with a "high degree of technical expertise and considerable organizational effort." In late August, Chancellor Friedrich Merz said of the incident: "The federal government will make the perpetrators of hybrid attacks pay a price. They will pay for this." At the time, he did not mention Russia by name. And even now, Merz himself has not commented on the matter. However, the price Russia will have to pay is relatively small. The Russian House cultural institute in Berlin is being shut down amid suspicions that it is serving as a cover for espionage. The Russian Consulate General in Bonn is also being closed. What's more, entry requirements for Russian citizens are set to be tightened, and Germany also plans to take tougher action against the Russian "shadow fleet" — the network of ships accused of circumventing fuel sanctions. Exactly how and when remains unclear, however. Mixed reactions to Germany's measures For the environmentalist Green Party in the Bundestag, however, the government's response was lacking. "The federal government's analysis came a bit late, and the steps it's taking aren't enough for me," said Sara Nanni, the Greens' security policy spokesperson, in a DW interview. "I don't think anyone in Moscow is afraid or giving it a second thought right now." As an example, she said Germany should be taking tougher action against the Russian shadow fleet. This would be necessary to "stop the flow of money to the Russian war machine," she said. Roderich Kiesewetter, security expert with Chancellor Merz' center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), is also dissatisfied. In the Handelsblatt newspaper, he called for the delivery of Taurus cruise missiles to Ukraine — and for the activation of Article 4 of the NATO Treaty, which requires allies to engage into consultations in the event of an external threat. He urged the German government to abandon "the politically convenient path of appeasement." However, wouldn't responding more assertively, as Kiesewetter has demanded, risk provoking a military confrontation with Russia, especially given that Russia has flatly denied responsibility for the Leipzig incident? On Tuesday, Russian President Vladimir Putin called the German sanctions against his country a "serious mistake" and accused Germany of fabricating evidence. The Foreign Ministry in Moscow announced that it would take countermeasures. Foreign Minister Wadephul sees Germany as a target Once again, the question of whether Germany is already at war with Russia is being raised — and this time with even greater urgency. But the federal government has unequivocally denied it. "We are not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," said Interior Minister Dobrindt on Tuesday, after he blamed Russia for the failed attack. Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told German public broadcaster ARD that Germany is not at war but is a Russian "war target." A year ago, in September 2025, Chancellor Merz said — though without naming Russia: "We are not at war, but we are no longer at peace either." This came against the backdrop of increasing attacks on data networks, critical infrastructure and hybrid threats. Security expert Sönke Marahrens from the University of Kiel offered a more nuanced answer: "No, Germany is not at war at the moment. We are facing hybrid activities by other countries, but we are not at war." In Western countries, he noted, declarations of war are regulated by law. And in Germany, according to the constitution, the Bundestag must declare that the country is at war, and that applies only after a physical attack. "Nothing currently meets that definition," he said. However, the Green Party's Nanni fears Russia will continue to escalate the situation. "We are not yet at war with Russia, but Russia appears to be preparing for a war not only against Ukraine but against all of Europe," she said, calling the incident in Leipzig an "attempted terrorist act." Not at war with Russia From a legal standpoint, too, Germany is not at war with Russia. No declaration of war has been made, no recognized armed conflict exists, and no collective defense obligation has been invoked under NATO's Article 5. Furthermore, consultations among NATO members, which must take place before a collective defense obligation can be invoked, have not been scheduled under Article 4. But things look different when it comes to hybrid warfare, which is not as precisely defined. Numerous security experts have argued that Russia is already waging just such a hybrid war against Western nations. This refers to attacks on infrastructure, cyberattacks, disinformation and traditional espionage. However, the line between hybrid war and an open act of war are blurry. Marahrens believes Russia is using hybrid actions — such as the one in Leipzig — to advance its strategic interests in Germany, the second-most important supporter of Ukraine after the US. Had the attack at the airport been successful, it would have relieved pressure on the Russian front, Marahrens said. He went on to say that "if Russia succeeds in convincing the German public not to support these political decisions [to support Ukraine], that would also directly reduce the pressure on the front lines." AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine The state election on Sunday in Saxony-Anhalt is one current example of Russian strategic interests. Many observers believe that this election is the most important in Germany in decades. The key question is whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — which is classified as far right by the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany's domestic intelligence agency — will secure an absolute majority and, for the first time, govern a German state. The AfD opposes further military support for Ukraine and would like to normalize relations with Russia. This resonates with many in eastern Germany, where the war in Ukraine is seen by many as none of Germany's business, and where there is a feeling that too much money has already been sent to Ukraine. This is why the federal government — composed of the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — is being careful about stepping up its rhetoric, as doing so could potentially help the AfD secure an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt. On the other hand, it can hardly afford to place the blame for the events in Leipzig on Russia while also responding in only a relatively mild manner. This dilemma may also be the reason why Chancellor Merz has so far refrained from speaking out to blame Russia. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: Unity at last: Is Libya's damaging power struggle at an end?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.50
There have been other attempts made in the past but this time, those involved hope it will finally work out: Thanks to mediation by the United Nations, the two opposing governments in the west and east of Libya have agreed that they will hold parliamentary and presidential elections within the next two years. "The agreement marks an important step in advancing Libya towards national elections and ending the transitional period," the UN's Support Mission in Libya, or UNSMIL, said in a statement. Among other things, the country's electoral commission will be restructured and, according to the UN, various points about the legal framework for the elections that had previously led to disagreements have now been resolved. But whether all this will actually result in free and fair elections in Libya remains to be seen. Divided for over a decade After former Libyan dictator Moammar Gadhafi was overthrown in 2011, Libya ended up divided in two. Since 2014, the country has been split between opposing governments located in the east and west of the country. A UN-backed administration known as the Government of National Unity is based in Tripoli in the west, and its rival, known as the House of Representatives, is based in the east, in Tobruk. Former warlord-turned-politician Khalifa Haftar, is based in the east while Prime Minister Abdul-Hamid Dbeibah is in charge in the west. Each is supported by a number of local militias and foreign powers, and each has tried to wrest control from the other. Up until now, attempts to hold an election that would unite the country have failed. For Andreas Dittmann, a geographic conflict expert and professor at the University of Giessen in Hesse, central Germany, the apparent unity is a positive. "Things could not continue the way they were," he told DW. After years of civil war and political division, the desire of many Libyans to end the fighting permanently has only grown. Dittmann believes the attitudes of political actors have also changed in this regard. Previously foreign actors had supported just one Libyan government, but now that has also changed and the prevailing argument seems to be that Libya can only develop further if both sides are incorporated into one administration. This is why the UN is trying to go beyond simply arranging a date for elections. It also wants to strengthen the electoral commission and work on electoral laws. The new and united government will be responsible for establishing the conditions for a secure and trusted electoral process. The UN has also set up what it calls "Structured Dialogues," during which consensus was sought on questions of leadership, security, the economy and reconciliation. Past agreements didn't work out Michael Bauer, who heads the Tunisia office of Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, believes the agreement is an important, if limited, step. Its success will depend on how binding any decisions are, he argued. After all, Bauer said, there have been plenty of political agreements in Libya in the recent past but none were really ever implemented. Parallel to the UN process, the US is also trying to work on bringing the disparate leadership together. Massad Boulos, the Trump administration's senior adviser on Arab and Middle Eastern affairs, has been trying to bring the Dbeibah and Haftar families together. In June, Haftar's son Saddam was in Washington where he met with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Bauer said the American way of dealing with Libya differentiates from the UN plan. "While the UN mission has basically been very inclusive, in my opinion, the American mission is trying to bring about a kind of deal between the country's elites," he told DW. He questions how such a deal would fit into free and fair elections in Libya. "Elections can only be meaningful if the outcome has not already been decided beforehand," Bauer said. The same is true for any pre-election allocation of political positions. Elites strike a deal? UK-based think tank Chatham House has already warned that a deal like this, around ministries and resources, will only institutionalize the existing rivalry between Libya's ruling elites. With such an arrangement the rival actors would just divide the state's resources between themselves, and corruption and patronage systems would continue. The country's division into east and west will be hard to overcome. A new united government would have to deal with preexisting power structures, rather than starting anew. Dittmann said there is a further problem. Much of the Libyan population lives in the western areas, especially in the Tripoli region. This would see the eastern half of the country lose power if elections are held. "If there are elections, and if those elections proceed mostly according to democratic principles, then the east can really only lose," he explained. Additionally, there are also external actors to consider. Russia has extended its positioning in the east while Turkey supports the government in the west. Alongside all of that is also the question of what the Libyan people want and what they expect from a united government. Bauer doubts elections alone can resolve Libya's problems. "The people have a particular interest in seeing the country's dysfunction end," he said. Libya is rich in raw materials and energy reserves, but also plagued by problems like power outages and inadequate public services. If the state was functioning properly, it would likely curtail the power of those currently benefiting most from the country's resources and, as Bauer argued, "why would they voluntarily give up these opportunities?" That will be the most difficult question for the next two years. The new agreement between Libya's political rivals must do more than simply establish a path toward elections. It must also create a framework in which those rivals accept the results of an election and in which public institutions function properly. This story was originally written in German.

item.title: Germany news: Police probe suspected power station attacks
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.50
What you need to know - Minor injuries reported after object explodes near Augsburg train station - Police are investigating 'criminal act' at power station near Cologne, North-Rhine Westphalia - Authorities also opened a terror probe over Tuesday's sabotage of a power station in Brandenburg - Germany is weighing further action against Russia after announcing it was behind the drone incident at Leipzig airport This blog is now closed. Read below for a roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Wednesday, September 2. Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. Thank you for reading Thank you for reading Wednesday's Germany news blog. We'll have more in a fresh blog on Thursday. Bis dann! Germany says EU countries handing out too many visas to Russians Berlin is pushing for other EU members to cut down on tourist visas to Russian citizens, essentially calling for stricter rules across the entire EU. More than 600,000 short-stay visas were issued by EU countries in Russia last year. Italy, France and Spain issued the most, while Germany approved a mere 20,000. Berlin says it wants to make sure that people who could pose a security risk are not allowed to enter the EU. The call comes as tensions between Germany and Russia peak over Berlin’s accusation that Moscow was the mastermind behind an attempted drone attack a German airport in August. Germany to spend €1 billion for drought-hit farmers This summer's massive heat waves and river droughts have faded from the headlines, but the record heat and drought are continuing to take a toll. It's harvest season, and farmers are struggling with lower yields and damaged crops. Berlin now wants to spend around €1 billion to support farmers in what Agriculture Minister Alois Rainer described as a crisis of national importance. The money won't be handed out directly but will come in the form of low-interest loans, tax relief, and subsidized fertilizer costs. The German Farmers' Association has already said the measures are not enough. The drought resulted in a more than 7% drop in the overall grain harvest, while rapeseed yields in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern fell by a staggering 25%. Farmers are also facing higher production costs due to rising fuel and fertilizer prices as a consequence of the Iran war. Political crisis deepens in eastern Germany Political tensions are deepening in the eastern German state of Thuringia after three lawmakers quit the populist BSW party. The three politicians say they are unhappy with pressure from the party’s national leadership in Berlin. They plan to form their own parliamentary group but continue supporting the state government. Founded by former left-wing politician Sara Wagenknecht, the BSW has left-wing economic policies, a conservative stance against immigration and criticizes military support for Ukraine. The split makes an already tricky political coalition even more tricky. Thuringia is currently being governed by an unusual coalition of the center-right CDU, center-left SPD and BSW. The coalition has no parliamentary majority and relies on the Left Party to pass legislation. The far-right AfD is the largest party in the state parliament, but other parties have formed the current coalition to kept it out of government. Ozempic pills enter German market As of this month, Ozempic — sold for weight management under the brand name Wegovy — is available in Germany as a pill. Until now, it had only been sold as an injection. The medication is not available over the counter and can only be obtained with a doctor’s prescription. However, it is generally not covered by statutory health insurance. The medicine is produced by Danish pharmaceutical giant Novo Nordisk and has been a major success for the company in recent years. The drug remains somewhat controversial, with reports of side effects alongside growing interest in other potential medical uses. WATCH: Sabotage fears hit Germany's power grid VW reportedly to close four Germany plants It's only media reports, but if they're to be trusted then Germany's car giant Volkswagen has made up its mind to shut down four of its German production sites. According to business magazine Wirtschaftswoche, a leaked paper from VW says that the Emden and Zwickau sites are to close in 2031, Hannover in 2032 and Neckarsulm in 2034. There's been no official VW comment on this but Germany's powerful IG Metall union has dismissed the reporting, saying that any such big decisions would need broad approval. But the report comes at a time where tension at VW are already at boiling point. The company faces — much like most of Germany's car industry — a deep structural crisis because of pressure from Chinese rivals, the transition to EVs, rising production costs and steep US tariffs. Ukraine says it's ready to ink drone deal with Germany Ukraine is close to finalizing a drone deal with Germany, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Wednesday after a call with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Zelenskyy also warned a surge in Ukrainian drones in Russia's skies meant Russian airspace would be "effectively" closed. Germany successfully tests Israeli ballistic missile A German frigate has tested the Israeli Lora missile system in the North Atlantic in an undisclosed operation, the country's navy said on Wednesday. Berlin is now considering buying the missiles which have a range of more than 500 kilometers (310 miles). Germany is in the process of modernizing and expanding its military in response to what it sees as a growing threat from Russia. The missile test came just hours after Germany said it held Russia responsible for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. "In terms of protecting Germany and our allies, this test marks a new chapter in deterrence and maritime defense readiness," navy chief Jan Christian Kaack said. The Lora missiles are designed for rapid deployment from ships at sea. Germany’s own Taurus missiles also have a range of more than 500 kilometres, but are launched from fighter jets. At the same time, Germany is working with its European allies to develop its own long-range weapons that would fly further than both the Lora or the Taurus missiles. Germany identifies suspects behind Leipzig drone attack German investigators have reportedly identified two suspects behind the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in August. According to reports on Wednesday from Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper, and public broadcasters NDR and WDR, one suspect is an ethnic Russian holding a Latvian passport. The second is a man from Belarus that holds a Russian passport. On Tuesday, Germany said it believed that Russia was behind the attempted drone attack targeting a Ukrainian transport aircraft at the airport in early August. Berlin said there would be strong consequences for the hybrid attack and has announced the closure of Russian consulate in Bonn and of the Russian House in Berlin, a cultural center that Germany believes to be inolved in in spying activity. Russia denies any involment in the Leipzig attack and on Wednesday summoned the German ambassador because of what it says are anti-Russian actions by Berlin. EU approves Germany's power capacity program The European Commission approved Germany's electricity supply support scheme. It is estimated to cost between €15.6 billion and €35.2 billion ($18.1 billion and $40.8 billion). Germany's plans to increase its electricity capacity by up to 11 gigawatts over five years required approval of the European Commission to ensure they do not distort competition within the bloc. The plan aims to ensure Germany has enough electricity capacity to meet rising demand. Contracts in the state aid plan can last up to 15 years and are open to existing and new providers with electricity delivery beginning in 2031. The energy companies receiving long-term contracts must be "hydrogen-ready" and must operate in a "climate-neutral" way by 2045. Germany set a goal of having at least 80% of its electricity come from renewable sources by 2030. Sabotage probe opened in second power station attack near Cologne North Rhine-Westphalia’s Interior Minister Herbert Reul on Wednesday said an incident at a power station in Bergheim near Cologne is preliminarily being investigated as an act of "anti-constitutional sabotage," using a German legal term applied for criminal acts aimed against the order of the state. On Tuesday night, police were called to the Amprion substation in Bergheim after bright flashes of light were reportedly visible. A short circuit affected several power lines, but officials said power supply to citizens was not affected. It was the second incident involving attempts at damaging electricity infrastructure in 24 hours. On Tuesday morning, power lines at a substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg hundreds of kilometers away were damaged by a projectile. Officials have yet to identify potential suspects involved in either incident. Based on the investigation so far, Reul said the investigation is looking at whether the sabotage attackoriginated from abroad or had a far-left extremist motive. Earlier this year, the far-left "Vulkangruppe" claimed responsibility for an attack on Berlin’s power infrastructure that left around 45,000 households without electricity for nearly a week during a cold winter spell. "Now we need to investigate," Reul said. "This was intentional; it was a crime," Ruel said. "More sabotage, more hybrid attacks ... interference like this is not happening far away, it's happening right on our doorstep," Reul told a press conference. "And anyone who acts this way is not just trying to hit cables; they're trying to hit our country," he added. Police open terrorism investigation after Brandenburg grid sabotage Police in the eastern German state of Brandenburg on Wednesday said they were investigating the possible formation of a terrorist organization in connection with an attack on a power plant and substation in the eastern state of Brandenburg. Officials said on Tuesday that a projectile managed to dislodge a high-voltage cable near the Jänschwalde coal-fired power plant and create a conductive connection to the ground, causing a brief outage. On Wednesday, Brandenburg's state Interior Minister Jan Redmann said "we were damn lucky" that only one of more than a dozen projectiles he said were "similar to fireworks" struck their target. He added the suspects had positioned the projectiles directly beneath the power lines near the Turnow-Preilack substation on the border with the state of Saxony. The search for suspects continues, and an investigation is looking into all possibilities. Brandenburg police said their investigation also includes disruption of public services, the causing of an explosion and the destruction of important equipment. "At this point, we must assume that the perpetrators had been on the scene for several days beforehand and had installed the necessary equipment," Redmann said. The construction and installation of the devices required a considerable amount of "technical expertise," he added. ICE train stops after door opened at 200 km/h A German high-speed Intercity Express (ICE) train was forced to stop near the entrance of a tunnel on Tuesday after a door mysteriously opened during the ride, police said Wednesday. The train had been moving at around 200 km/h (125 mph) and the conductor immediately applied the emergency brakes. There were 238 passengers on board the train, which was heading from Munich to Dortmund. No injuries were reported after police searched the tracks and ruled out the possibility someone could have fallen through the door. The passengers were able to get off the train in the town of Lohr am Main. Germany's Federal Police interviewed the passengers there and took down personal information. The officers also checked to see if any luggage had fallen off the train. The rail line was reopened around 2:30 a.m. According to a railway spokeswoman, there was no technical malfunction with the train. German rail operator Deutsche Bahn declined to comment on whether someone on board the train might have opened the door intentionally. "Doors on the ICE don't just open while the train is moving," according to a brief statement given to Germany's DPA news agency. "The specific cause is being investigated by the authorities," it added. Further details will not be available until the investigation is complete. IN DEPTH: Germany terminates lease for 'Russian House' in Berlin After Germany on Tuesday said Moscow was behind an attempted drone attack at an airport in Leipzig, Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said that the contract for the cultural center "Russian House" would be cancelled. The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations, it has long been the subject of fierce disagreements and a bone of contention in Berlin.

item.title: EU wants drones to spray pesticides, but it could backfire
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.43
In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed. The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package, which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030. Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light. Drone use doesn't automatically mean less pesticides "I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely. However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain." "At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection. Omnibus X aims to save administrative costs, cash Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved. When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism. Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it. To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment. The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release. Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years. Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans. But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence. The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important. Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said. Agriculture can work without pesticides Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved. But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012. Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author. Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically. The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security. What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: Germany's military wants to recruit tech-savvy gamers
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.28
Gamescom, which runs from August 26-30 in Cologne, is promoted as the world's largest video game trade show. Last year, two-thirds of its non-industry visitors were male, with over 40% of them between the ages of 16 and 25. Those are precisely the young people the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, is trying to reach as it urgently seeks to expand its ranks. Germany's military aims to have 260,000 active-duty soldiers by 2035. The German government has supplied hundreds of billions of euros to modernize the country's armed forces. Defense has become a priority for Germany in the face of the current global security situation. Career advice in camouflage The Bundeswehr set up shop at Gamescom for the first time in 2016. It's been back every year since. A brand-new, olive-green Caracal off-road vehicle is one of the main attractions. Alongside it are laptops belonging to the Bundeswehr's Center for Cyber Operations — tasked with cyber defense, among other responsibilities. Under a watchful eye, visitors can try their hand at hacking. At another station, visitors can put on VR headsets to get a glimpse into the working life of a soldier aboard a naval vessel. Pilots, aircraft mechanics and air traffic controllers present their professions in a 3D experience. Elsewhere, several fit mountain infantry soldiers stand beside a pull-up bar, where visitors are invited to test their strength. New this year is a career lounge where interested visitors can have what the Bundeswehr is calling "career counseling sessions." The atmosphere is positive, with soldiers promoting their jobs without being pushy, taking time to answer questions from visitors — who have primarily come to Gamescom to have fun, meet friends and play the latest games. Do gamers make good soldiers? A representative study by Germany's Bitkom digital association found that one in five people believed video and computer games teach skills that could be useful in wartime — training reaction speed and problem-solving, for instance. However, being a good gamer doesn't necessarily make for a good soldier. "We need people who are comfortable with technology," Lt. Gen. Robert Sieger, president of the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Personnel Management, told DW. "What we don't want are people who think we're playing an ego shooter or some kind of shooting game. That doesn't do justice to the seriousness of the situation at all. War isn't a game. As a soldier and a general, it is important to me that people understand the seriousness of what we do." For Sieger, educating people about the Bundeswehr and the range of careers it offers is a central reason for having a booth at Gamescom. "We're an integral part of our country's safety net. We have to simply be here and show what it means to stand up for the freedom of our country, be that as a soldier or a civilian." Criticism of Bundeswehr presence The Bundeswehr is represented alongside many other employers in the gaming trade show's Job Area, including Germany's federal police, retailer Edeka and software company DATEV. Gamescom is, however, still a video game trade show — and not everyone is comfortable with the Bundeswehr getting close to the gaming world. The German Peace Society — United War Resisters has criticized the Bundeswehr presence at Gamescom, along with booths operated by Germany's foreign intelligence service and defense companies such as Airbus and Rheinmetall. Peace campaigner Marius Pletsch said the Bundeswehr uses inappropriate slogans, designed to appeal specifically to gamers, and distorts the image of military service. "We think it's wrong to lure young people to the booth by appealing to their sense of adventure. We don't think the Bundeswehr should be represented at a trade show that is primarily about video games and leisure to boost its personnel numbers," he told DW. The peace organization will have a booth outside the trade show exhibition halls for two days, providing information about conscientious objection to military service. Bundeswehr: Not just any job "Being a soldier isn't a normal job," the peace initiative said in a statement. Lt. Gen. Sieger uses similar terms, but puts it somewhat differently: "Being a soldier isn't a job like any other. We put our lives on the line for the security of our people." Sieger reaches a different conclusion than the peace advocates, though. "It would be downright negligent for an organization responsible for our country's security not to be an inherent part of society," he said. "As an inherent part of society and a modern employer, of course we have our rightful spot here in the Job Area, just as we have over recent years." What did young Gamescom visitors make of the Bundeswehr's presence? "Morally questionable, but a good employer," said Dennis, a 22-year-old computer science student, although he said the Bundeswehr wasn't for him. Dominik, 26, said he was pleased that the German military was represented at Gamescom. "You can actually have a pretty good conversation with them. They're all very nice," he said. He said he may even consider working for the Bundeswehr's cyber defense division. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: EU summons Russian envoy over failed Leipzig drone attack
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.78
The European Unions's foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on Wednesday that she summoned Russia's envoy in Brussels over the alleged attempted hybrid attack involving an explosives-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month. Germany's foreign and interior ministers said in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the government in Berlin had concluded that Russia was responsible for the failed attack, reinforcing suspicions that arose as soon as the news broke in August. Kallas says incident has 'all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism' "We are discussing the Leipzig attacks, and also it is clear that it has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism," Kallas said ahead of an informal gathering of EU foreign ministers in Ireland. "The question is, what do we do about this? We have already summoned the Russian ambassador," she said. The former Estonian prime minister also said that the EU was continuing its work on its next package of some 1,600 sanctions listings related to Russia's war in Ukraine and said "maybe there is more to be added." France takes similar step, summoning charge d'affaires French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot also told reporters in Dublin that Paris was summoning a Russian ambassador in response. "I have summoned the Russian charge d'affaires in Paris to protest," Barrot said, adding that sanctions should be taken at a European level, notably against Russia's so-called shadow fleet of ships. Non-EU foreign ministers from Ukraine, the UK, Canada, Norway, Iceland and Switzerland also traveled to Ireland to attend Wednesday's informal talks. Germany's Wadephul says 'pressure on Russia is being stepped up' German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul told reporters that the EU would continue to work on additional sanctions "in the coming weeks." "Pressure on Russia is being stepped up and support for Ukraine also remains at a high level. That is the unity we are demonstrating at this time," he said. The Christian Democrat politician said that Russia had chosen to escalate, and "must now live with these consequences." He also defended Tuesday's announcement in Berlin, calling the government's response a "necessary and proportionate" one based on a "well-founded opinion and verdict." What did Germany say about its investigations? Wadephul and Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt announced in a joint press conference on Tuesday that the federal government in Berlin held Russia responsible for the failed attack. "Taken together, police investigations, patterns of the crime and intelligence findings substantiate Russian responsibility for the attempted attack at Leipzig Airport," Dobrindt said on Tuesday, without going into specifics. Wadephul said that the "means used — drone configuration, components, explosives and detonation systems — are known to us from other hybrid operations by Russia and its war against Ukraine." Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, have rejected the allegations and accused Germany of fabricating its version of events. Leipzig/Halle Airport is a key freight hub. Ukrainian airline and aircraft manufacturer Antonov uses the airport as a base of operations, frequently transiting material to Ukraine via the the eastern German city. Edited by: Zac Crellin If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Germany news: Summer was 2nd hottest of the century — DWD
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.59
What you need to know - Average summer temperature of 19.6 Celsius is second only to 2003 figures, Germany's DWD weather service says - Cologne police investigate early-morning shooting of empty cafe in south of city center - Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Tunisia and Algeria - Hamburg's new, larger Sternbrücke rail bridge opens for business, replacing a predecessor from 1926 - Chancellor Merz warns an AfD government would damage Saxony-Anhalt, with vote on Sunday This blog is now closed. Welcome to our roundup of news and analysis from and concerning Germany on Monday, August 31. Tired of missing our real time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google. Thank you for reading Thank you for reading. We'll be back with more German updates on Tuesday. Tschüss! G20: German finance minister 'irritated' by Russian invitation German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said on Monday that he was "irritated" by the decision by the United States to invite his Russian counterpart Anton Siluanov to this week's G20 meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. Klingbeil, who as leader of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) is also Germany's vice-chancellor, said he would have preferred the Americans "not to have welcomed [Siluanov] like a normal guest" given Russia's ongoing "brutal war" against Ukraine. "There is no normal situation with Russia at the moment," he said, adding that he told Siluanov "directly to his face that the Russian government must end this war" and that Germany would continue to support Ukraine. "Receiving the Russian finance minister here sends a signal I find troubling." Ahead of the meeting, Klingbeil said he made it clear to other European colleagues that he would not pose for a group photograph with the Russian minister and that he was "grateful" that they agreed. At recent G20 meetings, which bring together 20 leading and developing industrial nations, the Russian finance minister has been represented by under-secretaries. But this time, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sat down with Siluanov for bilateral talks during which Bessent advocated for President Donald Trump's peace plan for Ukraine, according to a US official. Asked about Siluanov's attendance, a White House spokesman told the AFP news agency that the Trump administration has been working with Moscow to push for a deal that "would stop the endless bloodshed that the president has really condemned." "The president and the administration will never shy away from talking with the folks we need to talk to, to further that," he continued. "That's what we're working on here at the G20." Klingbeil said he saw "no normalization or relaxation of the situation." He said Russia alone carries responsibility for ending the war, "not Russia and Ukraine." FDP leader: AfD in Saxony-Anhalt would not be 'collapse of democracy' The leader of Germany's Free Democrats (FDP), the business-focused party which formed part of the previous federal government before falling short of the minimum 5% hurdle at the last federal election, has said he does not think an Alternative for Germany (AfD) state government in Saxony-Anhalt would be a threat to democracy. "It would be bad but not a collapse of democracy were the AfD to govern in Saxony-Anhalt," Wolfgang Kubicki told broadcaster ntv on Monday, insisting that even an AfD government would have to adhere to federal laws. If necessary, he said, the federal government in Berlin could enforce this via "Bundeszwang" — or "federal obligation" — as stipulated by article 37 of the German constitution, or Basic Law. Kubicki said this could be the case for certain aspects of the far-right AfD's election program, such as a promise to remove foreign doctors. "It's not as straightforward under the rule of law as the AfD thinks," he said. "Every court would block them immediately. Nothing to worry about." Kubicki's FDP is currently the junior partner in the state government in Saxony-Anhalt, along with the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the Social Democrats (SPD), having won 6.4% of the votes at the last state election in 2021. Ahead of Sunday's vote, however, the FDP is polling consistently below the minimum 5% hurdle and, as it stands, is unlikely to even make it into the state parliament (Landtag). Merz warns against anger experiments in Saxony-Anhalt German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned of the consequences of a far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) state government in Saxony-Anhalt, saying the eastern state "must not become an experiment for enraged citizens." Merz was speaking in the town of Quedlinburg alongside current Saxony-Anhalt state premier Sven Schulze ahead of key state elections on Sunday. Schulze is also a member of Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) but has tried to distance himself from the unpopular chancellor during the election campaign. "Should a far-right populist party have an overall majority by Monday morning, international investors will think twice about investing in Saxony-Anhalt," Merz warned, repeating comments made in an interview on Sunday. "A lot rests on this election." According to current polls, the AfD (40-42%) has a significant lead over the CDU in Saxony-Anhalt (22-23%), but Merz insisted that his conservative party would perform better than the surveys suggest. "I am absolutely convinced that we will see a different result on Sunday than what we currently have in the polls," he said. "I want to win these voters for us. And if we've lost them, I want to win them back." 'Resign!': Chancellor Merz booed on northeastern campaign trail German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was greeted with boos, insults and calls to resign while campaigning in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (MV) on Monday. While speaking at a Christian Democratic Union (CDU) campaign stand on the seafront at the coastal town of Kühlungsborn near the city of Rostock, Merz was labeled a "warmonger" and "Pinocchio" by passers-by, some of whom called for him to "resign!" Other members of the public who were listening to him speak called on the critics to remain civil. Earlier, Merz had eaten a Fischbrötchen (a fish roll, a classic coastal snack in northern Germany) at a local restaurant. The owner's son, himself a fisherman, had complained about the problems faced by the fishing industry, including restrictions and seals eating his catch. He said they were on the way to "abolishing coastal fishing in MV." Merz responded that it was important to understand the roots of the problems and also to protect fish levels. Although the afternoon had begun in sunshine, it ended under dark clouds and the sound of thunder and lightning. Later on Monday, Merz was expected in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt ahead of key regional elections on September 6. Elections back in MV will follow three weeks later. German government plays down calls for increased use of coal-fired power plants The German government has rejected calls to ramp up the use of coal-fired power stations to curb rising electricity prices. "This is not entirely straightforward for technical and economic reasons, as well as for reasons relating to European law," an Economy Ministry spokesman said on Monday. On Friday, a leading member of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU) had suggested making more extensive use of coal-fired plants. Sepp Müller, deputy leader of the CDU's parliamentary group, said the environmentally unfriendly facilities should remain in operation until gas-fired power stations with a comparable capacity have been built, which is expected to be in 2030 or 2031. "[We're talking about] the coal-fired plants which are currently in reserve for times when wind or solar power isn't available," he told the economics magazine Wirtschaftswoche. "These plans should operate permanently." However, the Economy Ministry spokesman questioned the effectiveness of such a measure, describing the reserve power stations as old and inefficient. "That means we would have to assess whether they could actually have a positive impact on electricity prices," he said. Federal government spokesman Stefan Kornelius put a lid on the debate, saying: "This is not a question at the moment." Trains between Essen, Bochum disrupted by cable theft Railway traffic between Essen and Bochum in the industrial Ruhr region of western Germany has been disrupted after unknown perpetrators stole several copper cables. It's the latest of several sabotage incidents to impact the country's rail network this summer. A spokesman for Deutsche Bahn said that both regional and long-distance services had faced disruptions for several hours. He said the route from Essen to Bochum was closed for security reasons as staff rushed to repair the damage. He said the damaged cables and wires needed to be repaired and reconnected by hand in several places. A spokesman for Germany's federal police, which is responsible for transport network security, said officers were investigating a "particularly severe case" of theft involving some 15 meters of copper cables. He said that for now there were no leads on potential perpetrators. Arson attacks and other acts of sabotage have disrupted the rail network over the summer, most recently when unknown perpetrators cut through several cables on a Stuttgart railway line last week. In July, trains in northern Germany were brought to a halt by a suspected arson attack, just days after a similar incident in the west of the country. Women's Bundesliga: Leverkusen's Carlotta Wamser signs for Manchester City Manchester City have signed German international defender Carlotta Wamser on a four-year contract. The English Women's Super League champions on Monday confirmed the signing. Wamser, 22, joins from Bayer Leverkusen for a reported fee of €650,000 (roughly $750,000), which would be a Bundesliga record. "The English league is the best league in the world and Manchester City are one of the best clubs in the world," Wamser said in a statement on City's website. "I feel like I need the next step for my career and I feel that I can develop as a player here very well. And I like the challenge as well, so I think it's the perfect step for me right now," she added. Wamser, who plays at right back and grew up in the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, has 14 Germany caps and made her debut in the women's Bundesliga in 2020, before even turning 17. She was a regular fixture in Germany's youth teams before graduating to the seniors last year. City's director of football, Therese Sjögran, said that Wamser "is a player we've admired for some time and [we] know she will bring energy, passion and a willingness to learn to the team." Two German teammates await her in Manchester, Rebecca Knaak and Sydney Lohmann. Wamser was not in Leverkusen's squad for Sunday's Bundesliga match against Wolfsburg, which had already prompted speculation that a transfer announcement was likely imminent. August inflation rate climbs to 2.9%, driven by 10.5% energy bump linked to Iran war Germany's inflation rate rose slightly in August, reaching 2.9% year-on-year, versus 2.8% in July. That's above the national and eurozone target of 2%, if not by a particularly large margin. The increases were driven almost entirely by rising energy prices, which were 10.5% more expensive on average in August than in the same month last year. That's also a fairly sharp rise compared to July, when the energy inflation rate stood at 8.3%. Inflation for food and drink sank once again, to 0.1% year-on-year. Inflation in the services sector was close to the national average, at 2.8%. At present, the energy inflation stems in very large part from rising prices for oil and and gasoline — up by much more than the 10.5% average for the entire energy sector — amid the delivery problems in the Strait of Hormuz, not for gas and electricity. However, as the Iran war drags on and countries use up their gas reserves, this could be liable to change. Further inflationary pressure is likely in Germany in the coming months as a result of the drought and the hot summer and its impact on transportation, food production and industrial output. PROFILE — Sven Schulze, the politician leading the fight against the far-right in Saxony-Anhalt All political eyes in Germany, and indeed beyond, are turning to the small eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt this week, ahead of Sunday's state election in which the Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to perform strongly. But who's currently leading the coalition government in Saxony-Anhalt, Christian Democrat Sven Schulze? And what's his message on polling week, as he tries to stay in his job while facing not just the prospect of losing to radicals on the right of politics, but of perhaps needing support from those he might deem radicals on the left to avoid such a defeat? Woman confesses to pretending son had cancer to raise money A German woman on trial in Giessen, north of Frankfurt in Hesse, has confessed to pretending her young son had cancer to raise money online. Her lawyer said in court that she accepted and admitted to the allegations "without any reservation" and regretted what had happened. She's accused of obtaining a total of €358,000 (roughly $415,000 at current exchange rates) in donations between September 2021 and October 2024. The boy was aged 5 to 8 during this time period. The woman is alleged to have come up with the idea after a dermatological examination revealed an issue that turned out to be benign and require no further treatment. She then allegedly claimed that her son was suffering from malignant melanoma and urgently required expensive specialist treatment in the US, claims she also made to the media and online. Prosecutor Kai Karges said that hundreds of individuals and charities responded to the calls, and said that the child also believed he had cancer. The fraud was uncovered when the boy's pediatrician saw the calls for donations on social media and alerted child protection services. He has since been taken into care. Update: Cologne police issue details on suspect in cafe shooting, nobody hurt Just a quick follow-up on our top headline from the early morning today. Cologne police are still seeking a man believed to have fired shots at a Turkish cafe in the south of the city center. They confirmed that nobody was injured in the shooting. Police described the man as "baldheaded, roughly 1 meter 80 (5 foot 11 inches) tall," wearing "sports shoes, black trousers and a gray hooded jacket" at the time of the shooting. Investigators said residents saw the man fire the shots and flee on foot at around 7:40 a.m. that morning. "Based on preliminary investigations, four projectiles penetrated the cafe's front windows," police said, adding that Cologne's criminal investigation department or Kriminalpolizei had taken over the case. UK fuels 50% year-on-year growth in 2025 German foreign direct investment According to a report from the German Economic Institute (IW) think tank, foreign direct investment (FDI) into Germany rose markedly in 2025, reaching just over €86 billion (just under $100 billion at today's exchange rate). Investments from the UK were the largest driver of growth by far. IW put the level of FDI from the UK at more than €26.3 billion, saying it was a year-on-year increase of 284%.
