The drops acquired a tiny electrical charge between 0.2 and 2 nanocoulombs. After 3,000 drops, the equivalent of a single rainy day, the Teflon coating broke down, leading to the corrosion of the metal underneath. When the experiment was conducted with drops that had no electrical charge, neither the copper nor its Teflon coating suffered any damage. Take cover The findings revealed that even small amounts of charge can break through tough, heat-resistant, and water-resistant coatings. This suggests that water’s electrical state, and not just its acidity or chemical composition, can cause corrosion. The results of the study could help inform the design of protective coatings that are more resistant to electrically charged water drops. The data suggests that a thicker protective layer could do the trick, although more research is needed on designing a coating specifically geared toward protecting metal against tiny sparks.

item.title: Satellites Watched a Himalayan Glacier Speed Up for Weeks Before It Unleashed a Flash Flood That Killed Over 1,000 People
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.72
Relief workers and volunteers are still scrambling to save lives one week after a huge, glacier-coated chunk of mountain near Langtang Lirung peak collapsed catastrophically, raining rock, ice, and a debris-filled slurry of flood waters down into the Nepal-China border below. The current death toll has climbed to 1,114 people, according to the Nepalese government, with nearly 4,000 more still reported missing. The tragedy has pushed geologists, climate scientists, and geoscientists within the specialized discipline of glaciology to revisit what data they had on hand that might have helped sound the alarm before Nepal’s avalanche flooded rivers and washed away villages downstream. The warning signs were there, according to Virginia Tech geophysicist Manoochehr Shirzaei, who told the journal Nature that subtle but accelerating movement was visible in the mass of glacial ice and supporting rock beneath it for weeks before the disaster. Shirzaei and his colleagues analyzed data from the European Space Agency’s Sentinel-1 satellites, an “all weather” constellation that uses C-band synthetic aperture radar to peer through any degree of cloud cover to image the Earth below. They acquired Sentinel-1 data covering Langtang Lirung peak from January 8 to August 18, 2026—just a week before the avalanche cascaded down 3,900 feet (1,200 meters) into the Lhende Khola river below. “We detected evidence that the glacier–rock system was slowly moving downhill near the apparent collapse area, with velocities reaching roughly 10 millimetres [0.39 inches] per month,” Shirzaei told Nature. While that speed was not particularly alarming—glaciers can typically move at speeds around 10–200 meters [33–656 feet] per year—the pace at which that speed was ramping up was truly a worrying indicator. “The acceleration is more important than the velocity, because it suggests that the rate of slope deformation was changing in the days leading up to the disaster,” Shirzaei explained. “[Our] analysis also indicates acceleration of rock and ice near the potential failure zone.” Speed traps Shirzaei emphasized that monitoring for apparent acceleration along critical glaciers would only be one facet of a modernized early warning system for avalanches. Synthetic aperture radar systems like Sentinel-1 could only be a powerful pre-screening tool—best automated, Shirzaei believes, via algorithm. “Once a slope begins behaving anomalously, monitoring could become much more intensive,” he explained. “High-resolution commercial radar and optical satellites could be used, and where practical, ground instruments such as cameras and seismic sensors could be deployed.” But, Shirzaei noted, identifying a glacier at risk of collapse is only half the battle. Governments would have to highly tailor their responses and analyses, pairing advanced warnings with deep geophysical and hydrological research modeling local terrain, the conditions and risks posed to nearby rivers and lakes, and other specific information. Local conditions would be the only way to distinguish a more-or-less harmless glacial movement from one poised to incite the next major disaster. Future HiRISK situations Satellite imagery proved to be critical to another post-mortem conducted by experts with the Asian Mountain Academic Alliance, the Stimson Center, and China’s Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment. Like Shirzaei’s analysis, this coalition’s HiRISK report found that signs of a serious avalanche were present in the data days in advance. The report’s satellite observations, which included imagery from NASA’s Landsat 9 collaboration with the U.S. Geological Survey, documented evidence that water flow inside the glacier had also sped up before the collapse. Satellite imagery from August 24 appeared to depict meltwater that was visibly brown—a sign that the rocky ridges beneath the glacier were giving way. Geologist Jakob Steiner at the University of Graz in Austria, a co-author of the HiRISK report, echoed Shirzaei’s view that some form of AI-assisted monitoring would be a critical first step toward predicting future disasters like Nepal’s August 26 avalanche. “This is where I think we need to invest more,” Steiner told Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC). “There are thousands and thousands of glaciers in High Mountain Asia, so we have to find scalable solutions.”

item.title: Huawei’s Watch D3 Doubles as an Inflatable Blood Pressure Cuff
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.13
Huawei’s latest wearable goes a bit further than accelerometers or heart rate sensors to measure a wearer’s blood pressure. The new Huawei Watch D3 includes a watch band with an inflatable diaphragm that can act as a miniaturized blood pressure cuff. Plenty of other smartwatches now include some way of detecting signs of high blood pressure, but Huawei’s watch makes both on-demand and continuous readings throughout the day possible, offering a more detailed picture of your heart health over time. The Huawei Watch D3 is technically the company’s third iteration on this idea but arguably the first that looks like a normal smartwatch. The new watch includes a 1.92-inch AMOLED screen that reaches 3,000 nits of peak brightness, while the watch itself is 0.44 inches (11.3mm) thick and weighs 1.41 ounces (40 grams). A major part of Huawei’s improvements here are focused on the watchband, which the company says features a narrower airbag that’s both more comfortable to wear and more stylish in the Mocha Gold, Gold, and Black color options Huawei sells. Using the inflatable band, the Huawei Watch D3 can take blood pressure measurements in a similar fashion to the blood pressure cuff you might have used at a doctor’s office or have at home. The smartwatch also supports Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM), which means it’s able to measure your blood pressure at set intervals across a 24-hour period and pair it with other metrics the watch tracks, like your pulse. The Huawei Watch D3 can also remind you to take readings before and after workouts or when things that could affect your blood pressure, like elevation or temperature, change. Combined with features like workout and sleep tracking, it covers the smartwatch basics, too. The watch approaches blood pressure in a way that’s radically different than most smartwatch companies. Apple and Google offer what amounts to tracking blood pressure trends on their watches to avoid the regulatory scrutiny that comes from trying to determine systolic and diastolic blood pressure. Recent competitor Vital Signals is using similar sensors to the Oura Ring 5 but believes its unique algorithms could allow it to offer more detailed readings without the need to calibrate with a blood pressure cuff. No one approach is necessarily right or wrong, but Huawei is getting the closest to recreating the experience you’d get with professional equipment. The Huawei Watch D3 will be available for £400 or around $540, though due to the company’s products being banned in the U.S., it’s unfortunately not something we’ll be able to try over here anytime soon.

item.title: This New Dreame Robomower’s Side Piece Seems Great at Edging
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.60
I liked Dreame’s A3 AWD Pro robot mower when I reviewed it last month, and now, during IFA 2026, the company has announced a follow-up called the A4 AWD Pro that brings with it several key improvements. Among them is a robotic arm that the company says (based on its own lab testing, of course) can achieve “0 cm edge cutting.” The A4 AWD Pro is guided by LiDAR, like its predecessor, but also uses satellite navigation for “centimeter-level positioning.” It can also “see” obstacles defined by trained AI algorithms, and avoid them, and also features side-oriented time-of-flight sensors for keeping it from rolling over drop-offs, and infrared sensors to identify people and animals at boundary edges. These edge sensors also guide that robotic trimming arm, according to the company’s press materials. Dreame isn’t alone in its, uh, dream of a robotic side arm for trimming. I wouldn’t be surprised to hear other automowers that have little mechanical arms, the same way you see extending side brushes on so many robot vacuums. At the moment, the best that other robot mowers have been able to do is slide their mowing decks sideways to get closer to the side of your house or edge of a sidewalk. But it’s never close enough that you don’t have to go back and clean up afterwards with an old-timey handheld weed whacker. That robotic arm and new sensors and navigation aren’t all that’s new with the A4. In fact, Dreame seems to have rethought its approach entirely. The robot no longer has omnidirectional wheels in front, but instead uses swiveling, servo-driven caster wheels. The company says that it gives the robot “tight turns, smoother cornering, and flexible obstacle navigation from multiple angles with minimal turf wear.” That last bit is notable, since the A3 AWD Pro had a bad habit of tearing up bits of my lawn, leaving bald patches in the grass behind. The A4 AWD Pro has no official release date for the U.S. The culprit, of course, is the foreign robotics ban that requires manufacturers to prove that at least 65% of the parts making up their robot vacuums are made in the U.S.

item.title: iRobot’s New Roombas Can Clean Carpets 3x Deeper Than Older Models
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.58
Hot on the heels of its July release of five robot vacuums, Roomba is back with another two dirt-sucking discs, the $1,200 Roomba Max 875 and the $900 Roomba Plus 678. Announced at IFA 2026, both feature high suction—35,000Pa and 30,000Pa, respectively—and a new “SealForce Vacuuming Technology” that the company says makes for three times deeper carpet cleaning than non-SealForce robovacs. Now owned by Chinese robotics company Picea, iRobot’s latest Roombas sound a lot like all of the other robovacs from China. The Max 875 cleans and empties itself at its large dock, which washes its mop with 176-degree Fahrenheit water and automatically refills the robot with fresh mop water mixed with a cleaning solution before every clean. The Max 875 also has a mop roller that slides in and out of the chassis to get close to edges, and that automatically lifts and covers itself before driving over carpet—both features seen on devices like the Dreame Aqua10 Ultra Roller. As it cleans, the Max 875 sprays a continuous heated mist from its undercarriage, which iRobot says can help it clean crusty messes on hard flooring. It also has a hair-cutting main brush that keeps it from developing tangles. That’s somewhat unique compared to, say, the Ecovacs Deebot X12 OmniCyclone, which has front-mounted spray nozzles for wetting messes—whether it works any better, well, we’ll have to test that. I will say that roller-mopping robots tend to be superior to those with spinning mop pads for dealing with actual messes. The Max 875 navigates with LiDAR and avoids obstacles using front cameras. It stands just under four inches high, which is svelte but still taller than something like the 3.12-inch-tall Dreame X60 Max Ultra Complete. As for the Roomba Plus 678, it’s very similar to the Max 875 in a few ways, differing only in height (it’s 0.03cm shorter) and in its use of a high-pressure spray rather than the heated mist of the Max 875. It also lacks the self-sealing mop roller, although its mop does also reach for edges like that of the Max 875. Both of the new robot vacuums are priced lower than any of the costly options I’ve mentioned in this story, but they’re still expensive. My experience with robot vacuums packed with similar features to these new Roombas has taught me to be wary of them, and until we get to try one of this year’s iRobot crop (I’ll be testing the Roomba Max 775 this month), it’s a good idea to hold off on buying one until you’ve read some reviews and heard from other owners. If you can’t wait, though, both of the new Roombas are available now at the iRobot website.

item.title: Live Updates From IFA 2026 in Berlin 🔴
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.39
Before “techtember” and “techtober” hit, we have one big tech show to get through: IFA 2026. Gizmodo’s Kyle Barr and Wes Davis are returning to Berlin to check out the “Innovation For All” consumer tech show and live blogging the biggest announcements. You can think of IFA like a smaller version of CES 2026, with more of an emphasis on the smart home, lifestyle tech, and home entertainment. There are also usually a few interesting laptops, phones, and PCs worth seeing with our own eyes. This year, expect to see AI in everything, even devices that have no need for it. And just like last year, we’ll be handing out “Best of IFA” awards to the most innovative products. The rest of the Gizmodo Consumer Tech team will be supporting those two remotely here in this live blog. IFA 2026’s official dates are Sept. 4 through Sept. 8, but as always, companies will be announcing products early to get ahead of the noise. Stay up to date on everything IFA 2026-related by bookmarking this page! It’s the first official day of IFA for the public, but my first stop is a closed door RTX Spark showcase with Nvidia. But first, just look at this view of the wider Berlin skyline. — Kyle Barr Lenovo is leaning hard into its IdeaPad Vibe laptops and IdeaCentre all-in-one PCs’ vibrant palette. Beyond specs, I thought I’d give you a taste of the rainbow with every single colorway available right now. The desktops come with color-matched keyboards and mice. However, the coolest part of the new ecosystem is that the IdeaPad Vibe includes removable and swappable keycaps. These keycap packs are sold separately, and they come with a specialized key removal tool. You can either color match your laptop or add contrasting colors for your own preferred unique look. I only wish I could order a special kit for myself detailing which color keys I want across the entire typeface. The IdeaCentre AIO PCs are running on an Intel Core Series 3, aka Wildcat Lake, chip, while both 14- and 15-inch IdeaPad Vibe models are starting with either Qualcomm Snapdragon X chips or AMD Ryzen AI 400 series processors, with no Intel version in sight. Lenovo told me there may be more Vibes that come later with Intel Inside (TM). So go ahead, pick your favorite. —Kyle Barr Back in July, I started writing about the changes happening to OLED screen manufacturing, starting with TCL CSOT which developed a so-called “InkJet printing” method for creating OLED displays. Well, the good news is, it’s not just some vague notion. Lenovo is getting ready to sell its first monitor created using InkJet printing, the ThinkVision P27UL-40 monitor made for business folks who also enjoy pretty visuals. The screen is as nice to look at as most organic light-emitting diode displays, but both Lenovo and TCL have promised the screen type is more efficient and lasts longer than older-style OLEDs. —Kyle Barr DJI’s Osmo 360 II is the kind of sequel that only really means to fix a few of the first iteration’s issues. Case in point, the new swappable lenses in case one of them breaks. The camera is still using the same size 1/1.1-inch sensors, but now it promises better low-light shooting plus better contrast in video with more dynamic range. It may not be enough to truly compete with the leading Insta360 X6 360 camera, but DJI has one thing the competition doesn’t have: 60 fps shooting at 8K resolution. —Kyle Barr But instead, it’s the PrimeBot. Or, rather, these are PrimeBots. And believe it or not, it’s actually two models of them. According to the PrimeBot representative that was on hand tonight, the always-upright, humanoid Q1 will have a customizable 3D-printed outer shell that customers will be able to design by vibe coding it when they order. It probably won’t go on sale in the U.S. anytime soon, but hey, that’s life in the states these days. You know, maybe it’s fine, though. Because the T1, which transforms from a humanoid into a dog-style bot by BENDING ITS LEGS BACKWARDS AND FLOPPING DOWN ONTO ITS FRONT ARM TIPS LIKE SOME SORT OF DEMON OH GOD WON’T SOMEONE STOP IT, is a little spooky. Amusingly, though, its guts fell out after it performed its transformation, and a tech at the booth had to stuff them back in. Every time I pick up my gaming headset to game with friends, I ask myself why somebody couldn’t make something small and light enough I could wear it around as a regular pair of headphones. Beyerdynamics took the opposite tack, making a pair of headphones called Aventho Y that can work as a gaming headset in a pinch. I’m not complaining, since the Aventho Y includes a 2.4GHz dongle inside a slot found underneath the right-hand earcup, meaning it’s that much harder to lose among the detritus on your desk. There’s a slot for an attachable boom mic as well. Beyerdynamic promises the headphones should get 60 hours of battery life with ANC (active noise cancellation) on and about 90 hours without. The version I used includes the faux leather earcups, but there are more plush versions you can buy separately. The headset should cost $150. Also, just look how nice that peach color is on my very peachy head. —Kyle Barr …I am a Gym Monster 3/3S. Wait, no, that’s what this thing is. Made by a company called Speediance, it’s got some real as-seen-on-TV vibes. Except, as a person who has been trying to get back into a state of general physical fitness, it actually interests me. It has adjustable pulleys that you can swap between the bottom (for things like bicep curls) and vertical racks for things like chest presses and rows. The Gym Monster 3’s display shows you stats like those you see on screen here—how long you’ve been working out, your average power output, estimated calories burned, and so on—and it’ll even tell you if your range of motion is out of balance. (It told me my left side had a lower range, which is true—it’s been messed up recently due to… I don’t know, age and sedentary living?) According to the Speediance site, it can produce up to 260lbs of resistance (if you buy the higher-end 3S model), which is probably plenty for most home gym users. The kicker? You know it’s the price. It starts at $4,100. —Wes Davis I was ready to be disappointed by Tecno’s so-called “bezelless” phone. I watched Marques Brownlee’s video about the device and thought that it was just another pointless idea meant to pretend it’s the future of smartphones. After holding it, I now think that it’s only half of a gimmick. Tecno’s phone concept uses a unique screen-stacking technique to push the screen size practically to the edge of the device. There’s still the tiniest, almost imperceptible gap between the actual screen and the phone’s sides, but it is still striking to see practically no black bars surrounding the screen. Tecno’s concept device is also surprisingly light and comfortable to hold. Tecno told me this is actually a more recent iteration of their phone concept, where the screen no longer sits flush with the screen sides. There’s no more risk of accidentally tapping the sides of the screen above the phone’s edge. The China-based company wouldn’t tell me what’s running inside, but I can imagine future phones will use this feature as a major selling point. —Kyle Barr This may look like Oscar the Grouch on some sort of new mobility tech for people who can walk but would rather not, but it’s actually Ollobot, a tablet-faced “family” robot that can do things like emote, help kids learn another language, and do video calling. At least, that’s according to the Ollobot reps who were standing nearby. They also assured me that this robot won’t become totally useless without a subscription or internet connection, which it requires for full functionality. It just gets a little dumber, is all. —Wes Davis The original Aurzen Zip miniscule foldable projector disappointed us when we first got our hands on it in 2024. Now, Aurzen is back with a “Pro” version, and it may be the kind of projector you actually want. It’s now running at 200 ISO lumens, twice the brightness of its forebear. It’s also now capable of outputting at 1080p, rather than the original projector’s 720p. However, my favorite enhancement may be the inclusion of a small touchscreen on top. Now you can work with some of the devices’ actual controls without having to rely on the app all the time. It’s a larger, thicker, and slightly heavier device, but that doesn’t actually make it much less portable. It still folds up from its “Z”-shape to the size of a little bigger than a wallet, enough that it can fit into any travel bag where you may want to project your laptop or perhaps your Switch 2 handheld. There are two versions of the Zip Pro, a “Cyber Edition” with its cool transparent plastic cover and a regular opaque version. —Kyle Barr Oukitel isn’t a brand you’d know of unless you’re really into rugged devices made to take a blow from a sledgehammer on a work site. However, the Oukitel RG14-P is something worth knowing, since it can actually be powered—in part—by sunlight. There’s a large solar panel on the laptop lid that can power at 10W, which means that it may get you to a full 50% in six hours. In reality, the solar cells can help the laptop maintain a better battery life for longer when it’s under direct sunlight. Lenovo actually showed off a very similar Yoga PC concept last year, and I can imagine we may see more laptops that enjoy a ray of sunshine almost as much as we do. —Kyle Barr The Soundcore Sleep A30 have long been my favorite pair of sleep earbuds, and Anker is bringing a new twist to its offerings in the space. The Sleep Earbuds Pro 4 add a few things to the equation, including real-time tracking that can adjust sleep sounds on the fly and hopefully coax you into a deeper sleep if needed. There’s also a charging case with a touchscreen so you can control sleep sounds, alarms, and other stuff without pulling out your phone. The biggest question is whether they’re as comfortable as the Sleep A30, but Anker has a good track record so far, so my hopes are high. —James Pero Probably one of the most intriguing audio products out of IFA is the Anker soundcore SleepLab Pro, which claims to be able to track sleep metrics all the way from your nightstand. To do that, the SleepLab Pro uses a 60GHz radar, which Anker says can keep track of metrics like heart rate and sleep stages. The company even says the SleepLab Pro works when there’s another person in your bed. I’m sketpical of how well the sleep tracking works from a distance—even wearables that live right on your body can struggle with accurately assessing sleep—but the idea is at least an intriguing one. —James Pero Remember when people had dedicated stick recording devices so they could give themselves notes or record their thoughts and ruminations? Now imagine if the stick could talk back. The Relay Q is a push-to-talk AI gadget shaped like a Bic lighter, though with a button under the cap you can talk to an AI tied to your Mac (Relay promises it may come to PCs at a later date). Relay claims that, unlike other AI voice interfaces, its software isn’t just transcribing audio but is understanding the context of your voice recording, including intonation and pacing. So what is the AI using your voice for? Agentic actions, of course, like sending messages to friends. The Relay Q also comes with a magnetic base where it can act almost like a stick mic for talking with AI. Otherwise, it’s designed to be a little more discreet than when you’re supposed to yell at your Mac’s Siri interface. Still, if you’re so keen to talk to your AI assistant without anybody listening in, you could, you know, just type it out. —Kyle Barr As projector technology continues to improve, we’ll inevitably see them turn into two camps. One will be the dim, though highly portable, projector. The others will try to convince buyers they are TV replacements. The latest laser pointers debuting at IFA 2026 are seriously bright, with Awol Vision’s LuxVision short-throw projector reaching 6,000 ISO lumens. Other similar laser projectors like Xgimi’s Aura 3 Max also promise better contrast levels thanks to its dual-iris optical system. The big thing that will hold these projectors back is cost, but they are technically cheaper than those obscene 200-inch TVs that are only sold to the people with both the money and penthouse-levels of room (i.e., way too much money) to prop one up. —Kyle Barr The regular Aurzen Zip was not good. Gizmodo gave it a 2.5/5 for its low brightness, loud fans, short battery life, and pricey $400 price tag. The new Aurzen Zip Pro might be better. The company says the tri-fold pocket projector is brighter thanks to a “proprietary 10.7mm ultra-slim optical engine” and has a better thermal design, which—hopefully—means less fan noise. The Zip Pro also has higher resolution projection at 1080p versus 720p, supports two pairs of Bluetooth earphones versus one, and has longer battery life with 65W+ fast charging. All the extra performance does come at a cost: weight. The Zip Pro is 1.26 pounds compared to the regular Zip’s 0.62 pounds. The Pro version costs more, too: $629.99 ($579.99 limited-time introduction price). Preorders are available now on Aurzen’s website. —Raymond Wong I thought the detachable screen on the Insta360 Luna Ultra was sick, but get a load of the Hohem Eyepic’s whole removable lens and sensor body. It detaches from the 3-axis gimbal and can be mounted onto magnetic surfaces or used underwater up to 10 meters, according to the company. Kyle grabbed a photo of the Eyepic at Hohem’s booth: It looks way bigger than a DJI Osmo Pocket 3 or Insta360 Luna Ultra. And here’s a pic of the camera module in another accessory: Other tech specs include 4K video capture at up to 60 fps, a 2.51-inch touchscreen that rotates, and support with other Hohem accessories like a wireless mic. No pricing or launch details have been shared yet, but Hohem says it’s expected to arrive in Q1 2027. Somebody tell DJI to step things up. Its Osmo Pocket 3 is still stupidly popular for shooting steady video, but the Osmo Pocket 4 Pro just adds a second camera. Pretty boring compared to the Eyepic. —Raymond Wong The NXTPAPER AMOLED screen on TCL’s P80 Pro and P80 Ultra caught my attention at first, but then I learned that the phones have a slider key that launches an e-reading experience and extends battery life up to a week. There’s also an AI feature that can convert e-books into audiobooks and podcasts?! I have no idea how well that works, but I am dying to try it out. It’s a shame these phones are only launching in Europe. I’m sure plenty of us dumb Americans could use a paper-like screen with deep contrast and e-reader features. Anything to get us reading more books. Or listening to them if that’s more your thing. —Raymond Wong TCL’s new lineup of A1 TAB tablets is coming soon to select European markets, with optional NXTPAPER displays that have a matte finish and reduce blue light for an easier viewing experience. We have four options here: two with 11-inch displays (one with NXTPAPER and one without) and two with 12.2-inch displays (one with NXTPAPER and one without). The larger “Plus” models are being marketed as best for watching videos, as they’ve got a 3:2 aspect ratio. No word yet on pricing, but TCL’s tablets are usually on the budget side of the spectrum. Now if only we could get the company to sell them in the U.S. —Matt Wille Finally, here’s the really cool stuff. First is Lenovo’s Project AeroBlade, a laptop that is less than 10mm thin and weighs way less than two pounds. The other concept device for IFA 2026 is called Project Swan. If you remember Lenovo’s past rolling laptops that expanded vertically, this one takes a 14-inch screen and expands it horizontally to 17 inches. AeroBlade is easily the more practical of these devices, but Swan is inevitably what will attract more attention, especially if you can’t get enough of flexible screens. —Kyle Barr Lenovo is one of the first companies gearing up to make OLED monitors made with a new kind of production technique. TCL calls it “inkjet printing” OLEDs, which is supposed to make the process more effecient and cheaper with less waste. These screens are also supposed to be better and longer lasting. Lenovo’s first device not exclusive to China with this screen tech is the ThinkVision P27UL-40. — Kyle Barr Motorola’s new edge 70 plus phone is promising some big camera upgrades, now coming with a 200-megapixel main sensor that comes with image stabilization. The 6.8-inch AMOLED and a seriously-bright 5,200-nit bright screen round out a phone that, let’s admit it, looks very close to an iPhone, especially with its square camera bump. Motorola may not be as popular in the U.S., but it is certainly one of the largest in markets like Brazil. That’s where you’ll find the new Motorola Edge, rather than the U.S. —Kyle Barr Everybody’s got a giant watch built for fitness nuts. Now, even Motorola is coming up on the trend. It’s a WearOS watch with a 46mm stainless steel frame. More importantly, it works with the Polar ecosystem for its excessively data-driven health tracking features. It’s also Motorola’s first watch that supports both LTE and eSIM. —Kyle Barr Lenovo’s new IdeaPad Vibe is meant to fit your… well, vibe, I guess. The laptop comes in seven different colorways and can come with either a 14- or 15-inch screen and a choice between a Qualcomm or AMD chip. What’s your favorite (and why is it the red?). In addition, Lenovo’s launching new IdeaCenter all-in-one PCs that also have a selection of slick colors with tone-matched keyboards and mice. Apple may finally have some AIO competition with pretty colors. —Kyle Barr The Yoga Tab Plus Gen 2 is Lenovo’s more-powerful tablet that’s meant to take on the iPad Pro. Hey, you know what, it may actually have a chance thanks to its 13-inch 4K display. It comes with Tab Pen Pro 2 and you can also get its keyboard attachment. The keyboard is actually more stiff than it looks and its weighted so you may even be able to use it from your lap as a laptop replacement. —Kyle Barr Lenovo’s not losing out on Nvidia’s first CPU in way more than a decade. Lenovo’s first new RTX Spark PCs running an Nvidia N1X chip are the Yoga Pro 9n and the Yoga 9n 2-in-1. They both look good and promise seriously strong GPU performance, but my favorite is easily the convertible laptop thanks to its slick stylus features. You can use the new Apple Pencil Pro-like Yoga Pen on either the trackpad or the screen. —Kyle Barr If you’re wondering “who the hell is Qira,” Lenovo wants you to get to know the name if you happen to use one of its laptops or any Motorola mobile device. It’s meant to become an agentic chatbot, akin to Gemini or Siri, but work across the company’s ecosystem. Qira is currently available across 80 devices now, and the AI suite should ship in more devices before the end of 2026 including on wearables like smartwatches. Lenovo claims the file size for Qira has shrunk by 67%, though that doesn’t mean its a small part of these devices. It’s coming to Android 17 devices as well as Windows 11 laptops running with at least 16GB of RAM. —Kyle Barr Lenovo decided to host their own press conference all the way across town. This feels like a bigger arena than last year’s, if that matters. But we all know why we’re here: the cool Lenovo concepts it keeps pumping out that may actually be useful or, at least, cool. —Kyle Barr When Dell’s Alienware brand first suggested it was trying to push QD-OLED to esports pros, I wondered if the company was trying to imply these hardcore gamers would enjoy the deeper contrast these screens imply. In reality, the monitor is more designed to facilitate that 0.03ms pixel-to-pixel response time—the speed in which pixels can change color—that your usual fast TN IPS monitor cannot achieve. The 27-inch Alienware AW2527HX is a 1080p, 560Hz display that also manages with a matte display filter. It’s not built to make your games look their best—it’s a performance-first display. That includes a special button built into the back that stretches the screen resolution. Some Valorant or Counter-Strike 2 gamers prefer this stretched look, as it makes enemies appear larger and easier to hit (the jury’s still out whether this actually makes it easier to aim). Alienware also removed any emblems or icons from the front of the monitor to remove distractions. With a wide -45 degree to 45 degree swivel and a wide tilt range, the AW2527HX can maneuver so players can put their faces directly in front of the display. Listen, it may not be your cup of tea, but Alienware is trying to move esports gamers away from the old LCD model to something more modern. It will be interesting to see if they can budge these notoriously finicky gamers to leave their comfort zone. —Kyle Barr After launching the XPS 13, Dell decided it wasn’t done trying to beat the MacBook Neo. Its next lineup of relatively affordable laptops is the Dell 14S (you may remember Dell renamed its Inspiron lineup to just “Dell” back in 2025), and it still maintains the full aluminum frame, though it’s 0.3 pounds heavier (2.5 pounds total) and slightly thicker than the 13-inch XPS. For that size, it offers you an HDMI port and an even more solid feel. The XPS 13 had a subtle amount of give in the center of the keyboard, but the Dell 14S feels even more firm. I didn’t get to actually turn the screen on, but unlike the XPS, the 14S isn’t a touchscreen display, though you should be able to buy one with a 2.8K, 120Hz IPS LCD screen. And if you were wondering how the colors have come out, they’re very subtle depending on the ambient lighting. The pink tone is especially muted unless it’s under brighter, more natural light. The obvious standout is the “Velvet Green,” which has a metallic shade and black accents that make it look especially sleek. Dell hasn’t announced pricing yet, but the company told me that since the XPS is supposed to be the higher-end customer brand with its starting $800 price, the 14S may be even more affordable. If you ever wanted to see a tech convention in the days before it opens to the public, let me show you. At IFA, it looks like constant construction, with each building of the Messe Berlin reverberating with the sounds of construction. It’s 11 a.m. here, and most booths are barely even half constructed. The floor is littered with debris, sawdust, and garbage. These folk will be working until late in the night. They still have to replace the floors with something you can actually walk on. —Kyle Barr Similar to last year, Anker had a lot to announce at IFA 2026. While I already covered its SleepLab Pro speaker and its new sleep earbuds, there’s also a new pair of open wireless earbuds, a new pair of wireless headphones, and a new pair of in-ear wireless earbuds. The AeroClip 2 Pro are Anker’s new open wireless earbuds and are billed as “AI Note-Taker Earbuds.” They borrow some capabilities from Anker’s Liberty line of wireless earbuds, including note-taking and transcription. On the wireless headphones side, there’s the Space 2 Pro, which, thanks to Anker’s Thus chip, gets a major bump in active noise cancellation (ANC) and clear calling, according to Anker. Finally, there’s the Liberty Buds 2, which have features such as a “Comfort ANC” mode that’s meant to avoid uncomfortable ear pressure associated with wireless earbuds with silicone ear tips. The AeroClip price and availability are TBA, while the other two products will be available starting the week of Sept. 22, according to Anker. The Space 2 Pro cost $199, and the Liberty Buds 2 cost $129. —James Pero The company synonymous with USB chargers, cables, and power banks is consolidating all of its sub-brands under one brand: Anker. Yep, after almost 15 years of expanding through sub-brands like Eufy, EufyMake, Soundcore, and Solix, it’s all just gonna be Anker from here on out. “Category brands made sense when categories were separate. They no longer are,” said Anker CEO Steve Yang in a press release. “One brand, one promise – Ultimate Innovation, now unified across everything we make.” I, for one, am fine with the change, though that’s just for product naming. Anker hasn’t said anything about whether it’s going to unify all of its existing sub-brands through, say, a single app or connected experience. As far as I can tell, Anker hasn’t made any such claims. —Raymond Wong Luna just officially announced that its first wearable, the Luna Band, is now shipping worldwide. The screenless wearable’s main gimmick is that it recognizes patterns in user behavior and changes what it measures and how often it measures it to adapt to users’ “goals.” Unlike competitors like Whoop, Luna isn’t requiring a subscription for its health tracker. But it’s unclear how well it will actually be able to adapt to health patterns or even how well it will measure standard metrics like heart rate and blood oxygen levels. The company says more than 100,000 people signed up for its waitlist after the Band was first announced at CES 2026. —Matt Wille As I walked through Acer’s IFA 2026 showcase, my colleague Wes put his finger to the new Acer Swift Air 14 and shook his head. The device is meant to be relatively affordable with a lower-end Intel Wildcat Lake chip, but the trackpad was worse than cheap with a hinge mechanism that restricted a click until your finger was an inch away from the keyboard. Acer’s new Swift Blade 14 is even lighter than the Air at 1.7 pounds. That’s more than half a pound lighter than the $700 MacBook Neo. And still, the laptop shell had a little more give than I would prefer. The trackpad also had similar problems as the Air. As much as I want a super-thin, super-light design, there are going to be trade-offs. No matter what, though, I just want a single laptop maker other than Apple to create a mechanical trackpad that doesn’t suck. —Kyle Barr Packard Bell (no relation to Hewlett-Packard or Bell) makes some of the brightest, cutest laptops you cannot buy. That’s because the company hasn’t shipped its products to the U.S., despite being one of the companies to push PCs in big box stores. The company was acquired by Acer in 2013, and it’s been making laptops for the EU and African regions through various licensing deals since then. Now they’re working closer with Acer again, and that includes a new launch with extremely colorful laptops, keyboards, mice, and even a seriously cool record player. The DotBook laptop is emphasizing a very back-to-basics design but with an extremely colorful shell. Also, just look at these colorful keyboards with their rounded typewriter-like keys. Why do the Europeans get all the cool stuff? I talked with Eric Ackerson, Acer’s associate director of public marketing, and he agreed that it’s a shame that the U.S. market is dominated by dull gray designs. It’s a money thing, more than anything, but hopefully the mood is changing thanks to designs like the MacBook Neo and Acer’s own laptops like the Acer Swift Air 16 and Acer Swift Blade 14. Just give me a bright red laptop, dammit! —Kyle Barr Thanks to the MacBook Neo, every laptop maker is now trying to compete with a $700-800 computer that doesn’t suck. Samsung’s answer? A cheaper version of its 14-inch Galaxy Book6, starting at $799. Lowering the price means exactly what you think it does: weaker performance. The Galaxy Book6 comes with either an Intel Core 3 or a Core 5 CPU. The $799 model also only gets you 8GB of RAM. Samsung’s hoping its 25-hour battery claims will matter more, especially if you’re a student or a cubicle gremlin. At least the Galaxy Book6 has something the MacBook Neo doesn’t: tons of ports. It’s got a full-size HDMI 1.4, two USB-C, a USB-A, a headphone/mic jack, and a security slot for a Kensington lock. —Raymond Wong Kyle and I are at the IFA opening press conference. As a presenter spoke about the backlash to AI, he referenced how communities are increasingly protesting the build-out of data centers that make AI possible. I don’t think he meant that as an applause line, but someone clapped all the same. —Wes Davis We’re now attending the main IFA press conference. This is my third year attending the Berlin showcase, and it’s my colleague Wes Davis’ second time. And still, every time I come here, I cannot for the life of me navigate the Messe Berlin convention center. Seriously, it’s a maze. —Kyle Barr I’m with my colleague Wes Davis. We were promised sandwiches inside the IFA 2026 media center. There are no sandwiches. I have not had breakfast, and I am growing hangry. There is coffee and tea, and it will not tide me over. Please, if there is a drone company here (DJI, maybe), air drop me sustenance before I keel over. —Kyle Barr I found them in a darkened room. Warning to editors: Kyle and I are going to use them. By reading this, you agree to pay for injuries. – Wes Davis Acer’s gaming handhelds haven’t exactly made much of a statement, but its new concept device is actually making me consider what would happen if our “handheld PCs” acted more like actual PCs. The Project DualPlay Mini includes a flip-down display and an internal keyboard for when you need a backup workstation. On the other side, it includes all the regular gamepad controls you’re used to. It certainly looks janky, but this may be a better option than some of those boutique handhelds with their thin keyboard attachments. —Kyle Barr I’m still waiting for the Acer Predator Atlas 8 to hit the U.S. market, but Acer went ahead and made a smaller version, the Acer Predator Atlas 7, which may be a little bit cheaper. It features a smaller 7-inch display, but it will also run with either Intel Arc G3 Extreme or the lower-end Arc G3. We’re still waiting for a price point, but we can hope it may not be as expensive as other Intel handhelds have been. —Kyle Barr I represent the small, small minority of gamers who still want the Nintendo 3DS to make a comeback. Acer’s new Aspire G 3D 16 laptop may be exactly what I’m looking for. It includes a 4K stereoscopic display that can transform 2D content to make it look 3D. It’s also powered with an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 chip, a small rarity for gaming laptops that normally rely on a discrete GPU. This new Aspire is a ridiculous device, and it may not have that much content that can perform with 3D, but please forgive me; I can’t help but feel excited. —Kyle Barr I was chatting with my friend Wes Davis last night over a nice German beer about the weird state of screen extenders. They’re massive and bulky, and they don’t actually create the mobile multi-screen experience you’re looking for. So of course, Acer is making them look even sillier with its business-focused PD163QP3. As if two screens weren’t excessive enough, Acer imagines you might want three extra displays. —Kyle Barr Acer’s taking more than a few cues from Framework with its latest Vero laptops. The Acer Vero 16 is built for modularity, including the option to completely replace the mainboard with up to two generations of future chips. You can remove the screws surrounding the hinge to repair the screen. It comes with up to an Intel Core Ultra X9 388H processor and up to a 3K OLED display. —Kyle Barr Acer’s going back to the Swift series with what is one of its most petite offerings. I first saw the Acer Swift Air 16 at Computex 2026, but Acer is now offering a few more details. That includes the 13.5mm height when closed up. It was originally pitched as a relatively cheap device, making it out to be Acer’s MacBook Neo competitor, using an Intel Core Series 3 chip (dubbed Wildcat Lake). The thing is, the laptop also supports up to a 3K OLED display, so I can’t really say how much it may cost with the highest-end configs. But then there’s something even thinner. The Acer Swift Blade 14 is only 14mm thin, and it weighs 799g. It also comes with a 3K OLED display and the Intel Core Series 3 CPUs. Why is a “Blade” thinner than an “Air?” Somebody should talk to Acer about its naming conventions. —Kyle Barr Acer’s SFF RTX Spark is the company’s new tiny PC that’s employing Nvidia’s N1X chip, with the 20-core Grace CPU co-developed with MediaTek and the humongous 6,144-core Blackwell GPU. It’s a tiny PC that’s promising some serious graphics performance. We’ve yet to actually test any of these RTX Spark laptops or desktops. It seems powerful, but pure performance may not be the end-all-be-all. The actual mini PC itself looks like an old Volkswagen with the fake wood accents. —Kyle Barr Acer’s press conference is happening right now. I expect them to wax on about their upcoming RTX Spark laptop and mini PCs, but really all I want is for them to do is actually sell one of their gaming handhelds in the U.S. —Kyle Barr Smart home brand Homey’s latest in its line of hubs is an admittedly cute Homey Potal. Admittedly, the first thought I had was, “That looks like an Apple Watch.” In reality, the Homey Portal can hang out on your dresser or be mounted on a wall and be assigned a zone, where you use the 2.8-inch touchscreen to control your home’s lighting, temperature, speaker, and more. Alongside the touchscreen, the portal includes a rotating frame that acts as a dial for changing volume or the heat inside your home. You can also add different icons and widgets to the touchscreen for different flows, moods, or devices. The Homey Portal works with all of Homey’s latest smart home hubs alongside the Homey Self-Hosted Server and Homey Cloud. It’s available to preorder for $249 or 249 euros, but the full launch price will be $299. Homey says it expects to ship sometime in December. —Kyle Barr Although I’m not at IFA with the boyz, I do love to blog about weird-ass gadgets. Accessory maker Jsaux has a new controller brand called VoidJoy (uhh…) and the first two new products are definitely intriguing. There’s the Skylark S1 Pro Portable that you see above. This rectangular gamepad has dual recessed TMR joysticks (read: no drift), a D-pad, ABXY buttons, and “optical linear quick-switch” triggers. It’s not made specifically for the Switch or Switch 2, but it will work with it. It costs $49.99. Then you have the Elite Extender. It’s a doohickey that bolts onto a Switch Pro controller and adds a battery and four additional buttons that can be custom mapped. The gamepad also has a turbo mode. Yours for $39.99. Both are available for preorder today. —Raymond Wong Is there such a thing as a “gaming projector?” Perhaps, though the jury’s still out on whether JMGO’s new IRIS projectors are the best setup for your PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series X. These high-brightness projectors promise to hit 4K resolution at 120Hz. JMGO says the Iris series is making use of a “HyperPulse Actuator,” which shifts 480 times per second. The new projectors also support variable refresh rate (VRR), which will prove necessary if you plan to use this projector for gaming at unlocked frame rates. The top-end Iris Ultra Max claims a nice, bright 6,500 ISO lumens and a 10,000:1 native contrast ratio. The lesser Iris Ultra can only do 7,000:1, though both versions have dual-iris contrast control. The projectors were already announced for China, but JMGO is opening up pre-orders for the U.S. and Europe Sept. 4. If you imagine you want to play your games or watch sports on a gigantic bed sheet strung up in your backyard, this may be one of your better options. —Kyle Barr TP-Link promised it was coming, but we’re still somewhat surprised that the first Wi-Fi 8 routers are actually here at IFA 2026 before they’re set to launch in October this year. The pack with the new Wi-Fi standard is led by the Archer 8 Ultra, but there’s also a separate Deco 8 Ultra mesh Wi-Fi system. The big claim with Wi-Fi 8 is that it will finally add more connectivity to the dead zones in the corners of your home. These new routers are also supposed to keep speeds up even if you have multiple devices connected to the same router at once. Of course, you may still be using Wi-Fi 5 or Wi-Fi 6, and Wi-Fi 7 already seemed like a pipe dream. Hopefully we’ll get to test out some of these capabilities for ourselves in the near future. —Kyle Barr China-based mobile brand Tecno has a penchant for trying to push phones to their silliest. The latest concept to spill out from the company includes a “0mm” bezel-less phone with a screen the company claims can go truly edge-to-edge. Tecno says it achieved this via a complex method of screen-stacking, which it calls “advanced internal stacking, structural re-engineering, and novel screen packaging that reworks the display architecture.” The company is supposed to show this off at Showstoppers here at IFA 2026 on Sept. 3. However, Marques Brownlee already went hands-on with the phone and noted that Tecno has managed to achieve this feat by making the screen sit taller than the sides of the phone. Furthermore, Tecno is supposed to show off its MEGABOOK T15 360 Pro 2-in-1 laptop Thursday. I’m always interested in seeing more laptops that aren’t from the usual slate of makers you find in the U.S. So stay tuned. —Kyle Barr Nobody’s promising to make you into Iron Man, at least not yet, but there are several companies planning to debut new leg exoskeletons at IFA, all promising to make you somewhat better at climbing stairs. First up, we have Hypershell, which is planning to announce a new “Hypershell Halo” exoskeleton. Previous leg armatures like the Hypershell X Ultra S only attached to the thigh, but the new Halo has extra bands that go below the knee. This new model adds “four powered hip-and-knee joints” that may actually help you if you have some lower leg issues. Ever since I started writing about these exoskeletons, people have asked me if they’ll help you hike with bad knees. Here’s hoping these ones may actually make a difference. Hypershell is supposed to share more on Sept. 3. —Kyle Barr Just when you were growing tired of everything becoming an agentic “Claw,” LG wants to shove even more AI into all your smart home tech. The Korean tech giant described its “ThinkQ Claw” as an agentic chatbot designed to comprehend the daily context you feed it, then use all that data as a means to automate certain actions, like getting your ovens prepared for incoming guests or enabling your air conditioner or air purifier settings before you get home from work. How this differs from LG’s previous smart home concepts is a little more vague. However, LG says it’s building off its previous acquisition of AI startup Homey in 2024. If this year’s showcase is as cringe-y as it has been at previous IFAs, we’re in for even more Leave it to Beaver hilarity. —Kyle Barr Damn, I can’t believe I’m already gearing up for another one of these. The dread of trying to navigate the labyrinthine halls of the Messe Berlin convention center is ready to make me choke on a curry wurst. With that in mind, I need to carry a few extra gadgets to keep me going. So I’m keeping it classic with a MacBook Pro, better to help me when editing pictures from my Ricoh GRIIIX and newfangled GoPro Mission 1 ILS that I’m in the middle of testing. I have one of the action camera maker’s Media Mod with its attached mic alongside the company’s other Wireless Mic System. Hopefully, that camera and all its accoutrements doesn’t weigh me down. For extra juice on the go, I have a 10,000mAh Genki Energy Pack and an Anker Nano Power Bank. I have my 2TB Crucial portable SSD and my Lenovo travel dock to keep me company. And for my in-flight entertainment, there’s my Switch 2 now packing Metal Gear Solid Master Collection Vol. 2 that will finally give me the chance to play Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. I’ve also been jonesing to read Ursula K. LeGuin’s The Word for World is Forest. —Kyle Barr

item.title: Identity Verification Is Broken. The 153 Million Driver’s Licenses Now for Sale Are Proof
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 4.16
A dark web identity theft service is offering more than 153 million U.S. and Canadian driver’s license scans for sale, and the FBI is investigating where the data came from. The apparent breach is a particularly stark example of the problem with the modern identity verification economy where proving who you are means providing a third party with permanent copies of sensitive documents. According to KrebsOnSecurity, the service, called Nexus, launched on a Russian-language cybercrime forum and claims to have more than 153 million driver’s licenses, along with more than 10 million other identification cards, more than 3 million travel documents and international IDs, and hundreds of thousands of medical cards. The number is difficult to independently verify, but Krebs found evidence suggesting the service is not simply bluffing. The database contained the licenses of Krebs himself and U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, among other government officials. The licenses included multiple images of the documents, including front and back scans and, in some cases, infrared and ultraviolet versions. The data also appeared to be fresh. Nexus’s advertised collection grew by nearly 400,000 driver’s license records in roughly 24 hours, while the operators claimed they had been continuously exfiltrating information for more than a year. Krebs traced the apparent source to IDScan.net, a New Orleans-based identity verification company. The company says its technology processes more than 21 million identity verifications every month at more than 20,000 locations around the world. IDScan.net’s customer materials show just how deeply this type of infrastructure is embedded in everyday commerce. Its official site lists companies and brands including Holiday Inn, 7-Eleven, GameStop, DraftKings, Hertz, Target, FedEx, Shell, and Caesars Entertainment among its customers or integrations. The connection is particularly striking because Krebs found that timestamps attached to several leaked licenses corresponded with trips, hotel stays, car rentals, and other real-world interactions where people handed over their IDs. IDScan.net said it is investigating the incident but has not publicly confirmed that its systems were the source of the Nexus database. The company told Krebs that it was unable to provide additional information while its investigation continued. The FBI has also opened an investigation through its New Orleans field office into the apparent breach. ‼️ New article from Brian Krebs: FBI Probes Service Selling 153M+ Drivers Licenseshttps://t.co/S5KEn9pb5v Dark Web Onion discussed: http://nexusdbbulkq5345qlqyc2iprxzsrwvavd6r5qwel3o3vxs5svg5mjyd[.]onion pic.twitter.com/HVsrjGrL9x — Dark Web Informer (@DarkWebInformer) September 2, 2026 Shortly after Krebs published its report, the Nexus site itself disappeared from the dark web and was replaced with a message saying the service was no longer available. Peter Van Valkenburgh, a longtime cryptocurrency policy advocate and Coin Center Executive Director, argued in an essay that the breach was not some bizarre one-off accident. He called the hack “inevitable” and said society is “long, long, long overdue to reduce the amount of KYC we do.” Van Valkenburgh’s argument is fundamentally about data minimization. Every time a company demands a scan of a government ID, it creates another repository containing information that can potentially be stolen, resold, or abused. “We deputize a sea of s*itty quasi-government contractors to perform data collection and monitoring,” Van Valkenburgh wrote, arguing that the resulting databases become attractive targets precisely because they contain so much valuable information in one place. The problem gets even harder to ignore as governments and companies push identity verification into more parts of daily life. Age verification, financial compliance, hotel check-ins, car rentals, gambling, cannabis sales, and online services can all require some form of ID scan. Security and privacy researcher Zach Edwards, whose own driver’s license was found in the Nexus database, told Krebs that the incident highlights the risks of outsourcing identity verification to an expanding network of third-party vendors. “These systems are putting sensitive data into more and more 3rd party vendors, and we don’t have nearly the oversight to ensure they are safe,” Edwards said. Indeed, the very systems that have been built are a contradiction in themselves. While there are increasingly sophisticated processes put in place to determine whether someone is really who they claim to be, those systems often require collecting enough information to create a devastating situation if the security surrounding the associated database fails. And this is hardly the first time the scale of the problem has become absurd. In 2025, education software company PowerSchool was breached in an attack that exposed sensitive information belonging to tens of millions of students and teachers, including Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and medical information. In 2024, AT&T also disclosed that hackers had obtained the Social Security numbers, dates of birth, phone numbers, email addresses, and other information of 73 million current and former customers. A separate incident exposed phone records belonging to nearly all of the company’s customers. Solutions are Available Technical solutions to this underlying problem of creating honey pots of sensitive customer data are available. For example, zero-knowledge proofs can allow someone to prove that they satisfy a particular condition without revealing all of the information contained in the underlying credential. Instead of handing over a complete driver’s license to prove that you are over 21, a system could theoretically verify the relevant fact without receiving your name, address, license number, and other information printed on the card. 153M drivers licenses leaked! Identity documents should only be authenticated using zero-knowledge proofs. Stop revealing all your personal details just to prove you have a valid drivers license.https://t.co/ebdV54Zk78 — Remco (@recmo) September 2, 2026 While these technologies do not magically make identity verification secure in all scenarios, they offer a way to redesign the system so that verifying someone’s identity does not create other, second-order issues. Of course, there is also a less convenient reality behind all of this in that some of the data collection is not simply a matter of companies deciding they want more information. Laws and regulations can require businesses to collect, verify, or retain identifying information in certain circumstances. In other words, changes to the regulations around personal data collection are needed on top of the adoption of various technical innovations. Whether these technical or regulatory changes will be implemented anytime soon remains to be seen. “Risk-averse compliance departments and set-in-their-ways regulators prefer old practices and the appearance of rigorous compliance—box checking—to actually protecting people through data minimization and auditable, verifiable alternatives,” wrote Van Valkenburgh.

item.title: Acer’s Smaller Intel-Based Gaming Handheld Has Sky-High Ambitions
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.90
As Atlas holds up the sky, so too does Acer have high hopes for its next handheld, the Acer Predator Atlas 7. It’s a more compact handheld that may still offer strong performance at its lower spec. We’re still waiting to see how much it costs. The Acer Predator Atlas 7 is a little like the Predator Atlas 8 we saw back at Computex 2026, though the most obvious concession is that it trades the 8-inch display for a 7-inch, 1080p LCD display. The other major factor is that the smaller handheld can be equipped with an Intel Arc G3 or an Intel Arc G3 Extreme. The 8-inch Atlas was restricted to the Extreme version of the chip. To explain what that means, the non-Extreme chip includes the Intel Arc B370 GPU, rather than the higher-end Arc B390. That means it holds 10 Xe3 GPU cores instead of 12. Both versions of the chip maximize efficiency on the CPU side to let the GPU really shine. Just like the Atlas 8, this one is a Windows-based handheld. We’re still waiting for Intel and Valve to create some compatibility for SteamOS. The Atlas 7 can support up to 24GB of RAM and 1TB of SSD storage. It’s also packing a large 80Wh battery that should—hopefully—help it keep running for a bare few hours of gaming. Just like the Acer Predator Atlas 8, the 7-inch version can reach a max TDP (thermal design power) of 40W. That’s pretty good, but it means that this device will kick out a lot of heat. One of Acer’s touted design features is the handheld’s dual-fan design. The chassis includes a metal Predator Aeroblade fan alongside a plastic fan, which promises to expel enough heat to keep the Intel chip running efficiently. Design-wise, the handheld looks like the Asus ROG Ally from yesteryear, though with grips that are more reminiscent of the Lenovo Legion Go S. Acer is opting for high quality in this handheld, with TMR (tunneling magnetoresistance) thumbsticks that should better resist any breakage or stick drift. The flat, recessed buttons and dish-shaped D-pad are probably the most interesting part of the controls, but we’ll have to get hands on with it before judging the overall feel. We’ve yet to test the Arc G3 chip, but the Extreme version proved it could excel in performance on a $1,800 MSI Claw 8 EX AI+. And if you’re gagging at that price, we feel your pain. Acer has yet to reveal pricing for either its Predator Atlas 8 or Predator Atlas 7. The company has praised it; we’ll see the handheld come to North America sometime in Q4 this year. There’s a lot to like here, but without a price, we’ll have to wait to judge whether it’s worth considering compared to another handheld like the $1,300 Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20. The RAMpocalypse has not been kind to small gaming devices, and we’re still desperate to see a new handheld in 2026 cost $1,000 or less.

item.title: OpenAI Claims We’re in the ‘AGI Era’ With Release of GPT-6 Astra
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.77
We are approaching the precipice of the beginning of what could be the start of the first stages of the earliest version of artificial general intelligence. That seems to be the thrust of OpenAI’s pitch for GPT-6, its latest AI model that went live on Thursday. GPT-6 arrives about a year after the initial release of GPT-5 and about two months since OpenAI’s last update to GPT-5.6. It’ll be rolling out in waves as the company tries to manage access to what it is positioning as a very powerful model. According to CNBC, GPT-6 Astra will start rolling out to users of OpenAI’s ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise plans in the coming days, and will be available through OpenAI API and Amazon Web Services soon. It’s pretty common at this point for AI companies to engage in hype and hyperbole with the release of a new model, but OpenAI does seem particularly juiced about this one. According to Wired, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said, “It’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era,” regarding the release. “I think that if we fast-forward a couple of years, when we look back and say, ‘When was it really that AGI was created?’ I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model.” It’s worth noting that CEO Sam Altman said earlier this year that AGI is “not a super useful term,” but that was around the time when they needed to downplay competitor advancements. Now that they’re hyping their own, it actually is quite useful. Altman even said in July that he believes “we are now, like, in the singularity.” So OpenAI not quite declaring AGI but getting about as close to the line as you can without going over is in keeping with the clear effort to ramp up the hype. The company also called GPT-6 the “world’s best computer use model,” claiming that the model is significantly better at autonomously navigating computer systems than its predecessors or competitors—an essential advancement for the functionality of AI agents. OpenAI also made a special point to emphasize that GPT-6 is its safest model yet, with more work put into Astra’s alignment and lots of oversight of its chain-of-thought reasoning to make sure that it doesn’t go off the rails. Understandably, OpenAI would really want to ease concerns there, given that it’s still reeling a bit from the fact that one of its models (not GPT-6 but another, secret model) broke containment during training and hacked Hugging Face, and, reportedly, no one on the OpenAI team noticed it happened for about a week. GPT-6 is a major release for OpenAI, not just because it’s the latest version of its flagship model. The company is entering a make-or-break period as it prepares to ramp up for an initial public offering. GPT-6 succeeding could help the company achieve its reported goal of debuting with a valuation above $1 trillion. If it tanks, well, then it’ll probably only debut as a $950 billion company. What a shame that’d be.

item.title: ‘Never After Dark’ Filmmaker Will Next Remake the Already Perfect ‘Pulse’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.76
They remade Suspiria. A do-over of Possession is currently in production. And now, fans of already perfect films have another reason to weep. It seems a fresh take on Pulse, Kiyoshi Kurosawa‘s dread-infused 2001 chiller that predicted the isolating agony the then-novel internet would bring, is coming our way next. Pulse, which will creep into your brain, take hold, and make you sleep with the lights on, has actually already been remade. Though the 2006 American version was co-written by Wes Craven and starred Kristen Bell, it immediately faded into obscurity, trailing a pair of even more forgettable sequels in its wake. So why Pulse, again, now? As Deadline tells us, the filmmaker stepping into Kurosawa’s haunted footprints is Dave Boyle, whose breakout film, Never After Dark, hits theaters in a few weeks, buoyed by a successful festival run and words of praise from Stephen King and Black Phone filmmaker Scott Derrickson. “His hiring for Pulse tracks, as he’s long told stories either set in Japan or revolving around Japanese characters,” the trade notes, and that includes Never After Dark. However, we can’t assume it will take that focus for sure, since “plot details, including locale, for the new take are being kept under wraps. All that’s known is that it’s set in the modern era, revolving around a new set of characters.” Boyle is attached to direct and also do a fresh pass on the existing script by Luke Piotrowski; among the producers is Parker Finn, who directed the Smile films and… yes… the new Possession. Will you be checking out Boyle’s “modern” take on Pulse? Want more io9 news?
