item.title: How ‘Looney Tunes’ Icon Mel Blanc Influenced ‘Coyote vs. Acme’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.40
Saying the once-shelved Coyote vs. Acme got the last laugh during its opening weekend at the box office would be an understatement. Much has been written about the film’s underdog journey from a tax write-off to the number-one “non-arachnid” movie in the U.S. But the film also features an understated homage to Looney Tunes icon Mel Blanc. Director Dave Green and longtime series voice actor Eric Bauza were more than happy to lift the curtain on that tribute in an interview with io9. If you’ve watched any Looney Tunes cartoon, chances are Blanc’s screams are still permanently ringing in your ears. Blanc is as integral to Looney Tunes‘ DNA as composers Cliff Friend and Dave Franklin’s “The Merry-Go-Round Broke Down.” Known as “The Man of a Thousand Voices,” Blanc voiced practically every major Looney Tunes character: Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Porky Pig, Tweety, Sylvester, Foghorn Leghorn, Wile E. Coyote—the list goes on and on. He also lent his voice to other formative cartoons like Tom and Jerry and The Flintstones. Coyote vs. Acme‘s tribute to Blanc is subtle, but touching: the film uses archival audio of Blanc for one of Bugs Bunny’s screams. Having Blanc immortalized in the movie meant a lot to Green and Bauza, Blanc’s equally multi-credited torchbearer of Looney Tunes‘ personalities. “He’s a beacon. Mel Blanc was such a force as far as performers go. And in the world of voice-over, he was a pioneer,” Bauza said. “I equate him to human bagpipes. He had air coming out of every oropharynx on his person. Unmistakable, one voice from another—they’re so different. So unique. I always say Warner Bros. gave me the keys to the Cadillac, and I always promise not to scratch it and put it back with a full tank of gas. Being able to act in those roles on a bigger scale that isn’t a thirty-second shoe commercial—or even a seven-minute short harkening back to the originals—it’s something special. I’m super grateful for Dave putting me in that spotlight for his story.” Green credited gaining a deeper understanding of Blanc’s characters from working with Bauza throughout Coyote vs. Acme‘s recording sessions. During voice-over sessions, Green recalled a time when he asked Bauza, “Would Bugs say something like this?” Even after the script was nailed down, Green said he and Bauza would riff on ideas and alternate takes for Looney Tunes characters, thanks to Bauza’s years of fine-tuning Blanc’s characters since childhood, bringing a deep, surprising, and fun modern twist to them in his own voice. “I was watching Looney Tunes as well as a kid. I also grew up on Tiny Tunes, Pinky and the Brain—all of these things that were carrying the torch for Looney Tunes and the Acme brand at the time. I feel incredibly lucky to be one of the many custodians of the brand for just a moment,” Green said. Coyote vs. Acme is in theaters now. Want more io9 news? Check out when to expect the latest Marvel, Star Wars, and Star Trek releases, what’s next for the DC Universe on film and TV, and everything you need to know about the future of Doctor Who.

item.title: Bill Simmons’ Cozy Relationship With Tech Companies Is Blowing Up in His Face
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.24
Bill Simmons was re-apexing, but he’s now experiencing one of the top seven falloffs of all time. The sports columnist turned media empire empresario has had a hell of a week, catching flak first from his own colleagues for his adoption of artificial intelligence—first as a bit and then as a sponsor—and from regulators for openly discussing proxy betting. But all of Bill’s problems stem from the same starting place: his uncritical allyship with tech companies. Simmons has, to his credit and certainly to his benefit, always been ahead of the curve on tech adoption. People call him the Podfather because he was one of the earliest people to popularize podcasting back in 2007, and he’s still at it nearly 20 years later. He was blogging in the ’90s, which got him noticed by ESPN. He got Grantland, the prestige publication he launched under ESPN’s header, to make content for YouTube before the platform was a part of every media company’s strategy. After his exit from ESPN, he launched a new media operation called The Ringer that focused heavily on podcasts, almost out of spite because he felt ESPN never understood the value of the medium. Unfortunately, it seems he may have taken the wrong lesson from being on the cutting edge. Blogs, podcasts, and YouTube are all distribution methods for content. And Bill, for all his warts, makes damn good content. There just aren’t a lot of people out there telling stories about how they were in the middle of a colonoscopy when one of the most important players on their favorite team got traded. Artificial intelligence does not make good content. It makes, almost by necessity because of how the technology works, derivative content. Simmons has tried to play with that. On his movie podcast “The Rewatchables,” where he and a rotating cast of guests talk about movies that they watch over and over again, he started using ChatGPT to generate reviews in the style of Roger Ebert for movies that came out after his passing. The ChatGPT Ebert thing is a bit more than a true embrace of the technology, but his co-hosts almost always greet the segment with a cringe you can hear through your headphones and try to hurry him along, clearly uncomfortable with the concept, even as a joke. One fan of the segment, though, seems to be OpenAI. The company behind ChatGPT became a sponsor of Simmons’ podcast network earlier this year. The hosts of The Ringer’s other flagship film podcast, The Big Picture, are not fans. During an appearance on “Talk Easy” with Sam Fragoso, Sean Fennessey and Amanda Dobbins expressed dismay (and, in Dobbins’s case, shock) when confronted with The Ringer’s dealings with the AI firm. The Big Picture host Amanda Dobbins appears shocked that Bill Simmons is sponsored by ChatGBT Sean Fennessey later says he doesn’t approve of Bill’s ChatGBT-Ebert From the latest @TalkEasyPod pic.twitter.com/JImHnfoeGO — The r/BillSimmons Podcast (@rBillSimmonsPod) August 30, 2026 Simmons also managed to get himself into hot water by admitting to proxy betting on his podcast. During an episode of “The Bill Simmons Podcast,” the host said that he asked his daughter’s boyfriend to make bets for him on FanDuel—a request he had to make because FanDuel’s sportsbook is illegal in California, where Bill lives, but not in Massachusetts, where his daughter and her boyfriend live. Proxy betting is illegal, and the admission—for which Simmons seemed blissfully unaware would cause him any trouble—resulted in the Massachusetts Gaming Commission opening an investigation into the situation. FanDuel is, of course, a major sponsor of The Ringer. FanDuel advertisements regularly run during ad breaks; just about anything sports-related covered on The Ringer comes with odds presented by FanDuel, and Simmons regularly talks about trying to get FanDuel to create special bets for his audience. It’s notable that much of these matters have occurred after Spotify purchased The Ringer in 2020. On its face, this is the exact kind of deal that would make sense both for The Ringer and for Simmons’ better instincts. Getting sucked up by the biggest audio streaming platform in the world is a good fit for a podcast company, and it’d presumably give The Ringer more resources to do what it does best. Except Spotify doesn’t seem to realize that it’s an audio streaming company. It has increasingly pushed for video content in recent years—a decree that reached The Ringer and turned its podcast operation into a video podcast operation. And last year, the company entered an agreement to distribute its video podcasts on Netflix, meaning The Ringer podcasts went from something that could be recorded with a couple of microphones in a closet to something that requires makeup and a dedicated studio to make—not to mention the fact that The Big Picture’s hosts now find themselves compromised because they have to cover and review films produced by the same company that distributes their content. Simmons is a Mount Rushmore figure for digital media. But he doesn’t seem to realize that the internet has changed. It seems he viewed Spotify, Netflix, and OpenAI as tools to stay independent—same as his blog and his podcast—so he’d never find himself working under a big boss again as he did at ESPN. What he missed is that they have more control than a boss. They own and operate the biggest avenues for distribution, and he’s surrendered himself and his company to them. It’s harder to quit that than it is to quit a job.

item.title: While AI Industry Frets Over Safeguards, One Company Is Building a Model That ‘Doesn’t Say No’
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.01
In the wake of a string of major AI hacks that left Silicon Valley reeling, many tech companies have been focusing on how to make models better at refusing dangerous requests. Not all of them, though. Abliteration, a startup founded last year and based in Palo Alto, is loud and proud in its ambition to build what it describes on its website as AI that “doesn’t say no.” In other words, its models are intentionally trained to handle the sorts of questionable tasks that other AI systems on the market would decline. The company launched its latest model on Monday, called—in the awkward, multihyphenated style that’s become conventional in the AI industry—abliterated-model-large-v2. It’s built upon GLM-5.3, an open-weight model released last month by Chinese AI lab Z.ai, minus many of the usual safeguards. As Abliteration wrote in a X post about the new model: “it does the offensive cyber, red teaming, and agent testing work other models refuse to do.” But the startup isn’t completely devoid of ethical red lines: a spokesperson told Gizmodo that Abliteration’s models won’t generate text describing child sexual abuse material or self-harm. (It can’t generate images or video, either.) The company used a process called orthogonalization to find and remove the mechanisms within GLM-5.3 that refuses user prompts. “Everything else is left alone, so the reasoning, coding, and agentic strength of the base model carry over unchanged,” according to its website. It seems to be targeting a subgroup of developers who have been annoyed by what they regard as excessively touchy safeguards used by more mainstream developers, especially Anthropic. When that company released its Fable 5 model in June, many customers complained it was refusing to respond to requests related to sensitive subjects like cybersecurity and biology, even if the requests themselves were totally benign. But it’s reckless—to say the least—to try to respond to the problem of excessive refusals by just doing away with safeguards altogether. Ejaaz Amahadeen, an investor and the host of a podcast about AI, called it a “nightmare scenario,” and warned it “will spark a secondary ‘grey market’ for companies that seek to offer you the same model but effectively jail-broken.” As bigger developers like OpenAI and Anthropic move to slow down some of their internal R&D following the heavily publicized cybersecurity fiascos caused by their AI systems, opportunistic players could, like Abliteration, move in to fill the gap. All of this is happening within a gaping regulatory void. Last month, the Trump administration introduced a framework through which the biggest AI developers in the U.S. would voluntarily hand new models over to the federal government for a safety check prior to public release, though the details of what such a check would consist of—if they’ve been defined at all—haven’t been made public. All open source models are exempt. Aside from that, there are no policies at the federal level requiring developers to build particular safeguards into their models. Again and again, the administration has made it clear that its priorities lay chiefly in ensuring American dominance over China in the AI race, no matter the cost and despite the risks posed to the public by unconstrained AI. Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Abliteration’s latest model release should be a wake-up call for U.S. policymakers. “The fact that U.S. companies are currently commercializing access to dangerous capabilities without any regulation, and U.S. technology is actively enabling the development and operation of these models, is alarming,” he wrote in a X post on Tuesday.

item.title: Best Time to Visit Europe: Month-by-Month Guide
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.76
Europe has no single perfect travel month, which is convenient since there are twelve months to choose from. If you want the best time to visit Europe for sightseeing, start with May or September. May offers mild days, flowering gardens, and comfortable city sightseeing. September keeps the Mediterranean warm and reduces summer crowds. Dreaming of Greek islands or Croatian beaches? Aim for June to September. Planning an Alpine ski trip? Choose January to March, when resorts in Switzerland, Austria, and France are in their main winter season. Love big events? Reserve July for Tomorrowland in Belgium, August for the Edinburgh Festival Fringe, or September for Oktoberfest in Munich. December deserves special mention if Christmas markets are your thing. Vienna, Prague, and Strasbourg become wonderfully festive. So, when should you pack your bags for the ultimate Europe group tour? Take a month-by-month tour to discover the weather, destinations, events, and experiences to find the best time to visit Europe from India. Conditions vary considerably by region and elevation, so check the forecast for each destination before packing. January - Ski Slopes, Snowy Streets and Northern Lights If snow is your idea of good weather, January has plenty to offer. Ski the slopes around Innsbruck or St. Anton in Austria, or head to Zermatt in Switzerland for skiing beneath the Matterhorn. In Finnish Lapland, join a reindeer-sled ride, husky safari, or northern lights tour around Rovaniemi. After a day outside, warm up with hot chocolate in a Viennese café or glögg in Scandinavia. Winters in Europe are cold, but that is the point. Weather snapshot: Freezing and snowy in the Alps and Lapland; generally cold and damp in many central and northern European cities. Where to go: Austria, Switzerland, Finland, Norway Budget: Low-moderate, except ski resorts Best for: Skiing, northern lights and winter scenery February - Venice Carnival and Romantic Europe February gives you the best time to visit Europe from India to witness it at its most theatrical. In Venice, Carnival brings masked revelers, elaborate costumes, and events around St. Mark's Square and the historic center. If romance is your priority, stroll along the Seine in Paris, then escape the cold inside a Left Bank café. For snow, ski around Innsbruck or St. Anton in Austria or head to Finnish Lapland for husky rides and northern lights tours near Rovaniemi. Weather snapshot: Cold winter weather across much of Europe, with snow in Alpine and northern destinations and milder conditions around the Mediterranean. Where to go: Venice, Paris, Vienna, Prague Budget: Moderate Best for: Couples, culture and winter events March - Las Fallas and the First Taste of Spring March brings the first real signs of spring to southern Europe, along with some seriously colorful celebrations. In Valencia, Las Fallas fills the streets with towering satirical sculptures, marching bands, firecrackers and spectacular fireworks before the sculptures are burned in the festival finale. Seville and Lisbon are pleasant for walking tours and outdoor dining, while Rome is warming up nicely for sightseeing. Weather snapshot: Mild spring weather in southern Europe, while central and northern destinations remain cool and changeable. Where to go: Valencia, Seville, Lisbon, Rome Budget: Low-moderate Best for: Festivals, sightseeing and budget-minded travelers April - Tulips, Cycling and Springtime Europe April is when Europe starts looking like a travel brochure. Visit the Netherlands for spring flowers, explore Amsterdam by bicycle, or wander through Parisian parks as they burst into color. Italy is equally tempting, with Rome and Florence offering comfortable sightseeing before summer heat arrives. If you're excited to photograph Europe, this month offers plenty of colorful material. Weather snapshot: Generally mild but changeable, with a mix of sunshine, showers and cool evenings. Where to go: Amsterdam, Keukenhof, Paris, Florence Budget: Moderate Best for: Flowers, photography and city breaks May - The Sweet Spot for Your European Holiday If there is one month worth circling on your calendar, May makes a strong case. Explore Rome's Colosseum before the summer heat sets in, explore lower-elevation trails around Chamonix in the French Alps, wander the whitewashed lanes of Oia in Santorini, or follow Portugal's Atlantic coast from Lisbon to Lagos. May is especially appealing for honeymooners because you can combine romantic cities, coastal scenery, and outdoor dining without the high heat and crowds of July. Add a sunset dinner overlooking the Amalfi Coast and choosing your wedding date suddenly seems easy. Weather snapshot: Warm and comfortable in much of southern Europe, with mild days and cooler evenings farther north and at higher elevations. Where to go: Italy, Greece, France, Spain, Portugal Budget: Moderate Best for: First-time visitors, couples and outdoor adventures June - Long Days, Hiking and Mediterranean Beaches June is for travelers who would rather be outdoors enjoying summer in Europe than watching it through a hotel window. Cruise the Geirangerfjord in Norway, hike around Interlaken and Lauterbrunnen in Switzerland, or explore Hvar and the Dalmatian Coast in Croatia. In Greece, head to Naxos or Crete for swimming, island-hopping, and waterfront dinners. If you're considering Europe tour packages with island stops, book early. Popular ferries, trains, and hotels can fill quickly, and no one wants a dream Greek holiday derailed at the ferry terminal. Weather snapshot: Warm to hot around the Mediterranean, with long, generally mild days in northern Europe and cooler conditions in the mountains. Where to go: Norway, Switzerland, Croatia, Greece Budget: Moderate-high Best for: Hiking, families, beaches and road trips July - Tomorrowland, Island Hopping and Peak Summer If electronic music, huge stages and thousands of concert-goers sound like your idea of a great weekend, Tomorrowland in Belgium is worth planning around. Prefer saltwater to speakers? Swim off Mykonos or Naxos, island-hop around Croatia's Hvar and Bra?, or spend late evenings dining on tapas and watching the sunset along Spain's Costa del Sol. July is peak season, so expect higher prices and busy transport in popular areas. Weather snapshot: Hot and sunny across southern Europe; warm in central and northern destinations, although rain is still possible. Where to go: Belgium, Greece, Croatia, Spain Budget: High Best for: Festival lovers, beach travelers and families August - Edinburgh Fringe and Mediterranean Escapes August is when Europe fully commits to sunshine, swimming, and very late dinners. Each August, the Edinburgh Festival Fringe fills venues across the city with theater, comedy, music, and other performances. Head to Crete or Corfu for sandy beaches and warm Aegean waters, sail between Hvar and Bra? in Croatia, or explore Spain's Costa Brava between seaside towns. If you want culture without giving up sunshine, Lisbon and Porto are excellent choices. Summer in Europe is busiest, so expect crowded beaches, busy ferries, and higher hotel prices. Weather snapshot: Typically hot around the Mediterranean and pleasantly warm farther north, with occasional heat waves possible. Where to go: Edinburgh, Greece, Croatia, Spain Budget: High Best for: Festivals, beach holidays and families September - Oktoberfest, Wine Country and Golden Weather September may be Europe's most useful month because summer warmth often lingers while peak-season crowds begin to thin. In Munich, Oktoberfest fills Theresienwiese with enormous beer tents, Bavarian dishes, live brass music, fairground rides and traditional costumes. In Greece, swim off Naxos or Crete, while Italy calls you to explore Tuscany's vineyards, Rome's ancient landmarks, or the Amalfi Coast without July's intensity. Weather snapshot: Warm, often summery conditions continue in southern Europe, while central and northern regions begin to cool. Where to go: Munich, Italy, Greece, Portugal Budget: Moderate-high around major events Best for: Foodies, couples and festival travelers October - Autumn Colors, Wine and Comfort Food October is ideal if you want Tuscan vineyards, Bavaria's colorful forests and leisurely lunches with a glass of local wine. Autumn in Europe is especially beautiful around Chianti in Italy, Bordeaux in France, and the Moselle Valley in Germany, where vineyards take on rich seasonal colors. In Austria, explore the forests around Salzburg before settling into a comfortable traditional restaurant. Cooler temperatures also make walking through Rome, Paris, and Vienna far more comfortable than during the summer rush. Weather snapshot: Mild in Mediterranean destinations but increasingly cool, wet, and autumnal farther north. Where to go: Italy, France, Germany, Austria Budget: Moderate Best for: Foodies, photographers and couples November - Quiet Cities and the Start of Christmas Season November is quieter because the summer crowds are gone and the main Christmas season has not yet taken over. In Prague, explore Prague Castle, Charles Bridge and the Old Town Square, then warm up with coffee in a traditional café. In Vienna, visit Schönbrunn Palace, the Belvedere and the Kunsthistorisches Museum. Towards the end of the month, Christmas markets open at Vienna's Rathausplatz and Schönbrunn Palace while Strasbourg prepares its famous festive market. Autumn in Europe is fading, making November a good month for slower, less crowded city breaks. Weather snapshot: Cool to cold and often damp, with shorter days and the first wintry conditions in northern and mountain destinations. Where to go: Prague, Vienna, Munich, Lisbon Budget: Low-moderate Best for: Budget travelers and culture lovers December - Christmas Markets and Alpine Magic December is when you see winter in Europe, with its historic squares turning into glowing winter scenes. In Vienna, browse the Christmas market at Rathausplatz for handicrafts, seasonal treats, and hot punch, while Prague's Old Town Square pairs market stalls with its illuminated medieval buildings. In Strasbourg, explore the city's Christmas markets around Place Broglie and Place Kléber. For skiing, head to Zermatt in Switzerland or Innsbruck in Austria. Weather snapshot: Cold and potentially snowy in northern Europe and the Alps; generally cool and damp in central Europe, with milder weather around the Mediterranean. Where to go: Vienna, Prague, Munich, Strasbourg, Swiss Alps Budget: Moderate-high Best for: Families, couples, Christmas lovers and skiers There is no one best time to visit Europe, and that is its charm. Choose spring for flowers, summer for beaches and festivals, autumn for food and colors, or winter for snow and Christmas markets. Pick the month that fits your travel style, pack accordingly, and let Europe surprise you. This article was published in partnership with WanderOn Experiences Pvt Ltd.

item.title: Why Weekend Getaways Also Need Basic Travel Protection
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 4.99
Weekend trips may be brief, but illness, delays, baggage problems, or an unexpected change of plans can still disrupt them. Travel insurance for weekend trips can help limit the financial impact of covered events if the policy is consistent with the destination, bookings, transportation, and planned activities. Travel Delays Can Reduce Most of the Trip A weekend getaway usually follows a tight schedule. Travelers may leave Friday evening and return Sunday night. A delayed flight, train, or connection can consume much of the vacation. Some policies may cover eligible expenses from covered delays, such as extra accommodation, meals, or alternative transport. The exact benefit depends on the reason, duration, and policy terms. Sudden Illness Can Occur During a Short Stay Health problems are not limited to long vacations. A traveler may experience food-related illness, fever, injury, or other medical concerns when away. Reaching a doctor in an unfamiliar place may require quick decisions. Basic travel protection may cover emergency medical expenses during the journey. Travelers should check the geographical scope, benefit limits, and claim procedure before departure. This is especially important when visiting places where known medical facilities are distant. Baggage Delays Can Affect the Entire Break Many people carry only a small bag for a weekend trip. Even a short baggage delay can leave them without clothes, toiletries, medicine, or other essentials. A suitable policy may provide benefits for delayed or lost checked baggage, subject to its conditions. Travelers should keep baggage tags, boarding passes, receipts, and written reports from the transportation provider, as these records may support the claim. Prepaid Bookings May Not Be Recoverable Weekend plans often include advance payments for hotels, transportation, guided activities, or local experiences. When illness, a family emergency, or another covered event prevents travel, some bookings may not be refundable. Trip cancellation benefits may help with eligible prepaid expenses when the reason meets policy conditions. Travelers should read the approved reasons carefully and understand the required documents and notification timeline. Road Journeys Can Face Unforeseen Interruptions Not every weekend getaway involves air travel. Many travelers drive to nearby hill stations, beaches, heritage towns, or nature destinations. Road closures, poor weather, vehicle trouble, or an accident can interrupt the journey. Travelers should consider the complete itinerary, including transportation and planned activities. Coverage for delays, accidents, or emergency assistance depends on the policy, whereas ordinary vehicle breakdowns may require separate roadside assistance coverage. Short Trips Often Have Fixed Budgets Weekend breaks are usually planned within a set budget. An unplanned hotel stay, replacement ticket, or medical bill may affect the entire spending plan. The best travel insurance for a weekend journey isn't necessarily the policy with the longest list of benefits. It is the one that fits the destination, booking value, transport arrangements, and travelers' likely needs. Adventure Activities May Need Extra Attention A brief getaway may include trekking, cycling, water sports, or other outdoor activities. These plans can change the type of protection required. Travelers should check whether the selected activity is included and whether additional conditions apply. The activity provider's safety instructions should be followed. Insurance may offer financial support for covered situations but does not replace careful planning. Assistance Can Help in an Unfamiliar Place An unexpected situation becomes harder to manage when the traveler is unfamiliar with the local area. Finding a nearby hospital, arranging transport, or understanding the next step in a claim may take time. Some policies provide access to assistance services during the insured trip. Keeping the policy number, emergency contact details, and digital documents on the phone can make communication easier when help is needed. Quick access to this information also reduces uncertainty during an urgent situation. Before departure, keep digital and printed copies of your policy and other essential travel insurance documents. Final Thoughts Weekend getaways may be short, but they still involve bookings, transport, health concerns, and personal belongings. A minor disruption can affect a major part of the trip because there is little time to adjust the schedule. Basic travel protection can provide financial support for covered emergencies and travel-related problems. Travelers should review the benefits, limits, documentation requirements, and policy conditions before departure to ensure the selected cover suits the actual journey. This article was published in partnership with HDFC ERGO General Insurance Company Limited.

Organizations often design benefits that are easy to join but hard to get employees to stay committed—think carpool programs, wellness apps, or behavioral incentives. New research finds that...

item.title: What Happens When AI Starts Doing Business with AI?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.51
Summary. As AI agents increasingly interact with one another on commercial platforms, firms need new rules governing what those agents can see, decide, and do. In a controlled AI-to-AI simulation covering In late 2025, Perplexity’s Comet browser began logging into shoppers’ Amazon accounts and buying on their behalf. Amazon treated it as an intruder. It blocked the agent and when Perplexity slipped past the block within a day, Amazon took the dispute to federal court. WeChat drew the line differently. After shutting out ByteDance’s Doubao assistant, which used system-level access to navigate WeChat without permission, Tencent later opened what it describes as an agent-to-agent channel to selected assistants from Huawei, Xiaomi, and others to send messages and place calls. Under this arrangement, an external agent translates a user’s request into a structured instruction and passes it through a Tencent-controlled interface to WeChat, which executes the action inside its own environment. Tencent controls which agents can connect, which functions they can invoke, and what data and execution remain inside WeChat. In other words, one platform shut the door to AI agents outright; the other unlocked it on its own terms.

item.title: Inside McDonald’s New Strategy
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 4.50
Summary. McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski joined HBR editor at large Adi Ignatius for a wide-ranging conversation about the company’s new strategy, McDonald’s > Few companies have navigated shifting consumer expectations as consistently as McDonald’s. As inflation, changing dining habits, and intensifying competition are reshaping the restaurant industry, the company is continuing to evolve its strategy while serving millions of customers today.

item.title: Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.87
Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For Summary. Traditional “tough” questions often elicit polished talking points rather than candid answers. A more revealing approach is the curveball: a question that is closely tied to what We’re all taught to ask tough questions. Interviewers are coached to use open-ended prompts to get beyond rehearsed answers. Managers press for specifics when employees speak in generalities. Journalists and negotiators follow up when someone evades the point. The aim is the same: to uncover information the other person may be reluctant to reveal.

item.title: You Need to Understand Your Employees’ Caregiving Responsibilities
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.50
You Need to Understand Your Employees’ Caregiving Responsibilities Summary. Employees regularly balance work with caregiving responsibilities, whether it is child care, eldercare, or caring for another family member. Yet many organizations lack visibility into who their Most of us are caregivers. Seventy-three percent of all U.S. employees, and 71% of employees globally, identify as caregivers with responsibilities to look after children, aging parents, or other family members. Fifty-four percent of employees in their 40s identify as sandwiched caregivers, providing for the needs of parents aged 65 and older while also raising children or providing for a young adult child 18 years and older.

item.title: Do Your B2B Customers See the Value You Deliver?
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 3.00
Summary. Many B2B companies suffer from a “value gap”: Customers benefit from their products but cannot clearly measure, articulate, or defend that value to stakeholders within their companies. Most B2B companies have long harbored a costly blind spot: a gap between the value they create for customers and the value those customers can see, measure, and defend. For many, early strong growth masks the problem until sales slow or competitive alternatives drag down margins. Closing that gap is an executive decision—and one most leadership teams have never explicitly made.

item.title: How Japan’s Oldest Companies Navigate Uncertainty
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 2.76
Summary. In the period from 1994 to 2024, Japan’s family businesses matched or exceeded the returns of peers in the United States, Germany, and Canada while taking on far less risk. Their advantage In 1945, an air raid destroyed the main Tokyo factory of Toraya, a leading Japanese confectioner since the 16th century. Despite the ongoing world war, the company began rebuilding almost immediately; later, even when sugar became scarce and Japan’s future uncertain, it kept operating, experimenting, pressing on. The logic was simple: Toraya existed to make sweets and would continue to do so no matter what was happening around it. Today, with three factories and some 80 stores across Japan as well as a boutique in Paris, it still does.

item.title: The Store Isn’t Dead—but the Merchant Model Is
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 2.63
Summary. The decline of many retailers reflects not the death of the physical store but the failure of the traditional merchant model, which requires retailers to forecast demand, own inventory, and absorb Walk through a department store at the end of a season and the signs tell a familiar story: 40% off! 60% off! Clearance! Retailers often treat these markdowns as a tactical problem, the result of the wrong product, the wrong promotion, or bad weather effects. But they are better understood as confessions. They reveal the downsides of the traditional retailing model. The retailer acted as a merchant, committed to inventory before demand was known, absorbed the risk of being wrong, and then paid for that error in margin erosion and brand equity dilution. Under this merchant model, retailers routinely take on more risk than they can handle.

item.title: Home Assistant 2026.9 finally makes it easier to understand and control your smart home
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.84
Home Assistant 2026.9 update is out today. And it aims to solve the everyday guesswork that comes with running a smart home. The latest release answers questions like why an automation fired, which entities need your attention, or seeing how Matter devices are connected. The September update also has several other changes that make the open-source home automation platform more polished. Home Assistant gets better at showing you what’s happening Smarter alerts and long-overdue answer to ‘Why’ Home Assistant’s built-in security dashboard is getting two additions with version 2026.9. An Active alerts section now appears when something genuinely needs your attention. You get to decide which entities can trigger an alert and select the level of severity as Alert or Warning. So, a door left open doesn’t get treated with the same urgency as a smoke alarm going off. This way, the section disappears entirely when everything is working fine. The second addition inside the security dashboard is a new Favorites section. It lets you keep your frequently checked sensors, doors, locks, and other devices at the top of the dashboard so they’re never buried, and you don’t have to hunt for them. Another noteworthy feature with this update makes the Activity log more useful. Previously, you could see what changed but not why it changed. This meant guessing which automation or event was responsible for triggering it and then digging through the traces manually. Now, each Activity entry opens a detailed view laying out the chain of events, so when something gets triggered unexpectedly, you can see which automation or script was involved. Along with this, History and Activity also get a Sources pane to filter across both views by entity type or integration. Meanwhile, Tile Cards get three new control options—a light effect selection for compatible lights, fan-speed control for vacuums, and expanded target humidity for climate entities. Matter and Modbus devices are easier to manage A less intimidating experience Home Assistant is making it easier to set up Modbus devices like solar inverters, heat pumps, and energy meters. Previously, it meant manually configuring registers in YAML, which can be quite technical for beginners. In the 2026.9 update, integrations that understand how a device communicates with Modbus can now build that configuration through the UI instead of doing it yourself. If you use any Matter-enabled devices, this update makes it easier to see how everything is connected. Previously, there was a separate Matter Server web interface, but the latest release brings a proper Matter network map directly to the main interface. It gives you a topology view of Matter and Thread devices, showing how they connect to your Wi-Fi and Thread network. Taken together, Home Assistant 2026.9 gives you more information and takes more configuration work off your hands. The stable release is now available. Source: Home Assistant

item.title: How car A/C works, and the 5 tricks to keep it working
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.79
Most people don't think about their car's A/C until it stops working, and by then the repair bill is already uncomfortable. This is something you either crank up in July or forget about entirely until next summer. The problem is that neglect is exactly what kills it. A lot of the failures that send people to the shop are easily preventable if you start adding in a few habits. You need to keep your car A/C running Neglect is what breaks your car A/C Running your car's A/C for like 10 minutes a week, even in winter, is probably the cheapest and easiest way to keep it from dying on you early. It sounds weird to blast cold air when it's freezing out or like you’re wasting gas. But the whole climate control loop is a closed system that kind of needs regular use to stay healthy. The refrigerant absorbs and releases heat as it cycles through the system, and it carries the compressor oil around the system. That oil lubricates the fast-moving pistons and bearings inside the compressor and keeps all the rubber hoses, O-rings, and shaft seals soft and conditioned. When the system sits unused for a long time, gravity pulls that oil away from the seals. Leave it dry over a winter, and those rubber parts start shrinking, hardening, and cracking. Once micro-cracks form, you get tiny leak paths and pressurized refrigerant escapes. It doesn't take much time, and if you are a fan of lowering your windows instead of using the A/C, just make a habit of turning it on once a week. It’s worth the lowered EV range. Clean the junk out of your condenser Blocked airflow stops the system from cooling down The condenser sits at the front of your engine bay, in front of the radiator, and it's basically a cross-flow heat exchanger. Its job is to dump heat by taking superheated, high-pressure refrigerant gas from the compressor and releasing it into the outside air so the gas condenses back into a high-pressure liquid. To do that properly, it needs a ton of airflow. But since it's mounted forward-facing, the fins get hammered by bugs, dust, leaves, road grit, and a whole lot more. Those fins are packed super tight, so you want to clear that stuff off regularly. If you don't, it will clog, and then it won't work as well. You'll end up having to turn the A/C up because it won't feel as cold. Just check the front grille, use a soft brush or a low-pressure hose, and wash out the junk. Make sure to keep the water pressure low so you don't bend the fins. Change your cabin air filter on time A clogged filter chokes the airflow You should replace your cabin air filter every 12,000 to 15,000 miles. If you don't, your HVAC system basically starts choking. The whole heating and cooling loop depends on getting a steady flow of air, and once that filter cakes up, the airflow drops hard. A filter works the way it's named. It takes away the little stuff, and the more it adds up, the less airflow goes through. A clogged filter actually gets in the way of how much air can move across the evaporator core. Something most people don't think about is that a clean filter also keeps mold spores, dust, and allergens out of the climate-controlled housing. Eventually, you get that musty, stale smell coming through the vents every time you turn the AC on. It smells like old water, and it tells you that you desperately need to change your cabin filter. Just keep in mind that this isn't always the case for that smell; sometimes you just need to let the A/C go for like 10 minutes, and the smell will leave if your filter isn't the problem. Turn on your defroster during the winter Defrost mode runs the compressor to dry the air So windshield defrost isn't just a way to blow hot air on the glass to make it easier to look through. It's actually a whole climate control sequence that uses the AC system to pull moisture out of the air. When warm, humid air inside the car hits cold glass, it condenses, and suddenly you can't see. So the car runs the air across the freezing evaporator core first, then heats it. That cold surface forces the water vapor to condense out of the air before it ever reaches the windshield. Then the now-dry air gets routed past the heater core to warm it up. So you're blasting dry air at the glass, which acts like a sponge and clears the fog way faster than normal heat. That defrost mode actually runs your AC compressor even when the temp is set to full heat. Which sounds weird, but that's actually clever, because it keeps the system lubricated during winter when you never touch the AC. So don't hesitate to turn on that defroster. Keep your car battery in good shape Weak batteries mess with the cooling system Your car's AC is tied into the whole electrical system that is already really picky about voltage stability. Your cabin cooling setup pulls a lot of current; the blower motor, radiator fans, compressor clutch — all of that needs steady power. One thing I learned recently is that a low battery can mess with a lot of your car's systems. I had a battery I bought from AAA that died within three years, and I didn't assume it was the battery since that's a short time to last. Yet, my air conditioning wasn't spewing out air in some ports. I thought this would be a $1,000+ repair. However, when the battery that AAA sold me died much earlier than it should have, I replaced it with one from AutoZone. Afterward, my air conditioning worked just fine again. So it turns out that having battery issues can hurt your A/C a lot more than you'd think. So, if your A/C has been great but you're still having issues like low airflow, your problem may be the battery. You'll still have to fix regular issues It's really this easy to keep your A/C running well. Just keep in mind that even a well-maintained A/C system will eventually need a refrigerant recharge or a compressor repair, since some wear is just a matter of time and mileage. These new habits won't make the system immortal. The battery one in particular is worth keeping in mind if your A/C starts acting strange and you can't figure out why.

item.title: These 4 Windows tools helped me regain 16.1GB of storage without deleting a single file
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.68
Running out of storage usually means one thing—hovering over the downloads folder with increasingly desperate intent and looking for anything you can move to an external drive. But unless you’ve genuinely run out of files to delete, the problem likely isn’t what you have; it’s how much space Windows is quietly using behind the scenes. It turns out that a surprising amount of storage is tied to temporary files, recovery data, old updates, and system clutter. The good thing is that you don’t need another PC cleaner because Windows already has a capable cleanup kit built-in. These are the four built-in Windows tools that helped me claw back 16.1GB of storage space that my computer was wasting, and not a single personal file went away in the process. Disk Cleanup The most useful button is the one most people miss Storage Sense and Temporary Files cover the everyday surface layer, but Disk Cleanup goes underneath it. This is a classic utility tool that ships with Windows and one that goes further by surfacing options that aren’t obvious in the Settings panel. Search for Disk Cleanup in the Start menu, select your system drive, and let it scan. The tool displays downloaded program files, temporary internet files, Recycle Bin contents, and other system files. At the bottom of the window is one specific button called “Clean up system files” that most people overlook. It offers deeper cleanup with two additional options—Windows Update Cleanup and, on PCs that have been upgraded, Previous Windows Installation(s). The former removes superseded files from installation packages that the system holds onto after update completion, whereas the latter contains files from previous installations if you want to roll back to that version. Both of these can be an easy source of several gigabytes of storage space. So, unless you want to roll back to a past update or troubleshoot a recent one, they’re dead weight. On my machine, this step returned 8.48GB on its own. Storage Sense Keeps things automatically under control Storage Sense is turned off by default if you have an older PC running an older version of Windows. It is the easiest place to begin because it automatically cleans temporary files, empties the Recycle Bin on schedule, and sweeps out stale files without touching anything you’ve intentionally saved. To use Storage Sense, head to Settings > System > Storage > Storage Sense, and then flip the toggle on. You can set how often you want the tool to run, when the Recycle Bin should be cleared, and how long files can sit in downloads before being removed. For everyday junk that builds up between sessions, Storage Sense runs quietly in the background and handles it without you having to remember. I set mine to run every 14 days, and it freed up 1.86GB the first time I ran it. Temporary files Reveals hidden storage hogs Temporary files, as the name suggests, break down the disposable data Windows has accumulated. This includes cached thumbnails, Delivery Optimization files left over from Windows update downloads, error reports, and residual data from features you may not even use. Go to Settings > System > Storage > Temporary Files, and Windows lays out everything by category with a size estimate beside each entry. That makes it easy to see what's taking up room on your PC. Pay attention to categories such as Downloads before selecting them because the folder can contain files you actually want to keep. I prefer this approach the most instead of blindly running a cleanup utility because I’m informed about what is going away and how much space my PC will reclaim. Storage Sense and Temporary Files cover a lot of the same ground. Don't be surprised if the latter cleans up the system more lightly than expected, because it means that the former has been doing its job. I use Storage Sense for automatic maintenance, while Temporary Files gives me control over what gets removed. System Restore Shrink your safety net instead of deleting it Unlike other tools here, System Restore is basically an undo button for Windows system changes, like when a driver, update, or application causes problems. That makes restore points a sound precaution. However, it becomes far less useful when left unchecked because Windows can reserve a sizable chunk of your drive for them. The good thing is that System Restore lets you control how much space it claims going forward. Search for “Create a restore point” > Open the System Protection tab > Select the system drive > Click Configure. You'll see two figures: Current Usage, which is the amount of space your existing restore points occupy, and Max Usage, which is the space you’re allowing Windows to use. So, here you can put a hard ceiling on how much room restore points can consume. On my PC, the existing restore points were using 17.6GB, after which I lowered the maximum allocation to 5 percent or 11.86GB. So, this gave me 5.76GB of space back. It’s important to note that System Restore doesn’t back up personal files; it is primarily designed to restore the system files, drivers, registry settings, and other parts of Windows to an earlier state. None of these tools delete your personal files or require you to remove them. They simply clear up what Windows quietly accumulated on its own. Run all four on a machine that hasn't seen a cleanup in a year or two, and you might be surprised at how much breathing room you can get back.

item.title: How the humble parallel port outlived everything that was supposed to replace it
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.64
The parallel port is gone as of the time I'm writing this. But its demise was long and drawn-out, even as supposedly better alternatives came along and tried to take its place. Here's how it finally met its ultimate demise, long after it was supposed to. What's a parallel port, anyway? A look back at the connector that carried computing's data highway I'm not sure how many of you are too young to know what a parallel port is—I'm personally in my 20s, but I played around with my fair share of old computers back in the day and still do. But before USB became the default way to plug almost anything into a computer, the parallel port handled that job. Physically, it showed up as a wide, 25-pin D-shaped connector on the back of desktop PCs, commonly labeled LPT1 or LPT2. Its defining trait was right there in the name: unlike serial ports, which sent data one bit at a time down a single wire, a parallel port pushed multiple bits simultaneously across separate wires, one byte at a time. That made it noticeably faster than serial connections for the tasks it was built for, mainly, driving printers. The standard traces back to Centronics, a printer manufacturer that developed the interface in the 1970s to connect its printers to computers more efficiently. IBM adopted a version of it for the original PC, and it became a de facto standard across the industry long before any formal specification existed. That changed in the early 1990s with IEEE 1284, which codified the electrical and mechanical details and introduced faster, bidirectional modes like EPP and ECP, allowing data to flow both ways rather than just from computer to printer. Printers were the dominant use case, but far from the only one. Parallel ports also connected external hard drives, scanners, Zip drives, and even early network adapters in pinch situations. Software developers relied on them too, since the port's direct access to hardware made it a convenient way to attach copy-protection dongles or debug embedded systems. How did it last so long? Legacy hardware and industrial reliability kept it relevant Parallel ports should have disappeared not long after USB arrived in the late 1990s. USB was faster, simpler to use, hot-swappable, and didn't require a bulky cable with thumbscrews on either end. Yet parallel ports kept shipping on motherboards well into the 2000s, and in some corners of the industry, they never really left. The reasons come down to inertia, cost, and the specific demands of environments where replacing working equipment wasn't a priority. A huge installed base of printers, particularly dot-matrix and early laser models used in offices, point-of-sale systems, and warehouses, depended on parallel connections. Businesses had little incentive to replace functioning hardware just because a newer port style existed elsewhere on the machine. Receipt printers, label printers, and industrial control equipment often used parallel interfaces specifically because of their simplicity and direct, low-latency connection to hardware, something USB's more complex protocol stack didn't always replicate cleanly, especially in early implementations. Manufacturing and automation are where the parallel port really dug in. CNC machines, PLCs, and other factory-floor equipment frequently used the parallel port's pins for direct digital input and output, a technique still referenced in hobbyist CNC circles today. Because these systems were built around the port's specific timing and signaling behavior, swapping to USB wasn't a simple driver update; it often meant redesigning the control software or the hardware interface entirely. There was also a software dependency problem. Countless line-of-business applications, especially those tied to specialized printers or measurement equipment, were written with direct calls to the parallel port's I/O addresses. Rewriting or replacing that software carried real cost and risk, so companies kept the old ports around, and PC makers kept including at least one for compatibility, long after most people had stopped using them for anything else. How it finally died USB, integration costs, and shrinking motherboards sealed its fate By the mid-2000s, the parallel port's decline had become difficult to ignore. USB had matured into a genuinely universal standard, with USB 2.0 offering speeds that made the old parallel interface look sluggish by comparison, and manufacturers had refined driver support to the point where plugging in a device just worked, without the configuration headaches that sometimes accompanied early USB peripherals. Printer makers shifted their product lines almost entirely to USB, and consumer demand for parallel-equipped devices dried up accordingly. Motherboard manufacturers followed the market. Including a parallel port meant dedicating physical space on the board, adding a Super I/O chip to handle the interface, and paying for the connector itself, all for a feature an increasingly small share of buyers used. As PCs got smaller and slimmer, particularly with the rise of compact desktops and laptops, that tradeoff stopped making sense. By the early 2010s, most consumer motherboards had dropped the port entirely, and laptops had abandoned it years earlier. Operating systems played a role, too. Successive versions of Windows gradually reduced native support and made parallel port configuration more cumbersome, nudging remaining holdouts toward USB-to-parallel adapters instead of native ports. Those adapters worked well enough for basic printing but often failed with software that expected direct, low-level access to the port, which caused real problems for the industrial and embedded systems still depending on that behavior. Today, native parallel ports survive mainly in specialized industrial PCs, older CNC setups, and equipment where replacing the control software isn't worth the cost. For everyone else, the port lives on only as a USB adapter or a memory of unplugging a printer cable with two thumbscrews and far too much friction for something so mundane. A connector that refused to disappear quietly The parallel port outlasted its intended replacements not through superiority, but through sheer entrenchment in printers, industrial control systems, and legacy software that made switching more trouble than it was worth.

item.title: You will never own the definitive version of a movie
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.36
What you see up there are my two copies of Robocop. One is the version that people saw in theaters, and the other is the version that director Paul Verhoeven wanted people to see in theaters, but had to edit slightly to get past the ratings board. The differences between the two cuts are very small. In fact, if you hadn't seen the theatrical release a million times as I have, you might not even notice. But a more interesting question is which of these two movies is the definitive one? Is it the one that people first saw and put it on the map? Or the original vision of its creators? The truth is that there probably is no such thing as a "definitive" version of a movie. Blade Runner proves that “the definitive cut” is subjective This director never yells "Cut!" Blade Runner has existed as a workprint, US theatrical cut, international theatrical cut, 1992 Director’s Cut, and 2007 Final Cut, with meaningful differences in narration, violence, footage, and the ending. This famous cyberpunk pillar sparked plenty of controversy at its theatrical release. The producers thought the movie was too hard to understand and that audiences just wouldn't get it. So, they strong-armed Ridley Scott and Harrison Ford into recording narration that played throughout the film. Spelling out what viewers were seeing and how they were meant to interpret events. Ford's delivery of the narration is widely considered flat and poorly delivered. There's a fan theory that Ford did this on purpose to sabotage the narration being included, but he's denied that. However, Scott and Ford are on record as hating the narration. The 1992 Director's Cut rips out the voice-over, adds a unicorn dream sequence that has deep implications for the plot, and gets rid of a stupid, tonally-deaf happy ending that was also studio-mandated. So the 1992 cut of the film ends up being a much better movie, despite them leaving the awful Vangelis soundtrack in place. I'd love a "silent" cut where you could turn off the wailing synths. In 2007, we got The Final Cut, which keeps the positive changes from the 1992 version, extends the unicorn sequence, restores more violent versions of scenes cut from the original, and even includes a reshoot of a scene where the stunt double is too obvious. The special effects were updated, the video and audio cleaned up, and that's how you get this version. Personally, the 1992 cut is what I prefer to watch, but which is definitive? Ridley Scott says it's the 2007 version, but that's just his opinion. Making changes to the visual effects and altering the video and audio could be seen as inauthentic. Like painting over a historic mural, and that's something that means I can't consider it the definitive version. In the end, you just have to own all three collectively to have it all. Star Wars shows how a movie can be replaced by its revision Shots fired! We just don't know who started it George Lucas is notorious for going back and changing things in his Star Wars films. The original Star Wars trilogy has been repeatedly changed through new effects, altered dialogue, different color grading, additional scenes, and infamous revisions such as Greedo shooting first. For a long time, the only way to see the original theatrical cuts discs). The original cuts were included as a non-anamorphic bonus feature in the 2006 DVD release box set, but the proper wide-screen version of the movie people saw back in 1977 has not been released on modern formats. Disney announced on the Star Wars website that the original theatrical release would return to theaters for the film's 50th anniversary, so there is perhaps a (new) hope of getting a Blu-ray or even streaming release afterward. What is the definitive version of a Star Wars movie? Even George Lucas couldn't tell you. A movie collection is really an archive of competing versions I spent quite a bit of money to get my hands on the limited edition Blu-ray release of Neon Genesis Evangelion. Why? Because this version includes the original '90s English dub, which I consider crucial to the show's authenticity as I remember it from when I first saw it. At the same time, this version doesn't include the original ending theme because of licensing issues. Which means that if I ever get the opportunity to buy the original DVD releases, I'd likely go for it. Ending up with multiple versions of the same series. Neither is truly definitive, and as long as more than one version of a movie or show exists, there will never be a single version you can buy that's everything to everyone. The cynic in me sees this as a way to make more money from fans, but in the end, even great artists painted multiple versions of their most famous paintings too.

item.title: I traveled the world to visit an SSD factory and learned why they keep getting more expensive
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.76
As a tech journalist, it's easy for me to go ahead and criticize RAM and SSD makers for price hikes, and ignore the reasons as to why that might be happening. In reality, there's a ton of stuff that goes in our storage and memory—and I've personally been taking that for granted for too long. Now that I've gone and checked out Lexar's facilities in China by myself, I have a better understanding of why the increased demand from data centers has made all of our everyday tech more expensive all of a sudden. I was invited by Lexar with a group of journalists to visit the company's various facilities in Shanghai, Suzhou, Zhongshan, and Shenzhen, China, from June 8th to June 12th, as part of the company's "Behind the Build" media tour for its 30th anniversary. Lexar had absolutely no input in the content of this article. How is an SSD made? Inside the cleanroom where memory becomes storage Before touring the Longforce Production Line in Suzhou, my group had to change into full cleanroom suits and pass through an air shower designed to blast away any dust or fiber that might contaminate the line. That precaution alone tells you something about how sensitive this process is. Longforce is a joint venture between Longsys, Lexar's parent company, and Taiwan's PTI, and it functions as the manufacturing and packaging arm for both automotive and consumer storage products. Throughout the trip, Lexar was pretty proud to tell us that it's one of the few companies in the world that handles the entire process from when a wafer enters the factory to when an SSD, SD card, or RAM stick is shipped to consumers. That process starts with slicing the wafer into dies, and mounting said dies and a controller chip, which Lexar designs in-house, onto a printed circuit board, followed by wire bonding and encapsulation. What impressed me most wasn't the assembly itself, which is all handled on Longforce's facility in Suzhou, but the testing that follows it. And to see that, the tour continued to Longsys's Zhongshan campus, near Shenzhen, where the company runs its innovation and quality labs. Rather than pulling random samples from a batch, every single unit on this line gets evaluated for sustained write speeds, power consumption, and how it handles sector failures. From there, drives are subjected to thermal extremes, moisture exposure, physical shock, and X-ray inspection before anything ships. This facility is also where new products get validated against real-world devices rather than lab benchmarks alone—the company had a huge room full of pretty much anything users could buy that could take an SSD or an SD card, be it a console, a drone, a smartphone, or even a smart home display. One of the things engineers showed us was a design that combines the controller, NAND chips, and power management into a single unified chip, shrinking a standard M.2 2280 drive down to the far smaller M.2 2230 footprint without sacrificing capacity. That technology has since shipped as the Lexar Play X, a PCIe 4.0 drive rated for read speeds up to 7,400 MB/s and write speeds up to 6,500 MB/s. Seeing this process with my own eyes made it clear that an SSD isn't just a chip in a case. It's the product of sourcing, precision assembly, and exhaustive validation, all of which cost money well before a single unit reaches a store shelf. Why do they keep getting more expensive, then? AI data centers are eating the world's chip supply Touring a factory built for volume made the current price surge feel almost contradictory, until I looked at where that volume is actually going. The core issue isn't a shortage of factories. It's that NAND flash and DRAM production capacity is being redirected toward AI infrastructure at a scale the consumer market simply can't compete with. TrendForce has projected client SSD contract prices to rise at least 40% quarter over quarter in early 2026, with tight supply expected to persist through the full year, and that forecast has already been exceeded in practice. The mechanics behind this are straightforward once you see them laid out. Enterprise SSDs became the single largest NAND flash application segment in 2026, overtaking both client SSDs and smartphones. A single high-end AI GPU can require roughly 16TB of NAND storage to operate efficiently, and a full AI server rack can demand over a thousand terabytes of NAND capacity. Cloud providers buying at that scale simply outbid the consumer channel for the same wafers Manufacturers have responded by chasing the more profitable business. AI infrastructure consumes roughly three times the wafer capacity per gigabyte compared to conventional memory, and every wafer diverted to high-bandwidth memory for AI accelerators reduces the supply available for standard DRAM and NAND. Some brands have gone further and wound down consumer SSD lines entirely to focus on enterprise contracts. Remember that the factories building your consumer SSDs are now also the same factories building the hardware for those data centers. Standing on a production floor that was serving both markets, it was easy to see which side of that line is currently winning the allocation fight. Is it getting better anytime soon? Don't expect a price drop before 2027 ... or before the next decade Every person I spoke with in China framed this as a structural shift rather than a passing shortage, and the market data backs that up. Lexar itself wouldn't comment too much on concrete price predictions—the company's representatives stated that semiconductor pricing is cyclical and unpredictable, and that its way of staying competitive was focusing on its own internal R&D. Supply tightness is expected to persist through the rest of the year and into next year, with AI-related demand continuing to grow as a share of total NAND consumption and no incentive for foundries to redirect capacity away from high-bandwidth memory toward standard NAND. That's a meaningfully different situation than the cyclical downturns the memory industry has weathered before, where prices eventually corrected once demand cooled. Part of what makes this cycle stickier is that the biggest buyers have already locked in their access. Cloud giants including Microsoft, Google, and AWS have secured long-term NAND contracts, in some cases already negotiating supply allocations for 2027, which leaves less room for spot-market relief even if demand elsewhere softens. Overall NAND demand is projected to grow 20 to 22 percent year over year while supply grows only 15 to 17 percent, a gap that isn't expected to close in the near term. There is one wildcard worth watching. Chinese domestic NAND producers, particularly YMTC, are expanding their own manufacturing capacity, which could eventually loosen the market from a different direction than the established Korean and American suppliers. But new fab capacity takes years to come online at a meaningful scale, and nothing I saw or heard in Suzhou or Zhongshan suggested that relief is coming within the next few quarters. If you need a drive now, buying sooner rather than later is the more rational move. Waiting for 2024-era pricing to return isn't a strategy anyone in this industry is currently betting on. The real cost of an SSD The way an SSD is made is heavily documented online, but it's one thing to read about it and a different thing to see it by yourself. This trip was an eye-opener in many ways

item.title: Cheap smart LEDs look tacky, here's 3 easy ways to give them more ambient elegance
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.69
LED strip lighting is all the rage, and for good reason. It’s cheap, versatile, easily integrates with smart home platforms, and it’s easier than ever to make your own. But LED strips don’t always look good, and sometimes you need a little help to get that finished look. Hide LEDs for an instant glow-up Do this and you’re 90% of the way there The biggest mistake you can make with LED strip lighting is leaving the LEDs on display. These small, intense beads of light do a great job of illuminating your home, but they’re arguably not much to look at (unless you like them—in which case, you do you). For me, LED strips need some sort of diffusion, and the easiest way of doing this is to simply bounce them off a surface like a wall or countertop. Thankfully, the fix is remarkably easy: hide the LED as best as you can so that you get the benefit of the ambiance, without the harshness of the diodes. One way to achieve this is to place your LED strips strategically. My house is old enough to have picture rails, so I could feasibly hide thin LED strips by attaching them to the top of the picture rail. If you’re using LED lighting to illuminate an area like a kitchen worktop, you can mount them under a cupboard out of view. Sometimes, this isn’t enough. Adding a small lip to any edges where the lights are still visible can do the trick. Do this with a cheap piece of wood and finish or paint it to match whatever it is you’ve attached it to. Hide the LEDs, and you’re mostly there, depending on the density of your strips. Add diffusers to mask LED density Turn harsh light into a warm glow If you can’t avoid having your LED strips on display, or you don’t want to hide them, adding diffusers is a great idea. These sit on top of your LED strips and scatter the light, which can have a transformative effect. The main benefit of a diffuser is that the light is more evenly dispersed, which creates more of a glow. The light will be less harsh and your space more evenly lit. This makes for a gentler light, which works well in spaces like bathrooms, bedrooms, and walk-in wardrobes. The other benefit is that individual LEDs will be much harder (and sometimes impossible) to see. The effect is more pronounced with denser LED strips, where the gap between each diode is shorter. The idea here is to make your LED strip look like one long, neon-like light source. You can get really creative with this effect, especially if your lights are for more than just functional illumination. For example, creating sound-reactive lighting with WLED for your next party, or designing some sort of cyberpunk-esque feature light in a shape of your choice. It’s also worth noting that the diffusion effect is beneficial to LED lighting in general, even if you do a good job of hiding your strips in the first place. For an even glow, consider adding cheap diffusers or more expensive “neonizer” designs. You can even have a go at 3D printing your own. Color-match white temperature for a consistent look Pair strips with each other and the light outside Something else that can really spoil the look of your LED strip setup is mismatched white temperature. This isn’t a problem for lighting that is meant to be moody and colorful, but if you have LED strips and scenes that are designed purely for illumination, getting the white balance right really makes the difference. Thankfully, this is pretty easy. All you need to do is design scenes within your smart home platform of choice that specify the same temperature, which is measured in kelvins (K). You’re probably going to want to match these to existing light sources in your home, like non-smart bulbs. The other way to do this is to use an integration like Adaptive Lighting for Home Assistant. This will change the temperature of select lights automatically, based on the location of the sun. You will see warm hues at the start and end of the day, and more neutral daylight in the middle of the day. Adaptive Lighting is also available in platforms like Apple Home. It works best for lights that are on all day, or that are used to complement natural light sources like skylight windows and solar tubes or sun tunnels. The best way to add LED strips to your home is to use WLED with an ESP32 microcontroller. Check out five WLED-powered projects you can build in a weekend. You can even use WLED to make your own TV Ambilight.

item.title: I built a better Spotify Wrapped in Excel—and you can too
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.57
For the past couple of years, Spotify Wrapped has left me underwhelmed. The insights it serves up never feel all that “insightful” — which is strange, because Spotify clearly has a mountain of data on my listening habits. So I decided to get my hands on all that data and build my own Spotify Wrapped. I requested my full listening data from Spotify and processed it myself in Excel to dig up the kind of insights Wrapped never gives me. Downloading my Spotify data It’s easier than you might think First, we need to get our hands on the data. The typical route is by using the Spotify API. Now, if you're a developer or tech-savvy enough to already know how that works, you don't need me to walk you through it. However, if you don’t want this to get too technical, here’s a much simpler alternative for regular users. Simply open the Spotify web player at open.spotify.com, click your profile icon, and go to your account. In Account settings, go to Security and Privacy, then Account Privacy. Scroll down, and you'll find the option to Download Your Data. By default, it only selects “Account data.” Uncheck that and select “Extended streaming history” instead — that's the one that gives you your lifetime streaming history, which is what unlocks all the useful insights. Now, click “Request Data,” and you should get an email asking you to confirm your data download request. While the website says the process can take up to 30 days, in my experience, it’s nowhere near that long. I requested my extended streaming history on August 26 at 4:30 a.m., and the download link landed in my inbox the next day, on August 27 at 4:36 a.m. I imagine the turnaround might depend on how much data is in your account. Mine was created back in March 2019 and has over 133,000 plays logged, which I'd consider a fairly big account, and it still only took a day. So that's roughly what you can expect. Importing the Spotify data into Excel What Spotify sends you isn’t quite legible — yet Once the download is ready, Spotify hands you a ZIP file. Unzip it, and you'll end up with a bunch of JSON files containing your streaming history. Spotify doesn’t hand you a ready-made spreadsheet, so the next job is importing all those JSON files into Excel yourself. The simplest way is by using Power Query. If you're already familiar with it, you can probably take it from here. If not, here's the step-by-step process: - Open Excel. - Create a new file, and save it first — call it "Spotify Wrapped" or whatever you like. - Go to the Data tab and click Get Data -> From Other Sources -> Blank Query. - In the Power Query window that opens, click Home -> Advanced Editor, delete everything there, and paste in the code snippet I'm sharing below. You'll find the code snippet to paste into the Advanced Editor at the bottom of this article for convenience. This part is important. Before you hit OK, there are two things you need to change in the code. First, set FolderPath to the specific folder where all your Spotify JSON files live. The second is the TZ_OffsetHours value, which tells the query how far your time zone is from UTC. Without this adjustment, all your listening times will be shifted, and you won't be able to accurately see when you were actually streaming. For reference, US Eastern is -5, and US Pacific is -8. After tweaking the code, click Done, then go to Home -> Close & Load -> Close & Load To, choose Table and New Worksheet, and hit OK. And that’s it; you’ve successfully imported all your Spotify data into Excel. Give it a couple of minutes if your history is huge — it took around 90 seconds for me, and then all 133,999 plays stretching back to March 2019 were sitting in the spreadsheet. Here's my Excel-powered Spotify Wrapped It might not be pretty — but it’s comprehensive With all the data in Excel, it's time to process it and pull out meaningful insights. Now, I won't claim to be the most creative person when it comes to data extraction, and I'm definitely not a graphic designer. But I had a clear vision of what I wanted to see, and I built it all with Excel PivotTables. First, the overview sheet shows total plays, total hours, music time versus podcast time, skip rates, and a year-by-year breakdown of it all. Then there's the listening clock, where I charted which hours of the day I listened to music, year by year — in 2022, for instance, most of my listening happened between 7 and 11 p.m. There's also a day-by-day breakdown along the same lines. Also, if you look at my listening clock, it suggests I listen to Spotify at basically all hours of the day. That's not actually true — it's a side effect of the aggregation. Because of my job, I shift through sleep cycles: sometimes I sleep during the day and work at night, other times it's the reverse. Aggregate years of that, and it looks like I never stop listening. So I built the circadian drift sheet to visualize how my schedule actually drifts over time. Other than this, I built a view to see which devices I listened to Spotify on and how much. I also built a top artists list — when I listened to them, in which years, and how many times. Granted, none of this looks as pretty as Spotify's official Wrapped — but it’s a lot more insightful, which is what I was after. That said, if you're graphically inclined, you could always pull the key numbers into something like Canva and design a good-looking graphic out of them. You can use AI if you aren't well-versed in pivot tables You don’t have to know Excel to process your data I'm sharing my sheet so you can look at the pivot tables I built and reuse them for your own data: Spotify Wrapped Excel Sheet with Built-in Pivot Tables. It’s an XLSX file hosted on Google Drive. Please download it to your system and open it in Excel to avoid potential errors and glitches. That said, if you want access to a particular metric I haven't built, and you don't know how to create pivot tables yourself, you can always use AI. In fact, some of the pivot tables in my sheet were actually built with Claude's help. You can connect Claude to Excel and have it build them for you. Alternatively, you can just give Claude the master data table we imported earlier and ask it to process it, calculate whatever you're curious about, and surface those specific nuggets of information.
