item.title: Did a Chatbot Write That? 7 Red Flags to Help You Spot AI Text
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.47
The internet is absolutely inundated with AI-written content, and the pace of publication isn't slowing down anytime soon. That's because realistic AI text is super simple to generate (particularly with well-engineered prompts) and less obvious to catch compared with AI images or videos. I've spent a lot of time testing chatbots and reading AI writing, and these are the seven most reliable indicators of AI-generated text. 1. Unnecessary Encouragement or Enthusiasm AI chatbots tell you what you want to hear. So, if your prompt implies a certain point of view, the response you get will affirm that belief. This sort of structure in writing is the biggest tell of AI-generated text, especially if the actual context of the text in question doesn’t quite justify the level of encouragement or enthusiasm you see. For example, I developed a skincare routine with AI. When I send a description of my routine to ChatGPT, it tells me, “Overall verdict first: Your routine is extremely well thought-out and mostly solid.” (Yes, the bold text is part of the chatbot’s response.) ChatGPT then continues with its first major header, “What You Did Very Well,” which begins, “Honestly, you hit the three pillars of skin aging prevention almost perfectly.” 2. Overly Perfect Grammar and Punctuation If you read a lot, you understand the concept of creative (or artistic) license. This is the idea that writers break grammatical conventions or rules for effect, especially in fiction or poetry. For example, a writer might use a run-on sentence for emphasis. Or a sentence fragment. Furthermore, most people just don’t have an encyclopedic knowledge of grammatical rules, so they will make mistakes. If you look closely, you can find many instances of extra (or missing) commas in everyday writing. AI chatbots, on the other hand, rarely make those types of mistakes, unless you explicitly ask them to. In testing, I asked ChatGPT for a free verse poem, which means it has absolute permission to violate every grammatical rule under the sun. Nonetheless, much of my poem simply reads like grammatically correct sentences with line breaks. On the other hand, take a look at a free verse poem by E.E. Cummings, none of which reads like normal prose. Of course, not every free verse poem is as experimental as Cummings’ poetry, and AI chatbots don’t have perfect grammar in every single instance. However, if you notice a long Reddit post doesn’t have so much as a single grammatical issue, for example, that’s a red flag. 3. Routine Inclusion of Em Dashes You use an em dash when you want to break up a sentence for emphasis, as opposed to the shorter en dash you use to describe a range like 5-10. No—there’s nothing necessarily grammatically wrong with using em dashes, but chatbots historically incorporate these into their responses far more often than the average person. When I asked ChatGPT if I could recycle my spent water filters at one point, I got the following response: “Short answer: No—don’t put ZeroWater filters in your normal recycling bin.” Now, seeing a single em dash doesn’t mean something is AI-generated (I like using em dashes sometimes), but if you see a lot of them, that’s a potential giveaway. 4. Repetitive Phrases or Words AI-generated text isn’t new, so there are well-known phrases and words AI tends to use. You can simply pay attention to your conversations with chatbots to develop a sense of their favorite sayings or consult a list, of which there are many. Some examples of repetitive AI words are "harness," "illuminate," "pivotal," "realm," and "underscore," while examples of popular phrases are "at its core," "delve into," "that being said," "to put it simply," and more. Of course, these are pretty normal words and phrases, so seeing one doesn’t mean anything. But if you see many of these across a single article or post, that’s a sign that what you’re reading might be from a bot. 5. A Heavy Reliance on Lists, Headings, and Structure Ask ChatGPT, or any other chatbot, a question, and the response you get almost certainly includes bullet points, different headings, and a summary or conclusion section, alongside other similar formatting elements. That kind of structure makes sense in an article like this one, but it feels a lot more out of place in other contexts. As an example, if I ask ChatGPT if Pokémon Pokopia is worth buying, it begins with a short answer, then sets up the following headings (each with bullet points within) in order: "What Pokémon Pokopia Actually Is," "Reception (So Far)," and "When It’s Worth Buying." It then caps off its response with a brief conclusion section. This is a very different kind of writing than you’d get if you asked a friend or watched a video that covers the same topic. 6. A Lack of Unique Content AI chatbots run on large language models (LLMs) that are trained on vast amounts of preexisting data. Oftentimes, chatbots also search the internet for up-to-date information to inform their replies. As a result, when an AI tells you something, it’s regurgitating what other people already said, not forming an opinion itself. If you’re reading a blog post reviewing Pokémon Pokopia, but it covers only the same generic information you get when talking to ChatGPT about the game (which itself compiles from various reviews and previews of the game), that can be a red flag. But if the blog post has personal anecdotes or thoughts on the game, it's less likely to be AI. 7. Flags From an AI Detection Tool If you don’t want to put the work in yourself, that’s no problem, because a ton of online tools can analyze text and tell you how likely it is to be AI-generated. For example, I submitted a poem I generated with ChatGPT to Pangram, and it told me there was a 100% chance it was AI-generated. Meanwhile, when I submitted my own poems, it told me they were written by a human. However, keep in mind that these tools aren't perfect and might get things wrong. If you are going to rely on any of them, I recommend cross-checking results across several. But even then, you can't fully trust their answers. Look for Patterns, Not Any One Thing Every single attribute I identified above appears in legitimate writing from real people every day. Some people love grammatical perfection or highly structured writing, after all. However, if some writing online does most or even all of the things I call out, there’s a strong chance that a human didn't write at least parts of it. Don’t try to avoid the above characteristics when you write something, though. Not only is it likely going to sound awkward, but it's just unnecessary. It’s surprisingly difficult to replicate the feel of AI-generated text, and the telltale signs are changing all the time. When you write, just focus on being the best writer you can possibly be. As with spotting AI images or videos, spotting AI text is a skill that requires practice. Furthermore, AI models are constantly improving, so clocking AI-generated content will become increasingly difficult. Don’t sweat it if you mistake something fake for something real, as that’s just an inevitability in the AI age. I'll continue to update this article as new trends emerge, too. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: Eyeing a New iPhone 18 Pro? Do This to Get the Most Money for Your Old Phone
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.11
The iPhone 18 Pro is expected to hit this fall, and it's rumored to start at a steep $1,299, a whopping $200 more than the 17 Pro's debut price. If that price tag is a little hard to stomach, there is some good news. Apple also recently increased its trade-in values for the second time this year, making it a little easier to afford one of its new rumored iPhones. If you're preparing to trade in your old device to shave some cost off the upfront price, here's everything you need to know about Apple's boosted trade-in values and how to make sure your phone is prepped and ready to ship, so you can get the highest value in exchange. What's the Trade-in Value for an Older iPhone? Apple increased its trade-in values twice this summer, helping you get a little more money for your old device. If you have an iPhone 16, you can now get a maximum of $480 in trade-in value, an extra $20 since the last increase. Meanwhile, the iPhone 16 Pro could net you up to $630, up from $560. Similar increases have been added to the company's line of computers, tablets, and smartwatches. Here's the max value you can get for each type of iPhone: - iPhone 16 Pro Max: $720 (previously $695) - iPhone 16 Pro: $630 (previously $560) - iPhone 16 Plus: $485 (previously $465) - iPhone 16: $480 (previously $460) - iPhone 16e: $310 (no change) - iPhone 15 Pro Max: $530 (previously $490) - iPhone 15 Pro: $420 (previously $410) - iPhone 15 Plus: $340 (previously $325) - iPhone 15: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Pro Max: $405 (previously $375) - iPhone 14 Pro: $335 (previously $320) - iPhone 14 Plus: $235 (unchanged) - iPhone 14: $235 (previously $225) What to Do Before Trading in Your Old iPhone Now that you know the maximum trade-in value of your old phone, you'll want to take some steps to make sure it's backed up, unpaired, and cleaned up. Here are the steps you should take before you send in your old device. 1. Back Up Everything First, make sure you don't lose your data. Back everything up before you wipe it from your phone. To back up to iCloud from your device, go to Settings, select your name, and then choose iCloud > iCloud Backup > Back Up Now. To back up to your Mac, connect your iPhone and your computer via a cable or Wi-Fi. If you have macOS Catalina or later, go to Finder, select your iPhone, and then choose General > Back Up All of the Data on Your iPhone to This Mac > Back Up Now. If you have an earlier version or a Windows PC, you'd use iTunes. Open the program, click on the image of your phone, then select Summary > Back Up Now. 2. Unfind Your iPhone Apple’s Find My app can sometimes block activation by a new owner, so you should deactivate the app before you ditch the device. Though Find My is automatically deactivated when you erase all content and settings, which you'll do below, this is still a good step to take as a precaution. Go to Settings, select your name, then choose Find My and disable it for that device. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 3. Sign Out of Messages More than a decade ago, people who switched from iOS to Android without logging out of Messages on their iPhone found that texts were going to the old phone. The problem has since been fixed, but those still scarred by "iMessage purgatory" may want to go to Settings > Apps > Messages and disable iMessage. 4. Unpair Your AirPods Similarly, you can still connect your AirPods to a new iPhone without unpairing them from the old one, but it can't hurt to wipe the slate clean. Place your AirPods and iPhone near each other, then go to Settings > Bluetooth. Tap the information icon next to your AirPods, and select Forget this Device. 5. Unpair Your Apple Watch If you have an Apple Watch, save yourself a potential headache and unpair it from the iPhone you'll be selling. Place them near each other, then open the Apple Watch app on your phone. Go to My Watch > All Watches and select the info circle next to the watch you want to unpair. Tap Unpair Apple Watch and then confirm, which may require you to enter your Apple Account password. With a GPS + Cellular model, you're asked whether you want to keep or remove your cellular plan. Since you're selling the iPhone, you'll want to remove it. (If you don't plan to pair your watch with a new iPhone, you might need to contact your carrier to cancel.) Tap to confirm; you might need to enter your Apple Account password to disable Activation Lock. 6. Sign Out of iCloud You should sign out of iCloud, iTunes, and the App Store before selling your device. Tap Settings, select your name, and choose Sign Out. Enter your Apple Account password and tap Turn Off. 7. Wipe Your iPhone and Delete Data When your new phone is set up and you're ready to trade in or sell your old iPhone, head to Settings > General > Transfer or Reset iPhone > Erase All Content and Settings, then approve all subsequent prompts. 8. Remove the SIM Card (If You Have One) Apple went the eSIM route starting with the iPhone 14 lineup, but older devices will have a physical SIM card. In most cases, you can just deactivate your cellphone service on the device and trade it in with the SIM card intact. But that SIM card is the repository of your phone number, various bits of security data, and all the info needed for billing. It identifies you, your phone, and a lot of your activity on your phone. So you should remove it before you sell the phone. Fortunately, it's simple. Locate the SIM ejector on your phone, then insert a paper clip until the tray pops out. Remove the SIM card, replace the tray, and say goodbye to your old iPhone. The Best Places to Sell Your Phone I've also included some of the best sites for selling or trading in your phone. Some make it easy to send in your phone and get immediate cash, others let you control the price through bidding, and there are even options for receiving store credit from places you shop. To give you an idea of your trade-in power, I priced out what you can expect to get for an iPhone 15 Pro across all of them, and it varies wildly, as you'll see below. You can also trade your phone in with your existing carrier or switch to a new one. Many offer compelling trade-in promotions, so be sure to check out AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon, and others. Apple Trade In The Apple Trade In program pays you with a credit or gift card. If you pay for an Apple device in full up-front, a credit will be applied to your payment card once Apple receives your trade-in device and verifies its condition. If you're paying on an installment plan, the credit will be applied right away. Turning in an iPhone 15 Pro, for example, can get you up to $410 on a new iPhone now that Apple has increased some trade-in values by as much as $35. Best Buy If you're selling your iPhone and just want cash to buy electronics, you can cut out a step at Best Buy: Trade in your phone at a store or mail it in for a digital gift card. For a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition, expect to get about $275. eBay To sell your device yourself, there's always eBay. The site has a quick walkthrough where you can input your phone's stats. After entering my example device, a Black Titanium 512GB iPhone 15 Pro in good condition on Verizon, the page recommended that I list the phone at $510. GameStop Are most of your iPhone apps games? Then you'll probably do well to turn in your iPhone in for some store credit at GameStop. You can also get cold, hard cash for it there. Bring your device to your nearest GameStop, get a price quote from a sales associate, and then receive store credit or cash on the spot. I recommend getting an estimate on the site before you make the trip. I found that a 512GB iPhone 15 Pro from Verizon in very good condition will get you $267.30 in cash or $297.00 in store credit. Swappa Swappa is a marketplace where you can sell your iPhone directly. Select your phone model on the site, upload some photos, and set a price. Once someone buys it, you're paid immediately via PayPal. You're responsible for safely shipping your phone to the buyer. According to the site, an iPhone 15 Pro is selling for an average price of $544, while a trade-in to one of Swappa's partners could get me $311. uSell Want to sell your iPhone fast? One option is uSell. Select your model, carrier, capacity, and condition to receive an offer. If you choose to accept it, you ship your iPhone to uSell for free. If your device is in the condition you said it was, you're paid by check or PayPal. A 512GB iPhone 15 Pro on Verizon in good condition is currently worth about $268. Editors' Note: Trade-in values were accurate at the time of publication. Your mileage may vary. Chandra Steele contributed to this story About Our Expert As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: Uber Lays Off 3,300 Employees, Cuts Down on Middle Managers
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.06
Uber is laying off 10% of its global workforce, or 3,300 people, to reduce managerial layers. Impacted employees were notified of the change via email, while Uber published CEO Dara Khosrowshahi’s message to employees in a blog post. “The changes we’re making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future,” Khosrowshahi says. “It will also generate savings that we intend to reinvest in growth, innovation, and the capabilities that will matter most over the coming years.” As part of the restructuring, Uber will reduce by 20% the number of employees who sit seven or more levels below the CEO and by 50% the number of micro teams that work with just one or two members. "I’m sure many of you have felt that you spend too much time 'aligning' rather than building, shipping, or serving customers," Khosrowshahi writes. Uber will also be realigning its delivery teams across its restaurant, retail, and direct services into single-threaded teams at the global, regional, and country levels. “Running these three businesses separately made sense in their early days, but that structure is no longer serving us at scale,” Khosrowshahi notes. Finally, the company will rearrange where employees work from and reduce the number of key work locations. Global teams will work from New York and San Francisco; tech teams will work from designated tech hubs; and regional and local teams will work from their respective hubs. Once realigned, only 1% of the company’s total workforce will work remotely. As Bloomberg reports, Uber’s restructuring comes after it committed $10 billion to its robotaxi business. The company plans to launch robotaxis in 28 cities by 2028, and over the past year, it has invested in several companies focused on autonomous driving, including Avride, Lucid, Nuro, and Rivian. Before the latest organizational cuts, Uber reportedly replaced 10% of its customer service staff with AI in July. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: No, That's Not Really Paper: Acer Tips Touch-Screen Color ePaper Monitor
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.65
Combining paper-like visuals with glare-free use, the Acer EP130K ePaper monitor, announced today at IFA, is designed for professionals who perform deep work for long periods, avid readers, and mobile users whose work takes them outdoors. The EP130K supports touch directly on its ePaper screen, enabling stylus use as well as the intuitive feel of writing or drawing with a finger. Its 13.3-inch matte screen provides a resolution of up to 3,200 by 2,400 pixels in black-and-white mode and up to 1,600 by 1,200 pixels in color; it can render up to 4,096 colors. The screen supports wide viewing angles of up to 178 degrees, vertically and horizontally. The monitor’s bi-stability functionality allows the image on screen to remain in place even when all power sources are removed. Supported connectivity includes mini HDMI and USB-C; it draws power from its host computer over a USB-C cable. The EP130K includes a built-in pair of 1-watt speakers. The device also has an audio-out jack, should you prefer to use it with headphones or powered external speakers. Acer has integrated a tiltable kickstand into the product's design. EPaper is a display technology—best known from the E Ink brand commercialized by E Ink Corporation and widely used in ereaders such as the Amazon Kindle—that supports ultra-high pixel densities, reflects ambient light, remains readable in bright sunlight, and greatly conserves battery life. A commonly cited drawback of ePaper devices is that screens that use it tend to be very slow to refresh—some take well over a second—impairing, if not scuttling, their ability to render video and animations, but the screen that the EP130K uses has a full 60Hz refresh rate typical of desktop displays. EPaper is also used in some tablets, including those made by companies like Onyx and ReMarkable, but due to its cost, it has been largely limited to smaller-screen devices. There are, however, hopeful signs that mainstream monitor manufacturers are beginning to embrace this technology. At Computex in June, Asus announced its own 13.3-inch ePaper monitor, the ZenScreen Color ePaper MP13UC, which has yet to come to market. Unlike the EP130K, though, its refresh rate is only 35Hz. Pricing and availability info for the EP130K have not yet been announced. About Our Expert Since 2004, I have worked on PCMag’s hardware team, covering at various times printers, scanners, projectors, storage, and monitors. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: What Did You Want to Say? Microsoft Turns Off Default Text Suggestions
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.57
Text prediction tools are designed to speed up your writing, suggesting words and phrases you may want to use before you’ve finished typing a sentence. They're available in some versions of Microsoft software, but they no longer appear by default in Outlook and Word. Microsoft announced the decision in a blog post on Sept. 1, where it said it wanted to “provide a more consistent and user-controlled writing experience across Microsoft 365 applications.” It also said it wanted to reduce “unwanted interruptions for those who prefer to write without suggestions appearing automatically.” This appears to be part of Microsoft's latest attempt to improve its tools by listening to user feedback, such as when it removed Copilot tools from Notepad and Snipping Tool earlier this year. If that’s the case, Microsoft didn’t cite customer feedback as a basis for this decision. You can still use predictive text if you manually enable the feature. If you have the latest update installed on either, you may need to make some tweaks to regain access. This affects desktop versions of both tools on Mac and Windows, as well as their web editions. It may also impact your mobile version on Android or iOS, although some already have the tool disabled by default. There are a few complaints across social media about the default predictive text in these tools, but it doesn’t appear to be a widely cited problem. Microsoft has offered a way to turn the tool off for a long time, and it's likely that anyone who disliked it would have done so soon after launch. To turn the tool back on through desktop, head to Settings in Word and Outlook and look for a toggle under Advanced labeled "Show text predictions while typing." Tick this on, and press OK for them to appear across your future versions. For mobile, it’s the same method, but look for an option called Text Predictions. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: Acer's New Predator Atlas 7 Proves the Intel Arc G3 Can Fit Almost Anywhere
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.55
Acer has a new addition to its Predator handheld portfolio that promises the same flagship performance of its upcoming 8-inch model in a more compact 7-inch form factor. We got our hands on the Predator Atlas 8 at Computex in May, and the new Acer Predator Atlas 7 feels familiar. It has a 7-inch FHD touch screen with a 120Hz refresh rate, 500-nit peak brightness, Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) support, and a 16:9 aspect ratio. There are relatively few 7-inch gaming handhelds; they've coalesced around 8 or 9 inches, and none of those that do, such as the Asus ROG Ally X, use the Arc G3. Just like its big 8-inch brother, the Atlas 7 features contoured grips, an enlarged palm rest area, recessed keys, and an anti-slip texture that helps your hands settle into a steadier hold for cleaner input and better control throughout longer sessions. The joysticks come with a tunneling magnetoresistance option for greater precision, while Hall-Effect analog triggers offer greater pressure sensitivity. But the real draw of the Atlas 7 is what’s powering the device. The base version of the Atlas 7 will use an Intel Arc G3 Extreme processor and Intel Arc B370 graphics, and Acer will also offer an Arc G3 Extreme and Arc B390 configuration. We got our first taste of this processor's potential when we reviewed the MSI Claw 8 AI+. In our testing, we compared the Intel Arc G3 Extreme to AMD’s Ryzen Z2 Extreme and AI Z2 Extreme and saw improved frame rates across a wide range of titles. The dual-fan cooling system features a precision metal Predator AeroBlade fan with 89 blades, each just 0.1mm thick, which Acer claims will deliver up to a 10% increase in airflow. A secondary plastic fan works alongside it, guiding hot air out of the chassis more efficiently under sustained load. The Predator Atlas 7 also offers up to an 80Wh battery. The Predator Atlas 7 will be available in North America later this year, while the Predator Atlas 8 will be available this month. Stay tuned for our full reviews. About Our Expert I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.

item.title: Hertz So Good: Acer's Latest Predator Gaming Monitor Joins the 1,000Hz Club
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.53
At IFA 2026, Acer unveiled a gaggle of new gaming monitors, including the Predator XB253Q U1, the company’s first 1,000Hz model. The XB253Q U1 ($1,099) is a 24.5-inch display optimized for esports performance. It delivers a maximum 1,000Hz refresh rate at its native FHD resolution, which is not the case with some previously launched 1,000Hz monitors that require a step down to 720p. It also features Acer’s proprietary Visual Response Boost (VRB) Pro technology, which reduces motion blur and ghosting, making fast-moving objects on screen appear sharper and easier to track. Rounding out the Predator XB253Q U1's features are VESA DisplayHDR 400 certification, Circular Polarized technology to reduce glare and eye strain during longer gaming sessions, and support for AMD FreeSync Premium and Nvidia G-Sync for tear-free gaming visuals. It's not the first time Acer monitors have boasted a four-digit refresh rate. Earlier this year, Acer announced a 1,000Hz refresh-rate gaming monitor, the Predator XB273U F6, though it only supports 1,000 Hz at a 1,280-by-720-pixel resolution. Other manufacturers have also started building monitors with the 1,000Hz refresh-rate target in mind. LG's UltraGear 25G590B-B, which you can buy today, supports 1,000Hz at full HD, while Samsung announced the 27-inch Odyssey G6, the world’s first 1,100Hz gaming monitor, at Gamescom. Though like the XB273U F6, it only offers 720p resolution at the 1,100Hz refresh rate. Now, why would you bother with 1,000Hz refresh rates? Higher refresh rates lower input lag, reduce blur, and make the action on screen smoother because the display updates the image more times per second. For esports athletes, every millisecond counts, but even casual players can enjoy the benefits of faster input lag, even if it's not always immediately noticeable. The Acer Predator XB253Q U1 is not the only monitor Acer announced at IFA 2026. Other highlights include the 31.5-inch Predator X32 V3 ($899), a QD-OLED Penta Tandem panel with 3,840-by-2,160-pixel resolution and VESA DisplayHDR TrueBlack 400 certification. Also launched: a curved 34-inch Nitro XZ340CKR P monitor ($699), which pairs WUHD (5,120-by-2,160-pixel) resolution at 180Hz with Dynamic Frequency and Resolution (DFR) support for up to WFHD (2,560 by 1,080 pixels) at 360Hz. Finally, there's the Nitro XV270U Z3, which provides tri-mode DFR technology across QHD, FHD, and HD resolutions, and the Nitro XV275X P ($1,199), which offers a 5K resolution with 2,304-zone mini LED backlighting. The Nitro XZ340CKR P will be available later this year, while the rest of the new models will be available early next year, Acer says. Stay tuned for our full reviews. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.

item.title: Bigger Air, Lighter Blade: Acer Revamps Its Swift Laptops at IFA 2026
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.49
Acer dropped two new laptops at IFA 2026, expanding its thin-and-light lineup with the Acer Swift Air 16 and the Swift Blade 14. Aimed at multimedia productivity and portability, respectively, the two new systems share similar processing hardware and premium display technologies. However, you might see only one of these laptops hit US stores next year. Acer Swift Air 16: Intel Core Series 3 Power in a 16-Inch Canvas When the Acer Swift Air 16 was announced at IFA last year, we were wowed by how light it was, marveling that a full Copilot+ PC with a 16-inch display could weigh less than 2.2 pounds. Well, the new model isn't quite so feather light, weighing 3.3 pounds (1.5kg). However, it's still slim at just 0.52 to 0.53 inches (13.3 to 13.5mm) thick, and sold with up to a 120Hz, 3K OLED panel, packing a lot of capability into that thin chassis. The all-aluminum laptop comes in three colors: Elemental Blue, Sage Green, or Sandstone Gold. Intel Core Series 3 "Wildcat Lake" processors provide CPU muscle and NPU smarts, but it isn't listed as a Copilot+ system, even though it runs Windows 11 and offers AI-enhanced features. The top configuration, with an Intel Core 7 350, provides up to 40 trillion AI operations per second (TOPS) total across the system, falling below the 40 dedicated NPU TOPS required for Copilot+ certification. Beyond the CPU, the Swift Air 16 houses up to 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM and up to 512GB of onboard storage, with support for SSD upgrades up to 1TB. If you want touch controls, Acer also sells a 1,920-by-1,200-pixel IPS touch-screen option alongside the flagship 120Hz, 3K OLED panel. Audio quality also sees a boost from a quad-speaker array with DTS Virtual:X spatial audio, while a 1080p FHD IR webcam supports Windows Hello facial recognition for seamless, secure logins. Acer's port selection includes a pair of Thunderbolt 4 ports, a single USB Type-A port, and a 3.5mm combo audio jack. The whole thing is powered by a 70Wh battery that can fast charge to 50% in just 30 minutes. The Acer Swift Air 16 will start selling in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) in December 2026, with a North America launch in early 2027. Pricing has not yet been announced. Acer Swift Blade 14: 799 Grams of Magnesium and Carbon Fiber If you want the ultraportable lightweight design aimed at mobile productivity, then the 14-inch Swift Blade 14 is the laptop you want—if it were released in the States. The ultra-light design weighs just 799g (1.76 pounds) and measures just 12.9mm thick, achieving its feather-light portability through a hybrid build of a magnesium-aluminum alloy keyboard deck alongside carbon fiber top and bottom covers. Sold in Marshmallow White and Marshmallow Blue, it is built specifically for visual work on the go. The Swift Blade has the same Intel Core Series 3 hardware inside, with 12GB of LPDDR5 RAM and up to 1TB of PCIe Gen 4 SSD storage. Screen options peak at an impressive 14-inch, 2,880-by-1,800-pixel OLED display running at 90Hz with 100% DCI-P3 color gamut coverage. Additional hardware highlights include three USB 3.2 Gen 1 Type-C ports, an FHD webcam with a physical side-mounted camera switch, dual digital microphones, and a 50Wh fast-charging battery. However, North American shoppers might not see this ultralight 14-incher. While Acer confirmed the Swift Blade 14 will launch in Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA) in December 2026, the company made no mention of North American pricing or availability. At any rate, we're keen to test at least one of these slinky laptops soon. About Our Expert From the laptops on your desk to satellites in space and AI that seems to be everywhere, I cover many topics at PCMag. I've covered PCs and technology products for over 15 years at PCMag and other publications, among them Tom's Guide, Laptop Mag, and TWICE. As a hardware reviewer, I've handled dozens of MacBooks, 2-in-1 laptops, Chromebooks, and the latest AI PCs. As the resident Starlink expert, I've done years of hands-on testing with the satellite service. I also explore the most valuable ways to use the latest AI tools and features in our Try AI column.

item.title: A 560Hz OLED Gaming Monitor From Alienware? Yes, Please!
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.12
Alienware is at IFA in Berlin, where it's teasing two new gaming monitors, the 32-inch 4K OLED and the 24.5-inch 560Hz QD-OLED. The Alienware 32 4K OLED (AW3226Q) takes advantage of the same RGB Stripe Tandem technology as the recently reviewed Alienware AW3926QW, bringing it to a flat 32-inch, 165Hz 4K (3,840-by-2,160-pixel) panel with a 16:9 aspect ratio. RGB stripe tandem OLED combines the deep blacks and fast response times with improved brightness, color purity, and text clarity. It does so by stacking four emissive layers behind an RGB-stripe subpixel arrangement of red/blue/green/blue. This change leads to richer HDR scenes, cleaner detail, and sharper text for both gaming and everyday PC use. According to Alienware, the four-stack tandem emissive layer is a significant advancement in OLED technology. After proving the new tech’s effectiveness in the AW3926QW, which won an Editors' Choice award for Best Ultrawide Gaming Monitor, Alienware hopes to expand the technology into a form factor that fits more desks and budgets. The AW3226Q offers 1,000-nit peak brightness, an infinite contrast ratio, and is certified for VESA DisplayHDR True Black 400 and Dolby Vision. The panel is factory-calibrated to Delta E<2 color accuracy and covers 99% of the DCI-P3 color range, Alienware says. The monitor is also AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, Nvidia G-Sync, and VESA AdaptiveSync-certified. High-Refresh OLED: The Future of Esports? Alienware also revealed the 25 560Hz QD-OLED (AW2527HX), built for competitive FPS and esports players who prioritize refresh rate above resolution. Alienware co-developed this monitor with the pro esports players from Team Liquid, using their feedback during development to reflect the needs of elite competitive gaming. The 560Hz, 24.5-inch, 1080p monitor is the fastest Alienware has ever built, with a 0.03ms gray-to-gray minimum response time. The company says the monitor marks a generational leap over TN-based esports monitors that have long dominated competitive setups. Asus and Samsung have also announced 500+Hz OLED gaming monitors. Typically, esports gamers prioritize performance over visual splendor, but the AW2527HX aims to make that choice a thing of the past. The monitor is certified VESA DisplayHDR True Black 600, with infinite contrast, and zero backlight bleed. A matte anti-glare low-reflectance (AGLR) coating maintains image clarity under bright tournament lighting. You can expect 1,500 nits of brightness, as well. The screen is not the only part of the monitor tuned to esports gamers. You'll also find a telescopic stand that lets you tilt the screen to more extreme angles for greater ergonomic flexibility. Height and rotational markers let you replicate your exact setup at any venue, while the compact base is perfect for letting your keyboard rest on. A dedicated esports button switches between 4:3 and 3:2 aspect ratios instantly, and there’s a rear-flip headset hanger that keeps your headset within reach. The Alienware 32 4K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3226Q) is $699.99 and will be available this fall. The Alienware 25 560Hz QD-OLED (AW2527HX) will be available early next year. Stay tuned for our full reviews. About Our Expert I’m a PCMag reviewer and ISF-certified TV calibrator focused on computer accessories, laptops, gaming monitors, and video games. I’ve been writing, playing, and complaining about games for as long as I remember, but it wasn’t until recently that I’ve been able to shout my opinions directly at a larger audience. My work has appeared on iMore, Windows Central, Android Central, and TWICE, and I have a diverse portfolio of editing work under my belt from my time spent at Scholastic and Oxford University Press. I also have a few book-author credits under my belt—I’ve contributed to the sci-fi anthology Under New Suns, and I’ve even written a Peppa Pig book.

item.title: New iPhone 18 Pro Leak Points to 3 Colors, Skips a Regular Shade
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.05
Apple will unveil its latest iPhones about this time next week, and a new leak suggests the iPhone 18 Pro will be offered in three completely different colors than the iPhone 17 Pro. In a Weibo post on Monday, leaker Fixed Focus Digital revealed that the iPhone 18 Pro models have entered mass production and will be available in sky blue, black (dark gray), and a brand-new burgundy shade. Despite multiple leakers reporting the same three colors using different names, the absence of white/silver is quite surprising since Apple has offered that shade with each generation of its Pro models, starting with the iPhone 11 Pro in 2019. In response to a comment about silver’s absence, Fixed Focus Digital said they haven’t spotted the color anywhere in China. The leaker also attached an image of possible colors and noted that the light gray color, which a few other leakers have reported, is highly unlikely. If the rumor holds, Apple will be dropping all three colors it offered for the iPhone 17 Pro, including the extremely popular cosmic orange, silver, and deep blue. The good thing here is we won’t have to wait too long to find out if these claims are true. Apple is expected to unveil the iPhone 18 Pro models and the first-ever foldable iPhone at its annual fall event on Sept. 9. It will be the first event under new CEO John Ternus, with an iPhone Ultra foldable and a new “dark cherry” shade for the iPhone 18 Pro, which Fixed Focus Digital described as burgundy, are expected to be the main highlights. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: AG Promises to 'Track Down' Those Behind X Password Reset Requests
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.05
UPDATE 9/2: US Attorney General Todd Blanche today attributed the password-reset spree to "sophisticated cybercriminals" who targeted hundreds of X accounts. "X disrupted the attack to prevent user accounts from being captured," Blanche tweeted. "We are working closely with X to track down the criminals behind this week’s attack. There is no refuge for those [who] perpetrate their criminal schemes from behind computer screens." Original Story 9/1: Did you wake up this morning to multiple password reset requests from X? Dozens of users took to the social network this morning to report receiving at least 10 emails around 9:30 a.m. ET. The messages, which appeared in the inboxes of at least one PCMag staffer, looked legit; they came from [email protected] and included the six-digit confirmation code required to complete a password reset. "If you didn't make this request, ignore this email," it said. Easier said than done. The messages sparked a wave of concerned posts on X from people worried they had been hacked or targeted by a phishing campaign. X Product Engineer Mridul Singhai said the company is "actively investigating the issue and, so far, [has] found no evidence of any breaches. We apologize for the multiple emails and appreciate your patience as we work to resolve this.” Singhai attributes the concerning emails to X Money, Musk’s payment platform for X Premium subscribers that became publicly available in July. "Attackers appear to believe that, now that @XMoney is widely available, they can gain unauthorized access to accounts." How to Secure Your X Account If you’ve received suspicious emails, don’t click on any links. Go directly to the X mobile or web app to check your account status. If you don't have secondary security set up on your account, do that ASAP, whether it's two-factor authentication (2FA) or a passkey. Also consider enabling Password reset protect via Settings > Security and account access > Security > Password reset protect. "If you check this box, you will be prompted to enter either your email address or phone number, or your email address, then phone number if both are associated with your account, to send a reset password link or confirmation code if you ever forget it," X says. The same Security page is also where you'd go to set up 2FA or a passkey. For 2FA, you can use an authenticator app or a security key. To receive codes via text messages, you'll need to be a Premium subscriber, but we don't recommend using SMS for 2FA codes anyway. For more on passkeys, check out our explainer. About Our Expert I’m a New York-based writer currently serving as PCMag’s Editorial Intern. I cover the impact of technology and internet culture on our daily lives, with a specialization in video games and cultural criticism. I have written for Kotaku, The A.V. Club, Unwinnable, Aftermath, and more. In addition, I have a formal background in video game development and visual design. You can find all of my work on my website.

item.title: Stop Resizing Windows! This Built-In Windows 11 Trick Will Double Your Productivity
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.00
Managing open windows shouldn't feel like a full-time job. With Windows 11's Snap Layouts, you can instantly organize your workspace without the endless clicking, dragging, and manual resizing. Whether you're juggling two apps or managing a multi-monitor grid, this guide covers everything you need to master Snap Layouts, tweak your settings, and increase your daily productivity. How to Master Snap Layouts in Seconds To get started with Snap Layouts, simply hover the mouse cursor over the Maximize icon near the upper-right corner of a program window. You’ll see a choice of window layouts. Click a position to instantly snap the window to that location on the grid. The precise layout options here depend on the display you’re using. Common options include two side-by-side windows and a four-quadrant grid. Windows shows layouts for arranging three windows side by side if your PC has a high-resolution display, too. You will see the Snap Assist grid with previews of your open windows after selecting a location for the first window. Click them to quickly choose which windows you want in each position on your screen. It’s much faster than hunting down and resizing application windows one by one. Additionally, Windows lets you use Snap Layouts with drag-and-drop gestures. Drag and drop a window’s title bar to the left or right edges of the screen to place it on either side, or drag it into one of the four corners of the screen to place it in that quadrant. You can also drag and drop a window to the top of your screen. You’ll see the Snap Layouts options, and you can drop the window in your desired position on your preferred layout. This works on a touch screen, too: Place your finger on the window’s title bar and drag it to your desired position on your screen to start snapping. After you create a Snap Layout with a group of windows, you can see an app’s position in that arrangement via its taskbar thumbnail. Windows 11 also shows combined window groups in the window switcher (Alt + Tab)and Task View (Windows Key + Tab) overlays, allowing you to quickly switch between groups of windows. Ditch the Mouse: Lightning-Fast Keyboard Shortcuts Press the Windows Key + Z to start snapping a window from the keyboard. Snap Layouts will display numbers in a grid, and you can press a number to quickly assign a window layout. Additionally, Windows lets you move windows around the grid with Windows key shortcuts. Press the Windows Key + Left Arrow or the Windows Key + Right Arrow to snap the current window to either edge of your screen. You can also use the up and down arrow keys. For example, to snap the current window to the bottom-right quadrant of your screen, hold the Windows Key, press the Right Arrow key, then press the Down Arrow key. You will see the familiar Snap Assist interface after snapping the first window. You can use the arrow keys and the Enter or Space key to quickly make a selection. You can also press Esc to cancel Snap Assist. Tweak the Settings: Customize Your Snapping Workflow Microsoft lets you configure Snap Layouts from the Settings app, and you can even turn it off if it gets in your way. Go to Settings > System > Multitasking, then expand the Snap Windows section to see the available options. If you toggle the Snap Windows off entirely, you won’t even be able to snap a window to the left or right sides of your screen. Other options here let you turn off Snap Assist suggestions, Snap Layouts pop-ups, and the overlay that appears when you drag a window to the top of your screen. Additionally, you can hide groups of snapped windows from the app switcher view and the taskbar, if you prefer. The Multitasking settings window also has a toggle for a feature called Title Bar Window Shake, which lets you grab a window’s title bar with your mouse and shake it to minimize all other windows. Microsoft originally called this feature Aero Shake in Windows Vista, and the Snap feature was originally called Aero Snap alongside it. The Title Bar Window Shake option is off by default. Go Pro With FancyZones: Total Desktop Control If Snap Layouts isn't flexible enough for you, try the superpowered FancyZones utility included in Microsoft’s free PowerToys package. It lets you create custom layouts for window arrangements, which might be especially useful on higher-resolution monitors. You can create multiple sets of custom layouts and switch between them with keyboard shortcuts, quickly snapping your open windows to different arrangements. After you install PowerToys, FancyZones is active by default. Simply hold down Shift while dragging a window to see layout options for snapping it to a zone. It's possible to customize the keyboard or mouse actions that trigger FancyZones from within the PowerToys app, too. For more ways to upgrade your desktop experience, check out these hidden Windows 11 features. About Our Experts I've been testing PC and mobile software for more than 20 years, focusing on photo and video editing, operating systems, and web browsers. Prior to my current role, I covered software and apps for ExtremeTech and headed up PCMag’s enterprise software team. I’ve attended trade shows for Microsoft, Google, and Apple and written about all of them and their products. I still get a kick out of seeing what's new in video and photo editing software, and how operating systems change over time. I was privileged to byline the cover story of the last print issue of PC Magazine, the Windows 7 review, and I’ve witnessed every Microsoft misstep and win, up to the latest Windows 11. I’m an avid bird photographer and traveler—I’ve been to 40 countries, many with great birds! Because I’m also a classical music fan and former performer, I’ve reviewed streaming services that emphasize classical music. I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: Apple's First Foldable Is Almost Here: Everything We Know About the 'iPhone Ultra'
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.99
Apple has long taken a "wait and see" approach to emerging form factors, so it's no surprise that it's late to the folding phone party while its major rivals—Google, Motorola, and Samsung in the US, and many more abroad—take massive bites out of the hinged-handset pie. As a phone expert, I've tested intriguing foldables, from the not-so-great Microsoft Surface Duo to the more successful Samsung Galaxy Z Flip series, as well as the Google Pixel Fold and Motorola Razr lines. But where's Apple's fun and flexible iPhone Flip? I vividly remember when, in 2019, Apple co-founder Steve Wozniak told Bloomberg that "[Apple] is not the leader in areas like the folding phone, and that worries me because I really want a folding phone." Well, if the rumors are anything to go by, it looks like The Woz is finally getting his wish. Whispers about Apple's foldable project date back to 2016, but this year, reports have skyrocketed. As someone who's obsessed with both iPhones and foldables, I'm excited that these worlds may collide in an ambitious new piece of hardware that could make Apple's rivals sweat. Foldable iPhone: All the Credible Rumors So Far Given Apple's long-standing iPhone naming conventions, you may expect the company to announce the iPhone 18 Fold. However, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, one of the most credible Apple leakers, there may be a twist: Apple might go with iPhone Ultra, instead. Gurman claims the foldable is still on track for this fall, despite chatter about manufacturing snags. That said, the so-called iPhone Ultra is expected to launch at the Surprise and Shine Sept. 9 event, alongside the iPhone 18 series. What will Apple's foldable look like? Gurman called it "the most significant overhaul in the iPhone’s history and the first actual form-factor change." It won't open vertically like the Samsung Z Flip 7 or the Motorola Razr Ultra. Instead, it will open from side to side, like a book, revealing a larger display that's roughly the same size as the iPad mini. For reference, it won't be like the skinny Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 7, which is thinner than some regular phones. According to a recent interview with Tom's Guide, Gurman said that the iPhone foldable will more closely resemble the Galaxy Z Fold 8, adopting a wider footprint for its inner display. Apple reportedly plans to pitch the iPhone Ultra as a device that's more beneficial for web browsing, framing subjects with a gigantic viewfinder, and most importantly, watching video. Samsung leaned heavily into the fact that the Z Fold 8 reduced letterboxing for a more pleasant streaming experience—Apple may roll out similar marketing plans. Gurman also expects the larger display to make the iPhone Ultra “awesome for gaming,” delivering a far more immersive experience similar to handheld gaming consoles. Having tested the Z Fold 8, I completely agree. Gaming on a wider foldable screen is glorious. For the first time in years, I actually want to play mobile games because I’m no longer confined to a cramped, narrow display. Similar to the Z Fold 8, the iPhone Ultra won’t have a dedicated telephoto camera, so you’ll miss out on the enhanced zoom capabilities Apple will likely offer on its iPhone 18 Pro models. The rumored Apple foldable may also lack Face ID, meaning users could have to rely solely on Touch ID for biometric security. Bloomberg's sources say Apple will introduce "apps [that] look more like iPad software" to accommodate the upcoming foldable. Similar to the experience you'd find on rival foldables, the foldable iPhone will reportedly launch side-by-side apps. However, unlike the iPad, it can't run multiple windows at once. Although Gurman's reports often liken the rumored iPhone Ultra to a tiny iPad, it's worth noting that it's expected to run iOS, not iPadOS. We've already seen early glimpses of foldable-friendly software at WWDC. Apple's documentation emphasizes to developers the importance of creating apps that support a "dynamic range of sizes and aspect ratios." As for the processor, there's speculation that the foldable iPhone will run on Apple's A20 Pro chip, which is also expected to power the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. The real question is, how does Apple plan to stand out from the crowd? As mentioned, the Z Fold 8 appears to be quite similar to the rumored iPhone Ultra. On top of that, Apple faces stiff competition from devices like the Motorola Razr Fold and the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which we recently reviewed. Sources close to Apple's foldable project claim the iPhone Ultra will solve issues that other rivals struggle with, including that pesky crease in the middle of the display. Gurman acknowledged that Samsung has made “serious strides on the crease,” but told Tom’s Guide that Apple’s approach to tackling the center trench will be “a little bit better,” thanks to the stronger hinge rumored to be coming to the iPhone Ultra. Reportedly called Liquid Metal, the hinge is said to use a teardrop-shaped internal structure that helps distribute and reduce stress when folding. Another way the iPhone Ultra could stand out is with MagSafe. The iPhone Ultra will reportedly feature MagSafe support for case-free magnetic charging. Samsung’s foldables, on the other hand, aren’t quite there yet. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Z Flip 8 support wireless charging, but without built-in magnets, you’ll need a compatible case to use magnetic chargers. The Cupertino company's forthcoming foldable is expected to be priced between $2,000 and $2,500, which is not a surprise for envelope-pushing tech or for Apple. Apple's Surprise and Shine event is set to kick off in Cupertino at 10 a.m. PT / 1:00 p.m. ET on Wednesday, Sept. 9. We'll be there to bring you all the news. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s Senior Writer for Mobile on the Consumer Electronics team, diving into the latest phones, tablets, Bluetooth speakers, audio devices, and other portable gear. I’ve been covering consumer technology for six years. Before joining PCMag, I contributed my tech expertise to Laptop Magazine, Mashable, Tom’s Guide, Esquire, Good Housekeeping, and more.

item.title: Claude vs. Gemini: Smarter Brains or Better Features?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.78
Table of Contents AI chatbots are now a mature technology with impressive performance across the board and a large variety of features, so you might struggle to decide on which to use. Even if you narrow it down to Claude and Gemini, you will still find some notable distinctions. For instance, Claude specializes in exceptional model intelligence, while Gemini provides seamless features across nearly every Google app. I’ve spent countless hours testing both chatbots, so I've compared them across key categories, such as deep research, value, and vibe coding, to help you pick the best one for your needs. Full Specs | Claude | Google Gemini | | |---|---|---| | Free Version | | | | Free Version | | | | AI Model | | | | AI Model | Fable 5, Haiku 4.5, Opus 5, and Sonnet 5 | 3.7 Flash and 3.1 Pro | | Cites Sources | | | | Cites Sources | | | | Ability to Browse Web | | | | Ability to Browse Web | | | | Can Resume Prior Conversations | | | | Can Resume Prior Conversations | | | | Image Generator | | | | Image Generator | | | Price: Gemini's Free Tier and $5 Plan Leave Claude in the Dust You can use both Claude and Gemini for free, or you can opt for a paid subscription. Free versions for both come with significant feature and usage limitations. However, you still get a lot more from Gemini for free, such as access to deep research, Google Drive storage, image generation, and video generation. Outside of deep research, which Claude offers on paid plans, Claude doesn’t support any of the other features above across its plans. Paid versions start at $17 per month (billed annually) for Claude and $5 per month for Gemini. Both have plans that cost $200 per month; these unlock higher usage limits and more features, such as access to Claude Design or Google’s Antigravity coding app. The right plan for you depends on what you plan to do, but Gemini's base paid tier is far more affordable. And, as mentioned, Gemini’s plans also come with varying amounts of cloud storage, which can justify the subscription cost on its own. Winner: Gemini Platforms and User Experience: Claude’s Browser Ecosystem vs. Deep Google Integrations You can use Claude and Gemini on the web or via their desktop apps (macOS and Windows) and mobile apps (Android and iOS). Claude’s coding capabilities are a part of its desktop app, while Gemini maintains the separate Antigravity app. Claude has a Chrome extension for AI agent and assistant features in your browser, while Google integrates Gemini directly into Chrome. Of course, Google pushes Gemini in its Chromebook Plus lineup and presumably will do the same with Google Books. Anthropic doesn't provide any type of similar hardware integration. Claude’s and Gemini’s models are accessible across various online services, with Claude available on Perplexity and Gemini via Google’s partnership with Apple. You can also access Gemini across Google apps, such as Calendar, Docs, Drive, Gmail, Maps, Notebook, Keep, Photos, Sheets, and YouTube Music. However, I recommend sticking to their official apps and websites to access most of their features. The interfaces of Claude and Gemini are generally consistent and straightforward across platforms. Minor differences exist depending on the feature in question, but you can expect central text fields with sidebar menus on both. You can give both instructions to follow when chatting, but neither supports ChatGPT’s level of personality and tone customization. Winner: Tie AI Models: Claude's Four Intelligence Tiers vs. Gemini's Flash and Pro Claude’s lineup of AI models has four primary entries: Fable, Haiku, Opus, and Sonnet. Fable is Claude’s flagship model, and Anthropic says it's capable of the toughest challenges you have. However, expect to pay a hefty usage price to access it. Claude’s complex reasoning model, Opus, matches or surpasses Fable 5 in most areas and is much more efficient. Sonnet is Claude’s balanced, midrange model, whereas Haiku is Claude’s fastest, lightweight model, ideal for simpler tasks. It's possible to change the intelligence level of each Claude model. Gemini has Flash and Pro models. Flash is fast and suitable for daily use across most tasks, while Pro is Gemini’s complex reasoning model for tougher prompts. You can’t adjust the intelligence of Gemini’s models outside of its Antigravity app, though you can enable extended thinking. The latest model from Claude is Opus 5, while Gemini’s most recent is 3.7 Flash. Gemini also features image- and video-generation models, including Nano Banana, Nano Banana Pro, Omni, and Veo. Winner: Tie Web Search: Claude Goes Deeper With Prompts Both Claude and Gemini can search the web without issue and adequately source their findings. However, if you use Claude’s most capable models, especially at their highest intelligence settings, you can get better answers than what’s possible with Gemini’s 3.1 Pro model, even with extended thinking enabled. For example, I asked both bots about the current meta for The Finals, and Gemini’s answer lacked important details that Claude's included. Gemini has a dedicated shopping interface, complete with clickable tiles that make it easy to see product information and quickly open links to retailers. It also has a unique feature that lets you visualize how clothes will look on you. However, it doesn’t tell you anything about fit. Claude doesn’t have any meaningful shopping features. Nonetheless, I don’t recommend using AI as your only source of information when deciding what to buy. Winner: Claude Deep Research: Gemini’s Reports Are More Accessible and Detailed You can generate well-sourced reports on any topic with both Claude and Gemini. However, the quality of Gemini’s reports usually outshines Claude’s. For example, while troubleshooting a stuttering issue with my multi-monitor setup, Gemini’s report included helpful equations, tables, and a clear conclusion with steps to take. Claude’s report, on the other hand, was a lengthy block of text that concluded with a list of caveats and questions. Both interfaces have their strengths. Gemini lets me export reports to Google Docs with a single click and displays them in a large central window. Claude relegates reports to a sidebar for comparison. However, Claude provides a clearer visualization of its sources, making it easier to see how many pages from a particular site it accessed during the research. Claude doesn’t list the sources it ultimately cites, unlike Gemini. Winner: Gemini Image Editing and Generation: Claude Doesn’t Support Either Gemini’s AI image generation (and AI image editing) capabilities are top-notch, courtesy of its excellent Nano Banana series of models. Whether you want to make complicated diagrams, narrative-focused comics, or render scenes of any kind, Gemini can handle just about anything with minimal errors and distortion. Just keep in mind that editing images with Gemini can introduce some blurriness. Claude doesn’t support AI image editing or generation. However, you can make HTML-based visualizations with it. Below are some sample images I generated with Gemini’s Nano Banana Pro model: Winner: Gemini Video Generation: Gemini Wins by Default Video generation is another strength of Gemini, thanks to its best-in-class Omni and Veo models. Not only is Gemini capable of generating realistic video with audio, but you can also create videos from images or prompts. It's possible to extend clips with AI or even tap into some movie magic with Google’s AI filmmaking Flow tool. Since OpenAI killed Sora, Gemini and Grok are the only mainstream AI chatbots that support video generation, including Claude. Below is my favorite video clip generated with Gemini, courtesy of its Veo model: Winner: Gemini File Processing: Claude Identifies Fine Details That Gemini Misses In general, file processing doesn’t cause either chatbot to break a sweat. Both have large context windows, which is great for chewing through larger files, such as manuals or textbooks. Of course, that doesn’t mean Claude and Gemini will always answer every question about documents correctly, so make sure to verify anything critical. Although Gemini can understand images reasonably well, Claude’s image recognition is often more capable. For example, I presented both with an image of my computer's internals and a request to identify as many components as possible. Claude provided more specifics, such as correctly identifying my case and watercooling pump. Gemini’s identifications were far more vague. Winner: Claude Creative Writing: Both Deliver Competent But Cliche-Prone Writing Creative writing is a fairly trivial task for modern chatbots. From speeches to poems, you can prompt Claude and Gemini for pretty much any kind of writing. Just keep in mind that AI writing tends to have a distinct feel due to repetitive phrasings, topics, and word choices. For example, I asked Claude and Gemini for poems, and both focused on imagery seen during a walk: Winner: Tie Complex Reasoning: Claude’s Models Are Clearly Smarter Claude and Gemini can help with homework, whether you’re in high school or tackling a graduate-level course. Just don't assume they give you the correct answer every time. However, even Gemini’s Pro model with extended thinking enabled can't quite match Claude’s top models at their highest intelligence settings. For example, even with a relatively simple query about when Nioh 3’s final DLC will launch, Claude’s complex reasoning models gave a better answer. It included helpful details, such as the earlier-than-expected release of the first DLC, which Gemini didn't. You might not notice such a big difference with every prompt, though. Winner: Claude Coding: Gemini Just Isn’t a Great Coding Tool The AI coding market is fiercely competitive, with great options for both super-intelligent models and incredibly efficient ones. Gemini doesn’t stand out. It's impressively fast, but its intelligence pales in comparison to that of Claude’s models, such as Opus 5. Without careful prompt calibration, Gemini can and will mess up simple tasks that Claude handles easily. Although you might be able to incorporate Gemini into your workflows in some ways, Claude is a better choice for any hobbyist vibe coding projects. Winner: Claude Integrations: Gemini’s First-Party Support Is Peerless Claude supports a ton of integrations with a range of apps for both consumers and professionals, from Google Drive to Monday. The usefulness of these integrations depends on the apps you use and the available features, but they mostly just give you more ways to prompt Claude. For example, you can connect your Gmail and then ask Claude to tell you about your unread emails, among other things. Google embeds Gemini directly within Google apps. So, while you can open up Claude and ask it questions about your email, you could simply open up Gmail and prompt Gemini from the sidebar. This goes beyond email insights into upgrading your YouTube watching experience and much more. Furthermore, Gemini’s Personal Intelligence feature spans Google’s apps, allowing it to dynamically reference whatever information it needs to answer prompts. Claude doesn't offer anything similar. Winner: Gemini Agents: Claude Has No Answer for Gemini Spark Gemini Spark is my favorite AI agent, thanks to its generally competent performance, fast speeds, and impressive leverage of Personal Intelligence. For example, you can task Spark with finding you jobs, and it will automatically pull the resume you sent from your Gmail to match you with gigs that fit your experience. Claude doesn’t have an AI agent that competes with Spark in a meaningful way, and ChatGPT recently killed off its agent, so Gemini is one of the only chatbots worth using if you need regular AI agent access. Winner: Gemini Context Windows and Usage Caps: 1,000,000 Tokens on Both Claude and Gemini both have up to 1,000,000-token context windows, which is about as large as I've seen. This means both perform well when ingesting complex codebases, large documents, or anything else that might benefit from ample context. Both Claude and Gemini have five-hour and weekly usage limits that depend on your particular plan, but if you aren’t coding, you won’t have to pay much attention to those. Free users are likely to run into usage caps even if they aren't coding, however. For coders, Claude and Gemini (like other AI chatbots) may require more expensive plans, as usage can disappear quickly on both, depending on the task at hand. Winner: Tie Privacy: Neither Cares About Keeping You Safe Claude and Gemini collect a wide variety of data, and both use it to train their models by default. However, you can turn training off, and Google doesn’t use Workspace data for training by default, at least. Gemini feels particularly invasive with features like Personal Intelligence, though the functionality is unique. Neither chatbot has a history free of hacks or leaks, so I don't consider either of them especially reliable for safeguarding user data. You shouldn't share anything too sensitive with any AI chatbot. Winner: Tie And The Winner Is... Claude Both Claude and Gemini are impressive chatbots, but Claude wins this comparison because it excels in the area I consider most important: model intelligence. That makes it superior for everything from complex reasoning tasks to file processing to vibe coding. I’m much less interested in generating AI images and videos (which you can do to a limited extent for free with Gemini). However, if you care about media generation, frequently use Google apps, or want the best value in AI chatbots, Gemini is easy to recommend.

item.title: Microsoft Finally Backs Down: The Windows 11 Taskbar Update You've Been Waiting For
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.03
When Microsoft removed the option to move the taskbar with the release of Windows 11, that decision became a symbol of its refusal to listen to enthusiast feedback. Now, the company is reversing that stance. Next Tuesday, a movable taskbar is arriving on a PC near you, though the rollout may be a little messy. Once you get the update, you can also turn off Bing search results in the Start menu, effectively restricting searches to your files. This option addresses yet another major complaint I've heard about Windows. I watched from the audience at Build a few months ago as Satya Nadella proudly showed off the movable taskbar. Most Windows users will likely never move their taskbars, but Microsoft wants you to know you now have that freedom. As I've previously written, the Windows team is focusing heavily on feedback this year. I’ve been testing the taskbar and Start Menu features for months, so read on for everything you need to know about September’s forthcoming update, an easy-to-overlook update that makes OneDrive less annoying, and a convenient new keyboard shortcut tool you can download today. New Taskbar, Start Menu, and Search Options for the Masses (Eventually) Windows 11’s upgraded taskbar, Start menu, and search tools are available now in preview as part of the optional KB5120998 update, but Microsoft is likely to fully release them as part of a stable update on the next Patch Tuesday (Sept. 8). The preview update reportedly causes some glitches with mouse cursors, but I expect Microsoft to fix this issue before the final rollout. Once you install this update, you can move the taskbar to the left, right, or top edge of the screen. You can also shrink the taskbar to get more screen real estate. These options are under Settings > Personalization > Taskbar. The Start menu also gains toggles that hide the All, Pinned, and Recommended sections. Naturally, these options are accessible via Settings > Personalize > Start. Finally, you can turn off search results from Bing and the Store if you want to limit searches to just your files. Search options are under Settings > Privacy & Security > Search. I’ve been testing these features in Insider builds for a while, and they work so well that I no longer feel the need to use third-party tools like Start11 and ExplorerPatcher. Unfortunately, you might not immediately see these new features on your PC, since Microsoft’s patch notes indicate a “gradual rollout.” This means Microsoft will activate them on PCs over the coming weeks or months. You might not see them for a long time, or you might see them immediately. It's unfortunately random. OneDrive Becomes Slightly Less Annoying In more good news, Microsoft is backing off on pushy OneDrive prompts. Windows 11 still offers to back up your files to OneDrive, but a new “Opt out of backup” option lets you decline the offer indefinitely. Previously, Windows presented options, such as “Remind me in 3 days.” Although OneDrive is a high-quality cloud storage service, it's a perpetual annoyance in Windows. I've heard many user complaints about pop-ups, and I've even caught OneDrive silently enabling folder backup without asking first. The process of disabling OneDrive and getting your files back on your PC is often confusing, too. This change feels particularly welcome after a mysterious OneDrive Photos app appeared on many Windows PCs. Microsoft’s Jeff Teper, executive vice president of Microsoft apps and agents, says the company released the app by mistake, but it wouldn't shock me to see it resurface at some point. Window Hopper Brings a macOS-Style Shortcut to Windows Microsoft’s free PowerToys package has a new utility called Window Hopper, which brings a popular macOS-style keyboard shortcut to Windows. Window Hopper lets you switch between windows within your current app with the Alt+` keyboard shortcut. (That’s a grave accent symbol, which is located above the Tab key on your keyboard.) In other words, if you have five Chrome browser windows open, you can press Alt+` to switch between them. It’s a more focused alternative to the Alt+Tab shortcut, which shows open windows from all applications and can be quite cluttered. The Window Hopper utility is part of PowerToys version 0.101, which launched a few days ago. After installing the latest version, simply open PowerToys and toggle the Window Hopper option. You can customize Window Hopper’s keyboard shortcut, too. Ask Our Expert: How Do I Stop Windows From Pushing Microsoft Apps? Do you have a question about Windows? I’m here to share my knowledge! You can submit your question here, and I may answer it in an upcoming Windows Guide newsletter. If you’re not subscribed to the newsletter, head here to sign up, and check your inbox each week for the latest Windows updates from me. Now, on to this week’s question! Anita P. asks: “I understand why Microsoft wants me to use their products, but intrusively forcing their software on me only makes me mad. I am an old woman and set in my ways. I was perfectly happy with Windows 10. Now I have to deal with Edge, Bing, and OneDrive. Microsoft saves my passwords without my permission and didn’t tell me it was doing so. What can I do about this?” Hi Anita, thanks for writing in! Your concerns match how a lot of people feel about Windows. You might prefer Windows, but that doesn't mean you want to use Microsoft’s entire product line. Microsoft definitely uses Windows as a platform to promote its other applications and services, often in very pushy ways. Ultimately, you can bend Windows 11 to your needs (and feel more like Windows 10), but it might take a bit of work. While you can’t uninstall Edge (unless you live in Europe), you can set another browser as your default. As I mentioned above, Windows 11’s September update will let you turn off Bing search results in your Start menu. And Windows 11 also lets you uninstall OneDrive completely. You can remove it from the Settings > Apps > Installed Apps pane, just like you’d uninstall any other app. As far as passwords, Microsoft Edge and other modern web browsers are aggressive about saving personal details. If you stop using Edge, Windows shouldn’t automatically save any of your passwords. You can also stop your browser from automatically saving your passwords via the app's settings page. For example, if you use Chrome, go to Settings > Autofill and passwords > Google Password Manager > Settings, then turn off the Offer to save passwords and passkeys option. I recommend using a dedicated password manager instead. The process for disabling Chrome's autofill for addresses and payment methods is similar. In addition, you can delete many of Microsoft’s preinstalled apps from the Start menu: Just right-click their shortcuts and select Uninstall. Finally, we have a great guide to turning off the ads in Windows, which might help make the OS feel less annoying. About Our Expert I've been writing about technology for more than 15 years and using it in earnest for over twice as long. As a member of PCMag's software team, I focus on Windows coverage, but also write about other key desktop operating systems and system apps. (I used Windows 3.1 upon its release and have followed every subsequent release closely). Prior to joining PCMag, I wrote for How-To Geek starting in 2011, and my articles amassed over a billion page views. I went on to run the publication as editor-in-chief for four and a half years. I have also contributed to Computerworld, Fast Company, PCWorld, Reader's Digest, The New York Times, and many other outlets about everything from AI to PC hardware to Windows. I founded and ran my own direct-to-reader Windows-focused newsletters, Windows Intelligence and The Windows ReadMe, working in partnership with Thurrott.com.

item.title: Anthropic Fixed Fable 5.1's Worst Problems...So Why Am I Staying With Opus?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.85
Fable is perhaps the most intriguing AI model to date.
