Anthropic positioned it as the world’s most powerful LLM, comparable only with its big sibling, Mythos, which was too powerful for a public release. Then the US government banned it almost immediately, only to allow it to return in a less capable state. Now, Fable 5.1 is here. I’ve tried it, and I find it far more compelling, thanks to its friendlier pricing, relaxed censorship, and more. Here are the top five things Fable 5.1 gets right—and why all of these massive upgrades still aren't quite enough to change my daily routine. 1. Fable 5.1 Is Cheaper, Unlocked, and Here to Stay Previously, a cutoff date when Fable would only be accessible with purchasable credits rather than a regular Claude subscription loomed large over the experience, but that’s no longer the case. Now, you can access Fable via Enterprise, Max, and Team plans for up to 50% of your weekly usage. Of course, you still have the option to buy credits to keep using Fable beyond those limits. Fable 5.1 is also cheaper if you buy credits. According to Anthropic, you can expect savings of up to 25% in general and up to 45% for highly agentic work. This comes courtesy of reduced prices on cache reads, “where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored.” If you want to use Fable 5 heavily, these savings could potentially become significant. Just keep in mind that Opus 5 is still significantly cheaper per token and is available on all paid Claude plans. 2. Generous Usage Limits (With a Fine-Print Catch) Anthropic is currently (and has been since May) running a promotion that lets you enjoy 50% more weekly usage with Claude Code. However, when that promotion expires, Anthropic promises a permanent 25% increase to weekly usage across Enterprise, Max, Pro, and Team plans. So, although this means you can expect a 25% usage decrease versus what you’re getting now, that’s a permanent 25% bump over the baseline. Every bit of Fable usage counts, given the weekly usage limits. 3. Goodbye, Overly Aggressive Censorship Fable 5’s censorship was incredibly aggressive. Previously, when I asked benign questions such as, “What happened with Fable and the US government?" or “What’s new in chemistry?”, Fable bounced me back to Opus. And I couldn’t ask about potential exploits to any coding projects I was working on, either. Now, Fable 5.1 handles all of these prompts without issue. Safeguards are still in place, though, so don’t expect to hack into any mainframes with it. When Fable 5 came back online after its ban, Anthropic noted that it might falsely flag coding tasks. That tendency limited the LLM as a coding tool, but the company promised to continue refining its classifiers behind the scenes. It seems to have followed through on this initiative, as I haven’t encountered any issues with Fable 5.1 blocking coding-related prompts. Of course, your mileage may vary, but I no longer have any meaningful concerns about censorship. 4. Surprisingly, You Don't Need an ID Check When Fable 5 returned after its prohibition, Anthropic also updated its privacy policy to include a new section on ID verification. Considering the US government’s Fable ban focused on its use by foreign nationals, it seemed possible that you would soon need to provide ID to use Fable. However, this hasn't been the case. Although Anthropic notes that “a few use cases…might see a verification prompt when accessing certain capabilities,” this isn’t standard policy, and you can safely use Fable without the need to upload a picture ID. 5. Fable Reclaims Its Benchmark Crown From Opus Fable 5 was only briefly Anthropic’s most capable model. Opus 5 quickly outpaced it not just in efficiency but also in performance across Anthropic’s benchmarks for a variety of use cases, from agentic coding to biology. Since you could use Opus 5 with any plan to the full extent of your weekly usage limit, Fable 5 became difficult to justify. Now, Fable 5.1 tops Anthropic's list. So, if you actually need best-in-class performance, you should consider using Fable 5.1 first. That applies to everything from agentic coding tasks to complex business workflow development to scientific research and more. Why I'm Still Sticking With Opus Fable 5.1 is objectively much better than the original. If you have a tough task that Opus 5 just can’t handle, you can confidently turn to Fable 5.1 without spending extra money (or as much if you opt for credits), verifying your ID, or worrying about censorship. However, chances are that you won’t notice much of a difference versus Fable 5 or Opus 5 for simple coding projects or web searches. As always, I plan to keep testing Fable to see if any aspect of it could convince me to switch from Opus, but I haven't found one yet. About Our Expert I’ve been writing about consumer technology and video games for over a decade at a variety of publications, including Destructoid, GamesRadar+, Lifewire, PCGamesN, Trusted Reviews, and What Hi-Fi?, among many others. At PCMag, I review AI and productivity software—everything from chatbots to to-do list apps. In my free time, I’m likely cooking something, playing a game, or tinkering with my computer.

item.title: Say Goodbye to Microsoft Publisher. Try These 8 Alternatives Before It Disappears Next Month
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.76
Microsoft Publisher has survived as the default Windows graphic design app for 35 years, thanks to its simplicity and effectiveness, but its time is coming to an end. Whether you use it to create brochures, documents, flyers, newsletters, or simple ads, you will need to find an alternative once Microsoft kills it off in October. I've worked with many graphic design apps professionally over the years, and the ones I highlight below are the best alternatives to Publisher. Whether you want something with a similar feel or more advanced tools, you have plenty of excellent options. If You Want the Easiest Transition Possible If you don't want to learn how to use a new app or platform, the following recommendations will suffice. They should already feel familiar if you do any sort of typical office or productivity work. Microsoft PowerPoint Hiding in plain sight is a decent, basic layout app. It’s true—I've set up publication templates in PowerPoint for clients’ staff members who were unhappy using anything other than Publisher or Word for layout, neither of which is a good fit for that task. You just need to change your vantage point a bit. Consider setting up a document with 8.5-by-11-inch pages, rather than 16:9 ones. If you know how to use PowerPoint's Master Slides and Master Layouts, then you have a powerful master and parent page system at hand. The app also offers better-than-basic typography controls, such as custom bullet settings, line and word spacing, and more. It’s easy to create templates for others to use and to collaborate with your team. And don’t forget the handy access to Microsoft Copilot, which can help spark your creativity. PowerPoint is a part of Microsoft 365. Google Docs I surprised myself while writing this article in Google Docs. It's a great free alternative to Publisher, since it has most of the same capabilities and limitations. Additionally, you can create tables, dictate content, enjoy easy collaboration, export docs as PDFs, make custom bullet points, translate text, and even check your spelling and grammar. Its version history capability is also robust. Beginner-Friendly Design Platforms If Publisher's simplicity was the primary reason you stuck with it over the years, don't fret. For most community organizations, non-designers, and social media creators, the following apps are perfectly suitable and just as easy to use: Adobe Express Adobe Express offers a robust free version with high-quality fonts, professional photography tools, and sophisticated assets. Meanwhile, a paid subscription unlocks many goodies, such as 30 days' worth of version history, 100GB of cloud storage, a larger allocation of monthly AI credits, and significantly more fonts, stock content, and templates. It isn't quite as intuitive as Canva, but it strikes a nice balance between ease of use and polish for brand-keepers, freelancers, or small businesses that want better output quality without springing for a pro-level app. Canva Canva is more template-driven than Microsoft Designer. It offers a decent free version with lots of assets, while a paid subscription gets you additional tools, elements, features (such as a branding toolkit), and images. Think of Canva as a kitchen-sink-like app in which you can use customizable, predesigned templates to produce just about anything—flyers, presentations, websites, signs, social posts, and more. It makes it easy to get started, collaborate with others, organize your creations, and share your work. Microsoft Designer Microsoft Designer is available for free or with extra AI allowances and storage via a Microsoft 365 subscription. It's similar to Adobe Express and Canva in many ways, but it stands out for its prompt-first, AI-assisted design capabilities. As you begin typing your requirements and vision, Designer generates visuals and layout suggestions (much like templates)—it’s a good choice for quick creative iterations. However, it's not ideal if you have requirements for specific branding color formulations and Pantone-matching, or if you need to produce print-ready files. When You Need More Power and Precision Professional design applications have a steeper learning curve because they are orders of magnitude more capable than standard desktop publishing apps. For complex layouts, elegant long-format publications, high-level photo editing, packaging design, and ultra-precise typesetting using professional OpenType and variable typefaces, you need a pro-level app. Affinity Affinity is mid-to-high-tier, pro-level graphic design, layout, illustration, and vector editing software that’s easier to learn than Adobe InDesign. It's entirely free, too. Adobe InDesign Adobe InDesign is the industry-standard professional page layout and print design app for creating everything from brochures and posters to magazines, newspapers, and interactive ebooks. InDesign incorporates features, such as advanced typography capabilities, basic editing and importing of scalable vector graphics (SVG), and enhanced digital publishing and file export. Subscribers benefit from frequent updates that keep the software on the cutting edge of ever-evolving professional, social, and technical design trends. What’s more, individuals and teams can take advantage of Creative Cloud’s tight ecosystem of apps, which enables unsurpassed connectivity and collaboration among designers, authors, bosses, clients, and other creators. Powerful Free and Open-Source Alternatives Open-source apps are free for anyone to download and use. But, more importantly, they allow you to legally change or improve their underlying code and redistribute them. Behind most open-source projects are collaborative stewards within a community or organization—think non-profits, universities, and volunteers. Scribus Scribus is a desktop publishing and layout app that you can use to produce print-ready publications, such as booklets, brochures, magazines, and newsletters. It’s frame-based like Publisher, meaning it provides reasonable control over layouts. But it also includes color management features, export support for PDF and print formats, and typographic control. Goodbye, Publisher—Hello, Better Options Whatever app you choose, know that you're not stuck with it forever. Any of the replacement solutions above is a great starting point if you eventually intend to learn pro-level apps, like those in Adobe's Creative Cloud suite. You still have some time before Publisher is officially gone, but I think it's wise to get ahead of the change and figure out which app makes the most sense for you and your team of designers. You might not even miss Publisher once you make the switch. About Our Expert Shelby Putnam Tupper is founder and creative director of Shelby Designs Inc., a small-but-mighty, full-service, customer-obsessed design consultancy. She graduated from Trinity College in Connecticut with a BS in biology and a minor in French. She did post-graduate work at the School of the Art Institute in Chicago, where she received honors in the field of Medical & Scientific Illustration. She grew her entrepreneurial and design legs during her tenure at Harrison Design Group in San Francisco. Since its founding, Shelby Designs has received more than 100 local, national and international awards, has had their work published in books and top trade journals and exhibited in shows at The Palace of Fine Arts, The Masonic Auditorium and The SF Center for the Book. Outside the office, Shelby is a faceted artisan intoxicated by pre-1900s scientific illustration, engraving and typography. She also enjoys fiddling with her golden mean calipers and the number 1.618, and tinkers with computational graphics and Voronoi diagrams. She makes dimensional art from the pressroom’s recycled trimmings and fires up her torches to create jewelry from glass and steel. Shelby was born and raised in Oakland, where she lives with her husband, son and daughter, four cats, a gecko—and a tortoise named Darwin.

item.title: Laid-Off Developers Create AI Model to Replace CEOs and Other Executives
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.75
A group of developers who were let go due to AI efficiency savings have struck back at the executives who are often shielded from AI-induced layoffs by creating OpenExecutive, an AI tool designed to augment and replace executive decision-making, TechRadar reports. "Work happens around the clock. Leadership doesn't scale with it," a demo video says. Using the kind of language that executives have grown comfortable throwing around about AI replacing workers over the past years, it suggests the bottleneck to productivity and enhanced profitability at companies isn't a lack of worker enhancements; it's that leadership can't keep up. So why not replace them with AI? OpenExecutive presents as a singular AI for interactive purposes. However, in making its C-Suite-grade decisions, it leans on a virtual board of eight AI agents designed to emulate experts within an organizational structure. The singular voice is backed by an emulated CSO, CFO, HR officer, COO, marketing chief, a product officer, and a board comms director. Each of them can lean on the main executive AI to guide its actions and suggestions. They can all draw from company documents and data, remember their decisions, and trace back reasoning for that if you want to follow up on why they decided to do certain things. OpenExecutive is built on Anthropic's Claude AI model, using Claude Sonnet 4.6 by default, and Opus 4.7 for deeper reasoning tasks. It's distributed under the Apache 2.0 license, so anyone can use, modify, run it internally, or develop their own commercial product based on it. Although the whole project is somewhat tongue-in-cheek and a reminder to the higher-ups that AI may well come for us all eventually, it does have some legitimate uses. For smaller businesses that want organizational expertise to guide growth and expansion strategies, this kind of AI could be extremely useful. It might also be handy for any workers who want to get ahead of what their boss has planned for the future. Maybe you could offer useful suggestions for the business that would make you appear like a straight shooter with upper management written all over you. It also highlights the limitations of AI in meaningful ways that should be readily apparent wherever they're applied. OpenExecutive is designed as an advisory tool. It can't sign documents or hold legal weight; it can't actually replace decision-making positions. It augments them. While AI tools for employees are often suggested as replacements for workers, the technology can never replicate the nuance or taste of actual humans. Even if OpenExecutive isn't going to replace your boss's boss, maybe it can help them understand that. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: The New Roomba Max 875 Has Me Excited About iRobot for the First Time in Years
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.62
iRobot has finally stopped playing defense. After watching competitors dominate the high-end robot vacuum market with flashier bases and extendable arms, the pioneer of autonomous cleaning just unveiled its most ambitious flagship in years at IFA in Berlin: the Roomba Max 875 Combo. The headline feature isn't a gimmick; it's physics. The Max 875 uses a new SealForce chassis that lowers a skirt onto carpet fibers, creating an airtight seal to drag up deep-seated debris that traditional vacuums leave behind. If it performs in real-world testing the way it looks on paper, iRobot won't just be back in the conversation—it'll be setting the standard all over again. SealForce Tech: Fixing Robot Vacuums' Biggest Weakness The Roomba Max 875 has a lot of suction power—at 35,000Pa, it’s near the top of the industry. It’s also designed to create tornado-like airflow at up to 20 liters a second. Moreover, it uses what iRobot calls SealForce Vacuuming Technology, in which the chassis lowers a skirt over the carpet as it runs, creating a seal with the carpet fibers and focusing the airflow on the precise spot the vacuum is trying to clean. Between the powerful suction and airflow concentration, I’m hopeful that the 875 can tackle stubborn debris better than the competition. The tech comes with its share of questions. How good can the seal be if the vacuum keeps moving? Will the seal adapt to carpets of different lengths? Will it cause wear and tear on the carpet and strain its fibers by tugging on them? Will it scratch harder floors when traversing them? I’m looking forward to testing the 875 to find out the answers to these questions. If it doesn’t cause undue wear on flooring and creates even a semi-effective seal, it genuinely seems like it could be the first feature in a long time to meaningfully improve the vacuuming aspect of robot vacuums. ThermaMist and Mopping: Fighting Stains With Hot Steam The Roomba Max 875 isn’t just a vacuum. It also has a self-cleaning roller mop, which is my favorite mop design. To complement the mop and help it scrub tough stains, the 875 also features Ultrasonic ThermaMist. A nozzle in front of the mop sprays heated steam on the ground when it detects a stain, loosening the dirt and letting the mop do its job after the area is doused. The roller mop then scrubs with 18 newtons of downward pressure while spinning at 300 rotations per minute. When on carpet, the mop avoids cross-contamination by raising itself into the chassis, while a protective cover extends over it. Other models I've tested have spray nozzles and roller mops, so the Thermamist feature isn’t as innovative as SealForce. Even so, it still sounds promising. Everything Else: LiDAR, AI, and a Fully Automated Dock The Roomba Max 875 navigates with LiDAR and a camera with built-in AI to avoid obstacles. It can extend both its side brush and roller mop to the side to clean along walls. It can climb thresholds and doesn’t have a navigation tower jutting up from the top, so it can more easily fit under furniture. The base empties dirt into an allergen-sealed bag that can last for 90 days of ordinary use. It washes and dries the mop with hot water and hot air, respectively. It also has separate reservoirs for clean water, dirty water, and detergent. Altogether, the Roomba Max 875 is a competitive premium hybrid model. Its $1,199 price even undercuts some of our favorite high-end models, like the $1,599.99 Roborock Saro 10. Want It Cheaper? The Roomba Plus 678 Offers SealForce for $899 In addition to the Roomba 875, iRobot is debuting the Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $899. This upper-midrange model still uses SealForce Vacuuming Technology, but with slight steps down in power (30,000Pa) and airflow. The 678 still has a self-cleaning roller mop with 15 newtons of downward pressure for scrubbing. It doesn’t have the flagship's heated mist and instead uses a simple pressurized water jet to spray stains. This mop doesn’t have the retracting cover, but it will lift out of the way when traversing carpets. Otherwise, it has a base station that empties the dirt, washes, and dries the mop. The 678 navigates with LiDAR and an AI-equipped cam. It looks like a capable, well-equipped hybrid vacuum/mop and a more affordable way to access SealForce. The Verdict: Roomba Might Finally Be Back Traditional upright and cordless vacuums tend to create seals of varying quality as they work to optimize airflow. Robot vacuums have instead relied on brush rolls and body design to ensure airflow quality, enabling them to clean effectively while moving efficiently and autonomously. The retracting skirt of the Roomba 875 and 678 feels like an excellent compromise, and a potential step forward for the category. Both models are now available on iRobot's site and will hit retailers by the end of the month. I look forward to putting them to the test as soon as I can to see if they live up to their potential. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Get Peak Wi-Fi Speeds Everywhere In Your House With These September Mesh Network Deals
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 2.04
Updated September 2: Your home network probably has more devices hooked up to it every single year, from desktops and laptops to smart devices, phones, and who knows what else. The more connections, the harder your router has to work, and devices farther away can struggle for bandwidth. That's why modern homes should go for a Wi-Fi mesh network system, which uses adaptive signal distribution to pump out exceptional speed and stability across dozens of devices and thousands of square feet, with no slow spots or dead zones. PCMag has reviewed tons of mesh network systems, routers, and range extenders, submitting them to quantitative tests for signal strength, speed, square foot coverage, ease of setup, and more. These are the five best mesh Wi-Fi systems on sale this month. TP-Link Deal Let's start off with a $70 discount on one of the most capable Wi-Fi 7 mesh networks on the market, the TP-Link Deco 7 Pro. This three-node system took home an Editors' Choice award in our review, with PCMag expert John R. Delaney praising its "superb throughput and signal strength." The setup capitalizes on a huge swath of radio frequencies to spread the signal over up to 7,600 square feet, with support for as many as 200 hundred devices. Multiple gigabit Ethernet ports on every unit let you prioritize wired connections for gaming PCs, streaming hardware, and other bandwidth-hungry devices. As a cherry on top of the sundae, it comes with a lifetime free subscription to TP-Link’s HomeShield network security and parental control software. Google Nest Deal This is just a single node, but for this price the Google Nest Pro mesh router is a great way to dip your toe into modern networking without spending a ton. We had a generally positive review of this model, noting that it delivered solid performance and nice integrations with Matter and Threads-compatible smart devices. Installation is a breeze, with the intuitive Google Home app letting you run speed tests, set up passwords, and enable parental controls. Our signal strength tests were good, but if you want to stretch farther than the covered 2,200 square feet you'll need an additional node. At 50% off, it's a no-brainer to pick one up. Netgear Deal You can snag $50 off this very solid Netgear mesh system at Amazon right now. While it does support the Wi-Fi 7 protocol, it's restricted to two bands, leaving the 6GHz band on the table. That shouldn't be much of a downside for the vast majority of home systems, as it still delivers excellent throughput and stability. We have a comprehensive review of this system, noting that it was a breeze to set up, with plenty of configuration options and an intuitive mobile app. It also performed well in our real-world coverage tests. This three-node system is rated to cover up to 6,000 square feet, with 70 unique devices at the maximum. It does lack free parental control and security software, which Netgear offers from a separate subscription. Asus Deal For another Editors Choice-winning mesh option, this $200 price drop on the Asus ZenWiFi AX660 system is a sweet deal. In our review, we were dazzled by how capable its performance was, delivering lightning-fast throughput in every spot of our testing area. Installation was a piece of cake, with just a few easy-to-follow steps and great customer support if you need it. Under the hood, the hardware is top-notch, with six internal antennas per node reaching maximum data rates of up to 574Mbps on the 2.4GHz band, 1201Mbps on one of the 5GHz bands, and 4804Mbps on the other 5GHz band. We also liked the inclusion of a lifetime subscription to Asus’s AIProtection Pro, a Trend Micro-powered suite of security and parental control tools. MSI Deal If you have a smaller home but still need a multi-node mesh solution, you can't beat the price on the MSI Roamii BE Lite. We gave a positive review to this basic but capable dual-unit system, noting that it was simple to set up and configure and delivered solid multi-gig connectivity. Even though it lacks access to the 6GHz radio band that many other Wi-Fi 7 systems use, it still promises theoretical data rates of up to 688Mbps on the 2.4GHz band and up to 4,323Mbps on the 5GHz band, more than enough for lag-free gaming and video streaming. It has plenty of customization options for guest networks and the like, and includes free parental control and network security software. More Mesh Network Deals - TP-Link Deco BE63 BE10000 Tri-Band Wi-Fi 7 Mesh Sy... — $399.98 ($499.99) Save $100.01 - TP-Link Deco X55 AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 Mesh System (3-Pack) — $149.97 ($189.99) Save $40.02 - Netgear Orbi 870 Tri-Band Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System (3-Pack) — $899.99 ($1,299.99) Save $400.00 - Asus ZenWiFi BT10 Tri-Band Wi-Fi 7 Mesh System (2-Pack) — $549.00 ($689.99) Save $140.99 - Get the Best Prices On Routers — Download Our Free Price Comparison Tool $0 - Best Wi-Fi Mesh Network System Deals at Amazon - Best Wi-Fi Mesh Network System Deals at Newegg - Best Wi-Fi Mesh Network System Deals Walmart What Is a Wi-Fi Mesh System? Mesh Wi-Fi systems (or mesh Wi-Fi routers) are designed to extend the range of your wireless coverage. These systems consist of several networking components: a main router, which connects directly to your modem, and a series of satellite modules, or nodes, placed throughout your house. They are all part of a single wireless network, and they share the same SSID and password. Which Is Better: A Wireless Mesh Router or a Range Extender? Wi-Fi systems are user-friendly. Thanks to a companion app, they are a snap to set up and manage. Mesh systems offer whole-house coverage, and they provide seamless room-to-room roaming over a single network. On that second point, wireless extenders, in contrast, tend to require you to reconnect from network to network as you move in and out of range of the base router or the extender. For more about the differences between these two technologies, check out our explainer, Wi-Fi Range Extender vs. Mesh Network: What's the Difference. Do Wi-Fi Mesh Systems Support Wi-Fi 6? Most do, and it's the minimum Wi-Fi version you should look for on a Wi-Fi mesh system. Wi-Fi 6 (also called 802.11ax) offers fast throughput speeds (up to 9.6Gbps), low network congestion, and excellent range performance. However, if your budget allows, you should consider springing for a Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 system. The cutting-edge Wi-Fi 7 standard promises even better performance than those that preceded it, and it's backward-compatible, too. What Is the Best Wi-Fi Mesh System to Buy? That depends on your budget and individual connectivity needs. The Asus ZenWiFi BQ16 Pro is our current overall top pick for Wi-Fi mesh systems, while the TP-Link Deco BE63 is our pick for the best budget option. For even more details and options, check out our guide to the best Wi-Fi systems we've tested. What Are the Best Deals on Wi-Fi Mesh Systems? Expect to spend around $200 on a budget Wi-Fi 6 system for use in a smaller house with few devices, around $500 for a mainstream mesh kit, and $750 and up for a high-end Wi-Fi 7 option. If you find a well-rated system that's cheaper than these guidelines, jump on it! Do Wi-Fi Mesh Routers Go on Sale During Prime Day or Black Friday? Yes. Mesh systems are typically frequently discounted but often receive their deepest discounts during these sales events. Plus, Amazon owns Eero, one of the leading mesh systems manufacturers. So, you should expect exceptional deals on these award-winning systems during Amazon Prime Day. Are There Bundle Deals on Multiple-Node Systems? Yes. Mesh systems get cheaper on a per-node basis the more nodes you buy. However, you should first determine how many nodes your house actually needs rather than buying a three-piece system because it's a better per-node deal than a two-piece one. A good rule of thumb is to match your home's square footage with the manufacturer's rating for a given system, then add a node if you have thick walls, live in a dense neighborhood, have lots of small rooms, or have other similar situations. About Our Experts K. Thor Jensen is a writer and cartoonist living in the Pacific Northwest. He has contributed to dozens of prestigious outlets, including PCMag, Tested, Clickhole, and Newsweek. His second graphic novel, Cloud Stories, was released in 2017. I’m a managing editor at PCMag.com focused on PC hardware. Reading this during the day? Then you've caught me testing gear and editing reviews of Wi-Fi routers, printers, laptops, and tons of other personal tech. (Reading this at night? Then I’m probably dreaming about all those cool products.) I’ve covered the consumer tech world as an editor, reporter, and analyst since 2015. I've covered most major consumer tech events, including CES, Computex, Google I/O, and IFA. I've also appeared on CBS News, in USA Today, and at many other outlets to offer analysis on breaking technology news. Before I joined the tech-journalism ranks, I wrote on topics as diverse as Borneo's rainforests, Middle Eastern airlines, and Big Data's role in presidential elections. A graduate of Middlebury College, I also have a master's degree in journalism and French Studies from New York University. When she isn't perusing online stores for deals, Jade enjoys playing video games (mostly JRPGs and roguelikes), sorting board game components neatly into containers, and building Gundam models. Her love of electronics has persisted through her youth and has resulted in a collection of gaming peripherals including keyboards and controllers, scale figures, and art work. Jade lives in blissful harmony with her wife, cat, and two chinchillas—as well as a host of houseplants.

item.title: Claude Fable 5.1 sometimes guesses rather than searches. Here’s the fix
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 6.58
If you’re an experienced Claude user, here’s a phrase you know all too well: “Let me check rather than guess.” It’s one of those little Claude-isms that pops up every so often in Claude Code and other Claude platforms, right up there with “One thing worth flagging” and “Here’s the honest version.” In this context, “Let me check rather than guess” is Claude’s way of saying it’s about to kick off a web search rather than relying on its native memory, which has a cutoff date that can be weeks or even months old. Claude is being diligent about double-checking its facts rather than assuming. In my recent tests, most consumer-grade ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini models are quite diligent about searching rather than assuming, with even the puny-but-ultra-fast Claude Haiku 4.5 pausing to search before sounding off on, say, Apple’s just-announced Mac mini models. Surprisingly, Claude Fable 5.1—Anthropic’s most powerful new Claude model—does have a tendency to skip the searching and just guess, mainly when it’s set to low effort levels. Word of that curious quirk comes directly from Anthropic itself, which notes in its Fable 5.1 prompting guide that when its reasoning effort is set to “low,” the model “is less likely than Claude Fable 5 to call a search or retrieval tool, and more likely to answer from memory.” Anthropic’s first tip for making Fable 5.1 remember to search is to simply raise its effort level, keeping in mind that you can boost Fable’s effort setting for just a single conversational “turn” (and thus consume fewer AI tokens) rather than for the entire chat. There’s another option, however: a “nudge toward verification,” which comes in the form of a Fable 5.1-specific system prompt: When a query centers on a name you do not confidently recognize, or recognize from a fast-moving area like AI models and developer tools where the landscape shifts within months, the name itself is the thing to verify: search before answering, and include the name as the user wrote it in at least one query alongside any reformulations. This holds even when you have some background on it — partial background is exactly what makes an out-of-date answer sound authoritative, so familiarity is not a reason to skip the search. This prompt, which comes directly from Anthropic’s prompting guide (and can be added to the Instructions for Claude field in Claude’s app settings), effectively tells Fable 5.1 that “recognizing a name isn’t the same as knowing its current state, and that such names should be searched as the user wrote them,” according to Anthropic’s notes. While this “verify the name” prompt is written specifically for Claude Fable 5.1, it could come in handy for any AI model that tends to guess rather than check its facts, particularly local LLMs that aren’t as savvy as even the smallest ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini models.

item.title: How to reorder PDF pages quickly and easily
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.48
Need to rearrange the pages in a PDF without uploading the file to an online service? PDF Arranger lets you do exactly that. With multi-page PDF files, you may sometimes need to rearrange the pages. This isn’t possible with Acrobat Reader, and most other PDF viewers don’t support this either. The downside with using an online tool such as PDF24 is that you have no control over who can access your PDF. A simple but effective local solution is the open-source software PDF Arranger. On GitHub, click on the version number under Releases to download the MSI file and install the program. Once you’ve opened the tool, click on the hamburger menu with the three horizontal lines, select Open, and navigate to your PDF document. Foundry Alternatively, you can simply drag the file from File Explorer into the program window. PDF Arranger will now display thumbnails of the individual pages. You can drag and drop them into the desired positions. Click Save in the hamburger menu to save the new order. Because PDF Arranger runs locally, your PDF doesn’t need to be uploaded to an online service.

item.title: Firefox 155 patches 30 security flaws, adds sortable tab groups
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.25
The newest major release of Firefox 155 for Windows, macOS, Linux, and Android brings a number of improvements, including support for Nintendo Switch Pro controllers and sortable tab groups. Mozilla has also patched over 30 security vulnerabilities, and updates are also available for the ESR versions of Firefox for older systems. The release of the next major version, Firefox 156, is already scheduled for September 15th, with time for a bug-fix update on September 8th. What’s new in Firefox 155? The “AI” feature known as “Smart Window” (currently still labeled as a beta version) now makes it easier to revisit topics you’ve already covered. Questions are intended to be answered more quickly, complete with source references. It’s being rolled out gradually. The isolated tab environments introduced with Firefox 153 can now be sorted according to user preferences in settings. Tab environments isolate cookies from one another, allowing you to log in to the same website with different accounts across different tabs. This means you can, for example, actively use multiple Gmail inboxes at once. Another small improvement involves the display in the address bar that shows how many trackers were blocked on the current page. Firefox now allows this display to be disabled in the settings without turning off tracker blocking altogether. This feature is being rolled out gradually. The free built-in VPN feature, which was introduced back in Firefox 149, continues to offer the expanded selection of 32 virtual locations, but now that August is over, the unlimited data usage has been ended and is now capped at 50GB per month again. The free VPN is now also rolling out on Firefox for Android, with iOS set to follow soon. Other improvements include: the ability to scale up small PDF files to fit paper size when printing, and support for Nintendo Switch Pro controllers when playing browser-based online games on Windows. Since Firefox 154, there’s also been support for game streaming with Nvidia GeForce Now. Security flaws fixed in Firefox 155 In the security advisory for Firefox 155, Mozilla lists 29 security vulnerabilities that have been fixed, 25 of which were discovered and reported by external security researchers. Mozilla classifies 10 of these vulnerabilities as high risk, including several use-after-free (UAF) flaws that could allow malicious code to escape the browser’s sandbox. The last four entries in the security advisory (CVE-2026-84142 to CVE-2026-84145) summarize an unspecified number of internally discovered security flaws—most of which are classified as high risk—resulting from programming errors in memory management. The vulnerabilities are grouped according to which program versions are affected. Tip: Whether you keep your browser up to date, you need proper antivirus protections if you want your PC to remain secure and private. Check out our picks for the best antivirus software for Windows as well as best VPN services to stay ahead of security problems. Firefox ESR browser updates Alongside Firefox 155.0, the ESR versions 153.2.0, 140.15.0, and 115.40.0 are also available. The latter is only available for Windows 7 and 8.1, and macOS 10.12 to 10.14, and will remain so at least until March 2027. In the ESR versions, Mozilla has fixed the above-mentioned vulnerabilities that were also present in the code of those previous browser generations. This amounts to more than 24 vulnerabilities fixed in Firefox 153.2.0, at least 11 in Firefox 140.15, and at least six in Firefox 115.40. Firefox ESR 140 will receive a final update to version 140.17 at the end of September. This generation will then be replaced by Firefox ESR 153.

item.title: Windows 11 will now only make you restart once a month for updates
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.09
In summary: - PCWorld reports that Microsoft has changed how Windows 11 handles updates, now bundling drivers and firmware together with monthly security patches. - This means users will likely only need to restart their PC once a month during the regular Patch Tuesday cycle, reducing interruptions. - The change applies to versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H1, though critical Microsoft Defender security fixes may still trigger immediate restarts when necessary. Microsoft now bundles updates for drivers, the .NET Framework, and firmware together with the regular security updates that go out on Patch Tuesday every month. This consolidation brings one huge advantage to Windows users: your Windows 11 PC now only needs to be restarted once a month to remain up-to-date and secure. As reported by Windows Latest, this change affects Windows 11 versions 24H2, 25H2, and 26H1. Microsoft began rolling out this update bundle to compatible computers at the end of July, but starting with August’s Patch Tuesday, Microsoft began rolling out this change even more extensively (but still gradually) to all Windows 11 PCs. By bundling these updates, Microsoft is eliminating a real nuisance for Windows users. Until now, Windows has often (frustratingly) required several restarts per month, depending on whether driver, firmware, and .NET updates were released in addition to cumulative Windows updates. Now, however, the plan is for all updates requiring a system restart to wait quietly in the background for the next Patch Tuesday security update. As soon as the security update is ready for installation, Windows will also install all the other pending updates with it. Afterwards, Windows 11 will restart exactly once to complete the installation of all updates—and ideally, the restart will happen at a time that doesn’t interrupt your work. Microsoft explains in greater detail on this support page: Windows helps keep your device secure and reliable by downloading and installing updates automatically. Some of these updates need your device to restart before installation can finish. In the past, different types of updates could each ask you to restart at different times during the month — which meant more interruptions than necessary. Starting with the Windows updates released on and after July 28, 2026, Windows brings these updates together, so you restart just once a month. Instead of restarting for each update as it arrives and installs, Windows holds updates that need a restart and installs them together with the monthly security update. The result is a more predictable update experience with fewer interruptions. However, there are exceptions, namely updates that need to be installed as quickly as possible for security reasons. These include, for example, updates to Microsoft Defender and priority bug fixes that resolve critical issues outside the regular patch schedule.

item.title: This Windows security trick auto-locks your PC when you leave
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 5.02
I’m pretty good about remembering to lock my PC when I leave my desk, but every once in a while I forget. Thankfully, when I walk away from my computer and my brain is already halfway to the coffee machine, there’s an easy way to keep it protected. Windows’ Dynamic Lock gives you a handy backup plan by using your phone to tell when you’ve walked away. Joel Lee / IDG Dynamic Lock works via Bluetooth. Pair your phone with your Windows PC, then go to Settings > Accounts > Sign-in options > Dynamic lock and enable the option that lets Windows lock your device when you’re away. Once it’s turned on, Windows monitors the Bluetooth signal from your phone. When you walk far enough away that the signal drops out of range, Windows assumes you’ve left and automatically locks your PC. Microsoft says this should happen within about a minute after your phone goes out of Bluetooth range. In my experience, it usually takes less than 30 seconds. Dynamic Lock is really handy at an office, coffee shop, library, or anywhere else you might step away from your computer and need to secure it. While Dynamic Lock is a useful backup, it shouldn’t be treated as a replacement for directly locking your computer with Win + L. Dynamic Lock isn’t instant. There can be a short window between you leaving and Windows locking itself, and Bluetooth isn’t something I’d want to depend on as my only line of defense. When you can, always try to remember to press Win + L before leaving your PC. For more fun and helpful tips, tricks, and website and app recommendations, be sure to subscribe to our PCWorld Try This newsletter.

item.title: TP-Link’s first Wi-Fi 8 router promises speed and fewer dropped connections
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.80
In summary: - PCWorld reports that TP-Link has unveiled its first Wi-Fi 8 products, the Archer 8 Ultra router and Deco 8 Ultra mesh system, promising speeds up to 19 Gbps and 22 Gbps respectively. - Wi-Fi 8 focuses on Ultra High Reliability, with TP-Link’s new StabilityEngine technology designed to manage multiple devices and reduce interference for fewer dropped connections. - Pre-orders for the Archer 8 Ultra are expected to begin September 30th, positioning TP-Link as an early leader in next-generation home networking. Ahead of the IFA 2026 tech trade fair in Berlin, TP-Link has unveiled the first products in its all-new Wi-Fi 8 lineup, including the Archer 8 Ultra router and the Deco 8 Ultra mesh system, both of which are based on the IEEE 802.11bn standard (also known as UHR or Wi-Fi 8). Unlike previous Wi-Fi generations, which focused on increasing top data transfer speeds, Wi-Fi 8 is mainly designed to improve stability for more consistent connections. Hence, it being called UHR (Ultra High Reliability). With these products, TP-Link combines the Wi-Fi 8 standard with its own StabilityEngine, which uses several technologies to improve range, reduce interference, and manage multiple devices simultaneously. TP-Link The Archer 8 Ultra is a tri-band router with combined wireless speeds of up to 19 Gbps and wired connections of up to 10 Gbps. It has 18 built-in antennas and a sleek design that TP-Link hopes will encourage users to leave on display, thereby improving signal quality further. Pre-orders for the Archer 8 Ultra router open on September 30th. TP-Link Meanwhile, the Deco 8 Ultra is a tri-band mesh system with combined wireless speeds of up to 22 Gbps and Ethernet speeds of up to 10 Gbps. The Deco 8 Ultra is expected to be released in the first quarter of 2027. Pricing hasn’t been announced for either product yet.

item.title: Acer’s new gaming handheld has a tiny laptop hiding inside
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.39
Who’s going to spend $1,500 to $2,000 on a handheld gaming PC when we both need and want a laptop too? Apparently, Acer has been pondering this thought. In addition to a new conventional Steam Deck-style handheld, the company is showing off its DualPlay Mini concept—a handheld that can transform into a tiny laptop. And I do mean tiny. The screen on this device is 8 inches, which is chunky for a portable gaming device but old-fashioned netbook territory for a laptop. This isn’t the first time we’ve seen itty-bitty laptops with game controls attached, but I do believe this is the first time I’ve seen one with a screen that flips around and a hidden keyboard under the controls. Acer The screen seems to hinge around a point in the middle, rotating down and reversing orientation once you lift up the left and right sections. Bam, you’ve got a chunky little laptop with a backlit and apparently full-sized keyboard… notably one that lacks a trackpad. A shot of the DualPlay Mini in a haphazard shooter mode shows the user with a full-sized, wireless mouse, playing on a desktop. It’s unclear exactly how committed Acer is to the idea of this device as a productivity gadget, something you could really do work on. A promo shot of a person running Windows in an airliner seat certainly seems to imply that it’s possible. But Acer’s promotional text also points out that you can connect to an external screen if you want. Acer This is very much a concept device, with little available in terms of specs aside from the fact that it’s “powered by Intel” and using the same cooling architecture as the Predator Atlas 8. That’s using Intel’s new handheld-focused Arc G3 chips, so it makes sense. Whether we’ll ever see this interesting design on a store shelf will probably come down to both the initial response to its IFA reveal and what prices for RAM, storage, and chips will look like in a few months. Acer does have a smaller cousin to the Atlas 8—predictably titled the Atlas 7—ready to go in North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia “from September 2026.” Acer This slightly sleeker handheld will offer an Arc G3 or Arc G3 Extreme processor (Arc B370 or B390 graphics, respectively), a 7-inch 1080p IPS screen with 120Hz refresh rate, “up to” 24GB of RAM and 1TB of storage, and either a 60 or 80 watt-hour battery. Pricing is still a mystery. (That’s hardly surprising, since the Atlas 8 announced three months ago still doesn’t have an official price ahead of its October release.)

item.title: Acer’s new Swift Blade 14 might be the lightest 14-inch laptop yet
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 4.07
Are we in a thin-and-light laptop renaissance? Acer’s new sub-2-pound Acer Swift Blade 14 implies that we are. A few months ago, I balanced Acer’s TravelMate P6 14 AI in my hand. It weighed just 1 kg (2.2 pounds), limbo-ing under the 1kg bar like a feather. Now, Acer has debuted the Swift Blade 14 at an incredible 0.8 kg (1.76 pounds), shaving off an additional 0.2 kg from the TravelMate’s bulk. I can only imagine what that feels like! Put another way, if Acer somehow managed to repeat the process, that would put it at almost the exact weight of Apple’s smaller 13-inch iPad Pro… without its additional, optional keyboard. So, what changed? The processor, mainly. Intel designed its “Wildcat Lake” chip for cheaper, lighter devices and Acer’s Swift Blade 14 (SFB14-53CF) takes full advantage of that with an Intel Core 7 350 chip inside. (Acer is also launching a 16-inch version of the Swift Air 14, which it launched at Computex. It’s a 3.31-pound device, also based on the Core 7 350, and will ship in the first quarter of 2027.) Acer Productivity laptops have to balance two things: a large, bright, high-resolution-enough screen that’s comfortable to look at, and enough power efficiency to make that screen work without draining battery life. (The Swift Blade includes either 1920×1200 IPS, 1920×1200 OLED, or 2880×1800 OLED display options.) Adding a larger battery pushes that battery life number up, but at the cost of additional weight. The chassis plays a role, too. Here, Acer used a combination of magnesium-aluminum alloy plus carbon fiber to lighten the load. And while the TravelMate ships in business black, the Swift Blade 14 will be available in two colorways: marshmallow blue and white. Incidentally, while the Swift Blade isn’t the lightest laptop—the 13.3-inch Fujitsu Lifebook UH-X weighs 1.40 pounds—it might be the lightest 14-inch laptop announced so far. I don’t care as much about how thin a laptop is, though, and Acer seemingly agrees with me. The Swift Blade 14 measures 12.3 x 8.54 x 0.51 inches, which is thin but not too thin. If a laptop is too thin, it can suffer from bending and other structural issues. Intel’s Wildcat Lake was designed inside a single module, reducing the need for a bulky, heavier cooling system. At the time, Intel suggested it might use memory designed for smartphones to reduce cost. There’s no indication that Intel or Acer went that route, but there’s a standard loadout of 12GB of LPDDR5-6400, which differs a bit from the standard 8GB or 16GB options. Storage options will climb “up to” 1TB of PCIe Gen4 SSD storage. Also, Wildcat Lake lacks advanced I/O, so there’s only a pair of standard 10Gbps USB-C ports alongside Wi-Fi 6 and Bluetooth 5.3. Acer The other consideration, however, is performance. It’s here that Acer and other laptop makers suffer. Based on my review of the Lenovo IdeaPad Slim 3i, the Core 7 350 just isn’t that powerful. (It’s also worth noting that even the Apple iPad Pro uses an Apple M5 chip.) However, the 50 watt-hour battery inside that laptop allowed it to loop a 4K video for over 12 hours before the battery expired. My conclusion? The Slim 3i was a decent laptop by itself, but paled by comparison. However, the Slim 3i weighed 3.51 pounds—that’s two Swift Blade 14s, combined! The weight, then, opens up another opportunity for the Swift Blade 14 to attract potential buyers who are less interested in an ultra-endurance, powerful laptop and simply want a computing solution with as little bulk as possible. So, what do the availability and ship date look like? Well, that’s still a mystery. Ongoing shortages of memory and storage have made these questions perpetually difficult to answer, and Acer isn’t saying when the Swift Blade 14 will ship to US customers and what the price will be. (Europeans will receive it in December.) Here are the specifications for the Swift Blade, as presented by Acer:

item.title: How HDMI Technology Delivers Smoother, More Immersive Gaming
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.98
In computer and video gaming, connectivity plays a defining role in shaping the overall experience. HDMI® technology has established itself for delivering both high-definition video and high-resolution audio through a licensed, tested and certified seamless connection. Its widespread adoption across gaming consoles, PCs, displays, and home entertainment systems makes it the most versatile and reliable interface for gamers of all levels. One of HDMI technology’s greatest strengths is its ability to transmit uncompressed audio and video signals. This ensures that gamers experience content exactly as it was intended—without degradation or compromise. Support for advanced audio formats such as Dolby Atmos™ enables cinematic, immersive soundscapes that bring game worlds to life. On the visual side, HDMI technology supports resolutions up to 4K, 8K and even 16K. But don’t forget that current HDMI products’ support of 48Gbps and the upcoming support for 96Gbps enable support and display with higher color bit depth. An 8-bit image provides 256 shades for each primary color, producing approximately 16.7 million colors. This has long been the standard for traditional video. A 10-bit image increases that to 1,024 shades per color channel, producing more than one billion colors, while 12-bit color delivers 4,096 shades per channel for an incredible 68 billion possible colors. The additional color precision produces smoother gradients and more natural-looking images by reducing visible color banding. This is especially important for HDR gaming, where greater brightness, contrast, and wider color gamuts need more precise color reproduction. In fact, the ITU-R BT.2020 standard specifies 10-bit color as the minimum requirement for UHD HDR content. Whether navigating expansive open worlds or competing in fast-paced multiplayer environments, HDMI technology also ensures crisp visuals and smooth rendering and super-fast refresh rates. This high performance, combined with broad compatibility across devices, reinforces HDMI technology as the essential backbone of modern gaming systems. Advanced HDMI Gaming Features Beyond its core capabilities, HDMI technology continues to drive gaming experiences with features specifically designed to enhance gaming performance. Variable Refresh Rate (VRR) dynamically synchronizes the display’s refresh rate with the game’s frame rate. This eliminates screen tearing and stuttering, resulting in smoother gameplay—especially critical during high-speed action sequences or competitive play. Auto Low Latency Mode (ALLM) automatically switches compatible displays into low-latency game mode, reducing input lag and ensuring that player actions are reflected on-screen as quickly as possible. Quick Frame Transport (QFT) reduces display latency by transmitting frames at a higher rate. This minimizes the delay between a command input—such as pressing a controller button—and the corresponding on-screen action. HDMI Licensing Administrator, Inc Portable Consoles and Big-Screen Connectivity Portable gaming consoles have surged in popularity, offering powerful, console-quality experiences in compact, handheld formats. But their capabilities extend far beyond on-the-go entertainment. HDMI technology enables these devices to seamlessly transition into full home entertainment systems by connecting directly to HDTVs. With an HDMI cable connection, portable consoles can deliver high-definition visuals and immersive audio on large screens. This transforms personal gaming into a shared experience, ideal for social gatherings, family play, or competitive tournaments. The ability to scale from handheld to big-screen gaming adds significant versatility to these devices, especially with audio enhanced by an HDTV’s surround-capable soundbar. Many portable consoles include docking stations that provide HDMI outputs, allowing users to easily connect to an HDTV. Others support third-party docking solutions or adapters. Some consoles even feature built-in HDMI ports for direct connection, eliminating the need for additional accessories. This plug-and-play feature highlights how HDMI technology has revolutionized portable gaming. What was once limited to small screens can now be enjoyed in full cinematic scale, with enhanced visuals and audio that elevate the entire experience. Maximizing Performance with Certified HDMI® Cables For today’s high-performance gaming systems, a certified Ultra High Speed HDMI® Cable is needed. These cables support bandwidths up to 48Gbps, enabling advanced features such as higher resolutions, faster refresh rates, and uncompressed audio formats. Consumers should look for the official certification label on packaging to ensure authenticity and performance compliance. Certified cables undergo rigorous testing to guarantee they meet HDMI specifications, delivering reliable and consistent results.
