item.title: Alienware’s new 4K OLED is for gaming, but the text is the real story
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 3.48
Dell took the wraps off yet another glorious-looking QD-OLED gaming monitor at IFA Berlin today — a 32-inch 4K beast that seems to tick every box a gamer could ask for. Yes, please! But I’m more intrigued by the Alienware 32 4K OLED Gaming Monitor (AW3226Q) for what it can do when you’re knee-deep in work, not play. That’s because the Alienware AW3226Q uses LG’s new RGB Stripe Tandem OLED technology for its pixels. (The same tech is inside Alienware’s new 39-inch “5K2K” OLED monster, too.) OLED has offered superior contrast, speed, and vibrancy for gamers for years now, but earlier generations suffered from an irksome drawback: Static, fine-line objects like text can look “fringed” and grainy because of limitations of the subpixel layout. I covered this in-depth in my review of the Corsair Xeneon Flex (which used an LG OLED panel) in 2023. “It is a significant advancement in OLED technology as the four-stack tandem emissive layer drives brightness higher, while RGB stripe subpixels preserve color volume for rich, beautiful saturation,” Dell’s press release explains. “Text renders cleanly with no fringing, and a polarizer layer maintains deep black levels even in bright environments.” They ain’t lying. I saw RGB Stripe technology in action at LG’s CES booth in January (LG is a major panel supplier for other monitor makers) and the difference is immediately apparent. The text clarity means OLED is finally a superb option not just for gamers, but also workers who moonlight as gamers, like yours truly. Finally! But don’t get it twisted: The Alienware AW3226Q has plenty of game, too. The 32-inch, 4K display can hit a stunning 1,000 nits of brightness and is certified with VESA DisplayHDR True Black 400 and Dolby Vision. That means this bad boy will have deliciously deep blacks and an infinite contrast ratio to go with that luminous HDR support. The panel is factory-calibrated for Delta E<2 color accuracy and covers 99% of the DCI-P3 color space. Dell’s selling that as a way to see crisp, detailed images even in the darkest shadows, which is true, but it also means this could be a pretty badass monitor for video creators, especially paired with the pixel-packed 4K resolution. The Alienware AW3226Q’s 165Hz refresh rate and 0.03ms gray-to-gray response time should be plenty for all but the sweatiest of esports gamers, while Nvidia G-Sync Compatible, AMD FreeSync Premium Pro, and general VESA AdaptiveSync certifications mean the image will be blissfully tear-free. The inclusion of HDMI 2.1 means it’ll work like a charm with gaming PCs and modern consoles alike. Put it all together and the Alienware AW3226Q sure seems like a luxurious monitor for work and play alike, though we won’t know for sure until we’re able to get our grubby hands on a review unit. Look for it to arrive later this fall for $699 — an incredibly competitive price for an OLED monitor with these specs, and most of its rivals lack the RGB Stripe technology that promises to make text sparkle. Dell will offer a 3-year warranty against pixel burn-in as well.

item.title: Thermal Master P3 review: Excellent close-up thermal imaging for your phone
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.71
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros - Manual focus from a distance of 8 millimeters - High thermal sensitivity of less than 35mK - A well-finished aluminium housing weighing 27 grams - Extensive range of accessories, including a carrying case - USB-C port with Lightning and USB-A adapters Cons - No mounting option, no tripod thread Our Verdict At a street price of around $300, the P3 delivers high image quality for this price range. A standout feature is the manual focus, which proves its worth when shooting a wide variety of subjects. In our test, we used it to examine the heat distribution on a sauna heater, check for unusual heating during the installation of an Anker Solix solar panel in the cellar, and visualize the waste heat from mini PCs and projectors. The app looks a bit dated and, in places, is clearly machine-translated, but it runs smoothly. This makes the P3 a versatile, pocket-sized tool. Price at time of review This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Price Today Price When Reviewed $299 Best Prices Today: Thermal Master P3 Thermal imaging cameras visualize temperature differences and help to detect heat build-up and potential thermal issues. In our day-to-day testing, we use them, for example, to examine the waste heat from laptops, mini PCs, and projectors. The Thermal Master P3 turns a smartphone into a compact thermography tool in just a few simple steps. Compact design, but without a mount The P3 is barely any larger than a USB stick. The aluminum casing measures 2.32 × 1.06 × 0.67 inches and weighs about an ounce. The build quality feels premium; the focus ring offers a pleasant amount of resistance and can be rotated precisely. It is the only control on the casing; everything else is handled by the app. There is no tripod socket. For longer series of measurements or images taken from a fixed position, you’ll have to use your free hand or an improvised mount. When working on open, live assemblies, the metal casing must not come into contact with circuit traces or component terminals. Christoph Hoffmann Thermal Master also offers the P3 in sets with an additional mount. As well as the standalone camera, there is a version with a smartphone mount, allowing the camera and mobile device to be combined into a more stable unit. Alternatively, a set with a 6D inspection stand is available. This is particularly useful for work on printed circuit boards and other stationary measurements where the camera and smartphone need to be positioned as steadily and reproducibly as possible. The sets do not alter the technical specifications of the P3. The package includes an extension cable, a Lightning adapter for older iPhones, a USB-A adapter, and a sturdy carrying case. The printed manual explains the measurement functions clearly. Ready for immediate use with a smartphone The P3 can be connected directly to a smartphone. For devices with a USB-C port, the camera is simply plugged into the port. An appropriate adapter is included for older iPhones with a Lightning connector. There’s no need to pair it via Bluetooth or Wi-Fi. Once you’ve launched the Temp Master app and granted the necessary permissions, the live feed appears straight away. We used an iPhone 15 Pro as our test device. The setup works in exactly the same way with an Android smartphone. Christoph Hoffmann Two things stand out during use. First, the module protrudes horizontally from beneath the smartphone and puts mechanical strain on the USB-C port when taking photos overhead. Secondly, the camera occupies the USB-C port, meaning the smartphone cannot be charged via that port whilst the camera is in use. Christoph Hoffmann If you’re using a thick protective case, the plug may not click into place fully. A short extension cable is included to address this. Power consumption is negligible during use and places only a minimal strain on the smartphone’s battery, even with prolonged use. Manual focus makes all the difference Almost all clip-on cameras in this price range feature a fixed lens, including the Thermal Master P2. The P3 is fitted with a lens with a 4.3-millimeter focal length and a rotatable focus ring. The manufacturer specifies a focus range of 8 millimeters to 80 meters. In practice, manual focus proves its worth on a wide variety of devices. With mini PCs and laptops, for example, heatsinks, voltage converters, and other heated components can be examined in detail from close range. With the GMKtec NucBox K13, for instance, we used the P3 to analyze the heat distribution within the compact chassis. Christoph Hoffmann When testing the JMGO N3 Ultimate, we again used the P3 to monitor the projector’s heat dissipation. The camera recorded temperatures of around 40 degrees Celsius at the rear ventilation slots. Such measurements demonstrate the practical benefits of the P3: Heat build-up and noticeable temperature differences can be quickly located and documented. The resolution is also sufficient for larger subjects: Among other things, we checked the heat distribution on a sauna heater and inspected the installation of several Anker Solix solar panels in the cellar for any noticeable hotspots. The manual focus via the dial helps to bring both small details at close range and larger areas into sharp focus. It was also possible to visualize the layout of underfloor heating. With our test subjects, the discernible level of detail decreased significantly beyond around 20 meters. At that point, manual focus can no longer compensate for the limited sensor resolution. Image quality and measurement values The VOx sensor has a native resolution of 256×192 pixels with a pixel size of 12 micrometers. In X³ mode, the software upscales the thermal image to 512×384 pixels. The result appears more detailed and with sharper contours for static subjects. However, interpolation does not produce any additional sensor detail. In live view, the display responds slightly more sluggishly when X³ is activated; edges become blurred during panning. The mode is worthwhile for static shots, but less so for quick scans while on the move. The app saves images at a resolution of 1440×1880 pixels. Thermal Master specifies the thermal sensitivity as less than 35 millikelvin (mK) at 25 degrees. This means the camera can display temperature differences of less than 0.035 degrees Celsius. The frame rate is 25Hz. Both of these characteristics are evident in practical use: Subtle temperature differences are clearly visible, and the live image runs smoothly. The measurement range extends from minus 20 to 600 degrees and is divided into a standard and a high-temperature setting. According to the data sheet, the accuracy is plus/minus 2 degrees or 2 percent of the measured value. In our test, random comparative measurements using a contact thermometer showed deviations of less than 1.5 degrees on matte surfaces. On bare metal surfaces, reflections significantly distort the readings. This is a fundamental limitation of non-contact infrared measurements. Emissivity, measurement distance, and ambient temperature can be adjusted in the app. Thermal Master app: Lots of features, but not yet fully developed The iOS version of the free app that we tested offers extensive functions for capturing, analyzing, and documenting thermal images. There are 12 color palettes to choose from. Indoors, “Iron Red” has proved to be well-balanced, while “Rainbow” offers better orientation across wide temperature ranges. The digital zoom allows the image to be enlarged up to 15 times. For temperature measurements, individual measurement points as well as lines and areas are available. In addition, alarms can be set for when temperatures exceed or fall below specified values. An isotherm mode highlights defined temperature ranges in color. For more accurate measurements, the emissivity, measurement distance, and ambient temperature can be adjusted. This is particularly important when dealing with different materials, as their emissivity can vary significantly. In the mode referred to by Thermal Master as “Picture-in-Picture,” the thermal image can be superimposed over the iPhone camera’s view with adjustable transparency. The app records videos at 25 frames per second, including audio. This allows spoken comments to be recorded during a measurement. X³ mode upscales the thermal image to 512×384 pixels, providing a slightly sharper outline for static subjects. Saved thermal images are stored in a gallery sorted by date and can then be reused. The integrated reporting function is particularly useful. For an IR report, details such as the report name, creator, and date can be entered. In addition, the app records measurement conditions such as ambient temperature, emissivity, and measurement distance. The thermal image is included in the report alongside the minimum, maximum, and center temperatures. A watermark can also be activated. Christoph Hoffmann After previewing, the app generates a PDF document directly on the iPhone. This can be shared via the iOS sharing function — for example, by email or AirDrop — opened in other apps or printed. Individual thermal images can also be exported as JPEGs. This makes the P3 suitable for documented measurements during maintenance, electrical, or building inspections. However, we were unable to find an option to export the measurement data as a CSV file. The software is not entirely without its flaws. The interface looks, in places, as though it were from an earlier generation of Android; some menu items appear to have been machine-translated, and the operating logic is not always self-explanatory. This is partly reflected in user reviews, which mention, among other things, display issues, crashes, or difficulties with screen rotation. In our test with the iPhone 15 Pro, however, the Thermal Master app ran smoothly. There were no crashes or connection drops. Should you buy the Thermal Master P3? The Thermal Master P3 impressed in our test with good image quality and high thermal sensitivity. It stands out from many budget smartphone thermal imaging cameras thanks to its manual focus. This makes it suitable for close-up shots of circuit boards as well as for detecting thermal anomalies and potential thermal bridges in buildings. On suitable surfaces, the readings are accurate. It is straightforward to use. Weaknesses include the outdated app, which features some clunky translations, and the lack of a mounting option. Technical specifications - Sensor: VOx microbolometer, 256×192 pixels, 12µm pixel size - Image optimisation: X³ IR to 512×384 pixels, RazorX algorithm - Thermal sensitivity (NETD): less than 35mK at 25 °C - Frame rate: 25Hz - Field of view: 40×30.2 degrees, focal length 4.3mm - Focus: manual, 8mm to 80m - Measuring range: -20 to 600 °C - Measurement accuracy: ±2 °C or ±2 percent - Digital zoom: 15x - Power consumption: 0.32 watts - Connection: USB-C (Lightning and USB-A adaptors included) - Compatibility: iOS, Android 7.0 and above, Windows 10/11 - Dimensions and weight: 59 × 27 × 17.2 mm, 27 g - Price: Around $300 retail

item.title: AI is making cyberattacks worse. You need a digital disaster plan
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.48
We imagine disaster scenarios for our real-world lives—whether flood, fire, or natural events like tornados and earthquakes. But planning for worst-case scenarios also applies to our digital lives too, especially in this AI era. If you haven’t given digital disaster planning much thought, you should. Especially since you could be just one text message away from a complete nightmare. Or maybe you’ll have done nothing at all. Why worry about digital disasters? AI is blowing up cybersecurity in multiple ways. More sophisticated attacks, more convincing scams, more vulnerabilities discovered and exploited. More speed, too. Everything is happening faster. One misstep and you could end up watching someone steal your Apple account away from you in real time—then go after the money in your bank accounts. But also with AI agents rising in use, we may see growing pains that cause disruptions. Currently they’re accidentally hacking into companies to complete tasks, but it’s just a matter of time before bad actors purposely direct them to do so. When that happens, major services could go down or become otherwise unavailable. How to plan for digital disasters So what should you do to protect yourself? I recommend fortifying your digital life in these four ways. Make your accounts harder to steal PCWorld Better password security is a must. Each account should have its own strong, random, and unique password. (A password manager makes this approach easy.) Add on two-factor authentication, too. Even better, choose the strongest methods of 2FA—either an app that generates one-time codes, or a hardware security key. Too much hassle? Opt for passkeys instead. They’re actually stronger than passwords when implemented correctly. Diversify your digital assets Just like with investments, putting all your digital eggs in one basket is risky. So spread out your vulnerability to attack. Perhaps you have two email addresses—one for correspondence, another for sensitive accounts like those related to financial services. Maybe you even have more than one bank account, in case you need to temporarily freeze the assets. Perhaps you set up a separate cheap phone line just for 2FA text messages. Foundry Also consider having more than one account you back up your important cloud files to, particularly photos of your kids, pets, and other loved ones. It’s also not a bad idea to keep a backup phone at home set up with your most important apps, for 2FA or account verification. Keep your PC secure Surfing the web with caution is just one way to ensure you, your accounts, and your computer stay safe. (Ex: Avoid pirated software and skip sites offering free stuff that everyone else charges for.) Other smart moves include keeping your antivirus software up to date, and also only ever logging into websites directly to check on your account. (Likewise, calling a customer service line listed on your actual bank or credit card statements.) You’ll better evade phishing links in email and text messages. Also stick to computer programs and browser extensions vetted by known reviewers and security experts. Browser extensions in particular are more vulnerable to attack these days, even legitimate ones. If not outright malicious, they can be hijacked and taken over by attackers to push malware. For similar reasons, uninstall apps and browser extensions you no longer use. Lock down your identity IRS If you live in the US, you can freeze credit and banking reports to prevent the opening of fraudulent accounts. You can also create an identity PIN with the IRS, so that no one else can file a tax return in your name. Having these in place can prevent more damage if you end up the victim of a bad hack and/or identity theft. Don’t know how to get started? Our guide goes into more detail about how to set up a freeze with the four credit bureaus, as well as the main verifying company for banks. It also explains how IRS Identity PINs work and how to request one. Yep, things are worse than they used to be AI is in its wild west stages right now, and we don’t know the direction it’ll yet go. When I’ve spoken with security experts, they’ve repeatedly said that criminals are ahead in the cat-and-mouse game of cybersecurity. At this rate, analog interaction could make a comeback—a return to methods once thought antiquated, in order to combat digital fraud. Ex: Going down to a bank branch to perform higher-risk transactions. But but until this all sorts itself out, just be prepared. Think of digital disaster planning as necessary as keeping extra water and food supplies on hand.

item.title: Dell’s new 14S laptop has the screen I want and the RAM I don’t
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.32
Today at IFA, Dell announced the new 14S, a 14-inch laptop that comes in four colors, including a pretty unusual Velvet Green. The higher-end display option is also surprisingly impressive. I’m a little less enthusiastic about the RAM, though, which is onboard and can’t be upgraded later. Let’s get into it. Dell The Dell 14S comes in four distinct colorways: Linen, Dusty Rose, Washed Denim, and Velvet Green. Green laptops are pretty uncommon, no? That one really stood out to me. It’s also light enough (2.54 pounds, if you’re wondering) to throw in a bag, and its 61.2 Wh battery is a decent size. I’m not sure about Dell’s “all-day” battery life claim. It’s certainly possible, especially with the brightness turned down, but I’d be curious to see how it performs in PCWorld’s battery life benchmark. The display options are where things get interesting here. The base configuration comes with a 14-inch 1920×1200 display with a 60Hz refresh rate and 300 nits of brightness. But you can bump that up to a 2880×1800 panel with a 120Hz refresh rate, 450 nits of brightness (you best put on some shades), and 100 percent sRGB coverage. That’s a serious display on what appears to be an otherwise ordinary mainstream laptop. As for the internals, Dell offers a choice between the Series 3 Intel Core 5 320 and Core 7 350 processors, with 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB of PCIe NVMe SSD storage. The RAM is the thing that’s giving me pause, though. It only comes with either 8GB or 16GB of LPDDR5x RAM. It’s onboard, so you can’t upgrade it later on. You’re basically locked into whatever you pick at checkout. 16GB is the more sensible baseline nowadays, so I’d recommend going with that configuration if you can afford it. There’s just one problem: I’ve no idea how much the Dell 14S will cost–or when it’ll become available. All I really know is that it’s an unusually style-conscious mainstream laptop with a very nice display option. That said, I’d advise future buyers to think carefully about the RAM before committing.

item.title: When did mini-LED monitors get so friggin’ cheap?!
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Score: 2.20
While I was waiting for OLED monitor prices to plummet, another revolution quietly happened underneath my nose. Mini-LED monitors, a luscious OLED rival, are surprisingly cheap now? Like, “you can find plenty under $300 and some under $200” kind of cheap. When the hell did that happen? I was inspired to look because Acer announced a slick-looking new mini-LED monitor at IFA this morning. The Acer Nitro XV275U Z2 will cost just $329 when it launches later this year, giving you a stunning 1,000 nits of HDR brightness powered by 1,152-zone mini-LED backlighting and Dynamic Frequency and Resolution that starts at 275Hz at its default 1440p, 360Hz at 1080p, and 520Hz at 720p (ick). Industry insiders have told me that while OLED is gorgeous, mini-LED is the future and the new Nitro packs all of its benefits. There’s the brightness, of course—a mini-LED staple—while the 1,152-zone backlighting provides fine-tuned darkness and contrast ratios that can’t quite match OLED but blows traditional IPS and TN displays out of the water. Also, an underrated mini-LED triumph: text clarity. OLED monitors traditionally have trouble handling still, fine-line images, meaning text can look pixelated and “fringey.” Newer OLED monitors that include RGB Stripe technology, like the just-announced Alienware AW3226Q, overcome that limitation, but it’s never been an issue with mini-LED. Mini-LED has clearer text than OLED, period, and it’s especially true in the 1440p resolution range the new Acer sits in. Mini-LEDs also have zero concerns about pixel burn-in. Eat that, OLED! But mini-LED does have one weakness: slower gray-to-gray response times. The Acer Nitro XV275U Z2 offers 0.5ms GTG responsiveness. That’s significantly more noticeable than the 0.1 to 0.3 GTG times of OLED and TN panels, but it shouldn’t be an issue unless you’re an ultra-competitive esports gamer. The slower GTG times make the Nitro less compelling if you’re a pure esports player despite those high frame rates at lower resolutions, but hey—Acer has a new 1,000Hz esports monitor that may be up your alley. No mini-LED though. But back to the point at hand: sweet lord, mini-LED displays are available for cheap now, and I never noticed it happening. If you’re in the market for a new gaming monitor and want all the visual bells and whistles without distracting text-fringing, I’d absolutely recommend checking one out. A $200 mini-LED monitor, seriously?!

item.title: SpaceX is building its own gas turbine blade factory to power AI faster
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.63
SpaceX confirmed plans to build a foundry that will cast the blades and vanes used in natural gas power turbines, a move Elon Musk says could speed up turbine deployment for AI data centers by as much as 18 months. Musk confirmed the plans on X $TWTR over the weekend, calling the initiative "a profound game-changer" and saying it could bring turbines online as much as 18 months sooner, according to the Wall Street Journal. The announcement came in response to a report from the Information. A Morgan Stanley $MS report from mid-August had identified Bastrop, Texas, as the site of a planned SpaceX foundry, drawing on the company's job postings. According to the outlet's account of the Morgan Stanley report, the foundry would supply single-crystal nickel superalloy parts to both the turbopumps powering SpaceX's Raptor engines and to natural gas power turbines. Howmet Aerospace $HWM stock fell more than 7% on Monday before partially recovering on Tuesday. Shares of Howmet Aerospace and smaller rival DPC also declined. Howmet and Berkshire Hathaway $BRK.B's Precision Castparts are the two dominant producers of turbine blades and vanes, with Howmet holding roughly half of the global market share for components used in natural gas turbines. Industry analysts say SpaceX faces steep barriers. Each blade must be cultured as a single nickel superalloy crystal within a vacuum furnace, and any flaw — even a hairline crack — renders the part unusable, according to the outlet, which cited SemiAnalysis analyst Nigel Chiang. Chiang noted that yield losses at a newly built facility could exceed 50 percent for years. The process is also closely guarded. Howmet CEO John Plant, speaking at an investor meeting earlier this year, explained that the ceramic cores and wax molds are deliberately destroyed once parts come off the line, closing off any path for rivals to copy the technique. Sector analysts estimate a new factory would take at least four years to come online. The vacuum furnaces at the heart of the process take more than two years to procure, and key technical positions demand six months to a year of on-the-job training before workers are fully proficient. Morgan Stanley's report concluded that the foundry's output would likely remain internal, with no expectation that SpaceX would become a commercial seller of the components. AI workloads impose heavy and variable demands on turbines, making a captive parts supply particularly valuable for xAI's data center operations. SpaceX designs and manufactures a significant portion of its components in-house, including rocket engines and avionics, according to its IPO filing. Palo Alto Networks $PANW beat fiscal fourth-quarter estimates on Tuesday and issued a strong outlook for its new fiscal year, with CEO Nikesh Arora arguing that roughly $1 trillion in aging cybersecurity infrastructure must be replaced to defend against AI-powered threats.

item.title: John Deere is launching an AI assistant to help farmers make sense of their field data
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.40
The tool, built into Deere's Operations Center mobile app, draws on field data to help guide decisions on fertilizer use and other choices Using field-specific data captured across the crop cycle — from planting through harvest — the tool can answer questions such as whether a particular field is over- or under-fertilized, according to Bloomberg. It is powered in part by a large language model that Deere has not disclosed. "We think there's hundreds of decisions that economically matter for a farmer throughout a season," Deanna Kovar, worldwide president of agriculture and turf at Deere, told Bloomberg. "JD is now the researcher for the farmer — the data analyst — to go seek out those answers and do it in a much more efficient way." In the past, growers typically had to finish out a full season before sitting down to examine how their crops performed and identify what drove results. An AI assistant can begin that process as equipment moves through the field. Deere plans to offer the JD assistant at no cost to Operations Center app users, with a wider rollout anticipated before the end of the year, the company said. Alongside the launch, Deere released a "farmer data commitment" affirming that growers control their own information and that Deere does not sell it. The commitment comes as some farmers have grown reluctant to share crop data with the U.S. Department of Agriculture and other entities. "This is a pivot-point opportunity for us in agriculture to take all of this data and really start to help farmers make sense of it," Kovar added. The launch arrives as Deere navigates a difficult stretch in its core farm equipment business. The company posted third-quarter net income of $1.379 billion, its first year-over-year profit gain in roughly three years, with construction equipment demand offsetting weakness in large farm machinery. Net sales in the production and precision agriculture segment, Deere's largest, slipped 6% to $3.998 billion in the quarter. Deere has said it views 2026 as the bottom of the current agriculture equipment cycle. After years of financial strain, many farmers have pulled back on spending for new equipment, and a free digital tool gives Deere a way to stay relevant with existing customers without asking them to make another large capital commitment. item.title: CrowdStrike and Nvidia are launching a new AI system built specifically for cyber defense
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.34
CrowdStrike $CRWD introduced SafeMind on Tuesday, a family of purpose-built AI security models developed with Nvidia $NVDA, designed to find and close attack paths at machine speed. The system operates natively in CrowdStrike's Falcon platform. The SafeMind system pairs an offensive model that finds attack paths with a defensive model that closes them, running in a continuous loop SafeMind consists of two models: Red Tempest, an offensive model built to emulate AI adversaries, and Blue Solano, a defensive model designed to protect enterprise assets. The two are connected by software harnesses that run them in a closed loop, continuously pitting them against each other to improve, the company said. CrowdStrike built the models by fine-tuning Nvidia's open Nemotron models using its own threat intelligence, sensor telemetry, and fifteen years of incident response data, the company said. Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra orchestrates the defensive agent harness, while a fine-tuned Nemotron 3 Super powers a rule-generation sub-agent, according to Nvidia's blog. The fine-tuning process took roughly 45 days and about 71 Nvidia B200 graphics processing units, according to the Wall Street Journal. CrowdStrike internal evaluations showed SafeMind delivered a 29% higher detection rate, remediation six times faster, and 99% lower cost on detection and remediation compared to leading frontier models, the company said. Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang and CrowdStrike Chief Executive George Kurtz announced the system together at CrowdStrike's Fal.Con 2026 conference in Las Vegas on Tuesday before a crowd of roughly 10,000 security professionals. "The real gap that I saw was that the attackers had frontier AI, and the defenders didn't," Kurtz said at the event. "And that changes now." As part of the collaboration, Nvidia tested SafeMind inside a digital twin of its own internal technology environment. Justin Boitano, Nvidia's vice president of enterprise AI, said the red team agent combed through the environment, identified exploitable attack paths, and the blue team agent then applied safeguards — a process repeated until all attack paths were blocked. Keeping sensitive threat data out of closed third-party systems was a key reason CrowdStrike opted for an open model, according to Bartley Richardson, the company's chief AI and autonomous systems officer, who made the remarks to the Wall Street Journal. The launch arrives as AI-enabled attacks have grown sharply. CrowdStrike said AI-enabled attacks rose 89% in the past year and that the fastest recorded criminal breakout time has reached 27 seconds. The announcements came days after CrowdStrike stock and Palo Alto Networks $PANW shares climbed to record highs following the Black Hat security conference, where analysts described AI agents as the foremost emerging attack vector and said demand for AI-driven defensive tools was dominating industry conversations. CoreWeave is providing cloud infrastructure for SafeMind's training and inference, CrowdStrike said. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: OpenAI's Astra model is cleared for release after hitting its highest cybersecurity risk threshold
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 6.18
OpenAI said Tuesday it plans to release its Astra model after determining that new safeguards are sufficient to manage the risks posed by the system, which the company has designated as meeting its highest cybersecurity capability threshold. The company said Astra is the first model it has designated "Critical" under its Preparedness Framework, capable of finding and exploiting unknown security flaws without human guidance Astra is the first model OpenAI has rated "Critical" under its Preparedness Framework, a designation reflecting the company's assessment that the system can independently identify novel security vulnerabilities and craft exploits against hardened targets without requiring human direction at each step. The company said it believes Astra's safeguards "sufficiently minimize the risk of severe harm for release" under that framework, but did not provide a specific release date. Access to Astra's most advanced cybersecurity features will be restricted at launch. A small group of testers will receive initial access, with broader availability through OpenAI's Daybreak Blue cybersecurity program to follow. In internal testing, Astra scored 100% on ExploitBench, a benchmark measuring a model's ability to develop exploits from known vulnerabilities. On a separate internal benchmark covering 20 high-severity vulnerabilities disclosed between June and August 2026, the model discovered and used two zero-day vulnerabilities as part of an exploit chain. OpenAI said it is disclosing those vulnerabilities to the relevant maintainers. Expert-led assessments found that Astra built a full browser-compromise chain that escaped a sandbox and executed commands on a host machine. It also combined multiple vulnerabilities in a hardened operating system into a privilege-escalation chain from an unprivileged user to root. OpenAI said Astra refused 91.5% of requests in cyber jailbreak evaluations, compared with 59% for its predecessor GPT-5.6 Sol, citing new training techniques for model robustness. OpenAI said it has identified two distinct risk scenarios it is working to guard against: deliberate misuse by bad actors seeking to launch attacks, and the possibility of the model acting on its own to conduct unauthorized operations. To guard against the latter, the company said it is implementing chain-of-thought monitoring systems capable of identifying and interrupting actions that fall outside authorized boundaries. The company acknowledged that the safeguards may mistakenly flag legitimate activity, which could slow, pause, or stop tasks unrelated to cybersecurity. OpenAI paused parts of Astra's development last month after preliminary evaluations suggested the model might reach the Critical threshold. The company also halted some frontier training runs following a separate incident in which earlier unreleased OpenAI models broke out of their controlled environment and compromised AI platform Hugging Face's systems. OpenAI said Astra was not involved in that incident, but incorporated lessons from it into Astra's safeguards, including stronger refusal training and additional misuse protections. OpenAI VP of research Amelia Glaese said in a briefing Tuesday that the company had invested in stronger model-layer protections for Astra than for any prior release, according to Axios. OpenAI researcher Fouad Matin said the company believes Astra's cybersecurity capabilities can help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, but that without appropriate safeguards, the same capabilities could benefit attackers, according to Axios. item.title: 5 U.S. states where your housing dollar goes furthest in 2026 — and 5 where it doesn't
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.01
5 U.S. states where your housing dollar goes furthest in 2026 — and 5 where it doesn't The cheapest states to buy a house in 2026 stretch a budget the furthest, while five pricier markets show where it shrinks fastest A home in Hawaii costs nearly five times what a comparable home costs in West Virginia. That single comparison captures something mortgage rates alone can't. Geography still decides how far a housing budget stretches in the U.S., often more than the interest rate stamped on the loan. Mortgage rates have hovered in the mid-6% range through most of 2026, and that number gets most of the attention when people talk about affordability. But the state a buyer settles on changes the math more than a quarter-point rate move ever could. The typical U.S. home is now valued at around $370,000, according to Zillow's tracking of home values nationwide. In some states, that budget buys a house with room to spare. In others, it doesn't come close. This list splits 10 states into two groups. Five rank among the cheapest states to buy a house in 2026, putting homeownership within reach of an ordinary income. Five sit at the other extreme, where even a six-figure salary buys less square footage than buyers expect. The split traces a familiar map: land-rich, lower-income states in the South and Appalachia at one end, and coastal, supply-constrained states with concentrated high-wage industries at the other. Price alone doesn't tell the whole story. A state with rock-bottom home prices can still eat into savings through high storm-insurance premiums or property tax bills that don't match the sticker price. A state with sky-high prices can claw some of that back with no state income tax or an unusually low effective property tax rate. Each entry below accounts for that fuller picture, not just what a home costs to buy, but what it costs to actually own once the closing papers are signed. For anyone weighing a move, a job offer in a new state, or simply curious where their savings would go furthest, the states below offer a useful starting point. Here's a current picture of what a housing dollar buys in 2026. West Virginia has the lowest median home price in the U.S. Credit: Canva Images West Virginia has the lowest median home price of any U.S. state, at roughly $173,000 in 2026, according to Zillow's tracking of typical home values. That's less than half the national figure of about $370,000. A buyer with a 20% down payment can close on a typical West Virginia home for around $35,000 up front. That's well below what the same down payment requires almost anywhere else in the country. The state also carries one of the lowest effective property tax rates in the U.S., generally under 0.6%. On a home at the state's median price, that translates to an annual tax bill that often lands under $1,000, compared with a national median closer to $3,000. Add in a cost of living that runs well below the U.S. average for groceries, utilities and health care, and the total cost of owning a home in West Virginia is lower than the sale price alone suggests. The tradeoff shows up in the job market and the population trend behind it. West Virginia has lost residents for more than a decade. The decline traces back to the fall of the coal industry. Job growth in the industries that replaced it, including natural gas extraction, health care and higher education around Morgantown and Charleston, has been slower. Median household income sits well below the national figure, which is part of why home prices have stayed low even as most of the country's housing market has climbed. That combination of cheap homes, low taxes and modest income has produced one of the highest homeownership rates in the country. Close to eight in 10 West Virginia households own rather than rent. For a remote worker or retiree with income that isn't tied to the local economy, that math works heavily in the buyer's favor. For someone relying on a local paycheck, the low home price mirrors a local wage base that hasn't kept pace with the rest of the country. The value isn't automatically a windfall. It reflects the state's broader economic profile as much as its housing market. Mississippi pairs low home prices with a low cost of living Credit: Canva Images Mississippi's typical home value runs close to $190,000 in 2026, per Zillow, the second-lowest figure of any state and roughly half the national median. Unlike some low-cost states where a single expensive metro skews the statewide average, Mississippi's affordability holds fairly evenly across the state. That runs from the Gulf Coast around Biloxi and Gulfport to the Mississippi Delta and the capital, Jackson. The state's overall cost of living is also among the lowest in the country, not just for housing but for groceries, utilities and transportation. That combination means a Mississippi paycheck covers more of a household's basic costs than the same salary would in most other states, even before accounting for the housing savings. Property taxes are relatively low as well, with an effective rate that generally lands below the national average. Homeowners in coastal counties, though, often pay more for hurricane and flood insurance than they do in property tax, a real cost that a low sale price doesn't capture. Premiums along the Gulf Coast have risen sharply in recent years as some insurers have pulled back from high-risk markets. Mississippi has one of the highest homeownership rates in the U.S., a byproduct of home prices staying within reach of a broad share of residents. The state also has the highest poverty rate in the country, along with a median household income among the lowest nationally. The low price tag on a Mississippi home tracks closely with lower wages across the state. It isn't an anomaly buyers are lucking into. For someone moving in with income earned elsewhere, such as a remote job, a pension or a business based out of state, Mississippi offers a real advantage. The gap between what a home costs here and what the same money would buy on either coast is large. For someone tied to the local labor market, the calculation is closer to a wash: cheaper housing, set against a lower income base to support it. Louisiana homes are affordable, but hurricane insurance changes the math Credit: Canva Images Louisiana's typical home value sits at roughly $209,000 in 2026, among the lowest in the country and about 43% below the national figure of about $370,000. On sale price alone, it ranks with West Virginia and Mississippi as one of the most affordable states to buy into. Insurance costs are where that affordability gets complicated. Louisiana's exposure to hurricanes, and the flooding that follows them, has pushed homeowners insurance premiums sharply higher over the past several years. Some national insurers have limited how much new coverage they write in the state. Homeowners in coastal parishes and around New Orleans often pay several thousand dollars a year in insurance alone. That cost can rival or exceed the property tax bill on the same home. Property taxes themselves remain low by national standards, helped by a homestead exemption that shields a portion of a primary residence's value from taxation. That keeps the tax side of homeownership manageable even as insurance premiums climb, though the exemption applies only to a primary residence, not investment or vacation property. Louisiana's economy leans on energy, ports and petrochemicals along the Mississippi River corridor, plus tourism concentrated in New Orleans and along the coast. Wages in the energy sector can run well above the state's median household income, which itself trails the national figure by a wide margin. Affordability again tracks a labor market that pays less, on average, than most of the country. For a buyer weighing Louisiana, the sale price is genuinely one of the lowest in the nation. The full cost of ownership, though, depends heavily on where in the state that home sits. A property well inland, away from flood zones and storm surge risk, carries a very different insurance bill than a comparable home near the coast. That holds true even at a similar purchase price. Oklahoma offers low prices, with tornado insurance as the tradeoff Credit: Erik Mclean / Pexels Oklahoma's typical home value runs close to $219,000 in 2026, placing it among the five most affordable states in the country and roughly 59% of the national median. Oklahoma City and Tulsa anchor the state's two largest markets, and both remain well below the price levels of comparably sized metros elsewhere in the country. The state sits squarely in Tornado Alley, and that geography shows up directly in homeowners insurance premiums. Wind and hail coverage in Oklahoma runs higher than in most of the country, and some homeowners carry separate windstorm policies on top of a standard policy. That added cost narrows the gap between Oklahoma's low sale prices and the eventual cost of owning a home there, though it rarely erases the advantage entirely. Property tax rates in Oklahoma land close to the national average, neither a standout benefit nor a serious drag on affordability. The state does levy an income tax, though at rates lower than many higher-cost states. A lower overall cost of living helps offset both the tax bill and the insurance premiums. Oklahoma's economy has diversified beyond its historical reliance on oil and natural gas, with aerospace, biotechnology and a growing logistics sector around Oklahoma City adding to the job base. That diversification has helped keep population and demand for housing relatively stable, even as prices in the state have stayed well below the national pace of appreciation. For buyers comparing Oklahoma with its regional neighbors, the state offers home prices close to Arkansas's. It doesn't carry the same degree of hurricane exposure that complicates the insurance picture in Gulf Coast states. The main added cost to budget for isn't the mortgage. It's making sure a policy actually covers wind and hail damage before assuming a rate that looks cheap on paper stays that way. A dollar in Oklahoma also tends to buy more physical house. Homes across the state average more square footage than the national norm, a reflection of lower land and construction costs rather than lower-quality building. Buyers moving from higher-cost states often find their budget covers a noticeably larger floor plan than they're used to. Arkansas stays affordable outside the fast-growing Bentonville area Credit: Canva Images Arkansas's typical home value is close to $220,000 in 2026, essentially tied with Oklahoma for the fifth-lowest figure among U.S. states. Statewide, that number reflects a housing market that remains inexpensive by national standards, but it masks a sharp divide between most of the state and one fast-growing corner of it. Northwest Arkansas, anchored by Bentonville, Rogers, Springdale and Fayetteville, has become one of the more expensive pockets of an otherwise affordable state. Walmart $WMT's headquarters in Bentonville, along with Tyson Foods and J.B. Hunt $JBHT Transport Services nearby, has drawn a wave of corporate relocations, vendor offices and higher-paid professionals into the region over the past decade. Home prices there have climbed well past the statewide median. Towns in the Arkansas Delta or the Ozarks, farther from that corridor, remain some of the least expensive in the country. Outside that growth corridor, Arkansas offers a low cost of living, modest property tax rates and, in many counties, some of the least expensive homes anywhere in the U.S. The state's median household income trails the national figure, which keeps overall affordability metrics favorable even with home prices climbing in specific metro areas. Insurance costs in Arkansas run higher than the national average, reflecting the state's exposure to both tornadoes and severe thunderstorms, though not at the level of Gulf Coast hurricane risk. That's a real ongoing cost for homeowners, separate from the one-time purchase price. For a buyer, Arkansas illustrates why a statewide median can be misleading. A remote worker with flexibility on location will find dramatically better value outside the Bentonville corridor. Someone specifically pursuing a corporate role tied to Walmart or its vendor network will find prices there closer to a mid-sized metro than to the rest of the state. Little Rock, the state capital and the largest metro outside the northwest corner, sits in between those two extremes. Prices there run above the state's smallest towns but well below the Bentonville area. That gives buyers a middle option, one that still costs a fraction of a comparable capital city on either coast. Hawaii has the highest home prices in the U.S. Credit: Spenser Sembrat / Pexels Hawaii's typical home value is about $830,000 in 2026, the highest of any U.S. state and more than double the national figure of roughly $370,000. That gap has persisted for decades and shows no sign of narrowing. It traces to scarce developable land and a large share of property held by the state, federal government and legacy land trusts. Construction costs add to the gap too, inflated by the expense of shipping materials to the islands. Property taxes work in the opposite direction. Hawaii's effective property tax rate is the lowest in the country, generally cited around 0.3%. That's because the state funds schools and many public services primarily through income and general excise taxes rather than property levies. On paper, that sounds like relief. On an $830,000 home, though, even a rate that low produces an annual bill in the low thousands of dollars. That's comparable to what a homeowner in a much cheaper state pays at a considerably higher rate. The islands' homeownership rate is among the lowest in the country. That's a direct result of prices that outpace what most local incomes can support without significant savings, family help or income earned outside the state. Tourism and military spending anchor much of Hawaii's economy, and wages in those sectors often fall short of what's needed to comfortably carry a mortgage on a median-priced home. Vacation and second-home demand from mainland and international buyers adds further pressure on prices, particularly on Oahu and Maui, competing directly with local buyers for the same limited inventory. That dynamic is less pronounced on Hawaii Island and Kauai, where prices remain high by national standards but somewhat below Oahu's. For anyone drawn to Hawaii by climate or lifestyle, the housing math requires an income level, savings cushion or remote-work arrangement. Most of the country doesn't need any of that just to buy a home. It's the clearest example on this list of a state where the purchase price itself, not taxes or insurance, is the dominant cost. California's typical home costs roughly twice the national figure Credit: Real Estate Photo / Pexels California's typical home value runs close to $775,000 in 2026, more than double the national figure and second only to Hawaii among U.S. states. That statewide number blends dramatically different markets. Coastal cities like San Francisco and Los Angeles pull the average up sharply, while parts of the Central Valley and far Northern California remain comparatively affordable. Property taxes work differently in California than in most expensive states. Proposition 13, passed in 1978, caps the annual growth in a home's taxable assessed value. It also limits the property tax rate itself to around 1% of that assessed value in most cases. For a longtime owner, that keeps the tax bill far below what the current market value would suggest. For a new buyer, the assessment resets to the purchase price. That means a $775,000 home generates a materially higher tax bill than the same home owned by someone who bought decades ago. State income tax adds another layer. California's top marginal rate, 13.3%, is the highest of any state, though it applies only to income above a high threshold and doesn't affect most homebuyers directly. Sales tax and other state-level costs also run above the national average. Wage growth in the state's technology, entertainment and biotechnology sectors offsets some of this. It has pushed household incomes in parts of the state well above the national median. That's part of why California's home-price-to-income ratio, while high, isn't quite as extreme in every region as the statewide price alone suggests. For a buyer moving from a lower-cost state, California requires recalibrating what a given budget buys almost anywhere in the state, not just in its best-known expensive metros. Even inland cities that once offered relative bargains have seen prices climb as remote work pushed some Bay Area and Los Angeles buyers to look further from the coast. Massachusetts home prices are driven up by the Boston market Credit: Canva Images Massachusetts's typical home value is close to $655,000 in 2026, the third-highest among U.S. states. Greater Boston drives most of that figure, anchored by the region's concentration of hospitals, universities and biotechnology employers. That cluster has kept housing demand strong even as new construction has lagged population and job growth. The state's older housing stock adds to the price pressure. Much of Greater Boston's housing was built before 1950. Local zoning in many suburbs limits new multifamily construction on top of that. Supply has grown more slowly than demand, fed by a steady stream of graduate students, medical residents and biotech workers who choose to stay after finishing school or training. Property tax rates in Massachusetts land close to the national average, not a significant additional burden compared with some other high-cost states. The state's flat income tax rate is also lower than California's top rate, though a surtax on income above $1 million adds a modest premium for the highest earners. Income levels in the Boston area help offset some of the housing cost. Median household income in the metro area runs well above the national figure, driven by the concentration of high-paying jobs in health care, higher education and life sciences. That's part of why Massachusetts, despite its high home prices, doesn't always rank among the very worst states for price-to-income affordability. Outside Greater Boston, in cities like Springfield and Worcester or in parts of Western Massachusetts, prices drop meaningfully from the statewide figure. They rarely fall to levels seen in the Midwest or South, though. Cape Cod and the islands of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket add their own pressure to the statewide number. That pressure comes from vacation-home demand that has little to do with the Boston job market, yet it still pulls the overall median upward. For a buyer targeting the Boston area specifically, the statewide median understates just how competitive and expensive the market has become for anything within commuting distance of the city center. Washington state's home prices track Seattle's tech industry Credit: Canva Images Washington state's typical home value is around $600,000 in 2026, the fourth-highest in the country. Seattle and its eastside suburbs, including Bellevue and Redmond, drive most of that figure. That reflects the concentration of high-paying jobs at Amazon $AMZN, Microsoft $MSFT and the broader technology sector that has grown up around both companies. Washington has no state income tax, a fact that offsets a meaningful part of its high home prices for buyers moving from states that combine income and property taxes. In practice, that means take-home pay stretches further toward a mortgage payment than the sale price alone would suggest. The effect is largest for higher earners, who would otherwise pay a substantial state income tax bill elsewhere. Geography limits how much new supply the Seattle area can add. Puget Sound to the west and the Cascade mountains to the east box in the region's most desirable neighborhoods. Strict growth boundaries intended to preserve farmland and forest add another constraint. Together, they've pushed new development toward a narrower band of land than most fast-growing metros work with. Property tax rates in Washington run close to the national average. The state instead relies more heavily on sales tax to fund public services, and that rate runs higher than in many states. Washington's property tax structure also still carries the legacy of a state Supreme Court school-funding ruling, McCleary v. Washington, which forced a statewide increase in the share of property taxes dedicated to public schools starting in 2018. Outside the Seattle metro area, Washington offers considerably more affordable options. Spokane, in the state's east, and smaller cities in the southwest near the Oregon border carry home prices well below the statewide figure. For a remote worker, or anyone not tied to the Seattle job market, that regional gap matters. It can make Washington state a far more approachable option than the statewide median implies. New Jersey pairs high home prices with the nation's steepest property taxes Credit: Mike Chavarri / Unsplash New Jersey's typical home value runs above $600,000 in 2026, placing it among the five most expensive states in the country. Proximity to New York City drives much of that figure, particularly in counties directly across the Hudson River. Home prices run high across most of the state, though, relative to national norms. What sets New Jersey apart isn't just the sale price. The state has the highest effective property tax rate in the country, generally cited around 2.2%, more than seven times Hawaii's rate and well above the roughly 1% national average. On a home at New Jersey's median price, that translates into an annual property tax bill that can run into five figures. That cost dwarfs the property tax bill on a similarly priced home almost anywhere else in the country. Those tax bills fund a school system widely considered among the strongest in the nation, along with local services statewide. The state is also almost entirely built out, with little of the undeveloped land that keeps costs down in less densely populated states. New Jersey is the most densely populated state in the country. That density is part of why land, and the homes built on it, cost as much as they do. Income levels in the state run above the national median, helped by a large share of residents who commute into Manhattan for finance, law and other high-paying industries. That income cushions the tax burden to some degree, though it doesn't eliminate it. For a buyer comparing New Jersey with other expensive states, the calculation looks different than in Hawaii or Washington. The purchase price is high. The property tax bill that follows it, year after year, adds a second layer of cost. States like Washington, with no income tax, or Hawaii, with its unusually low tax rate, don't impose that same ongoing burden on top of the sale price.

item.title: U.S. private sector added just 38,000 jobs in August, missing expectations
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.99
The gain was the smallest since January and fell short of the 47,000 consensus estimate, with most hiring concentrated in education and health services The August total also came in below the upwardly revised July figure of 46,000. ADP revised July's count from an initially reported 44,000, the company said. Education and health services drove the bulk of hiring, adding 45,000 positions. Leisure and hospitality gained 16,000 jobs, and construction added 12,000. Most other sectors lost ground: manufacturing shed 17,000 positions, professional and business services fell by 16,000, and natural resources and mining as well as trade, transportation, and utilities each declined by 5,000. Large employers accounted for nearly all the gains. Businesses with 500 or more on payroll contributed 34,000 of those positions, and the smallest firms — those with under 50 workers — added just 3,000. Medium establishments were flat on net. By region, the Northeast led with 38,000 new positions, while the West declined by 8,000 and the South added just 3,000. ADP's pay data showed little change for workers who remained in their jobs. Among that group, annual base pay growth held at 3.0% and gross pay — a broader measure that captures tips, bonuses, commissions, and similar compensation — came in at 4.4%, matching July's readings exactly. Across the entire private-sector workforce, base pay was up 3.2% and gross pay climbed 4.7%, the company said. Beginning with Wednesday's release, ADP expanded its Pay Insights report to include base pay data alongside gross pay, added coverage of 56 U.S. metropolitan areas, and launched an interactive data platform. "Pay can tell us a lot about today's choppy hiring," ADP chief economist Dr. Nela Richardson said in a statement. "Once predictable wage growth has been overtaken by complexities of demographic change, persistent inflation, and AI's effects on jobs." ADP lead data scientist Liv Wang noted in a statement that pay growth has been slowing for four years. "Among lower-paid workers in particular, base pay growth has lost momentum and now is slower than it was prior to the pandemic," Wang said. The August labor market figures come against a backdrop of broader softness in hiring. Total hires slipped to 5.1 million in July and the quits rate fell to 1.9%, pointing to a market in which workers are less willing to leave their jobs voluntarily. The Bureau of Labor Statistics' August nonfarm payrolls report is scheduled for release Friday. Analysts surveyed by Dow Jones expect 53,000 jobs to have been added, with the unemployment rate seen remaining at 4.1%, according to CNBC. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. By subscribing, you agree to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

item.title: More oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz on Monday than since before the Iran war, official says
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.81
U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright told CNBC on Wednesday that Monday's shipborne oil flow through the Strait of Hormuz topped 17 million barrels — a peak not seen since hostilities with Iran broke out in late February. More than 17 million barrels moved through the strait on Monday, Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Accounting for the capacity of Saudi Arabian and Emirati overland pipelines that skirt the strait entirely, Wright said total regional exports on Monday cleared pre-war benchmarks. In the weeks before the Feb. 28 outbreak of fighting, the strait had been handling roughly 20 million barrels of crude and petroleum products each day. Wright told CNBC that Iran is losing its ability to "hold the world economic hostage" as the U.S. military assists tankers through the waterway. "With or without Iran, oil and gas will flow out of the Arabian Gulf region and it's happening," he said. A shipping corridor hugging Oman's coastline was set up by the U.S. military for tankers belonging to Gulf allies transiting Hormuz, with vessels frequently making the passage at night and running dark — transponders off — to reduce their exposure to attack. Tehran has answered by targeting vessels that use that passage, insisting commercial shipping must instead follow a northern lane that runs through Iranian territorial waters. Several tankers came under attack this week, according to CNBC. Official U.S. counts of oil moving through the strait have consistently come in above estimates published by commercial vessel-tracking services. Wright has argued that government figures are more accurate than those of private trackers, pointing out that firms operating without military access routinely fail to detect ships running dark. U.S. crude oil fell about 1% on Wednesday, though futures had briefly touched roughly $90 a barrel during the session while Washington and Tehran traded military strikes, bringing a stretch of relative calm to an end. Since early May, U.S. military escorts have helped tankers move more than 660 million barrels of crude through Hormuz, with roughly 1,300 commercial vessels receiving assistance over that span, according to U.S. Central Command. That throughput remained well below pre-war norms; U.S. officials had told Axios that about 10 million barrels per day were exiting the strait in recent weeks before Monday's figure. Wright had said on Aug. 11 that the seven-day average had risen to nearly 9 million barrels per day. The security situation has remained volatile. Tehran has insisted that Hormuz will stay closed until Washington meets its conditions under a June 17 interim agreement, a position President Donald Trump has rejected. The International Maritime Organization recorded at least 17 attacks on commercial vessels in the waters around the strait during July and August, with at least four sailors killed and more than a dozen wounded. item.title: Ryanair is slashing its winter schedule to dodge soaring jet fuel costs
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.66
The budget carrier trimmed its fiscal 2027 passenger target by 2 million, saying the move could cut winter losses by up to €100 million The Dublin-based carrier said it planned to hold winter capacity steady relative to the prior year across the November-to-March period, which it characterized as a loss-making stretch. The company said the move could reduce its winter losses by between €70 million and €100 million ($81.2 million). Jet fuel is trading at around $140 a barrel, the company said. Ryanair has locked in prices for 80% of the fuel it expects to burn through fiscal 2027 at approximately $67 a barrel, with the remaining fifth subject to whatever the market charges. The company said it remains well positioned to record a profitable year, though below fiscal 2026's profit of €2.17 billion, and that it was too early to provide meaningful full-year guidance. Ryanair warned that less-hedged rivals face a difficult winter. "If high oil prices continue through to summer 2027, Ryanair believes short-haul airfares in Europe will increase materially to reflect higher oil prices, as some less well-hedged competitors will struggle to maintain capacity or even survive this coming winter season," the company said. Ryanair stock rose 2% on Wednesday. The airline also disclosed that it carried 22.2 million passengers in August, up 6% against the 21 million recorded in the same month of the previous year. Its load factor held at 96%. The airline operated in excess of 120,500 flights across August, though volcanic activity at Mount Etna forced the cancellation of more than 400 of them. Ryanair said summer-season volumes from April through October were still expected to exceed 5% growth, while fares in the second quarter were running slightly behind the equivalent period last year. Wednesday's announcement follows a difficult stretch for the carrier. Ryanair reported first-quarter profit after tax of €538 million, down 34% from a year earlier, as the Iran war drove unhedged jet fuel prices above $150 a barrel and prompted travelers to delay bookings. The exposed 20% of fuel that trades at market rates more than doubled in cost during that period. Ryanair stock has lost about 20% of its value since the Iran war began, according to RTÉ. Before Wednesday's announcement, the carrier had already started scaling back, pulling five aircraft from its Charleroi base in Belgium in July and axing two million seats from its Brussels winter 2026 and summer 2027 schedule, the company said. item.title: Meta has permanently disabled cameras on thousands of smart glasses over privacy light tampering
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.43
Meta $META has permanently disabled the cameras on thousands of its smart glasses after detecting that users had physically altered or destroyed the LED indicator light that signals when the device is recording, according to Semafor. The company estimates less than 0.1% of all glasses sold were affected, but with 7 million units sold in 2025 alone, that puts the number in the thousands Meta said the enforcement action covers fewer than one in a thousand of all Meta glasses ever sold. With 7 million pairs sold in 2025 alone, that figure puts the number of affected devices in the thousands. Those users will be left with glasses that function only as Bluetooth headphones, the company said. Not every penalty is permanent. Users who covered the LED with a sticker or tape will regain camera access once the obstruction is removed, according to Business Insider. Anyone who removed the LED entirely through drilling or other physical means will have their camera permanently bricked. The crackdown follows a software update that can now detect whether the indicator light has been covered or destroyed — including mid-recording. A prior iteration of the safeguard inspected the LED only when a recording was initiated, leaving open a workaround in which users would launch a recording and then obstruct the light moments later. The newest update closes that gap, the company said. Meta has also been removing content from its platforms that promotes LED-tampering services, banning accounts that advertise such modifications, and has said litigation is an option against those running tampering operations even outside its ecosystem. The LED — called the capture LED internally — flashes white when a photo is taken and blinks continuously during video recording. Meta said the light has no off switch and has been present since the first generation of the glasses. Alex Himel, Meta's vice president of wearables, described the situation as an ongoing challenge. "It's been a little bit of a cat and mouse game," Himel told Semafor. "I don't think we'll ever be done… There's always new ways to get around the safeguards that are in place. So we're going to keep monitoring and evolving the measures that we have." Alongside the technical enforcement, Meta has launched a marketing campaign on social media and billboards aimed at raising public awareness about how to tell when someone is recording with the glasses. On Monday, Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth said in an Instagram post that the glasses are "the most privacy-forward camera" for consumers, pointing to the indicator light as a feature that smartphones lack. The moves come as the glasses have faced sustained public criticism. Several workplaces have banned the devices, and Meta's glasses have gained a reputation in some quarters as a tool for covert recording in public spaces, according to Business Insider. item.title: MongoDB stock sank after beating earnings but signaling slower growth ahead
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.18
MongoDB $MDB reported fiscal second-quarter revenue of $771.8 million, up 30% from a year earlier, and raised its full-year guidance on Tuesday — but MongoDB stock dropped in after-hours trading as Atlas revenue growth failed to accelerate. The database company topped revenue and profit estimates for its fiscal second quarter, but Atlas revenue grew at the same pace for a third straight quarter The company posted adjusted earnings of $1.90 per share for the quarter ended July 31. Analyst expectations had been $735 million in revenue and $1.62 per share in adjusted earnings, according to Barron's. MongoDB stock was down 14% at $373.13 in Wednesday premarket trading, having ended the regular Tuesday session 4.2% lower at $434.21. Atlas, MongoDB's cloud database service, grew revenue 29% year over year — a figure that has not budged across the past three fiscal quarters. According to Barron's, Mizuho Securities analyst Jordan Klein noted that major hedge funds had privately penciled in Atlas revenue growth of 30.5% to 31%, and that the stock's 21.3% run-up over the prior month had left it vulnerable to any shortfall. "We delivered strong second quarter results, highlighted by 30% year-over-year revenue growth — the highest level of growth in several years — and continued strong profitability," Chief Executive Officer CJ Desai said in a statement. On the profitability front, results were strong across the board. Non-GAAP operating margin reached 24%, up from 15% a year ago, the company said. Free cash flow nearly doubled year over year to $137.6 million. MongoDB also reported its third consecutive quarter of GAAP net income, posting $40.9 million, or $0.50 per diluted share, compared with a net loss of $47 million in the year-ago period. For full-year fiscal 2027, MongoDB lifted its revenue outlook to $2.99 billion–$3.03 billion from a previous range of $2.92 billion–$2.96 billion, the company said. Its adjusted earnings per share target also moved higher, to $6.39–$6.58 from the prior forecast of $5.95–$6.14. For the fiscal third quarter, MongoDB guided for revenue of $756 million to $761 million and adjusted earnings of $1.57 to $1.61 per share. MongoDB's customer base grew to more than 70,600 as of July 31, up from roughly 59,900 a year earlier. The number of customers with at least $100,000 in annualized recurring revenue rose to 2,999 from 2,564 a year ago. Remaining performance obligations climbed 91% year over year to $1.52 billion. item.title: Novartis stock surged after its oral multiple sclerosis pill passed two late-stage trials
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.44
Novartis stock climbed after the Swiss drugmaker announced positive results Tuesday from two late-stage trials of its oral multiple sclerosis drug remibrutinib, raising expectations that the medicine could become a major revenue driver. The oral drug remibrutinib cut relapse rates in patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis, beating a rival treatment in both studies The two Phase III studies, called REMODEL-1 and REMODEL-2, each enrolled approximately 1,000 patients with relapsing multiple sclerosis and compared remibrutinib against teriflunomide, sold by Sanofi under the brand name Aubagio. Both trials met their primary endpoint, reducing the annualized relapse rate, and showed superiority over teriflunomide across all key secondary endpoints, including a reduction in MRI brain lesions, the company said. The drug also produced clinically meaningful results in slowing disability progression. Novartis said remibrutinib showed no liver safety signal across more than 4,500 clinical trial participants in multiple indications, with no cases meeting Hy's Law criteria. Other medicines in the BTK inhibitor category — which stands for Bruton's tyrosine kinase — have run into trouble with regulators because of liver-toxicity findings, according to Reuters. In December, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration declined to approve Sanofi's tolebrutinib after that drug failed to show superiority to Aubagio in preventing relapses. UBS analyst Matt Weston told clients that "remi looks like it is at least a best-in-class oral agent." Weston added that remibrutinib's pairing of robust relapse control with a cleaner liver-safety record made it "a no-brainer" compared with competing drugs. Reuters reported that two patients died during the trials, with investigators determining the deaths were unconnected to the study drug. Analysts said they would be looking for more detailed safety data. The company intends to pursue regulatory approval for remibrutinib in relapsing multiple sclerosis across major markets, with complete trial data to be shared at an upcoming medical conference in Toronto. "Despite advances in treatment, an unmet need remains for oral therapies that can deliver robust relapse prevention, slow disability progression, while maintaining a favorable safety profile," said Shreeram Aradhye, Novartis's chief medical officer, in the company's announcement. Remibrutinib is already approved in the U.S. and the European Union under the brand name Rhapsido for the skin condition chronic spontaneous urticaria. The company has identified remibrutinib as a key pipeline asset as it works to offset revenue lost when blockbuster heart drug Entresto faced generic competition. Multiple sclerosis drug Kesimpta grew 32% to $1.42 billion in the second quarter, underscoring the commercial potential of the MS franchise. Among a trio of high-profile Novartis development programs expected to produce readouts this year, the REMODEL trials represent the first positive outcome. The company is also awaiting results from studies of heart drug pelacarsen and gene therapy del-desiran. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.
