item.title: Apple stock is becoming investors' go-to hedge as the AI trade wobbles
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 3.30
Apple $AAPL stock rose 2.6% on Tuesday as the broader technology sector sold off, extending a stretch of outperformance that has positioned the iPhone maker as a de facto hedge against turbulence in the AI trade. According to a CNBC analysis using ThinkOrSwim data, the 30-day correlation between Apple and the Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 bottomed out at -0.86 last Thursday and was sitting at -0.82 as of Wednesday, a degree of inverse movement between the two that has not been recorded since 2005. Apple commands a 7.5% weighting in the Nasdaq-100. Apple shares have climbed 7% over the past month, a stretch during which the Nasdaq-100 managed only a 1% advance. Having trailed the index for the first half of 2026, Apple has climbed 20% for the year, outpacing the Nasdaq-100's 15% advance. "When the AI trade gets questioned, Apple doesn't sell off with it, because it was never carrying that risk in the first place," Dave Mazza, chief executive officer at Roundhill Investments, told CNBC. "It has become the hedge inside the Nasdaq." Mazza is the head of an Apple-focused exchange-traded fund whose strategy involves using swaps to pay out weekly income to shareholders. Options market activity on Tuesday reinforced the bullish positioning. ThinkOrSwim data show call volume reached nearly 1.5 million contracts on Tuesday against fewer than 700,000 puts, with approximately 543,000 of those calls appearing to have been buyer-initiated, compared with under 220,000 on the put side. Flows analysis on Barchart showed the net delta across Apple's options market was skewed meaningfully in the bullish direction, according to CNBC. SpotGamma and Cboe LiveVol data indicate that Tuesday's Apple options volume came in at approximately double the trailing 30-day average. Apple's divergence from its Magnificent Seven peers reflects its conservative posture on AI capital spending. As investors have grown wary of runaway infrastructure costs, Apple's restrained approach has drawn attention. Alphabet $GOOGL, Amazon $AMZN, Meta $META Platforms, and Microsoft $MSFT have committed hundreds of billions of dollars to chip purchases and data center construction, with industry-wide AI capital expenditures on track to exceed $700 billion in 2026, a roughly 70% year-over-year increase. Apple reported its strongest June quarter on record last month, with revenue of $109.4 billion, up 16% year over year, and diluted earnings per share of $2.02, up 29%. The company has also crossed $5 trillion in market capitalization, becoming only the second publicly traded company to do so. John Ternus, the company's hardware engineering chief, took over as chief executive officer on Tuesday from Tim Cook. Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz. item.title: These are the 10 best love songs of all time
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 2.08
These are the 10 best love songs of all time From 1960s soul ballads still anchoring wedding playlists to viral-era tracks that became cultural moments overnight, the greatest love songs ever A great love song rarely announces itself as one on paper, since the actual mechanics behind it, a chord progression, a vocal run, a lyric that lands at exactly the right moment, resist easy explanation even after decades of listeners trying to pin down why certain tracks keep working. Some love songs arrive polished and immediate, built specifically for a first dance from the moment they’re released. Others take a stranger route, wrapping real devotion inside melancholy or uncertainty until the romance only becomes clear on a second or third listen, long after the initial impression has already settled in. This range shows up clearly across any serious ranking of the genre’s best work. Soul and R&B pillars from the 1960s and '70s still anchor wedding playlists decades after their original release, proving that a well-built ballad rarely goes out of style once it finds its footing in public memory. Alongside those standards, a newer generation of artists keeps adding fresh entries to the canon, some through pure songwriting craft and others through the accelerant of viral platforms that can turn a single lyric into a cultural moment almost overnight. Both paths lead to the same place: a song people keep returning to long after its release date stops mattering, whether that’s forty full years later at a wedding reception or forty days later on repeat. The songs below appear in Time Out, covering the top 10 entries from the publication’s larger ranking of the 30 best love songs of all time, as curated by Time Out’s editorial staff and contributors. Counting down from tenth place to the single song currently sitting at the very top, each entry below covers the artist, release year, and the specific quality that earned the track its spot this high on the list. 10. All of Me becomes wedding season’s default song John Legend’s “All of Me” has spent well more than a full decade now as roughly the very closest thing modern weddings have to a default first-dance song, and that considerable reputation shows no real sign of fading anytime soon, even with the passage of time. Written specifically as a heartfelt dedication to Legend’s then-fiancée and now wife, Chrissy Teigen, the track works simultaneously as both a deeply personal love letter and something general enough for couples everywhere to claim entirely as their own at their own weddings. The earnest, understated piano ballad builds its emotional case slowly and deliberately, letting Legend’s vocal carry most of the weight instead of leaning on elaborate production or a dramatic key change to manufacture its impact. This restraint gives the song a lasting, unmistakable sense of intimacy that louder, more theatrical wedding staples often lack entirely, closer to quietly overhearing a private conversation than watching a stadium-sized declaration of love unfold on stage. Streaming data itself strongly backs up the song’s staying power beyond simple anecdotal popularity, with Spotify $SPOT itself reporting that “All of Me” consistently ranks among the most-added tracks across listener-curated playlists built specifically around love and romance. This kind of sustained, voluntary curation strongly suggests the song has moved well past its initial release-year popularity into something closer to a true, lasting standard in the modern love-song canon. Few tracks released in the past decade feel this universally applicable while still carrying real specificity about one particular relationship beneath the surface. “All of Me” earns its spot on this list by threading that needle convincingly, giving couples a song that feels truly personal to Legend and Teigen while somehow still working for practically anyone else who plays it at their own wedding celebration. 9. Thinkin Bout You opens space for queer R&B Frank Ocean’s own “Thinkin Bout You” first arrived on 2012’s widely acclaimed Channel Orange as more than a well-crafted love song built around gorgeous vocal work and soaring instrumentation, though it succeeds plenty well on those musical terms alone regardless. The track also quietly opened up a notably significant conversation about queer identity within Black artistry, particularly inside a hip-hop and R&B landscape that was still actively struggling with homophobia and rigid, outdated ideas about masculinity at that particular time of its release. By carefully weaving in a wide, thoughtful range of references drawn from queer cultural history and lived experience, Ocean built an entire song that reads simultaneously as a specific, deeply personal statement and a considerably broader, meaningful act of representation for listeners who rarely saw themselves reflected this directly in mainstream R&B music at that particular time in history. This dual function gives “Thinkin Bout You” lasting cultural weight that extends well beyond its considerable merits as a piece of pure songwriting craft and raw vocal talent. The song itself captures the specific curiosity and lingering uncertainty that comes with an all-consuming crush, treating that emotional state as worth taking seriously instead of reducing it to a simple romantic cliché. An entire generation of young listeners who played Channel Orange on repeat in their bedrooms found something validating in that treatment, discovering through Ocean’s music that romantic longing belonged to everyone, regardless of who they happened to love. Few love songs released this century carry this much cultural significance while still functioning as an effortlessly catchy, endlessly replayable single overall. “Thinkin Bout You” earns its place on this list by managing both at once, proving that real representation and real pop craft were never actually in conflict with each other to begin with. 8. All Night closes Lemonade with quiet healing Beyoncé’s own “All Night” closes out 2016’s sprawling, ambitious, remarkably expansive Lemonade, an hour-long visual album that spent its previous eleven tracks carefully exploring the full, complicated emotional territory of marital infidelity in considerable depth, including deep betrayal, jealousy, rage, and pointed revenge running throughout. After that sustained emotional intensity across the record, “All Night” arrives as a welcome tonal shift, trading confrontation for something more tender, reflective, patient, and reconciliatory. Reportedly Beyoncé’s own personal favorite track from the entire record overall, this particular song, “All Night,” itself trades away the fury of songs like “Hold Up” or “Sorry” for a quieter, more compassionate meditation on healing after real heartbreak and consciously choosing to move steadily forward together instead of walking away entirely. This choice to end the project on reconciliation instead of pure catharsis gives Lemonade a far more complicated emotional arc than a simple betrayal-and-revenge narrative would have allowed. Soulful, richly layered vocal work and a haunting, sparse, deliberately minimal guitar line run consistently throughout the entire track from start to finish, giving “All Night” a considerable, unmistakable warmth that distinguishes it quite clearly from the more explosive, percussive tracks that precede it much earlier on the same full album overall. This restraint mirrors the song’s lyrical content, favoring quiet tenderness over the kind of big, dramatic gesture that might otherwise feel more expected for a closing album statement of this kind. Few love songs released this decade tackle the specific, rarely explored territory of preservation and reconciliation within a long-term committed relationship, rather than the more common narratives of new romance or dramatic breakup. “All Night” earns its place on this list precisely by choosing that harder, less flashy emotional territory and handling it with real care throughout. 7. Higher & Higher lifts surrender into celebration Jackie Wilson’s own true classic 1967 hit “Higher & Higher (Your Love Keeps Lifting Me)” captures a very specific, unmistakably joyful feeling that plenty of love songs attempt and comparatively few artists actually manage to nail: the sensation of fully letting go and falling headlong into the uplifting embrace of romantic love without holding anything back at all. Instead of treating that surrender as something vulnerable or risky, Wilson’s performance frames it as pure, unqualified celebration from the very first note onward. This celebratory, unrestrained energy sets the track apart clearly from the more common yearning or melancholic love songs that dominate large portions of the genre’s overall back catalog. Where plenty of classic, well-worn love songs slowly and carefully process longing, doubt, or loss, “Higher & Higher” simply commits fully and unreservedly to pure joy, treating uncomplicated happiness as worth truly celebrating just as much as any considerably more dramatic romantic complication found elsewhere. Wilson’s remarkable, athletic vocal performance throughout the track demands real, considerable technical skill, built around a soaring, athletic delivery that few singers anywhere today can convincingly replicate, even decades after the song’s original release. This particular difficulty has genuinely become quite something of an ongoing, familiar running joke among casual amateur singers pretty much everywhere today, since attempting “Higher & Higher” at any karaoke night tends to expose a considerable, humbling gap between the song’s effortless-sounding original recording and what most amateur voices can actually deliver live on stage. Few love songs from this era sound this purely, uncomplicatedly happy while still delivering real vocal fireworks throughout the performance. “Higher & Higher” earns its lasting place on this list by proving that pure celebration can carry just as much staying power as more conventionally complicated romantic material. 6. I Will Always Love You bids a mentor farewell Dolly Parton herself originally wrote and composed “I Will Always Love You” as a heartfelt, deeply sincere, and genuine farewell to her own longtime musical partner and mentor, country music legend Porter Wagoner, at the exact moment she finally chose to leave their partnership and pursue a solo career entirely on her own terms. Released in 1974, the song became a notable, widespread sensation almost immediately, capturing a specific, bittersweet emotional territory that few love songs before it had ever articulated quite this clearly or directly. Few songs in popular music capture the sentiment of loving something enough to set it free with this much clarity, warmth, tenderness, and emotional precision. Parton’s own original version treats that painful departure with real tenderness instead of bitterness, honoring what the relationship truly meant even while insisting on the necessity of moving on toward something new and uncertain ahead. Whitney Houston’s own later, considerably more famous cover version eventually became the more commercially dominant take on the song, reaching an even wider global audience decades after Parton’s own original recording had first appeared publicly on the airwaves. This commercial reality doesn’t diminish Parton’s original composition, however, since the song’s structure and emotional logic remain entirely her own creative achievement, regardless of which recording eventually reached the largest audience over time. Few vocalists anywhere at all beyond Houston herself can convincingly replicate the song’s most demanding high notes, yet that considerable difficulty hasn’t stopped generations of listeners from singing along anyway, chasing the same cathartic release Parton originally built into the composition. “I Will Always Love You” earns its place on this list by giving heartbreak an unusually generous, big-hearted emotional register that still resonates across five full decades later. 5. Let’s Stay Together sets marriage vows to soul Al Green’s own timeless classic “Let’s Stay Together” takes the solemn, deeply practical language found squarely within actual, spoken marriage vows and lasting promises made between two people, promising steady, lifelong commitment through both good times and bad alike, and transforms that everyday promise into something that sounds notably transcendent once filtered carefully through Green’s own unmistakable voice. Released in the early 1970s, countless artists across many genres have covered the song many times since, though few versions come particularly close to matching the warmth of Green’s original recording. This considerable warmth comes through most clearly in how effortlessly and quite naturally Green himself delivers each and every line that could easily sound stiff or ceremonial in lesser, less capable hands, turning what amounts to a fairly straightforward commitment statement into something that feels spontaneous and deeply felt instead of rehearsed, stiff, or obligatory. Few singers working anywhere today manage to make sincerity sound this effortless across an entire recorded track from start to finish. The song itself found a considerable second life in 1994 when director Quentin Tarantino featured it quite prominently in Pulp Fiction, introducing Green’s original recording to an entirely new generation of listeners who might never have encountered classic soul music any other way. This cinematic placement helped cement “Let’s Stay Together” as a true cultural touchstone well beyond its original chart run decades earlier. Perhaps the song’s single most memorable modern moment came around 2012, when then-President Barack Obama sang a brief snippet of the track during a campaign fundraising event, instantly turning “Let’s Stay Together” into a viral moment that introduced the song to countless listeners who might have otherwise overlooked it entirely. Few love songs anywhere manage to stay this culturally relevant across more than five full decades of continuous rediscovery by new audiences. 4. Vision of Love introduces Mariah’s signature whistle Mariah Carey’s own landmark 1990 debut single, “Vision of Love,” formally and confidently announced an entirely new, quite remarkable vocal talent to mainstream pop audiences everywhere at that particular moment in time, built around a gorgeous, gospel-tinged pop-soul arrangement that builds steadily and quite patiently toward a notably thrilling musical climax. This particular climax showcases Carey’s now-signature whistle register for the very first time on a major commercial single, a vocal technique that would go on to define much of her considerable subsequent career in music. Though Carey would go on to write and perform considerably more sophisticated, layered love songs across the following decades of her long career, “Vision of Love” still captures something that her later, more polished work sometimes loses entirely: the real, uncomplicated giddiness of early romantic infatuation before any complications or history have had real time to accumulate. This emotional register gives the song lasting freshness, even decades after its original chart-topping run. As a debut single specifically, this particular track carried considerable pressure to properly and convincingly introduce Carey definitively to a mainstream audience that was entirely unfamiliar with her voice, and the song’s steady build toward that vocal climax works almost as a structural metaphor for her own dramatic arrival as a major new artist in music. Few debut singles in pop history have announced a notably new vocal talent this convincingly on a first outing. Few love songs released at the very start of the entire 1990s hold up quite this well against the considerably more polished production techniques that followed across the rest of that decade. “Vision of Love” earns its lasting place on this list by capturing something truly unrepeatable about a specific artist’s arrival, a moment no amount of later technical polish could ever really fully recapture again. 3. A Couple Minutes captures the sting of lost love Olivia Dean’s own “A Couple Minutes” clearly stands out today as one of the strongest, clearest highlights from her Brit Award-nominated album The Art of Loving, no small achievement given how consistently strong the rest of that particular record plays throughout, from start to finish. The song opens by quietly noticing a small, telling detail about an ex-partner’s changed habits, a deceptively simple entry point into a much larger, more complicated emotional reckoning with loss. This opening detail sets up an emotional gut-punch that unfolds gradually across the rest of the track, rather than announcing its full weight immediately. Dean’s songwriting, singing, and the song’s overall composition work together with real precision, building a sense of bittersweet loss that feels earned rather than manufactured for maximum immediate impact on a first listen. The track’s central subject matter, the specific ache of noticing how much has quietly changed in someone you once knew intimately, gives “A Couple Minutes” real emotional specificity that plenty of breakup-adjacent love songs never quite manage to achieve this convincingly. This precision comes through clearly in how the song builds its own narrative around one small, concrete moment instead of relying on broader, more generic romantic language throughout the track and full record. The song’s considerable emotional weight comes with a built-in warning label for anyone still processing their own breakup, since the track’s specificity tends to hit uncomfortably close for listeners in a similar emotional place. “A Couple Minutes” earns its spot on this particular list precisely by committing fully to that discomfort instead of softening it for easier, more casual listening, trusting the audience to sit with something genuinely uncomfortable instead of smoothing it over for radio-friendly consumption. 2. At Last still owns every first dance Etta James’s own 1960 recording of “At Last” remains the single most unapologetically romantic slow-dance song in all of popular music history, the kind of track so thoroughly associated with weddings and first dances that its sheer familiarity has arguably become part of its considerable charm instead of a mark against it. From the very first single note played, listeners already know exactly where the song goes next, and that anticipated arrival somehow never loses its considerable, unmistakable emotional power, no matter how many times it plays. James’s soulful, deeply controlled vocal delivery elicits a real, physical reaction in listeners virtually every time it plays, no matter how many times a person has already heard the recording in their life. This consistency across so many repeat listens speaks to how carefully constructed the performance is beneath its seemingly effortless surface, since manufacturing that same reaction reliably requires real vocal control, considerable patience, and precise pacing throughout the recording. The song’s cultural reach expanded dramatically in 2009, when Beyoncé performed a memorable rendition of “At Last” at the presidential inauguration ball for Barack Obama, reportedly moving both the new President and First Lady visibly during the performance. This memorable moment introduced the song to an entirely new generation of listeners while reinforcing its status as the definitive choice for important romantic occasions of every kind. Few songs in popular music carry this much cultural weight while still functioning as a purely, straightforwardly beautiful vocal performance on its own terms. “At Last” earns its position this high on the list by remaining the clearest possible answer whenever someone needs exactly one perfect song for exactly one perfect romantic moment. 1. Birds of a Feather blurs sweet and intense Billie Eilish’s own “Birds of a Feather” proves quite clearly that a truly great love song doesn’t necessarily always need to arrive as a straightforward, gushing ballad to land with real emotional force, hitting an unusual middle ground between joyful and melancholy, light and notably haunting throughout its entire runtime, tone, and structure. At first listen, the track reads as simply cute and lightly romantic, an easy, breezy pop song built quite neatly around an appealing melody and catchy hook. This initial impression shifts considerably once the song’s central lyrical idea eventually and quietly becomes clear: a declaration built entirely around the literal inability to imagine living without one particular person, phrased in a way that blends real devotion with an undercurrent of considerable intensity beneath the surface. This combination gives “Birds of a Feather” a complexity that many more straightforward love songs never reach, sitting somewhere between deeply romantic and quietly unsettling depending on how a listener chooses to read it. Released in 2024, the song spread across TikTok with remarkable speed and staying power, dominating the platform for most of a year instead of the brief viral spike that defines most platform-driven hits. This sustained cultural presence suggests listeners responded to something deeper than a catchy hook alone, connecting with the song’s more complicated emotional undercurrent beneath its accessible surface. Few recent love songs feel this immediately catchy while still rewarding closer, more attentive listening the way “Birds of a Feather” consistently does throughout its runtime. The track earns the top spot on this list by proving that real romantic intensity and mainstream pop accessibility were never incompatible, whatever conventional wisdom about the genre might suggest to casual listeners.

item.title: Alabama-Coushatta opens temporary Naskila Casino as permanent resort takes shape nearby
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 4.78
The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas has opened Naskila Casino Leggett, giving Polk County its first operating piece of a much larger casino resort planned for the property. Tribal members marked the occasion Monday (August 24) with a Tribal Membership Opening Day ceremony. Doors opened to everyone Tuesday and visitors began lining up early. Operating around the clock, the temporary casino offers 300 electronic gaming machines and a dining facility. Local reporting says the operation has brought roughly 100 new jobs to the area. For tribal leaders, Leggett also signals a new period of economic development after years spent fighting in court over gaming. In 2022, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that Texas could not apply its gaming laws to stop electronic bingo on tribal land when state law did not prohibit the activity outright. Texas later abandoned its longstanding lawsuit against the Tribe. Naskila Casino Leggett opening signals wider tribal gaming and economic expansion Construction is already underway nearby on the permanent Naskila Casino Resort, which broke ground in June. Plans cover roughly 685,000 square feet, with about 3,400 electronic bingo machines and a 366-room hotel. Guests are also expected to find restaurants, bars and lounges, a resort-style pool complex and around 35,000 square feet for conferences and events. A grand ballroom is designed for crowds of up to 1,000 people. The opening of the first phase is targeted for late 2028. The development builds on Naskila’s existing operation near Livingston, which has been running since 2016. Tribal officials point to its wider role in the East Texas economy, including jobs and spending with regional businesses. An economic-impact study cited by the Tribe put that contribution at about $251.7 million annually. Federal agencies had previously confirmed the Leggett property could host gaming. The land has been held in trust since 2001, and tribal membership approved the location in September 2025. The federal status stands in contrast with another current tribal gaming dispute. In California, the Scotts Valley Band of Pomo Indians sued the Interior Department on August 7 after officials reversed their position on gaming eligibility for roughly 160 acres in Vallejo. Interior had approved that property in January 2025 as “restored lands” under federal gaming law, using broader readings of “occupancy” and “vicinity”. After another review, the department reversed course July 30. Scotts Valley called that decision “arbitrary, capricious, contrary to law, unsupported by the administrative record” and said it was “compelled to suspend gaming operations” at its Class II facility. The tribe had pursued a temporary “preview casino” while the dispute continued. In Leggett, meanwhile, the temporary casino is operating while construction moves ahead. The Alabama-Coushatta Tribe called its membership celebration “a new chapter” as it prepared to welcome the wider public. Featured image: Alabama-Coushatta Tribe of Texas via Facebook

item.title: FanDuel voids Bill Simmons bets after proxy betting admission
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 4.31
FanDuel has voided wagers placed on behalf of Bill Simmons and taken action against his account after the sports media personality admitted using his daughter’s boyfriend to make bets for him in Massachusetts. The sportsbook said it also reported the matter to the Massachusetts Gaming Commission (MGC), which is reviewing Simmons’ admission. “We became aware of the issue and handled it consistent with our Terms and Conditions and Massachusetts Gaming Commission regulations, including reporting the matter to the MGC, voiding the bets, and actioning the account,” a FanDuel spokesperson said. FanDuel did not disclose what action it had taken against Simmons’ account. Its terms prohibit customers from allowing other people to access their accounts or wager on their behalf, a practice known as proxy betting. The incident is also being examined by Massachusetts regulators. “The Commission is aware of the comments made on the Bill Simmons Podcast and staff are currently reviewing the matter,” MGC spokesman Thomas Mills told Front Office Sports. The Simmons case comes as the MGC is already examining sportsbook VIP programs following a separate FanDuel controversy involving Philadelphia Phillies star Bryce Harper. Harper said a personalised Cameo video he recorded as a holiday greeting was later branded and used by FanDuel as a gambling promotion without his knowledge or consent. The MGC said in July that it was aware of the case and was looking into VIP programs “as a whole,” with an update potentially reaching its agenda this fall. Simmons admits sharing FanDuel login to place bets remotely Simmons, founder of The Ringer and a former ESPN columnist, disclosed the arrangement while discussing bets he wanted to make from Los Angeles, where online sports betting is not legal. He explained that his daughter and her boyfriend, Hank, had both recently turned 21 and that Hank was in Massachusetts, where FanDuel operates. “There was a couple of bets I really wanted to get in,” Simmons said, mentioning UCLA and Houston before describing how he provided access to his account. “I let Hank log into my FanDuel as me. I get the code to make sure it’s me to my phone, I give him the code, he logs in,” Simmons said. Simmons said money from successful futures bets the previous year remained in the account and Hank used it to place wagers on his behalf. “And he’s putting in bets for me, and honestly, it was the closest I’ve ever felt to Hank,” Simmons joked. “It was a real bonding moment for us.” The arrangement was not limited to one occasion. Simmons said that a week later he contacted Hank again and “we did some more.” His description amounts to proxy betting, which Massachusetts rules require licensed sportsbooks to prevent. FanDuel’s own terms similarly state that accounts are for personal use and prohibit allowing another person to log in to place a wager on the account holder’s behalf. FanDuel voids wagers and reports Simmons to regulator Simmons’ comments quickly attracted regulatory scrutiny, particularly because he described not only having another person place the wagers but also sharing the authentication code sent to his phone. Massachusetts law requires sports wagering operators to prevent people from placing wagers as agents or proxies for others. State regulations also provide mechanisms for cancelling wagers involving prohibited bettors. FanDuel subsequently confirmed that it had reported the matter to the MGC, voided the affected bets and taken action against Simmons’ account. The case has an additional commercial dimension because FanDuel is The Ringer’s exclusive sports betting partner. Neither FanDuel nor the MGC has publicly detailed what further consequences, if any, Simmons could face. The commission said only that its staff were reviewing the matter. Simmons says he misunderstood proxy betting rules Simmons addressed the controversy again on his podcast after FanDuel acted, saying he had not realised the arrangement violated proxy betting rules. “I talked about how I got my daughter’s boyfriend to place some bets for me in Massachusetts, because I was in LA,” Simmons said. “Did not know about the proxy rules. Yeah, there’s some real rules with this stuff,” he added. Simmons confirmed that the wagers had been voided and said he had learned from the episode. “Apparently, proxy betting not allowed. I actually thought it was, but that’s fine.” He continued to joke about the involvement of his daughter’s boyfriend, before acknowledging the consequence for his wagers. “All those bets went out the window. All that special time I had with Hank, out the window as well.” Simmons said he expected to be back in Boston and could place wagers himself in the future, concluding: “Lesson learned.” The MGC has not yet announced the outcome of its review. Featured image: Bill Simmons via BeyondAvgMick on X

item.title: Churchill Downs urges FTC review of HISA as regulator suspends trainer over alleged Albuterol violations
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 3.66
Churchill Downs Incorporated has asked the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) to order an independent review of the Horseracing Integrity and Safety Authority, escalating scrutiny of the regulator days before HISA provisionally suspended trainer Angel Quiroz over a series of alleged medication and horse-welfare violations. In an August 28 letter to FTC Chairman Andrew Ferguson and Commissioner Mark Meador, Churchill Downs said a series of recent events had raised “significant questions about the governance, transparency, technology controls, and accountability” of HISA. The company asked the FTC, which oversees HISA, to require or initiate a formal independent review covering racing and wagering integrity, non-public information and the safeguarding of sensitive industry data. The intervention follows controversy over the so-called “Fair Hill Five” betting episode and HISA’s handling of confidential veterinary information accessed through its online portal by horse racing data analyst and owner Marshall Gramm. The latest enforcement action came on August 31, when HISA served Quiroz with a notice alleging violations of Rules 2215 and 2221. His registration was provisionally suspended from noon EDT on September 1, pending a provisional hearing. The notice says HISA believed there was “clear and convincing evidence” that his actions or inactions presented an immediate threat of serious injury or death to covered horses or riders. HISA alleges three horses under Quiroz’s care, Bonita Rough, Scootaloo and Tepeyac, returned adverse analytical findings for Albuterol, which is classified as a banned substance unless prescribed in specified circumstances. Each alleged anti-doping violation involving a banned substance carries a potential two-year period of ineligibility and $25,000 fine. Quiroz suspended after three horses test positive for Albuterol The first case involved Bonita Rough, whose blood sample was collected after a Vet’s List Workout at Fair Hill Training Center in Maryland on July 10. According to the notice, laboratory analysis detected Albuterol, while HISA Portal records showed no dispensation, prescription or treatment with the drug during the period Quiroz was the horse’s Responsible Person. HISA’s filing says Quiroz subsequently told investigators he had nebulised Bonita Rough with Albuterol obtained from the horse’s veterinarian at Gulfstream. “You stated that you nebulized Bonita Rough with Albuterol that you received from Bonita Rough’s Veterinarian at Gulfstream,” the charge letter quoted in the notice says. “You stated the Veterinarian had prescribed the medication to another horse but informed you that you could use it on Bonita Rough if needed.” HISA alleges that this amounted to administering a controlled medication outside a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship. Its notice also says no corresponding Albuterol treatment records existed in the HISA Portal for Bonita Rough, Scootaloo or Tepeyac. The regulator said Quiroz was notified of the potential Bonita Rough violation on July 28. Thirteen days later, an out-of-competition sample was collected from Scootaloo at Saratoga Race Course and subsequently tested positive for Albuterol, according to the notice. A sample taken from Tepeyac at Fair Hill on August 13, 16 days after the initial notification concerning Bonita Rough, also returned an adverse analytical finding for Albuterol, HISA said. HISA said the alleged discovery of banned substances in multiple horses after Quiroz had already been notified of the first case posed an “immediate threat of serious injury or death to Covered Horses or Riders”. The allegations remain subject to the disciplinary process. Quiroz also faces a separate allegation that he caused Bonita Rough to breach her provisional suspension by posting a timed and reported workout at Fair Hill on July 29. Churchill Downs says HISA scrutiny goes beyond Gramm The Quiroz action comes as Churchill Downs is challenging HISA over broader questions about its technology, oversight and disclosure practices. Its August 28 FTC letter focused heavily on the controversy surrounding Gramm’s access to confidential veterinary and horse-health information through the HISA Portal. HISA announced on August 17 that it had charged Gramm with multiple rule violations, including fraud, after an investigation into confidential information appearing in past-performance reports for Deterministic and Griffin’s Wharf. HISA said the information should only have been available to the horses’ connections and regulatory veterinarians. HISA said its investigation, which included an independent forensic cybersecurity analysis, concluded Gramm had deliberately accessed confidential information over approximately six weeks and developed an automated method for obtaining it “at scale” in a way designed to mimic authorized activity and avoid detection. Gramm has disputed HISA’s characterisation of his conduct. In a public statement, he said the information was available through his authorised HISA account and that he used his own credentials, did not conceal his identity and bypassed no security protocols or safeguards. “I intend to vigorously defend myself in the HISA proceedings,” Gramm said. He acknowledged exercising “poor judgment” by failing to alert HISA sooner to the vulnerability after the issue became public, but argued that focusing on him distracted from weaknesses in HISA’s systems. The Jockey Club separately said Gramm had accessed veterinary information relating to horses he did not own and announced that its stewards would meet to take steps to remove him as a member. Portal controversy raises questions over HISA security controls Churchill Downs told the FTC it was not seeking to “excuse, minimize, or prejudge” any alleged misconduct by Gramm. Instead, it argued that the controversy exposed a separate institutional problem. “But the institutional question is separate and more fundamental: why was such information accessible in the first place?” the company said. The company stressed what it characterized as a reversal in HISA’s public explanation of the episode. According to the letter, HISA CEO Lisa Lazarus had initially said screenshots circulating online could not have originated from the HISA Portal, before HISA later acknowledged the health information had come from its system. Churchill Downs said HISA’s subsequent focus on allegations of “fraud”, “misappropriation” and other wrongdoing by Gramm did not answer critical questions about the regulator’s own controls. Among them were how an authorised user could access records for horses with which they had no legitimate connection, whether similar vulnerabilities existed elsewhere, whether other users accessed comparable information, how long the vulnerability existed and why it was not detected sooner. HISA, meanwhile, said it had changed its technology systems to prevent similar unauthorised access and was devoting additional resources to protecting confidential information. “There must be significant consequences for individuals who violate the integrity of our rules and obtain and abuse confidential horse health information,” Lazarus said. “HISA will take every necessary step to fiercely protect the integrity of Thoroughbred racing and ensure that violators of our rules are punished appropriately.” Churchill Downs seeks independent review of HISA governance Churchill Downs wants the FTC review to extend well beyond the Gramm case. Its letter calls for an independent examination of the Fair Hill Five episode, the timing and disclosure of a previously undisclosed banned-substance positive connected with the matter, the HISA Portal vulnerability, whether other users downloaded or shared confidential information, and HISA’s relationships with technology providers. The company also questioned whether HISA’s procurement, vendor oversight and information-security governance were appropriate for an organisation exercising federally authorised regulatory powers. “HISA’s legitimacy depends on confidence that it is transparent, accountable, technologically competent, and subject to meaningful oversight,” Churchill Downs said. It added that restoring confidence would require more than assurances that individual wrongdoers would be punished. “It will require an independent accounting of what happened, why it happened, whether it could happen again, and whether HISA’s governance and technology infrastructure are adequate for the responsibilities it has been given,” the company said. HISA’s own materials state that it operates under FTC oversight and that its national racing integrity framework is subject to federal review. Featured image: HISA via press release

item.title: Kalshi fights New York bid to move prediction market case to state court from federal court
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 2.53
Kalshi is pushing to keep New York’s lawsuit against the prediction-market operator in federal court, saying the state’s case cannot be resolved without answering key questions about federal commodities and gambling law. In an August 21 filing in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, Kalshi challenged Attorney General Letitia James’ effort to send the dispute back to state court. “This case should not be remanded,” Kalshi said in the filing. New York sued Kalshi on July 31, accusing the company of operating an illegal gambling business without a state gaming license. The case cites the federal Wire Act alongside New York constitutional, criminal, racing and wagering laws. Officials want to stop Kalshi’s operations in the state and are seeking restitution, disgorgement, civil penalties and accounting information. Kalshi moved the lawsuit into federal court that same day. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) granted Kalshi designated contract market status in 2020. Kalshi maintains that its contracts are federally regulated derivatives and fall under the CFTC’s exclusive jurisdiction when traded on its market. Kalshi says federal commodities law overrides New York gambling claims Sports contracts joined Kalshi’s offerings in January 2025. When those products were self-certified, the CFTC asked Kalshi for information showing they complied with federal law, according to the filing. Kalshi responded, and the regulator took no further action. “The State’s claims necessarily raise disputed and substantial federal law issues,” Kalshi said. Kalshi points to three reasons the federal court should retain the case. Its first argument focuses partly on New York’s Wire Act claim. Deciding it, Kalshi says, means determining whether event contracts qualify as betting or wagering and examining the Wire Act alongside the Unlawful Internet Gambling Enforcement Act and Commodity Exchange Act. The company says the same federal questions underpin New York’s state gambling allegations because a court must decide whether federal law permits the contracts as swaps regulated by the CFTC. Kalshi also invokes the federal officer removal statute and argues that its CFTC designation gives it a federally derived property right. Separately, it says New York cannot sidestep federal jurisdiction by excluding the CFTC as a party. The jurisdiction battle follows regulatory clashes. On August 11, the CFTC issued an emergency order directing Kalshi to continue normal operations while the litigation proceeds, after warning that New York’s requested restrictions could disrupt derivatives markets. New York has also pursued a separate Gaming Commission investigation and previously ordered Kalshi to cease operations. “The federal issue—whether Kalshi’s event contracts are unlawful gambling or authorized swap transactions traded on a federal exchange subject to the CFTC’s exclusive jurisdiction—is ‘actually disputed,’” the company said. Kalshi now wants the federal judge to reject New York’s remand request and keep the dispute in federal court. Featured image: Canva / Kalshi

item.title: CFTC backs case against US soldier accused of Polymarket insider trading
item.description:
Source: ReadWrite Score: 2.34
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) is backing the criminal case against Gannon Ken Van Dyke, a US Army master sergeant accused of using classified military information to make more than $400,000 trading Polymarket event contracts tied to Venezuela and Nicolás Maduro. In an August 21 notice, the CFTC asked the US District Judge Margaret M. Garnett for permission to file an amicus brief supporting prosecutors as Van Dyke seeks to dismiss Commodity Exchange Act charges. He argues the contracts are not swaps under federal law and says applying its anti-fraud provision to his conduct would be unconstitutional. “Both contentions are wrong,” CFTC Counselor Cameron Sinsheimer wrote in the letter. The regulator argues Congress defined swaps broadly enough to include the event contracts Van Dyke traded. It says adopting his interpretation could also significantly restrict federal oversight of prediction markets. “Van Dyke’s distortion of the CEA’s text, if accepted, would undermine the Commission’s jurisdiction over a huge range of event contracts whose notional volume totals into the tens of billions of dollars,” Sinsheimer wrote. CFTC says Polymarket event contracts fall under federal swaps law in US soldier case Van Dyke, 38, served with US Army Special Operations Command at Fort Bragg, North Carolina. Prosecutors say his role in Operation Absolute Resolve gave him access to classified and other nonpublic details about a mission targeting Maduro. “The core theory of the Indictment is that Van Dyke took information that he had pledged to keep confidential and, though he was duty-bound not to do so, he used it to make a personal profit,” prosecutors said. Van Dyke had signed nondisclosure agreements covering classified material. One agreement concerning “Western Hemisphere Operations” said information obtained through his work “is now and will remain the property of the United States Government.” According to prosecutors, he opened a Polymarket account on December 26, 2025, before spending about $33,934 on contracts involving Venezuela and Maduro through January 2. US special forces captured Maduro and his wife in Caracas on January 3. Prosecutors say the successful trades left Van Dyke with more than $400,000 in net profit. A grand jury indicted him in April on five counts covering confidential government information, commodities and swap fraud, wire fraud and an unlawful monetary transaction. He pleaded not guilty and was released on $250,000 bail with travel restrictions. Prosecutors have called it the Justice Department’s first criminal insider-trading prosecution involving prediction markets. Van Dyke moved to dismiss the indictment on July 31. Van Dyke “committed an old crime on a new platform,” they said. “Because the Indictment alleges all that it must,” prosecutors said, “the next step is trial.” The CFTC also rejects Van Dyke’s argument that he lacked sufficient notice that federal law covered his alleged conduct. It points to the Commodity Exchange Act, its own regulatory actions and similar contracts traded on CFTC-registered exchanges. The agency says its proposed filing could help the court address legal questions with implications beyond Van Dyke’s prosecution. “Here, the proposed amicus brief is both timely and useful, and will aid the court in its deliberation of this matter by offering insights not available from the parties,” Sinsheimer wrote. Featured image: CFTC via Wikimedia Commons / Canva

item.title: Review: Grayl GeoPress Water Purifier
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 3.97
The Grayl GeoPress Water Purifier is a bottle-based water filter that removes bacteria, viruses, and protozoa from contaminated backcountry and international water sources. It's easy to use, portable, and safe for individuals to use for day hiking, fishing, or international travel, especially when you don't want to deal with a more complicated hose, bladder, or pump-based water purifier. The Geopress also addresses cross-contamination, which happens when you accidentally re-contaminate the drinking vessel or water you've just purified. - Removes: Protozoa, Bacteria, and Viruses - GeoPress purifies and filters 24 fl. oz. of water in 8 sec. - The purifier's (replaceable) cartridge is rated for 350 cycles (65 gal./250L) or 3 years have elapsed since first use - Meets the EPA guide standard and protocol for testing microbiological water purifiers - Filter medium: Electroabsorption/activated carbon - Dry weight: 15.9 oz - 10.4 x 5.6 x 3.4 inches The GeoPress has an outer and inner bottle (top photo), with a filter at one end and a screw-on drinking spout at the other. To use it, pull the inner bottle out of the outer bottle, fill it with suspect water, then push the inner bottle into the outer bottle like a French press. It takes some elbow grease (force) to push the inner bottle down, but doing so forces water through the purifier's filter element, filling the inner bottle with purified water. To drink it, unscrew the cap at the top and sip. It's that easy. Depending on water quality, the purifier's filter element lasts for about 350 uses. When new, it takes about 8 seconds to push the inner bottle with its attached purifier filter into the full outer bottle, containing suspect water. When the amount of time to perform this action takes longer than 35 seconds, you know it's time to change the purifier filter, which unscrews with a twist of the wrist. Replacement purifier filter elements are sold separately for about 30 bucks each. When filtering, you can loosen the top cap a 1/2 turn to let the air out of the inner bottle and make the pressing motion a little easier. Once purified, clean water fills the inner bottle. You have the option to drink it immediately, carry it as you would with any water bottle, pour it into a separate bottle if you prefer to carry it that way, or share it with others. Cross-contamination Cross-contamination occurs when you accidentally contaminate the part of your purifier or filter system that you drink from. This can occur if you touch a drinking spout with wet hands from contaminated water or if the mouthpiece of your hydration bladder drops in the dirt. The only way to decontaminate the drinking spout is to sterilize it by washing it with chlorinated water. Cross-contamination is one of the key reasons people still get sick on hikes, even when they use a water filter or water purifier. The Grayl GeoPress guards against cross-contamination because it has a screw top that covers the drinking spout. As long as you keep that drinking spout away from unpurified water, you can safely drink from it or pour the bottle's contents into other containers for consumption. Recommendation The Grayl GeoPress is a bottle-based water filter and purifier that's ideal for removing bacteria, viruses, and protozoa from backcountry or international water sources. Weighing 15.9 ounces dry, it's too low volume for general-purpose backpacking, where you probably want to process several liters of water at a time (since it can only purify 24 ounces at once). Instead, I've found it to be a great water treatment solution for outdoor recreational activities like day hiking or fishing, where there's plenty of water around, so you don't have to carry any, and you can drink when you're thirsty. The GeoPress is also simple enough for anyone to use casually without a lot of training, making it a valuable general-purpose solution for all your family members. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. I’d used an older 16oz model of the Grayl water purifier for hiking and backpacking but discontinued using it. I found the filter cartridge to plug very fast with waters heavy with color bodies, such as tannins and humic substances, found in some areas that I hike (example: Dolly Sods, WV). I would use it 2-3 times to filter that water after which it was completely unusable to ‘french-press’ the water. I’m surprised. I used an old one too in NH and VT full of trees and red tannic water without issues. What’d you switch too? I switched to a Sawyer Squeeze. With regular backflushing, the Sawyer has worked well for two years now. It’s not a purifier, though. The Geopress filter has pores small enough to remove viruses; the Sawyer doesn’t. That’s why is silts up more quickly.

item.title: Adobe is making its tools available in Slack
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 6.82
Customers can now use Adobe’s apps like Firefly, Adobe Express, Photoshop, Premiere, Acrobat, InDesign, Illustrator, Stock, Lightroom, and others directly with Slack’s AI chatbot, Slackbot, Adobe announced on Monday. In addition, more than 70 Adobe tools will become available in Slack through the Adobe for Slack MCP app. With the Slackbot integration, users will be able to describe what they want to do, and the bot will call the right Adobe tool to complete the task. Adobe said that while calling its tools, Slackbot also takes in the context of the conversations. For instance, users can get information from conversations or Canvas and turn it into PDFs, images, and videos. They can also bring in assets from previous campaigns or the Creative Cloud asset library into a chat and edit them. At launch, this integration will be available to Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ teams. While productivity and creative companies have been busy adding AI features into their tools, most people still work in conversational boxes. This pushes the tool providers to make their features available through services like ChatGPT, Claude, and Slack. Last month, Adobe introduced a similar integration for ChatGPT and is planning to launch a Gemini integration soon. Deepti Pradeep, senior director for Agentic AI at Adobe, told TechCrunch over email that people are using the company’s tool in other apps for repeatable workflows like batch-editing images or resizing creatives without leaving the app. “In focus groups, people talked about the value they get from this experience very clearly: saving time, getting to the outcome they want faster without having to micromanage every step, being able to access Adobe wherever they’re already working. That’s been interesting for us because it’s pushed us to think less about individual edits and more about the larger outcome someone is trying to get to,” Pradeep said. Other creative tools like Canva and Figma are also making their capabilities available in chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude. On the other hand, companies like Anthropic are releasing tighter integrations in Slack, because team context is often captured through those conversations. Pradeep said that consumers having choices between tools is a good thing, but Adobe has the advantage of providing both creative and productive tools across different modalities.

item.title: HiddenLayer nabs $100M as enterprises rush to secure their AI deployments
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 6.80
When AI security startup HiddenLayer raised its $50 million Series A three years ago, one of the big questions in the space was whether the AI threats the startup was protecting against would manifest in enough quantity to make for a real market. As my former colleague Kyle Wiggers noted at the time, it was difficult to pin down real examples of attacks against AI at scale. How quickly things have changed. Security companies are now scrambling to build products that can monitor not just agents but also the tools and add-ons they use. While there still aren’t many headlines about agents being exploited, the risk of agents going haywire during production is nevertheless real. And so the market for tools to prevent that from happening has exploded: Gartner estimates companies will spend $2.83 billion this year on products meant to secure AI tools, 83% more than 2025, and expects spending to reach nearly $4.78 billion next year. HiddenLayer, which makes tools to protect AI models, agents, and workflows from adversarial attacks, vulnerabilities, and malicious code injections, has been able to take good advantage of that shift. Its co-founder and CEO, Chris Sestito, tells TechCrunch that the startup’s annual recurring revenue grew more than 10x over the past year. He declined to give an exact number but said ARR is now in the “tens of millions” of dollars, and over 90% of that growth was driven by new customers signing in the past year. Financial services and large tech companies building AI products are currently the company’s largest verticals, and it also has contracts with the Department of Defense and intelligence community. One of its customers is apparently a “leading frontier model provider” with “more than 700 million weekly users,” which sounds like OpenAI or Anthropic to me. To make the most of that momentum, the startup has now raised $100 million in a Series B funding round that was led by Delta-v Capital, with participation from Ten Eleven Ventures, Morgan Stanley, Microsoft’s M12, Booz Allen Hamilton, and others. The Austin-based startup broadly still sells what it used to in 2023, but Sestito told TechCrunch that the biggest change it’s had to make was to extend its existing products — discovery, runtime protection, attack simulation, and supply chain security — to address prompt injection, agent manipulation, and malicious tool use. “Inference is still inference. So whether it’s on a traditional machine learning model, whether it’s GenAI, whether it’s an agentic work stream, a lot of our technology still applied. So really, we haven’t had to pivot, but we’ve had to grow our scope … from traditional modeling to GenAI to agentic,” he said. Sestito stressed that runtime security has especially become a priority as AI deployments grow common across businesses and likened it to traditional endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions, but specifically for AI. The company’s new products reflect that shift, and Sestito highlighted a new opportunity for attackers in exploiting open source models. “We parse and scan about 50 different AI file frameworks to make sure that, especially in the case of open source, open-weight models, that the tool you’re working with is the one you believe it to be, and it’s the one it’s purporting to be. We’re looking at things like models purporting to be one thing, but they’re another — hidden models inside of models,” he said. The startup says the new $100 million is going to help it build in that direction, though with more of a focus on sales and distribution, while continuing to expand its engineering and research. It also plans to expand into Europe and EMEA. HiddenLayer may find itself tapping that war chest for more, though. Large cybersecurity companies, like Cisco, Palo Alto Networks, and Check Point often prefer to buy rather than build this sort of tech, while startups like Noma and Zenity have raised over $100 million each to take on adjacent or overlapping areas of this space. Sestito acknowledged that some parts of the AI security products his company offers could eventually be bundled into the platforms built by companies such as Microsoft, OpenAI, and AWS. However, he expects AI infrastructure will grow toward governance features such as discovery, identity, and policy controls, rather than the kind of tools that his company builds. For now, he says HiddenLayer’s job is to “scale vertically alongside artificial intelligence,” and eventually expand horizontally into parts of cybersecurity that increasingly depend on AI. That’s an ambitious goal, but the startup first has to prove it can turn its head start into an enduring business before the rest of the industry catches up.

item.title: India’s richest man now wants to turn aging computers into AI-ready PCs
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 6.50
Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Jio is opening its cloud PC service to any internet user in India, positioning it as a way to turn aging computers into AI-ready machines without hardware upgrades. On Wednesday, Reliance Jio expanded JioPC, originally launched in July 2025, beyond its own broadband subscribers, making the service available as a stand-alone subscription to users with an internet connection, regardless of their telecom or broadband provider. The service streams a virtual PC from Jio’s cloud to an existing computer, with plans offering up to eight virtual CPUs, 16GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage. Jio says the service can give even computers as old as eight years access to the computing power needed for modern AI applications, without users replacing their machines or installing new hardware. Plans start at ₹1,000 (about $11) for two months, while a 12-month subscription costs ₹4,000 (around $42) for 8GB of RAM and 500GB of storage, or ₹5,000 (about $53) for the 16GB and 1TB configuration. India had more than 65 million PCs in use in 2025, including about 34 million consumer and 31 million commercial machines, according to estimates from IDC, which expects the installed base to approach 69 million by the end of 2026. Ambani’s move comes amid widening replacement cycles. Consumers and small businesses in India typically replace their PCs every five to six years, compared with four to five years in 2022, IDC’s senior market analyst Bharath Shenoy told TechCrunch. Enterprises are stretching their machines for longer too, with replacement cycles reaching about four years, up from three previously. Jio is betting that cloud computing can stretch those lifecycles further. By shifting much of the processing and storage away from the device and into its data centers, India’s most valuable company can keep adding computing capacity without requiring users to replace the machines sitting on their desks. Prabhu Ram, vice president of the industry research group at the Gurugram-based market analyst firm CyberMedia Research, said JioPC could instead create a market where consumers pay for computing capability rather than repeatedly spending on hardware upgrades. “Jio is broadening its value proposition by opening JioPC to non-Jio users, while also challenging the traditional hardware upgrade cycle,” Ram told TechCrunch. However, he does not expect that model to replace conventional PCs. JioPC, he noted, could create a parallel, price-sensitive tier for households, students, and others “for whom buying a new AI-capable PC was never really on the table to begin with.” Indians have traditionally preferred owning their hardware over paying for PCs as a service, Shenoy said. Jio will have to convince consumers that a recurring subscription is worth giving up some of the advantages of a conventional PC, including the ability to keep working without the internet. That dependence could be particularly prominent in the smaller cities and towns where affordable computing has the most room to grow. JioPC requires a stable internet connection, and any disruption can affect the user experience, unlike a conventional computer. Additionally, there is competition at the low end from refurbished PCs, which Shenoy said allow consumers to own inexpensive hardware without remaining dependent on connectivity. Jio’s pitch of an “AI-ready” PC through JioPC also challenges the conventional idea of what an AI PC looks like. The company has not disclosed much about the underlying hardware powering the cloud service. However, the specifications it has provided do not mention dedicated AI accelerators for on-device generative AI workloads, which is a key feature of the new generation of AI PCs. Moreover, the real test for Jio, Ram said, is whether people come to see cloud computing as a “daily utility” rather than an “opportunistic workaround,” and are willing to pay for computing power instead of buying new hardware.

item.title: OpenAI’s new reasoning technique alarms AI safety experts
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 6.27
OpenAI’s new Astra model will use a reasoning technique called “recurrent depth” that allows it to operate outside of the sequential thinking that characterizes most reasoning models, The Information reported on Tuesday. This technique, also called “opaque recurrence,” will likely make the model’s chain of thought more difficult to monitor — and that has AI safety experts rattled. While Astra’s use of the technique is reportedly limited, its emergence has still raised significant concerns among AI safety experts. “I am extremely concerned by the reporting that Astra uses opaque recurrence,” wrote Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris in a post after the news broke. “I don’t know whether Astra is much less CoT monitorable than previous models. But if OpenAI pushes this technique further, they’ll have the option to massively increase the recurrence and totally destroys CoT monitorability.” Longtime AI safety advocate Zvi Mowshowitz also weighed in and wrote that laws might be necessary to prevent a “race to the bottom” among AI labs. “The technique is playing with fire, risking a taboo that OpenAI and Anthropic have fought to establish that we work hard to maintain Chain of Thought faithfulness and monitorability for as long as we can,” Mowshowitz wrote. “More intensive use of such techniques would probably damage monitorability.” Under normal circumstances, a reasoning model’s chain of thought provides the sequential steps taken by the model as it attempts to solve a problem. While the representation is imperfect, it still serves as a valuable tool for monitoring misbehavior or misalignment. In the case of OpenAI’s recent rogue agent activity, chain-of-thought records were an important tool in teasing out why agents behaved the way they did. In opaque recurrence, the model takes a less linear approach, processing the same query several times in a loop. The result leaves fewer legible traces, effectively side-stepping a conventional chain-of-thought record. Crucially, Astra’s use of the technique appears to be limited. The model’s chain of thought is still expected to be legible, and the company pushed back against any suggestion that it would shift to “neuralese.” OpenAI has already announced plans for extensive chain-of-thought monitoring systems as part of its forward-looking safety plans. In a post on X, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki emphasized the lab’s commitment to legible chains of thought. “OpenAI has worked to preserve and utilize chain-of-thought monitoring since our very first reasoning models,” Pachocki wrote. “It’s a core goal of our current research program. All AI models do some quantity of opaque reasoning, and few researchers take chain-of-thought logs as a direct representation of a model’s reasoning. Still, those caveats don’t dispel the concern that opaque recurrence may make AI reasoning harder to monitor, particularly as it grows in use across different models. In a follow-up report Wednesday morning, The Information reported that both Anthropic and Google DeepMind were already discussing the technique. In a post responding to the news, Redwood Research chief scientist Ryan Greenblatt said opaque reasoning could easily scale faster than conventional chain-of-thought reasoning, effectively removing all reasoning from visible channels. “My biggest concern is that a natural progression from here would involve scaling up the opaque reasoning to the point where the model reasons entirely or almost entirely in latent space,” Greenblatt wrote. “I hope it isn’t too late to avoid the most concerning architectures and that OpenAI will stop here.”

item.title: Utilities are racing to link up with fusion startups, with Realta Fusion the latest to benefit
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.71
Fusion startup Realta Fusion this week announced a deal with Madison Gas and Electric that will place one of the first grid-connected fusion power plants in the country in Wisconsin. The partnership comes as utilities around the world have been jockeying to court fusion startups, a courtship that says as much about utilities’ anxiety over future power supply as it does about fusion’s progress. For founders and investors watching the sector, these tie-ups serve as a kind of real-world credibility check. A deal with a utility offers several advantages for a fusion startup, ranging from engineering support and permitting assistance to site selection for grid interconnection and land leases. For utilities, such deals give them early access to a technology with the potential to reshape the grid for decades to come. To date, only a handful of fusion startups have announced deals with utilities, which makes agreements like this one so newsworthy. Realta’s deal with Madison Gas and Electric will explore the construction of a 200-megawatt power plant — roughly enough capacity to power a small city — sometime in the mid-2030s. The utility also made an equity investment as part of the deal, though Realta did not reveal specifics and did not immediately reply to TechCrunch’s request for more information. The startup is currently converting an old Oscar Mayer factory in Madison to serve as its research and development facility. In addition to funding, Realta gains access to interconnection sites, a key advantage as power providers and users scour the country for a place to hook up to an increasingly connected electrical grid. Realta will also receive engineering and technical assistance along with financing for the eventual power plant. Utilities, which are typically cautious, weren’t always so forward: For decades, fusion power appeared to be just over the horizon, but for nearly as long it failed to deliver on its promises. In the last few years, though, fusion startups have made significant strides on both scientific and engineering challenges. Those advances, juxtaposed with soaring demand from AI data centers, have brought utilities to the table. Fusion power offers a natural fit for many utilities, which have been tested by the growth of wind and solar. Both are cheap and clean, but they only generate power when the wind blows or the sun shines. And while batteries have offered a new tool to stabilize intermittent power flows from renewables, utilities have also been searching for fossil fuel-free alternatives that can provide consistent power 24/7, so-called baseload power plants. Fusion power plants, which are being designed to operate round the clock, must appear tantalizingly familiar to grid operators, even if their inner workings have a whiff of science fiction about them. Among the few other fusion startups to ink a deal is Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS), which is perhaps the farthest along, given it’s now nearly two years into its partnership with Dominion Energy. CFS has agreed to lease land from Dominion for Arc, its first commercial-scale power plant. Arc will connect to the grid near Richmond, Virginia, and it’s expected to generate 400 megawatts of electricity. Google and Italian energy company Eni have both agreed to buy electricity from the power plant, which is expected to come online in the early 2030s. On the other side of the country, Helion has been working with the Chelan County Public Utility District in Washington State for its first power plant, Polaris. The startup, which leases land from the utility, intends to turn on the 50 megawatt facility in 2028 to fulfill a deal to provide electricity to Microsoft. In between Helion and CFS, Type One Energy is planning to build a 350-megawatt power plant on the site of a former coal plant near Oak Ridge, Tennessee, part of a larger deal the startup has with the Tennessee Valley Authority. The startup hopes to start supplying the grid with electricity from the Infinity Two power plant sometime in the mid-2030s. Meanwhile, in Europe, Proxima Fusion is looking to rehab an old power plant site in southern Germany. In February, the company said it would build its first commercial power plant, Stellaris, on the grounds of an old fission power plant that is being decommissioned by RWE (one of Europe’s largest utilities, formerly a major operator of Germany’s nuclear plants) after Germany decided to pull the plug on the nuclear technology. RWE is also an investor in Proxima. The startup is aiming to turn on Stellaris in the late 2030s. For now, the benefits of these deals are more tangible for startups, which gain access to expertise and real estate that might otherwise be costly or simply out of reach. It’s a capital-efficient way to de-risk a famously capital-intensive business. For utilities, the potential rewards are farther afield though the payoff in terms of new power supplies could be significant. Utilities are used to tackling projects with long timelines, though they aren’t accustomed to taking big risks, of which fusion power is one. Still, an underpowered grid would be an even bigger gamble. Better to bet now on a technology that promises to save their business years down the road. It might take a decade to build a commercial fusion power plant, and while that might seem like a long time, to utilities, it’s practically tomorrow.

item.title: Palo Alto Networks paid $500M for Thrive-backed Console, sources say
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.40
Palo Alto Networks paid $500 million in cash and stock to acquire Console, a two-year-old startup that uses AI agents to automate routine IT help desk tasks, according to two people with knowledge of the deal. The companies officially announced the acquisition on Tuesday but didn’t reveal terms of the deal. Since its founding in 2024, Console has raised $29 million across two rounds: a $6.2 million seed led by Thrive Capital and a $23 million Series A co-led by DST Global and Thrive. Before the sale, Console was valued at $157 million, according to PitchBook, delivering a rapid return for investors including SV Angel, Abstract Ventures, and notably Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora, who participated as an angel investor. Palo Alto Networks declined to comment. The cybersecurity giant said that it will integrate Console into Cortex, its platform that uses AI to automatically detect and neutralize threats. Console’s agentic functionality will allow security teams to investigate and resolve alerts using natural language, giving Cortex “the arms and legs to deliver autonomous security outcomes across the entire enterprise,” as Arora described in a statement. Console was founded by Andrei Serban, coming shortly after his previous startup — code-security platform Fuzzbuzz — was acquired by Rippling. The startup, whose customers included Ramp, Flock Safety, and Scale AI, automated tasks like password resets, granted access to apps like Figma and Miro, and performed routine troubleshooting without direct human involvement. As a startup, Console competed primarily with Serval, another ServiceNow challenger that hit a $1 billion valuation after raising a $75 million Series B round led by Sequoia last December. Serval started as an AI tech support tool and quickly expanded to provide AI assistance for human resources, legal, and finance departments. Console’s acquisition leaves Serval as the category-leader-to-watch among startups automating IT service management, one investor, who is not a backer of Serval, told TechCrunch. Console is Palo Alto Networks’ seventh acquisition in 2026, according to PitchBook. Other VC-backed companies scooped up by the cybersecurity behemoth this year include Greylock and Lux Capital-backed observability platform Chronosphere, at a valuation of $3.35 billion, and Koi, a cyber startup backed by Battery and Team8, for $400 million.

item.title: Norway considers ban on camera-enabled wearable ‘pervert glasses’
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.27
Norway is considering a ban on smart glasses and other camera-enabled wearable headsets as it seeks to regulate the controversial technology amid privacy concerns. The country’s digital minister Karianne Tung, as quoted by the AFP news agency, said that the government is looking to regulate the use of camera-enabled wearables, such as those made by Meta and Snap. These wearables feature cameras, are internet-connected, and may soon include facial recognition, drawing ire from civil liberties advocates, who say the devices intrude on people’s privacy. Some call the devices “pervert glasses,” prompting considerable consumer backlash. Norway’s Tung said there is a “clear trend toward combining artificial intelligence with cameras and microphones built into glasses, headphones, hats and other objects we use in everyday life.” “We must prevent this equipment from being used to monitor other people in public places,” said Tung, who added that this may include banning the use of facial recognition of other people in public places. Tung plans to set up a group of experts to advise the government on better protecting people’s privacy rights.

item.title: Delivery Hero board backs Uber’s $15B takeover bid
item.description:
Source: TechCrunch Score: 5.23
Delivery Hero’s board has signed off on Uber’s $15 billion takeover offer and recommended shareholders approve the deal, which would create one of the largest on-demand food delivery platforms in the world. After reviewing the offer, Delivery Hero’s supervisory and management boards said it was in the best interests of the company, its shareholders, employees, and other stakeholders. The boards also deemed that the price was “fair and adequate” and said the deal had the “potential to accelerate product innovation.” The deal, if approved, would double Uber’s global footprint and make its delivery platform one of the largest in the world outside of China. It could also put Uber in a better position to compete with DoorDash and Just Eat Takeaway. Uber, which was already the largest shareholder in Delivery Hero, set a minimum acceptance threshold of 50%, plus one share of Delivery Hero’s outstanding share capital. Prosus, another major shareholder, has agreed to sell its 17% stake in Delivery Hero as well, according to the announcement. Delivery Hero previously agreed to sell its businesses in 14 markets where Uber Eats already operates to New York-based investment firm SSW Partners for $1.6 billion. The tie-up is the latest example of consolidation in the on-demand delivery industry.
